blocks.body: This lesson covers task 1.1 of the SAP-C02 exam, Architect network connectivity strategies, within Domain 1 (Design Solutions for Organizational Complexity). It is the network-design half of multi-account and hybrid architecture: how many VPCs talk to each other, how data centers join AWS, how names resolve across the boundary, how services are shared privately, and how you see and troubleshoot traffic. Questions mapped to this lesson are weighted toward AWS Transit Gateway, AWS Direct Connect, AWS PrivateLink and interface endpoints, hybrid DNS, centralized egress and inspection, and static egress addressing.

Domain weight: the exam-guide percentage for Domain 1 was not available when this lesson was built, so it is not quoted here; check the current official exam guide. The mapped practice questions show that this task is a large, recurring theme, with 88 questions in the bank mapped to it.

blocks.title: Prerequisites
blocks.body: You should already know VPC basics: CIDR blocks, subnets, route tables, internet gateways, security groups (stateful, instance level) versus network ACLs (stateless, subnet level), BGP at a conceptual level (autonomous system numbers, prefix advertisement, route preference), and AWS Organizations with AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM, the service that shares resources such as transit gateways and subnets between accounts).
Objectives. After this lesson, you will be able to:

items: Choose between VPC peering, AWS Transit Gateway, AWS PrivateLink, and AWS Cloud WAN for a given multi-VPC or multi-account requirement, and justify the choice with transitivity, scale, overlapping-CIDR and cost facts.
Design hybrid connectivity with AWS Direct Connect (private, public and transit virtual interfaces, Direct Connect gateway) and AWS Site-to-Site VPN, including resilient topologies and VPN backup.
Design hybrid DNS with Amazon Route 53 Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints, forwarding rules, private hosted zone associations, and Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall.
Design centralized egress and inspection (NAT gateways, Gateway Load Balancer, AWS Network Firewall) and provide static, allow-listable IP addresses for outbound and inbound traffic.
Select and configure VPC endpoints (gateway versus interface), endpoint services and private DNS, and reach services privately from on premises and other Regions.

Pick the right monitoring and troubleshooting tool (VPC Flow Logs, Traffic Mirroring, Reachability Analyzer, Network Access Analyzer) for a given question, and select Regions and Availability Zones for latency and cost.

blocks.body: Services and patterns covered: VPC addressing and peering, DHCP option sets, VPC sharing, NAT gateway and egress-only internet gateway, AWS Global Accelerator for static ingress addresses, AWS Transit Gateway (route tables, appliance mode, peering, RAM sharing, pricing, quotas), AWS Cloud WAN, AWS Direct Connect and Direct Connect gateway, AWS Site-to-Site VPN (including accelerated and private IP VPN) and AWS Client VPN, AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints, endpoint services, cross-Region), gateway endpoints, Amazon Route 53 Resolver and Route 53 Profiles, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall, Gateway Load Balancer, AWS Network Firewall, VPC Flow Logs, Traffic Mirroring, Reachability Analyzer and Network Access Analyzer.

blocks.title: How to study this lesson
blocks.body: Every topic starts from the decision it supports. Memorize the decision rules and the quotas called out in tables, and cross-check anything flagged 'not verified against AWS docs in this build' in the console or current documentation before relying on it.

Everything else in this lesson sits on top of VPC addressing. Begin with the IP addressing plan. VPCs and on-premises networks that may connect through VPC peering, AWS Transit Gateway, or a Direct Connect gateway should use non-overlapping CIDR blocks. Use Amazon VPC IP Address Manager (IPAM) to allocate address space and monitor utilization. If overlapping ranges already exist, private NAT gateways or AWS PrivateLink can provide interim connectivity while you plan phased readdressing or migration.

VPC peering is a one-to-one routed connection between two VPCs, in the same or different accounts and Regions. It uses the existing VPC infrastructure, so AWS states it introduces no separate single point of failure or bandwidth bottleneck. Traffic on inter-Region peering stays on the AWS global backbone. Three things must be in place for peering to carry traffic: the accepter VPC owner must accept the request (an unaccepted request expires after one week), each side needs a route table entry for the peer CIDR pointing at the peering connection, and security groups and network ACLs must permit the traffic.

rows: Peering does not support transitive relationships. If A peers with B and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B. Full mesh needs one connection per pair; Transit Gateway or Cloud WAN is the alternative.

You cannot create a peering connection between VPCs with matching or overlapping IPv4 or IPv6 CIDR blocks. If any of multiple IPv4 CIDR blocks overlap, the peering fails even if you intend to use only the non-overlapping blocks. A request between overlapping VPCs ends with status failed.
Only one peering connection between two VPCs at a time.

You cannot connect to or query the Amazon DNS server in a peer VPC. Private DNS resolution of peer hostnames to private IPs needs DNS resolution support enabled on the peering connection (relevant when the peer CIDR is outside RFC 1918).
50 active peering connections by default, adjustable up to 125. Outstanding requests: 25 by default.

blocks.body: Peering is the simplest option at small scale (a handful of VPCs, no need for transit). It stops being practical when the number of VPCs grows (the pair count grows quadratically and the per-VPC quota can be raised to at most 125), when you need transitive routing to on premises, or when you need central route control.

blocks.title: Common mistake: edge-to-edge routing
blocks.body: A peering connection does not let the peer VPC use your VPN, Direct Connect or internet gateway as a transit path. The whitepaper statement is that VPCs not directly peered cannot be reached by using a third VPC as transit. If the stem needs a shared on-premises connection for many VPCs, the answer is Transit Gateway (or a Direct Connect gateway with virtual private gateway associations), not peering.

Subnetting and re-addressing. A subnet's CIDR cannot be resized in place, so re-carving a VPC without downtime means adding new subnets with the new layout, shifting the workload (for example, by editing the Auto Scaling group subnet list so new instances launch in the new subnets), and then retiring the old subnets. VPC-level connectivity (VPN, Direct Connect, peering) stays attached to the VPC and is not interrupted. Plan VPC address space for the services that consume IPs: Amazon ECS tasks in awsvpc network mode each need their own IP address and elastic network interface, and if subnets run out of addresses, the number of tasks cannot scale up. Use larger CIDRs or new subnets when a subnet approaches capacity.

The Amazon EC2 documentation confirms that after you create a subnet you cannot change its CIDR block. The generic re-addressing sequence above is standard practice rather than a quoted procedure, so confirm the exact steps in the VPC user guide before relying on them.

DHCP option sets. A VPC is associated with one DHCP option set at a time. The set can carry domain name servers, a domain name, and NTP servers (up to four IPv4 and four IPv6 addresses). The Amazon Time Sync Service is reachable at the link-local address 169.254.169.123 and can be listed in the option set; for a different time source such as an on-premises stratum-0 appliance you list its IP addresses in the DHCP option set (reachability over VPN or Direct Connect must exist, including UDP 123 in security groups, network ACLs and routes). Option sets cannot be modified after creation, so changing them means creating a new set and associating it with the VPC.

VPC sharing. Instead of creating a VPC per account, a network account can own a VPC and use AWS RAM to share individual subnets with other accounts in the same organization. Participants create and manage their own resources in the shared subnets and cannot see or change other participants' resources or the owner's. Sharing suits workloads that need high interconnectivity within one trust boundary, relies on the VPC's implicit routing (no peering or Transit Gateway between participants), and still lets the shared VPC connect outward through PrivateLink, Transit Gateway and peering. Because Availability Zone names map differently per account, use AZ IDs (for example use1-az2), which are consistent across accounts, whenever you coordinate placement across accounts (shared subnets, PrivateLink services, cross-account latency and data transfer).

Selecting Regions and Availability Zones for network and latency. Choose Regions close to users or data centers, subject to data residency and service availability. For production, select at least two Availability Zones and spread resources evenly; dev and test may use one to save cost. Local Zones place subnets and instances near population centers that have no Region, while keeping high-bandwidth connections to the parent Region, for low-latency requirements. Keep chatty tiers in the same AZ where you can: cross-AZ traffic adds latency and cost (the RDS knowledge-center article makes this point with AZ IDs across accounts).

Static addressing at the edge. An Elastic IP is a static public IPv4 address tied to one Region. AWS Global Accelerator instead gives two global static anycast IPv4 addresses (four if dual-stack: two IPv4 and two IPv6) announced from edge locations. An accelerator can front Application Load Balancers, Network Load Balancers, EC2 instances, or Elastic IPs in one or more Regions, so you can allow-list a fixed address set, steer traffic using the AWS global network, and change endpoints without telling clients. You pay an hourly fee plus data transfer charges for each accelerator, and you lose the addresses if you delete the accelerator.

No separate hub device, so no added bandwidth bottleneck or single point of failure (peering pricing not verified in this build); not transitive
Many VPCs/accounts, any-to-any or segmented, shared on-premises link
Hub-and-spoke, route tables, thousands of attachments
One service exposed one-way to many consumers, overlapping CIDRs OK
Consumer VPC gets an ENI; no VPC-level routing between sides
Many accounts in one trust boundary, avoid per-account VPCs
Shared subnets owned by a network account

blocks.body: Keywords: 'overlapping CIDR' removes peering and Transit Gateway-based VPC-to-VPC routing and points to PrivateLink (one-way service access) or a private NAT gateway. 'Static IP addresses for customers to allow-list' on an ALB-fronted app points to Global Accelerator (or NLB/Elastic IP patterns) rather than the ALB's changing addresses.

links.label: Share your VPC subnets with other accounts

blocks.body: AWS Transit Gateway (TGW) is a Regional virtual router that connects VPCs, VPN connections, Direct Connect gateways, Connect (GRE/BGP) attachments, and other transit gateways (peering). Traffic is routed at layer 3 by transit gateway route tables, and each attachment is associated with exactly one route table, but it can propagate its routes to one or more route tables. That association/propagation model is the whole segmentation story.

blocks.title: Route tables, association and propagation
blocks.body: A transit gateway automatically gets a default route table that is both the default association and default propagation route table. If you disable both default association and default propagation, no default route table is created. Additional route tables isolate subsets of attachments. Association decides which table an attachment's incoming traffic is looked up in; propagation decides which tables learn the attachment's routes. A blackhole route drops matching traffic. Route selection: the most specific prefix wins; for the same prefix, static routes are preferred over propagated routes, and among propagated routes Direct Connect gateway routes beat Connect routes, which beat VPN routes. Also remember that each VPC attachment still needs routes in the VPC subnet route tables that point at the transit gateway.

headers: How it is built with route tables
rows: One route table; all attachments associated and propagating to it
Production/development isolation, shared services reachable by both

Two spoke route tables (prod, dev); associate prod VPCs with prod table and dev VPCs with dev table; propagate each VPC to its own table only; propagate the shared-services attachment to both; propagate prod and dev routes into a shared-services table associated with the shared-services attachment

Spoke attachments associated with a table that has a static 0.0.0.0/0 route to the egress VPC attachment; egress VPC attachment associated with a table that learns spoke CIDRs; optional blackhole route to stop spoke-to-spoke traffic
Spoke table default route to the inspection VPC attachment; inspection VPC attachment table routes back to spokes; enable appliance mode on the inspection VPC attachment

blocks.body: Appliance mode. By default, the transit gateway keeps traffic in the Availability Zone it originated in, so the forward and return packets of one flow can reach stateful firewalls in different AZs. With appliance mode enabled on a VPC attachment, the transit gateway picks a single network interface in that VPC using a flow hash and uses the same one for the return traffic for the life of the flow. Appliance mode is only supported for VPC attachments, route propagation must be enabled on the table associated with that attachment for AZ-aware routing, and you must connect exactly one transit gateway to the appliance VPC to guarantee stickiness. Enabling it on an existing attachment can rebalance current flows.

Cross-account and cross-Region. A transit gateway is shared for VPC attachments across accounts or an organization using AWS RAM; RAM sharing must be enabled with AWS Organizations first. Inside an organization with sharing enabled, principals get access to the shared transit gateway automatically without accepting an invitation; accounts outside the organization (or inside it when sharing with AWS Organizations is not enabled) must accept an invitation. The consuming accounts then create VPC attachments. Peering attachments connect transit gateways in the same or different Regions and accounts; the owner of the accepter gateway must accept the request, and you must add a static route in each transit gateway route table pointing at the peering attachment (peering routes do not propagate dynamically; AWS recommends unique ASNs per peered gateway for future propagation capabilities). Inter-Region peering traffic is encrypted with AES-256 at the virtual network layer and stays on the AWS backbone. Transit gateway peering does not support resolving private DNS names across the peering through Route 53 Resolver in another Region.

rows: Total routes (dynamic + static) across all route tables of one gateway
Bandwidth per VPC attachment per Availability Zone
Up to 100 Gbps each direction (the docs say AWS will try to provide more)
Packets per second per VPC attachment per AZ
Direct Connect gateway or peering bandwidth per AZ in the Region
Up to 1.25 Gbps standard; ECMP across tunnels needs dynamic routing
Up to 5 Gbps each; 4 peers per attachment (20 Gbps)

blocks.title: Outdated number to avoid
blocks.body: Older AWS material (and older exam questions) say a TGW attachment bursts to 50 Gbps. The current quotas page says up to 100 Gbps per VPC attachment per AZ and for Direct Connect gateway or peered gateway connections, with AWS able to provide more. When a question's premise is a 50 Gbps ceiling, expect the distractor logic to rest on that outdated premise; the answer that avoids the hub entirely (a direct peering connection between the two VPCs) still avoids any hub limit.

Pricing dimensions. You pay an hourly charge per attachment and a per-GB data processing charge for traffic sent from a VPC, Direct Connect, VPN or Network Firewall attachment to the transit gateway; by default data processing is charged to the account that owns the source attachment (flexible cost allocation can change that). The VPC account owner pays for VPC attachments, the transit gateway owner for VPN and Connect attachments, the Direct Connect gateway owner for Direct Connect attachments, and each owner for its side of a peering attachment. Data processing is not charged for data sent from a peering attachment to a transit gateway. Standard data transfer charges apply as well. Whether peering is cheaper than Transit Gateway for a given pair depends on current peering and data transfer pricing, which was not verified in this build; what Transit Gateway buys is management and scale.

Transit Gateway versus the alternatives. Peering: no transitivity, no hub quota, lowest cost for a few high-volume pairs. Transit Gateway: transitive hub, thousands of attachments, centralized route control and segmentation, native attachment of VPN and Direct Connect, a single Region (peer gateways to span Regions). PrivateLink: one-way, service-level, tolerates overlapping CIDRs. AWS Cloud WAN: a managed global network built from a core network policy with segments and core network edges in each Region. It supports Direct Connect gateway attachments directly (no intermediate transit gateway), automatic BGP route propagation, policy-based segmentation and tag-based attachment automation. Choose Cloud WAN when the requirement is a centrally governed, policy-driven global network with segment-level isolation across many Regions; choose Transit Gateway with peering when the footprint is smaller or you need the specific TGW features. Not verified against AWS docs in this build: feature-by-feature parity between Cloud WAN and Transit Gateway.

Operations. Transit Gateway Flow Logs export flow-level records for traffic crossing the gateway, including traffic over Direct Connect and VPN, without needing tooling in the data center. Transit Gateway Network Manager can surface routing updates for monitoring route-quota consumption. Automating spoke onboarding: create the gateway in a central account, share it with AWS RAM, and use an infrastructure-as-code mechanism such as AWS CloudFormation StackSets that creates the VPC, the attachment and routes in each new account.

Large multi-account footprint with per-account autonomy over local route tables plus central egress: a Transit Gateway hub with spoke VPC attachments is the scalable answer; peering meshes do not scale and VPN-attached firewalls add operational overhead. If the requirement is 'segmentation by OU or environment', look for separate TGW route tables (one gateway) or separate gateways; tags do not control TGW routing.
Internet egress design is an exam favorite because it combines cost, availability, static IPs and security inspection. Start with the building blocks.

NAT gateway. A NAT gateway is a managed, zonal service: each one lives in one Availability Zone with redundancy inside that zone. If several AZs share one NAT gateway and that zone fails, resources in the other zones lose internet access, and you also pay cross-zone data transfer. The resilient pattern is one NAT gateway per AZ, with each private subnet's route table pointing at the NAT gateway in its own AZ. It supports TCP, UDP, and ICMP. It handles 5 Gbps and automatically scales to 100 Gbps, and it handles 1 million packets per second, scaling to 10 million, beyond which it drops packets. Each associated IPv4 address supports up to 55,000 simultaneous connections to each unique destination (destination IP, port and protocol); you can associate up to 8 IPv4 addresses (1 primary and 7 secondary), but by default only 2 Elastic IPs per public NAT gateway (increasable by quota request). Exhausting ports shows up as the ErrorPortAllocation metric. Connections idle out after 350 seconds, so use TCP keepalives below that for long-lived flows. A public NAT gateway uses an Elastic IP; a private NAT gateway has no internet path and is used for traffic between VPCs and on premises through a transit gateway or virtual private gateway, including to preserve private addresses, to present a small pool of allow-listed addresses, and to connect overlapping networks.

Static outbound IP. When a third party allows only one or a few source IPs, run the workload in private subnets and send egress through a public NAT gateway with an Elastic IP; the Elastic IP is the address to allow-list. For a VPC-attached Lambda function the same applies: Lambda in private subnets with a route to a NAT gateway in a public subnet; give the provider the NAT gateway Elastic IPs (one per AZ if you use several NAT gateways). If the provider accepts only one CIDR block, bring your own public IP range (BYOIP) through IPAM and allocate Elastic IPs from it so every NAT gateway presents addresses inside the one block. The network border group of an Elastic IP must match the Availability Zone's border group or the NAT gateway fails to launch. A VPC-attached Lambda function reaches an internet SaaS API only through a NAT path (a VPC endpoint covers AWS services only).

IPv6. IPv6 addresses in a VPC are global unicast and do not need NAT; you cannot allocate Elastic IPs for IPv6. For outbound-only IPv6, create an egress-only internet gateway and route ::/0 to it, which lets instances reach the internet without allowing internet hosts to initiate connections. For IPv6-only workloads that must reach IPv4 services, a NAT gateway performs NAT64 together with DNS64 on Route 53 Resolver. A regular internet gateway with a ::/0 route is used for subnets that must accept inbound IPv6 connections.

Centralized egress with Transit Gateway. Deploying a NAT gateway in every spoke VPC means an hourly fee and data processing charge per gateway across hundreds of accounts. Instead, create an egress VPC in a network account with a NAT gateway in each AZ; attach spokes and the egress VPC to a transit gateway; give the spoke route table a static 0.0.0.0/0 route to the egress attachment; and route the return path through the egress route table. You then pay one set of NAT gateways (charged to the egress VPC owner) plus extra Transit Gateway data processing per GB, so for a VPC that sends very large volumes, keeping a local NAT gateway can be cheaper. Use gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB in each spoke to keep that traffic off both the transit gateway and the NAT gateway. Attach the transit gateway to every AZ the workload uses so traffic stays in-zone. Centralizing egress also centralizes inspection and gives one place to log outbound traffic.
Inspection options for egress and east-west traffic:

rows: A load balancer that encapsulates traffic in GENEVE and distributes it to a scalable fleet of third-party virtual appliances, with health checks
Endpoints sit in the inspection VPC; flow stickiness for 5-tuple or 3-tuple; combine with TGW appliance mode so firewalls need no SNAT to keep symmetry
Managed stateful and stateless firewall with firewall endpoints in subnets; rule groups

Models: distributed per VPC, centralized inspection VPC, or TGW-attached firewall; TLS inspection is supported in some models (see the table in the blog post linked below); policy is centrally managed through AWS Firewall Manager in the distributed model
Filters DNS queries leaving the VPC by domain list
Not a packet firewall; see hybrid DNS topic

blocks.body: GWLB egress inspection flow: spoke traffic crosses the TGW to the inspection VPC, a route table sends it to the GWLB endpoint in the same AZ, the GWLB encapsulates it in GENEVE to a security appliance and returns it, then forwards it to a NAT gateway in the same AZ and out through the internet gateway; return traffic reverses the path through the same endpoint. For east-west inspection, the TGW spoke route table points 0.0.0.0/0 at the security VPC attachment and the security VPC route tables send traffic via the GWLB endpoint and back to the transit gateway.

blocks.title: GWLB versus Network Firewall versus Traffic Mirroring
blocks.body: GWLB and Network Firewall sit inline and can block. Traffic Mirroring is out-of-band copy for analysis and cannot block. If the stem says the company must keep using a specific third-party appliance and scale it, GWLB is the match; if it says managed firewall with the least operational overhead, Network Firewall.

Cost-driven egress for 100+ accounts: centralize NAT in an egress VPC behind a transit gateway (and add gateway endpoints for S3/DynamoDB). Distractors: a NAT instance per VPC (operational burden), an internet gateway per VPC with public IPs (no central control), peering to an egress VPC (no transit, does not scale). Static source IP for a Lambda function or AWS Elastic Beanstalk worker: private subnets plus NAT gateway with Elastic IP, with the Elastic IP provided to the vendor.

topics.title: Direct Connect and Direct Connect gateway

blocks.body: AWS Direct Connect (DX) is a dedicated private network connection from a data center or colocation facility to AWS. A dedicated connection is a physical Ethernet port reserved for you, whereas a hosted connection is provisioned by an AWS Direct Connect Partner. You carve the connection into virtual interfaces (VIFs), each a VLAN with its own BGP session. Choosing the VIF type is the core skill.

rows: VPC private IPs, through a virtual private gateway (VGW) on one VPC, or through a Direct Connect gateway to VGWs in many Regions
AWS advertises the VPC CIDR only; it cannot advertise or suppress individual subnets. Up to 20 VGWs can be associated with a DX gateway
AWS public service endpoints using public IPs
You cannot create a public VIF to a Direct Connect gateway
One or more transit gateways through a Direct Connect gateway
AWS advertises only the prefixes you list in the allowed prefixes of the association; connects many VPCs across accounts through the TGW

blocks.body: Direct Connect gateway. A Direct Connect gateway is a global construct (not created in a Region) that lets one connection (through a private or transit VIF) reach VPCs in any Region except the China Regions. You associate it with VGWs (private VIF design) or with transit gateways (transit VIF design), but a single DX gateway cannot hold both: you cannot attach a DX gateway to a transit gateway if it is already associated with a VGW or attached to a private VIF, and you cannot attach it to a VGW when it is already associated with a transit gateway. Rules that cause exam traps:

items: VPCs behind a DX gateway cannot have overlapping CIDR blocks, and a DX gateway does not provide VPC-to-VPC routing. Traffic between VPCs associated to the same DX gateway, between VIFs on one DX gateway, and between a VIF and a VPN on an associated VGW is not supported. If VPCs must talk to each other, use Transit Gateway or peering as well.

A virtual private gateway can be associated with only one VPC and one DX gateway, so each VPC needs its own VGW; the number of VGW associations per DX gateway (20) is therefore a scale limit, which is the reason to move to a transit VIF and a Transit Gateway for 'hundreds of VPCs'.

For a transit gateway association, the allowed prefixes you enter are advertised to on premises exactly as entered (originating from the DX gateway ASN); for a VGW association they only filter the VPC CIDR and must be the same as or wider than the VPC CIDR. Allowed prefixes of multiple associated transit gateways cannot overlap.
If you connect to transit gateways in different Regions, use unique ASNs per transit gateway. A point-to-point /30 connectivity range does not propagate to a transit gateway.

Cross-account: for a transit gateway, the TGW owner creates an association proposal for the DX gateway and the DX gateway owner accepts it (and can set or update the allowed prefixes on acceptance or later). VGW associations across accounts follow a similar proposal flow (not verified in detail). Automating this from a project account typically uses a cross-account IAM role assumed by a CloudFormation custom resource (exam-pattern reasoning, not quoted from a page read).

blocks.title: Source disagreement
blocks.body: Different AWS pages disagree on some Direct Connect numbers: the Transit Gateway quotas page, the Direct Connect User Guide, and the General Reference all list 6 transit gateways per DX gateway, while a knowledge-center article says up to three, and the total VIF count is shown as 51 on the User Guide quota page but 54 in the General Reference table. Treat these as 'verify current quota in the console', and do not build an answer on the exact number.

Routing control with BGP. When multiple VIFs advertise the same prefixes you control path choice with local preference BGP communities: 7224:7100 (low), 7224:7200 (medium), 7224:7300 (high). Use the same tag on all paths for active/active (ECMP among the remaining paths if one fails), and a higher tag on the primary for active/passive. Local preference communities are evaluated before AS_PATH. If you set no community on a private VIF, outbound routing defaults to an AWS Region-based choice that depends on the relative distance from the Region, in which case AS_PATH prepending may not change the result. Advertising a more specific prefix on the primary also attracts traffic. Advertise the same prefixes on DX and VPN backups so failover is clean.

Resiliency. The Well-Architected guidance (REL02-BP02) defines maximum resiliency (99.99% SLA) as separate connections on distinct devices in more than one on-premises location and more than one Direct Connect location, which survives device failure, connectivity issues and a complete location outage. High resiliency (99.9%) uses two connections to multiple locations, with each on-premises location connected to a single DX location, which protects against fiber cuts and device failure and mitigates a complete location failure. A second connection at the same location, or from the same provider path, still shares fate. A Site-to-Site VPN ending on a transit gateway is a cost-effective backup: ECMP across VPN tunnels can reach up to 50 Gbps even though each tunnel is capped at 1.25 Gbps, but Direct Connect remains the best choice for stable, consistent connectivity because the VPN rides the internet. Use dynamic BGP routing so traffic fails over automatically. The Direct Connect Resiliency Toolkit helps design the topology.

Encryption. Direct Connect is private but not encrypted by default. MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) provides layer-2, hop-by-hop, near line-rate encryption on 10, 100, and 400 Gbps dedicated connections at selected locations (not on 1 Gbps dedicated or hosted connections); it needs a MACsec-capable device with direct layer-2 adjacency to the Direct Connect device and 256-bit keys. For any speed, or for end-to-end encryption, a Site-to-Site private IP VPN can run over a transit VIF and Direct Connect gateway to a transit gateway, using private addresses so the tunnel never touches the internet.

Cloud WAN. A Direct Connect gateway can be attached directly to a Cloud WAN core network (no intermediate transit gateway) with BGP route propagation, policy-based segmentation and tag-based attachment automation. Use that when the rest of the network is already a Cloud WAN core network.

Pricing and capacity planning: Direct Connect charges include port capacity and data transfer; the pricing model and the claim that Direct Connect lowers outbound data transfer cost versus internet egress were not verified against AWS docs in this build, so do not quote numbers. What the docs do support is the consistency and private-path argument.

'Multiple Regions over one connection' = private VIF to a Direct Connect gateway with VGW associations, or a transit VIF to a DX gateway with transit gateway associations (and TGW peering for transitive VPC-to-VPC routing). 'Hundreds of VPCs / accounts' = transit VIF + Direct Connect gateway + Transit Gateway shared by RAM. 'Redundant, 99.99%' = two locations, two devices each. 'Cost-effective backup' = Site-to-Site VPN, preferably on a transit gateway with BGP. A second DX connection to the same location, or both links to one on-premises router, is not resilient.

topics.title: Site-to-Site VPN, Client VPN and resilient hybrid design

blocks.body: AWS Site-to-Site VPN creates IPsec tunnels between a customer gateway device on premises and a virtual private gateway (one VPC) or a transit gateway (many VPCs). Each VPN connection has two tunnels, each with its own public IP address and ending in a different Availability Zone. Configure both: traffic from on premises to AWS can use both tunnels, traffic from AWS prefers one and fails over to the other, and AWS performs routine maintenance that can briefly disable one tunnel.

rows: Up to 1.25 Gbps per standard tunnel (140,000 packets per second); large bandwidth tunnels up to 5 Gbps (400,000 pps) are listed in the quotas page; VPN Concentrator tunnels up to 100 Mbps. None is adjustable. Whether and how a large bandwidth tunnel is enabled was not verified in this build.

On a transit gateway, ECMP across tunnels adds bandwidth, but only when the VPN uses dynamic (BGP) routing. ECMP is not supported with static routing, and it does not work across multiple VPN connections terminating on one virtual private gateway.

With static routing, AWS sends traffic to on premises over a single tunnel and you cannot choose the preferred tunnel when both are up (to prefer tunnel A, keep tunnel B down). Dynamic BGP gives automatic rerouting and path preference.

Optional accelerated VPN uses AWS Global Accelerator to enter the AWS network at the nearest edge location, avoiding congestion on the public internet; AWS creates two accelerators for you (one per tunnel) that you cannot manage directly. It is configured on VPN connections to a transit gateway (per the launch blog).

Built over Direct Connect using private IPs on a transit VIF and Direct Connect gateway; adds encryption without the internet. No extra TGW data processing beyond the underlying Direct Connect attachment.
You pay the Site-to-Site VPN connection charge; on a transit gateway you also pay the VPN attachment hourly charge (billed to the transit gateway owner) and data processing.
CloudWatch TunnelDataIn and TunnelDataOut (Sum, 5-minute period) let you compute throughput and alarm before a tunnel saturates

blocks.body: Customer gateway redundancy. A single customer gateway device is a single point of failure. The Well-Architected guidance is to use two tunnels per connection, each ending in a different AZ, with redundant on-premises hardware, ideally multiple ISP connections with diverse paths, and BGP for failover. Two customer gateways connected to one virtual private gateway through two VPN connections give device-level redundancy; with static routing, AWS-to-on-premises traffic uses a single tunnel and ECMP is unavailable, so BGP is preferred.

AWS Client VPN is a managed remote-access VPN service for individual users. Core objects: the Client VPN endpoint (in the same Region as the target VPC), a client IPv4 CIDR that must not overlap with VPC ranges, one or more associated subnets (the target network), authorization rules (who may reach which destination CIDR; they can be tied to Active Directory or SAML groups) and endpoint routes. To reach additional networks such as a peered VPC, an on-premises network, or the internet, you add both an endpoint route and an authorization rule for each destination. Authentication options shown in the docs are mutual (certificate), Active Directory and federated SAML 2.0. Use Client VPN when remote employees need private access to applications in private subnets without exposing them publicly; use Site-to-Site VPN for site-to-site links.

rows: Tunnel-level only; single customer gateway is a single point of failure
Two VPN connections, two customer gateways, BGP
Device and tunnel redundancy over the internet
Moderate availability, no Direct Connect lead time
One DX connection + VPN backup (TGW, BGP)
Survives DX failure at lower bandwidth and variable latency
Cost-sensitive backup; VPN throughput is enough in failover
Separate connections on distinct devices in 2+ DX locations and 2+ on-premises locations (maximum)
Mission-critical; optional VPN as extra backup

blocks.title: DX plus VPN gotchas
blocks.body: Advertise the same prefixes over the DX BGP session and the VPN BGP session. Prefer DX with local preference or a more specific prefix. On a virtual private gateway, VPN connections cannot be aggregated with ECMP, so large VPN backup for a fast DX link should terminate on a transit gateway. If the ask is a backup for several VPCs on a single DX connection, a transit gateway keeps the VPN count small; per-VGW VPNs also work but multiply.

Backup for a DX link: VPN. Consistent latency and bandwidth for failover: a second DX connection at a different location. 'Lowest cost' backup: VPN, with BGP. Users working from home on laptops: Client VPN, not Site-to-Site VPN.

links.label: Access resources in a peered VPC over Client VPN

blocks.body: AWS PrivateLink provides private connectivity between VPCs, AWS services and on-premises networks without exposing traffic to the internet. A VPC endpoint is the consumer-side object. There are two types of endpoints for AWS services (gateway and interface), plus interface endpoints for your own and partner services.

rows: Most AWS services, plus your own endpoint services, SaaS partners; S3 and DynamoDB also support interface endpoints
A route table target (prefix list); traffic uses the service's public IP addresses over the AWS network
Elastic network interfaces with private IPs in your subnets
Endpoint-specific DNS names (and optionally private DNS names for the default service name)
Not reachable from on premises or another Region
Reachable from on premises (VPN/Direct Connect) and from other Regions using peering or Transit Gateway
Billed (hourly and data processed; rates not verified here)

blocks.body: Interface endpoints can coexist with gateway endpoints in the same VPC. Practical rule: use gateway endpoints for in-VPC S3 and DynamoDB access (free, and they also remove NAT gateway and Transit Gateway data processing); use an interface endpoint for S3 when you need private IP access from on premises or from another Region.

Private DNS for interface endpoints. If private DNS names is enabled on the endpoint, a private hosted zone is associated with the VPC so that the default service name (for example the regional service name for an AWS API) resolves to the endpoint network interface IPs. This requires both VPC attributes enableDnsSupport (DNS resolution) and enableDnsHostnames (DNS hostnames) to be true, and the queries must go to the Amazon-provided DNS of the VPC (base of the VPC CIDR plus two) or a DHCP-option-set resolver that eventually reaches it. The CreateVpcEndpoint API describes the default for private DNS as true for interface endpoints. If you do not enable it, you can still use the endpoint through its generated endpoint-specific regional DNS name, but the default service name keeps resolving to public IPs, which is the classic 'we created the endpoint but names still resolve publicly' symptom. For on-premises clients, use the endpoint-specific DNS names (or forward queries to the VPC); an interface endpoint for S3 requires the endpoint-specific S3 DNS names.

Endpoint services (the provider side). To expose your own service, put it behind a Network Load Balancer (or a Gateway Load Balancer for appliances), create a VPC endpoint service configuration, and optionally require acceptance of each connection request; permissions list allowed principals. The consumer creates an interface endpoint to the service name. Consumer and provider can be in different VPCs and accounts and can have overlapping IP ranges, because the consumer reaches only the ENI in its own subnet and only the consumer can initiate connections. Details that matter:

items: Endpoint services are Regional; within a Region the consumer can only create endpoints in AZs the service also uses. AZ names differ across accounts, so match on AZ IDs. Providers should span at least two AZs.

Source IP seen by the application is the private IP of the load balancer nodes, not the consumer; enable proxy protocol on the load balancer to receive consumer addresses and endpoint IDs in the proxy protocol header.
A Network Load Balancer can be associated with a single endpoint service, but an endpoint service can have multiple NLBs; configure them identically.

An Application Load Balancer can be placed behind the NLB as an ALB-type target group to combine ALB routing with PrivateLink. An endpoint service needs the NLB (or GWLB) front end; the ALB cannot be the endpoint service directly (the documentation states that endpoint services require a Network Load Balancer or a Gateway Load Balancer, but no page read for this lesson explicitly says ALBs cannot back an endpoint service).

Scale: each endpoint supports 10 Gbps by default per AZ and scales automatically up to 100 Gbps per AZ; PrivateLink is described as having virtually unlimited scale in number of endpoints, while VPC peering is limited to at most 125 active connections per VPC. Metrics include PacketDropCount, BytesProcessed and ResetPacketsReceived.

blocks.body: Cross-Region PrivateLink. A provider can host a service in one Region and make it available in a set of supported Regions; the consumer selects the service Region when creating the endpoint. It is supported for NLB-based services (the launch blog states that it did not cover AWS or Marketplace services at launch; a later blog extends it to AWS services). Prerequisites and rules: the IAM permission-only action vpce:AllowMultiRegion; the condition keys ec2:VpceSupportedRegion and ec2:VpceServiceRegion; opt-in Regions must be enabled on both sides; the host Region cannot be removed from the supported set; providers need at least two AZs; consumers need not match AZs. Some AZs (use1-az3, usw1-az2, apne1-az3, apne2-az2, apne2-az4) are not supported for cross-Region access. AWS recommends intra-Region access wherever possible because it has lower latency and cost. The docs also note that consumers can reach an endpoint service from other Regions using VPC peering or a transit gateway. A further workaround, an NLB in the consumer Region with IP targets that reach the provider over inter-Region peering, is reasoning from exam practice and was not verified against a docs page in this build.

Securing access. Endpoint policies and resource policies restrict who can use an endpoint. For S3, a bucket policy with the aws:SourceVpce condition limits access to a specific endpoint; an Allow statement alone does not stop authenticated principals using other paths, so pair it with an explicit Deny using StringNotEquals on aws:SourceVpce when you must force the endpoint path. Private API Gateway REST APIs are reached through an interface endpoint for execute-api (including from on premises over Direct Connect) and use a resource policy keyed on aws:sourceVpce to control invokers. Security groups can be associated with the network interfaces of interface endpoints (the default security group of the VPC is used if you specify none), so make sure their rules allow the clients that use the endpoint.

PrivateLink versus peering versus Transit Gateway. PrivateLink: one-way client/server, unidirectional initiation, overlapping CIDRs are fine, scales to many consumers, no route tables to manage. Peering and Transit Gateway: two-way routing at network level, need non-overlapping CIDRs, and expose the whole network to each other (controlled by security groups and routes). When 200 accounts need to consume a few microservices, endpoint services scale better than a mesh. For a SaaS provider and a customer that agree to connect privately inside the same Region, the customer creates an interface endpoint to the vendor's endpoint service (deployed in multiple AZs for availability).

Cues for PrivateLink: 'overlapping CIDR', 'expose only one application/service', 'unidirectional', 'SaaS provider in a different account', 'no VPC peering or route tables', 'consumers must not reach anything else in the provider VPC'. Cues for gateway endpoint: S3/DynamoDB from inside the VPC, lowest cost. Cues for interface endpoint to S3: on-premises or cross-Region access to S3 over private IPs. 'Private DNS resolves to public IPs' = turn on private DNS names on the endpoint and make sure the VPC DNS support and hostnames attributes are enabled.

blocks.body: Every VPC has an Amazon-provided DNS resolver at the VPC CIDR base plus two (and at 169.254.169.253). It answers VPC-internal names, public DNS and private hosted zones associated with the VPC, but it accepts queries only from inside the VPC. Hybrid DNS is the set of constructs that let on-premises resolvers query AWS-hosted names and let VPC resources resolve on-premises names, without building DNS servers on EC2.

rows: On premises to AWS (private hosted zone names, VPC names)
ENIs with private IPs in your VPC; on-premises DNS servers use a conditional forwarding rule that targets those IPs
ENIs in your VPC used as the source of forwarded queries; one rule per domain name with the target on-premises resolver IPs; rules are associated with VPCs
Rule sharing with AWS RAM; private hosted zone association; Route 53 Profiles
One outbound endpoint can serve many VPCs when you share its rules

blocks.body: Inbound endpoint requirements. Route 53 requires 2 to 6 IP addresses, and AWS recommends spreading them across at least two AZs; create one more network interface than the steady-state need so surges and maintenance do not reduce capacity. The endpoint security group must allow inbound TCP and UDP port 53 from the on-premises DNS servers; network ACLs must allow port 53 inbound and ephemeral ports 1024-65535 outbound to the on-premises servers; the subnet route table needs a route to the on-premises network over Direct Connect or VPN so responses return; and the on-premises DNS server needs a conditional forwarder for the domain. Test with telnet to port 53 and with dig or nslookup. Outbound endpoint security groups need outbound rules for TCP and UDP port 53 (or the port your on-premises resolvers use).

Design pattern for many VPCs. In a shared services VPC, associate the central private hosted zones, create one AZ-redundant set of inbound endpoints for on premises to call, and create outbound endpoints with forwarding rules for on-premises domains, then share the rules with the other accounts through RAM and associate them with every VPC that needs them. You do not need an outbound endpoint in every VPC. Documented limitations of the endpoint approach: up to about 10,000 UDP queries per second per endpoint IP address (as low as roughly 1,500 when connection tracking applies, for example behind a Network Load Balancer), and the query source address the on-premises server sees is the endpoint IP, not the original client.

blocks.title: Quotas and behaviors worth remembering
blocks.body: Each EC2 network interface can send 1,024 packets per second to the Route 53 Resolver (.2 address), and this cannot be increased. Flow Logs do not capture traffic to the Amazon DNS server; use packet capture or Traffic Mirroring (and Resolver query logs, which only see queries that reach the resolver) to diagnose DNS throttling. VPC peering does not let you query the peer's Amazon DNS server, and transit gateway peering does not resolve private names across Regions.

Private hosted zones across VPCs and accounts. A private hosted zone answers only for VPCs it is associated with. To associate a zone in account A with a VPC in account B you cannot complete the association from the console on one side alone: in the zone owner's account run create-vpc-association-authorization (hosted zone ID, VPC Region and VPC ID), then in the VPC owner's account run associate-vpc-with-hosted-zone with the same values (the knowledge-center article also notes that you can remove the authorization afterwards; confirm cleanup steps in the current docs). For ~50 or more accounts, hand-made authorizations become an operations burden, which is the motivation for Route 53 Profiles.

Route 53 Profiles let you group private hosted zone associations, Resolver forwarding and system rules, DNS Firewall rule groups, interface VPC endpoint DNS settings, query logging configurations, and some VPC-level settings (reverse DNS behavior, DNS Firewall failure mode, DNSSEC validation) and apply them to many VPCs in a Region. You associate one Profile per VPC, and you can share a Profile with accounts, OUs or the whole organization through AWS RAM. Updates propagate to all associated VPCs. This is the current low-overhead answer for sharing private DNS across many accounts; older exam answers use per-account PHZ association authorizations or shared Resolver rules.

Resolver DNS Firewall filters outbound DNS queries from VPCs. You build domain lists (your own or AWS managed), put rules in a rule group (allow, block with a custom response such as NODATA, or alert), give each rule a priority (lowest number evaluated first), and associate the rule group with VPCs. A rule group is created per Region. The closed 'walled garden' pattern is a rule that BLOCKs the domain list containing `*` plus higher-priority ALLOW rules for the domains you trust, so partners using a proxy fleet can reach only approved domains by name. AWS Firewall Manager can manage DNS Firewall across an organization. DNS Firewall controls name resolution; it does not stop a client that connects to a raw IP address, so pair it with Network Firewall or security controls when that matters (reasoning, not a quoted doc statement).

'On-premises must resolve cloud.example.com' = inbound endpoint plus conditional forwarder on premises. 'VPCs must resolve corp.example.com on premises' = outbound endpoint plus forwarding rule associated with the VPCs. Both = both, with the PHZ associated to every VPC that must resolve it. Do not choose 'run BIND on EC2' unless the stem forbids managed endpoints. 'Share across 50 accounts with least overhead' = RAM-shared Resolver rules and Route 53 Profiles; per-pair PHZ association authorizations are the heavier alternative.

links.label: How Resolver endpoints forward DNS queries from your VPCs
Resolver endpoints and forwarding rules (hybrid DNS whitepaper)

blocks.body: Network tooling is split by question: what flowed (Flow Logs), what is in the payload (Traffic Mirroring), can it flow at all (Reachability Analyzer), and what unintended paths exist (Network Access Analyzer).

rows: Who talked to whom, accept or reject, bytes
Records for a VPC, subnet or network interface, published to CloudWatch Logs, Amazon S3, or Amazon Data Firehose; collected out of the traffic path so there is no throughput or latency impact

Not real time; configuration and record format cannot be changed after creation (delete and recreate); cannot enable for a peered VPC unless the peer is in your account; does not capture traffic to the Amazon DNS server; with secondary IPs or NAT use pkt-srcaddr/pkt-dstaddr fields to see original addresses
Flow-level records for traffic crossing the transit gateway, including to on premises
Complements VPC flow logs and attachment metrics
Full packets for deep analysis, intrusion detection, reverse-engineering an attack
Copies inbound and outbound traffic from ENIs to a mirror target (an ENI, an NLB with a UDP listener or a GWLB with a UDP listener) encapsulated in VXLAN

Target security group must allow UDP 4789 from the source; source subnet route must reach the target; target software must decode VXLAN; source and target can be in different VPCs via peering, transit gateway or GWLB endpoint; mirrored TLS stays encrypted unless decrypted at the target (reasoning, not quoted from a page read)
Whether a path between two resources is configured to work, and which component blocks it
Builds a model of the configuration; sends no packets and does not analyze the data plane; shows the shortest reachable path or the blocking components
Configuration only; cannot find an application that is down. Works across accounts through Network Manager
Unintended network access, internet exposure, segmentation validation
Static automated-reasoning analysis against a Network Access Scope you define; no packets sent
Use regularly and in the Network account of a multi-account design
VPN TunnelDataIn/Out, NAT gateway ErrorPortAllocation and ActiveConnectionCount, PrivateLink PacketDropCount and BytesProcessed, Network Manager route events

blocks.body: Flow log reading tips. A flow log record carries an action (ACCEPT or REJECT); compare records from the network interfaces on both sides of a hop to localize a drop. Query CloudWatch Logs with Logs Insights, or S3 with Athena, to aggregate by source, destination and port. The flow log limitations page notes that dstaddr and srcaddr can show the interface's primary private address in some cases (secondary IPs, forwarded traffic), so add the pkt-srcaddr and pkt-dstaddr fields when you need original addresses, for example around a NAT gateway. Flow Logs are not real time, so use them for analysis and troubleshooting, not as a live control.

items: Check the route tables on both ends: subnet route table entry to the peering connection, transit gateway, virtual private gateway, NAT gateway or endpoint, then the transit gateway route table associated with the attachment, then the return path (routes must exist in both directions).
Check security groups (stateful) and network ACLs (stateless, ephemeral port range for return traffic) on both sides, including endpoint and Resolver endpoint security groups.
Check overlap: overlapping CIDRs break peering, DX gateway and TGW designs; look for the longest-prefix route that is winning.
Check DNS: does the name resolve to the private IP you expect (private DNS names on the endpoint, PHZ association, Resolver rules, VPC DNS attributes)?

Check hybrid paths: BGP session state, advertised prefix counts versus quotas (a Direct Connect BGP session goes DOWN if you advertise more than the configured routes), VPN tunnel status and throughput, transit gateway route table propagation, and the 'allowed prefixes' on the DX association.
Check symmetry for stateful appliances: appliance mode on the inspection VPC attachment, and a single transit gateway attached to the appliance VPC.
Run Reachability Analyzer for a configuration verdict, then Flow Logs for evidence of actual packets, then Traffic Mirroring or packet capture when you need payload.

blocks.body: 'Analyze payloads to reverse-engineer an attack' = Traffic Mirroring (Flow Logs have no payload). 'Prove that an instance can reach a database through a TGW without sending traffic' = Reachability Analyzer. 'Find out if any path exposes a subnet to the internet' = Network Access Analyzer. 'Who is sending unsolicited inbound traffic' = Flow Logs with a query.

links.label: Logging IP traffic using VPC Flow Logs

blocks.body: Scenario 1: 300-account retailer with segmentation, central egress and hybrid DNS.

items: Requirements: prod, dev and shared-services segments; prod and dev must not reach each other; all outbound internet traffic inspected and logged centrally; two data centers connected privately; on-premises and AWS must resolve each other's private names; teams keep autonomy over their own VPC route tables.
Existing environment: AWS Organizations with a network account, non-overlapping CIDRs assigned from IPAM, two data centers with existing routers.

Architecture: one Transit Gateway per Region in the network account, shared with the organization through RAM; spoke VPC attachments in each account (attached to every AZ in use); route tables 'prod', 'dev', 'shared' and 'egress' with default association and propagation disabled so nothing lands in a default table by accident; spokes get a static 0.0.0.0/0 route to the inspection VPC attachment (appliance mode on); inspection VPC runs Gateway Load Balancer with endpoints and firewall appliances, then NAT gateways per AZ; gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB in each spoke.

Hybrid: two Direct Connect locations with transit VIFs to a Direct Connect gateway associated with the transit gateway; allowed prefixes list the summarized AWS CIDRs; Site-to-Site VPN on the same transit gateway (BGP, same prefixes) as backup.

DNS: PHZs associated with a shared-services VPC, a Route 53 Profile shared to the organization with the private zones and forwarding rules, inbound endpoints (3 IPs in 2 AZs) for on premises, outbound endpoint with forwarding rules to on-premises resolvers.

Security and cost: Flow Logs on the transit gateway and inspection VPC to a central S3 bucket; Network Access Analyzer scheduled in the network account; NAT/TGW data processing is centralized and charged to the networking account unless flexible cost allocation is used; gateway endpoints cut NAT and TGW processing for S3/DynamoDB.

Rejected: full-mesh peering (not transitive, 125-connection ceiling, no central control); a VGW per VPC on Direct Connect (limited VGW associations per DX gateway, no VPC-to-VPC); NAT gateways in every spoke (hourly cost across 300 accounts, no inspection point); EC2 DNS forwarders (operational burden versus managed Resolver).

blocks.body: Scenario 2: SaaS provider exposes an API to customers whose networks overlap.

items: Requirements: customers in many AWS accounts, some with the same CIDR ranges, consume a private API; traffic must not cross the internet; customers must not reach anything else in the provider network; onboarding must be controlled.

Architecture: the API runs behind a Network Load Balancer (an ALB can sit behind it as an ALB-type target group if path or header routing is needed); the provider creates a VPC endpoint service with acceptance required and allowed principals; each customer creates an interface endpoint in subnets in the service's AZs (matched by AZ ID), enables private DNS names if the provider verified a private DNS name, or uses the endpoint-specific DNS name; the provider enables proxy protocol if it needs consumer addresses; for customers in another Region, enable cross-Region access on the endpoint service for the supported Regions.

Security and cost: only the customer can initiate connections; endpoint policies and security groups on the consumer side (security groups can be associated with interface endpoint network interfaces) limit who inside the customer VPC can use it; cost is the interface endpoint hourly and data processing charges plus load balancer charges (rates not verified here); cross-Region adds latency and cost, so prefer same-Region endpoints when possible.

Rejected: VPC peering or Transit Gateway (overlapping CIDRs, exposes entire networks, per-pair management); public API with IP allow lists (traffic traverses the internet and allow-lists break when customers change addresses); site-to-site VPN per customer (operations and overlapping ranges).

blocks.body: Scenario 3: Two-Region company with a single data center, 99.99% hybrid availability, private access to S3 from the data center.

items: Requirements: on premises reaches VPCs in two Regions; hybrid link must survive device and location failures; backup jobs must write to S3 over private IPs, not the internet; VPCs in the two Regions must also reach each other.

Architecture: two Direct Connect locations with separate devices on each side, transit VIFs to a Direct Connect gateway associated with one transit gateway per Region; the two transit gateways peered with static routes in both route tables (inter-Region traffic is encrypted and stays on the backbone); BGP local preference communities make the nearer location primary; a Site-to-Site VPN on each transit gateway acts as a last-resort backup; an interface endpoint for S3 in each Region with endpoint-specific DNS names used by the backup software (gateway endpoints are not reachable from on premises); Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoints if the data center needs to resolve AWS private names.
Cost: transit gateway attachment hours and data processing (including the Direct Connect attachment), interface endpoint charges, Direct Connect port and data transfer charges (not quantified here).

Rejected: a single DX connection plus VPN (does not meet the SLA design); private VIFs with a VGW per VPC (does not scale and has no inter-Region VPC routing); a gateway endpoint for S3 (not usable from on premises); a public VIF to S3 (traffic uses public addressing, though not the internet, and the stem asks for private IPs).

links.label: Building a scalable and secure multi-VPC network infrastructure (whitepaper)
Direct Connect gateways and Transit Gateway associations

blocks.body: The snippets below follow the structure and commands shown in the AWS pages listed under each topic where possible. The policy shape for cross-Region PrivateLink and the CLI and CloudFormation snippets that are not quoted from a docs page were authored from the documented object model and have not been executed; validate with cfn-lint, the CLI --generate-cli-skeleton option and a non-production account first (this is listed under unverified).
1. Segmented Transit Gateway hub.

items: Console: VPC > Transit gateways > Create. Choose an ASN, and turn off default route table association and propagation if you want explicit segmentation.
Share it: AWS RAM > Create resource share > select the transit gateway > principals: the organization or OU. (RAM sharing with AWS Organizations must be enabled first.)
In each spoke account: VPC > Transit gateway attachments > Create > VPC > choose subnets in every AZ you use.

In the network account: accept attachments if auto-accept is off, then, under Transit gateway route tables, create the tables, associate attachments, enable propagation, and add static routes (for example, 0.0.0.0/0 to the egress or inspection VPC attachment).
In each spoke VPC route table add the destination CIDRs (or a summary/prefix list) that point at the transit gateway; the attachment alone does not route anything.

blocks.label: CLI
blocks.body:
# 1. Create the gateway without default association/propagation
aws ec2 create-transit-gateway \
  --description "network-hub" \
  --options AmazonSideAsn=64512,DefaultRouteTableAssociation=disable,DefaultRouteTablePropagation=disable

# 2. Route tables, attachment (appliance mode for an inspection VPC), association, propagation, static route
aws ec2 create-transit-gateway-route-table --transit-gateway-id <tgw-id>
aws ec2 create-transit-gateway-vpc-attachment --transit-gateway-id <tgw-id> --vpc-id <inspection-vpc-id> \
  --subnet-ids <subnet-az1> <subnet-az2> --options ApplianceModeSupport=enable
aws ec2 associate-transit-gateway-route-table --transit-gateway-route-table-id <rtb-id> --transit-gateway-attachment-id <attachment-id>
aws ec2 enable-transit-gateway-route-table-propagation --transit-gateway-route-table-id <rtb-id> --transit-gateway-attachment-id <attachment-id>
aws ec2 create-transit-gateway-route --transit-gateway-route-table-id <spoke-rtb-id> \
  --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --transit-gateway-attachment-id <inspection-attachment-id>

# 3. Share with the organization (RAM sharing with Organizations must be enabled)
aws ram create-resource-share --name tgw-share \
  --resource-arns arn:aws:ec2:<region>:<account-id>:transit-gateway/<tgw-id> \
  --principals arn:aws:organizations::<management-account-id>:organization/<org-id>

blocks.label: CloudFormation
blocks.body:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Description: Transit gateway with segmented route tables (sketch)
Resources:
  Tgw:
    Type: AWS::EC2::TransitGateway
    Properties:
      AmazonSideAsn: 64512
      DefaultRouteTableAssociation: disable
      DefaultRouteTablePropagation: disable
      AutoAcceptSharedAttachments: disable
      Tags:
        - Key: Name
          Value: network-hub
  RtProd:
    Type: AWS::EC2::TransitGatewayRouteTable
    Properties:
      TransitGatewayId: !Ref Tgw
  RtShared:
    Type: AWS::EC2::TransitGatewayRouteTable
    Properties:
      TransitGatewayId: !Ref Tgw
  AttProd1:
    Type: AWS::EC2::TransitGatewayAttachment
    Properties:
      TransitGatewayId: !Ref Tgw
      VpcId: <prod-vpc-id>
      SubnetIds:
        - <prod-subnet-az1>
        - <prod-subnet-az2>
  AttShared:
    Type: AWS::EC2::TransitGatewayAttachment
    Properties:
      TransitGatewayId: !Ref Tgw
      VpcId: <shared-vpc-id>
      SubnetIds:
        - <shared-subnet-az1>
        - <shared-subnet-az2>
  AssocProd1:
    Type: AWS::EC2::TransitGatewayRouteTableAssociation
    Properties:
      TransitGatewayAttachmentId: !Ref AttProd1
      TransitGatewayRouteTableId: !Ref RtProd
  AssocShared:
    Type: AWS::EC2::TransitGatewayRouteTableAssociation
    Properties:
      TransitGatewayAttachmentId: !Ref AttShared
      TransitGatewayRouteTableId: !Ref RtShared
  PropProdIntoShared:
    Type: AWS::EC2::TransitGatewayRouteTablePropagation
    Properties:
      TransitGatewayAttachmentId: !Ref AttProd1
      TransitGatewayRouteTableId: !Ref RtShared
  PropSharedIntoProd:
    Type: AWS::EC2::TransitGatewayRouteTablePropagation
    Properties:
      TransitGatewayAttachmentId: !Ref AttShared
      TransitGatewayRouteTableId: !Ref RtProd
2. Direct Connect gateway with a transit gateway.

items: Create the Direct Connect gateway (global), then create a transit VIF on your connection pointing to it and bring up BGP.
Associate the transit gateway to the DX gateway, listing allowed prefixes (cross-account: the TGW owner creates an association proposal, the DX gateway owner accepts).

Associate the transit gateway attachment (Direct Connect gateway attachment) with the right route table and enable propagation so VPCs learn on-premises prefixes and on premises learns the allowed prefixes.
Create the backup Site-to-Site VPN on the same transit gateway with BGP and advertise the same prefixes; verify local preference (7224:7300 on the primary).
Verify: BGP session status UP, prefixes received, and the transit gateway route table shows the on-premises prefixes propagated from the DX gateway attachment.

blocks.label: CLI
blocks.body:
# Associate a Direct Connect gateway with a transit gateway and set allowed prefixes (shape shown in the AWS networking blog)
aws directconnect create-direct-connect-gateway-association \
  --direct-connect-gateway-id <dxgw-id> --gateway-id <tgw-id> \
  --add-allowed-prefixes-to-direct-connect-gateway cidr="10.24.10.0/24" --region <region>

# Update allowed prefixes later
aws directconnect update-direct-connect-gateway-association \
  --association-id <association-id> --add-allowed-prefixes-to-direct-connect-gateway cidr="10.30.0.0/16"
3. Hybrid DNS and cross-account private hosted zones.

blocks.label: CLI
blocks.body:
# Inbound endpoint: 2 IPs in 2 AZs; security group allows TCP+UDP 53 from the on-premises DNS servers
aws route53resolver create-resolver-endpoint --name inbound-hybrid --direction INBOUND \
  --creator-request-id inb-001 --security-group-ids <sg-id> \

A Direct Connect gateway is global and connects private or transit VIFs to VGWs or transit gateways in many Regions, but it does not route between its associated VPCs, and a DX gateway cannot hold both VGW and transit gateway associations.

blocks.title: Key concepts
blocks.body: Connectivity is chosen by transitivity, overlap, scale, direction and path (private versus internet). Transit Gateway route tables (association plus propagation) implement segmentation. Direct Connect is private and consistent but not encrypted by default; resiliency comes from separate devices and locations. PrivateLink gives one-way service access across overlapping address space. Hybrid DNS is built from Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints, rules, PHZ associations and Profiles.
Decision rules:

items: Two to a handful of VPCs, no transit: peering. Many VPCs or accounts, central route control: Transit Gateway; global policy network: Cloud WAN.
Overlap or one-way service exposure: PrivateLink. Private NAT gateway for overlapping network-to-network cases.
One DX connection to many Regions: DX gateway. Many VPCs/accounts on DX: transit VIF + DX gateway + transit gateway.
Backup or encryption on DX: VPN (BGP, transit gateway) or private IP VPN; MACsec on supported dedicated ports.
Central egress: egress VPC with NAT per AZ behind a transit gateway; inspect with GWLB or Network Firewall; gateway endpoints to save processing cost.
Static outbound IP: NAT gateway Elastic IPs (BYOIP for a single CIDR). Static inbound global IPs: Global Accelerator.
Hybrid DNS: inbound for on premises to AWS, outbound + rules for AWS to on premises, share rules and Profiles across accounts.

Task 1.2 of the SAP-C02 blueprint, 'Prescribe security controls', is about choosing the right preventive, detective and identity controls for an organization that already runs many accounts, many identity sources and sensitive data. The exam rarely asks 'what does service X do'. It asks which combination of policies, keys and services satisfies a set of constraints (cross-account, least privilege, minimal change, central visibility) with the least operational overhead.

blocks.title: Prerequisites
blocks.body: You should already know basic IAM (users, groups, roles, identity-based policies), S3 bucket policies, what a KMS key is, VPC basics (subnets, security groups, endpoints) and the idea of AWS Organizations with OUs and member accounts. Task 1.4 (multi-account design) covers Organizations and Control Tower in depth; here we use them only as the scope for controls.

Skills this lesson maps to (verbatim from the exam guide): evaluating cross-account access management; integrating with third-party identity providers; deploying encryption strategies for data at rest and data in transit; developing a strategy for centralized security event notifications and auditing. Knowledge areas: IAM and IAM Identity Center; route tables, security groups and network ACLs; encryption keys and certificate management (AWS KMS, ACM); and security, identity and compliance tools (CloudTrail, IAM Access Analyzer, Security Hub, Inspector).
Learning objectives. By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

items: Trace a request through policy evaluation and state, for any given principal and resource, which policies must allow it for same-account and cross-account cases.
Choose between a cross-account role, a resource-based policy, S3 Access Points, S3 Access Grants and a token-vending broker for a given sharing requirement.
Design a guardrail stack using SCPs, permissions boundaries, session policies and tag-based (ABAC) conditions, and predict the effective permissions.
Select an identity integration (IAM Identity Center with Active Directory or an external IdP, SAML or OIDC federation to IAM) for a workforce or CI/CD scenario.
Specify the KMS key policy and IAM policy pieces needed for cross-account use of encrypted S3 objects and Secrets Manager secrets, and place ACM certificates correctly.
Design organization-wide detection and auditing: CloudTrail organization trails, Access Analyzer, GuardDuty, Inspector, Config aggregators and Security Hub aggregation, with EventBridge notification.

Security controls appear both as stand-alone questions and as the deciding constraint inside multi-account and data-sharing questions, so this lesson overlaps heavily with Task 1.4 and Task 2.3.

links.label: Four ways to grant cross-account access in AWS

blocks.body: Everything in this task rests on how AWS decides to allow a request. Within one account, AWS evaluates identity-based and resource-based policies together and the result is the union: an Allow in either is enough, and an explicit Deny in any policy overrides every Allow. Permissions boundaries, SCPs and session policies can then only narrow what is granted (see the next topic).

blocks.title: Cross-account is different
blocks.body: When the caller and the resource are in different accounts, the resource-based policy alone is not enough for a principal that is an IAM user or role: the caller's own account must also allow the action through an identity-based policy. Both sides must grant. The one common exception is a resource-based policy that names a specific IAM role session or federated session as principal. This both-sides rule was not stated in a single quotable sentence on the pages read; it is shown concretely by the KMS and S3 cross-account walkthroughs below and the 'Four ways' post, which says cross-account access is granted by identity-based and resource-based policies.

Two ways to give another account access to your resource. (1) Resource-based policy: you attach a policy to the resource (S3 bucket, KMS key, Secrets Manager secret, SQS queue) naming the other account or principal. The principal keeps its own identity and its own account's permissions, and still needs an identity policy on its side. (2) Cross-account role: you create a role in the resource account whose trust policy names the other account (or specific principals) and whose permissions policy grants the access. The caller calls `sts:AssumeRole`, receives temporary credentials, and acts as the role, so only the resource account's role policy matters for the resource, plus an identity policy in the caller's account allowing `sts:AssumeRole` on that role ARN. The AWS Security Blog notes that KMS keys and role trust policies require a resource-based policy even for same-account principals.

blocks.body: S3 object ownership matters for cross-account writes. When ACLs are enabled, the AWS account that writes an object owns it by default, so a bucket owner may not own objects uploaded by another account. The S3 documentation says that with the 'bucket owner enforced' Object Ownership setting the bucket owner owns every object and ACLs are disabled, and that this is the default for new buckets. With ACLs enabled, `ObjectWriter` makes the uploader the owner of cross-account uploads, and `BucketOwnerPreferred` gives ownership to the bucket owner only when the uploader sends the `bucket-owner-full-control` canned ACL. The modern answer is therefore: keep ACLs disabled and control access with bucket policies and identity policies.

Third-party access and the confused deputy. When a vendor assumes a role in your account, the vendor is a 'deputy' acting for many customers. If the role trusts only the vendor's account, another customer who learns your role ARN could trick the vendor into using it against you. An external ID, which the vendor generates for you and you place in the role's trust policy as a `sts:ExternalId` condition, prevents this. AWS does not treat the external ID as a secret (anyone who can view the role can see it); its purpose is to bind the assumption to one customer. The AWS documentation describes this scenario for third-party service providers. For your own auditor with a single account the external ID is optional but harmless, and the best-practice answer is still a read-only role assumed by the auditor, never shared IAM users or access keys.

Role session limits. A role session requested with `AssumeRole` can last from 900 seconds up to the role's configured maximum session duration (1 to 12 hours; default requested duration 3600 seconds). Role chaining (using a role session to assume another role) limits the CLI or API session to one hour, and asking for more than one hour fails. `GetSessionToken` credentials, used for MFA, follow a different range: credentials requested with IAM user credentials can last from 900 seconds up to 129,600 seconds (36 hours), with a default of 43,200 seconds (12 hours), while credentials requested with root user credentials are limited to 3,600 seconds.

rows: Yes, up to 10,000 (Service Quotas, N. Virginia)

blocks.body: Scaling implication: a trust policy listing thousands of individual account IDs or principal ARNs hits the trust policy length limit, and a bucket policy naming every account hits the bucket policy size limit (that S3 limit was not looked up here). For sharing with hundreds or thousands of accounts, prefer a broker or condition-based design (for example `aws:PrincipalOrgID` in a resource policy, which this lesson did not verify, so confirm it in your own environment) or an identity broker that vends short-lived credentials, over enumerating accounts.

items: Common mistake: attaching only a bucket policy in the resource account and forgetting the identity policy in the caller account.

Common mistake: trusting `arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:root` and assuming only one user can assume the role. Trusting the account root delegates to that account's IAM admins, who then decide which of their principals may assume it.
Best practice: grant to roles rather than individual IAM users, scope trust to specific principals where practical, and add conditions (external ID, MFA, source identity, org ID).
Best practice: use a separate identity account or IAM Identity Center rather than creating IAM users per account when you need prod/test separation.

If one option uses a cross-account role and another uses long-lived access keys or shared users, the role is almost always the intended answer.

topics.title: Guardrails: SCPs, permissions boundaries, ABAC and MFA conditions

blocks.body: A guardrail limits what can be granted; it never grants anything itself. The exam tests whether you can pick the right guardrail for the scope (organization-wide, one account, one delegated administrator, one session) and predict the combined result.
