blocks.body: SCP details to know cold. An SCP never grants permissions; it defines the maximum available permissions. An account has only the permissions permitted by every parent above it (root, each OU, the account itself), so a block at any level, implicit by omission from an Allow list or explicit by Deny, cannot be overridden by `AdministratorAccess` in the account. SCPs affect only IAM users and roles that the organization's accounts manage, not resource-based policies directly: the documentation example is a bucket owned by account A in the organization whose bucket policy grants account B (outside the organization); the SCP on A does not apply to B's users. SCPs have no effect on the management account, and they do not affect service-linked roles. The effective permission is the intersection of applicable SCPs, the principal's IAM policies and any resource policies.

Permissions boundaries are the delegation tool. A boundary on a role or user caps what its identity policies can grant. The classic use is letting a team create roles for their workloads without letting them exceed a ceiling: require, with an `iam:CreateRole` condition on `iam:PermissionsBoundary`, that new roles carry the boundary, and allow only specific roles to be passed to services via `iam:PassRole`. The boundary condition-key pattern is standard IAM practice, but the sources reviewed for this lesson described the boundary mechanism and intersection rule, not the exact `iam:PermissionsBoundary` condition key syntax, so check the IAM reference before relying on key names in production. One nuance from the boundaries page: within the same account, a resource-based policy that names an IAM user ARN is not limited by an identity policy or boundary implicit deny, whereas one that names a role ARN is limited by a permissions boundary or session policy.

Tag-based control (ABAC). Attribute-based access control compares tags on the principal with tags on the resource, so one policy scales with the number of teams. With IAM Identity Center, you choose attributes from the identity source on the 'Attributes for access control' page; Identity Center passes them to the target account as session tags that policies reference with `aws:PrincipalTag/<key>`. The docs list benefits: fewer permission sets, permissions for new resources granted automatically when tagged, and CloudTrail records the user attributes for session tracking. With SAML federation, the identity provider sends session tags in the assertion; with plain IAM roles you can also set tags on the principal. ABAC only works if resources are tagged, so pair it with preventive controls that require tags on creation. For a minimal-disruption retrofit on a single account with many teams, a Deny statement keyed on mismatched tags is often the smallest change, compared with restructuring accounts.

MFA enforcement and the BoolIfExists trap. The key `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` is absent when the request uses long-term access keys, so a `Bool` condition set to false cannot evaluate to a match and the deny does not fire. IAM documentation therefore says to use `BoolIfExists` with value false in a Deny statement. For CLI users with IAM access keys, the user calls `sts:GetSessionToken` with the MFA device serial number and token code, receives temporary credentials marked as MFA-authenticated, and uses those; the deny policy blocks everything else except the actions needed to set up MFA and call GetSessionToken. A Knowledge Center article shows the same policy and notes console users get MFA-based temporary credentials automatically while CLI users with long-term keys are not prompted.

items: Region restriction is usually an SCP Deny with `aws:RequestedRegion` and exceptions for global services. The Region-condition idea is common practice; the exact global-service exception list was not verified in the pages read.
Preventive versus detective: SCPs and boundaries stop the action; Config rules and EventBridge notify after the fact. 'Prevent' in a stem points to the former, 'detect and alert' to the latter.
Delegated administrators: SCPs apply to member accounts that are delegated administrators, but not to the management account, which is why you should keep workloads out of the management account.

Service Catalog launch constraints give end users least privilege: the constraint names an IAM role that Service Catalog assumes to launch, update or terminate a product, so end users need only Service Catalog access, not CloudFormation or the underlying service permissions. A constraint applies to a product within a portfolio, not to the whole portfolio at once.

blocks.body: Words like 'maximum', 'cannot exceed', 'regardless of what IAM policy allows' point to SCP or permissions boundary. 'Delegate role creation to developers safely' points to permissions boundary. 'Per-team access with a single policy' points to ABAC. 'Developers must not need broad CloudFormation permissions' points to a Service Catalog launch constraint. A stem that says the account is not in the organization rules SCPs out; use identity-policy conditions instead.

topics.title: Workforce identity: IAM Identity Center and federation

blocks.body: Workforce identity answers 'how do people and pipelines get into accounts without long-lived IAM users'. Three mechanisms matter: IAM Identity Center for people across many accounts, SAML 2.0 federation directly to IAM roles, and OpenID Connect (OIDC) web identity federation for workloads such as CI/CD systems.

blocks.title: IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS Single Sign-On)
blocks.body: Identity Center provides single sign-on to accounts and applications from one place. Documentation and prior exam material may still say 'AWS SSO'; the service is named IAM Identity Center and the pages read call it the successor to AWS Single Sign-On. An organization instance is the recommended, fully featured type, enabled in the Organizations management account (a delegated administrator can manage it). An account instance is bound to a single account and Region and suits simple scenarios, including accounts outside Organizations. Newer docs therefore say Organizations is recommended rather than strictly required.

Identity sources. An instance connects to one identity source at a time: the Identity Center directory (default), Active Directory (AWS Managed Microsoft AD, or a self-managed AD through a two-way trust or AD Connector), or an external IdP using SAML 2.0 (Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Ping and others) with SCIM v2.0 for automatic provisioning of users and groups. The AD documentation adds constraints: the directory must live in the management account (or the delegated administrator account if one exists); only one AD Connector or one AWS Managed Microsoft AD directory can be connected at a time; use AWS Managed Microsoft AD for multiple domains or forests; and Simple AD (Samba 4 based) is not supported. For AWS Managed Microsoft AD, enable Identity Center in the same Region as the directory. AD Connector is a directory gateway that forwards requests to your on-premises AD without caching information in the cloud, which makes it the low-change answer when an existing VPN or Direct Connect link already reaches the domain.

blocks.body: How permission sets work. A permission set is a template of policies. When you assign it to a user or group for an account, Identity Center creates an IAM role in that account whose name begins with `AWSReservedSSO_`, attaches the policies, and lets assigned users assume it from the AWS access portal or CLI. These roles are modified only from Identity Center, not IAM (the IAM console returns a 'protected role' error). When you delete all assignments to a permission set in an account the role is deleted, and a new assignment later creates a role with a new suffix, so resource and KMS key policies that referenced the old role ARN break; reference permission-set roles by a pattern or via conditions rather than a hard-coded suffix. Customer managed policies referenced from a permission set must exist in each target account with the same name and path.

blocks.body: The IAM role quota (default 1,000 roles per account) also bounds how many permission sets you can provision into an account, because each becomes a role.

SAML 2.0 federation directly to IAM. Your IdP authenticates users and returns a signed SAML assertion; the user (or application) calls `sts:AssumeRoleWithSAML` or posts the assertion to the AWS sign-in endpoint. The role's trust policy lists the SAML provider ARN in `Principal.Federated` and should check `SAML:aud` equals `https://signin.aws.amazon.com/saml`. Importantly, the SAML IdP resource must be in the same account as the role, so multi-account SAML federation means one provider per account (or Identity Center). The assertion maps users to roles, so troubleshooting 'access granted to the portal but cannot reach the console or a specific role' starts with the assertion's role attribute, the trust policy and whether the role ARN and provider ARN pair is correct. `AssumeRoleWithSAML` is an unsigned call, so session policies should only be sent through a trusted intermediary.

OIDC web identity federation for pipelines. In IAM you create an OIDC provider for the token issuer and a role with `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`. For GitHub Actions the Knowledge Center example trust policy uses the provider `token.actions.githubusercontent.com`, requires audience `sts.amazonaws.com` and restricts the subject claim (`sub`) to a repository and branch. Without a `sub` condition any repository could assume the role. This replaces the IAM user and stored secret key in the pipeline.

Common mistake: forgetting that Identity Center manages assignments but the AD (or IdP) remains the source of truth; changing the source later is disruptive, so decide early.
Best practice: give permission sets least privilege, use groups not individual assignments, use ABAC attributes to reduce permission-set count, and keep break-glass access outside the primary IdP.
Credential type guidance: prefer temporary credentials from SSO, roles or federation over access keys; when keys are unavoidable add MFA through GetSessionToken.

topics.title: Encryption and secrets: KMS, S3, Secrets Manager and ACM

blocks.body: Encryption questions on this exam are really access-control questions: who is allowed to use the key, in which account, and through which service.

blocks.title: KMS key policy is mandatory
blocks.body: A KMS key policy is the primary access control for a key. Unlike most resource policies it does not automatically trust the owning account. The default key policy contains a statement that makes the account root principal an allowed principal for `kms:*`; this does not hand access to root, it lets the account use IAM policies to delegate. Without that statement IAM policies that allow key access are ineffective (IAM policies that deny still work). The AWS Security Blog also notes KMS keys and role trust policies need a resource-based policy even for same-account use.

Cross-account use of a customer managed key needs two parts. In the key owner's account, the key policy must allow the external account or specific external principals the required actions. In the external account, an IAM policy must delegate those actions to its users or roles. Effective permissions are the overlap: if the key policy names specific external roles, an IAM policy can only give the permission to those roles; if it names the whole external account, any principal there can be granted; and IAM actions not present in the key policy are not effective. KMS grants are an alternative to IAM policies for delegating access.

S3 with SSE-KMS. When objects are encrypted with a customer managed key, a reader needs S3 permission and permission to use the key (decrypt at minimum; the KMS doc example for sharing a key lists Encrypt, Decrypt, ReEncrypt*, GenerateDataKey* and DescribeKey, and the writer needs the generate-data-key and encrypt style actions). A 403 on download from an SSE-KMS bucket therefore has several candidate causes: IAM policy, bucket policy, the KMS key policy or IAM delegation, an S3 VPC endpoint policy, an SCP or a permissions boundary. Isolate by checking which layer denies; an explicit deny anywhere wins. If the object is encrypted with the AWS managed key `aws/s3`, you cannot edit that key policy to add another account, which is why cross-account sharing normally requires a customer managed key; AWS documentation states that you can grant cross-account access for a customer managed key but not for an AWS managed key, because you cannot modify an AWS managed key's policy. To change existing objects from SSE-S3 to SSE-KMS, set default encryption on the bucket for future objects and update existing objects with the S3 `UpdateObjectEncryption` API (also available as the S3 Batch Operations Update encryption operation), which changes SSE-S3 to SSE-KMS in place without a copy; copying objects over themselves also works.

Secrets Manager. A secret is encrypted with a KMS key. To share across accounts the owner attaches a resource policy to the secret allowing `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` to the other account's principal, and the KMS key policy must allow `kms:Decrypt` to that principal (the Knowledge Center example constrains it with `kms:ViaService` and the `kms:EncryptionContext:SecretARN` key). The article states that the secret must use a customer managed key specified by its full ARN to be reached from another account, not an alias. A different pattern avoids the key problem: the caller assumes a role in the secret's account and uses that role's local access to read the secret and decrypt with the key, as in the cross-account role pattern described earlier. To revoke access to a secret you shared, edit or delete the resource policy statement, and remember a deny wins; use IAM Access Analyzer to confirm external access is gone.

ACM certificates. ACM provisions and renews public and private TLS certificates for integrated services such as Elastic Load Balancing, CloudFront and API Gateway; imported certificates are not renewed by ACM. A certificate is Regional: ACM certificates used with CloudFront must be requested or imported in US East (N. Virginia), while for ELB the certificate must be in the same Region as the load balancer. You cannot move a certificate between Regions; request a new one. The AWS security reference architecture states externally facing ACM certificates must reside in the same account as the resources and cannot be shared across accounts. ACM public certificates are normally deployed by terminating TLS on an integrated service. Only public certificates requested with export enabled (certificates created before June 17, 2025 cannot be exported) can be exported and installed on EC2 instances, containers or on-premises hosts, and they carry a charge at issuance and at renewal.

The key policy first; IAM policies only if the key policy enables them
Key policy allow in key account AND IAM allow in caller account (or a grant)
Secret shared with another account needs
Resource policy on secret, customer managed key with ARN, key policy allowing decrypt
ACM renews automatically for integrated services; imported certificates are not renewed by ACM

Common mistake: giving a cross-account role `s3:GetObject` but not `kms:Decrypt`, then seeing Access Denied.
Common mistake: editing only the IAM policy when the key policy lacks the account-root enabling statement.

Cost dimension: the KMS and Secrets Manager pricing models were not retrieved in this build; ACM public certificates are described in the FAQ as available for use with integrated services, but price statements are not asserted here.

blocks.body: When a stem says 'the data is encrypted with a KMS key and cross-account access fails', answer with the pair 'key policy in the owner account plus IAM permission in the caller account'. If the secret uses the default AWS managed key, a resource policy is not enough: either move to a customer managed key or have the caller assume a role in the secret's account.

blocks.body: Network controls sit next to identity controls: identity says who, the network says from where. SAP-C02 questions combine them, for example 'must not traverse the internet and must be least privilege'.

rows: Stateless; return traffic must be allowed explicitly
Rules in ascending order until first match
Primary per-workload control, can reference other security groups
Coarse subnet boundary, explicit denies for known bad ranges

blocks.body: The VPC FAQ adds that network ACLs do not filter traffic between instances in the same subnet. The pages state you can secure instances using only security groups, with network ACLs as an additional layer. To block a specific IP range, only a network ACL can express a deny.

Protecting an ALB origin behind CloudFront. CloudFront documentation describes limiting the ALB security group to the AWS-managed prefix list `com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing`, which blocks traffic not from CloudFront at layers 3 and 4. The Knowledge Center adds a secret custom header (for example `X-Origin-Verify`) that CloudFront sends and an AWS WAF rule on the ALB checks, and recommends using both together for strongest origin protection: the prefix list restricts to CloudFront network addresses (any CloudFront distribution), and the header proves the request came from your distribution. The prefix list is managed by AWS, so it stays current without custom Lambda automation. It counts as 55 rules toward the security group rule quota (default 60), so it leaves little room for other rules in the same group.

S3 Access Points. An access point is a named endpoint with its own policy and its own network origin. Access point policies behave like IAM policies, support a subset of S3 actions, and combine with the bucket policy as an intersection. The blog describes delegating access control from the bucket policy to access points so that each application has its own policy rather than one giant bucket policy. A VPC network origin makes the access point reachable only from the named VPC and, per the documentation, effectively denies requests where `aws:SourceVpc` does not match (works with a gateway or interface S3 endpoint); with an internet origin you must add an explicit Deny on `aws:SourceVpc` and a VPC endpoint so the key is populated. The S3 FAQ notes you can use an SCP to require that new access points be created with network origin `vpc`. One blog caveat: VPC-origin access points cannot be used from the console. This pattern fits 'hundreds of applications, many accounts, no public internet, least privilege'.

S3 Access Grants. Access Grants maps identities to S3 locations. It supports IAM principals (same or other accounts) and, when associated with an IAM Identity Center instance, corporate directory users and groups through trusted identity propagation. You create one Access Grants instance per Region, register a location (for example `s3://`, a bucket or a prefix) mapped to an IAM role that Access Grants assumes to vend temporary credentials, then create grants. Choose it when the requester is an end user from your directory rather than an application role, and you want scale beyond bucket-policy size.

Block Public Access and Access Analyzer for S3. S3 Block Public Access prevents public exposure at bucket and account level; Access Analyzer for S3 lists buckets whose ACL, bucket policy or access point policy grants public or cross-account access, and lets you block public access with one action. It needs an analyzer in each Region you monitor, with an account as the zone of trust, and the storage blog says findings update about 30 minutes after a change to policies (up to six hours for account-level Block Public Access changes). Use CloudFront Origin Access Control to serve private S3 content rather than making the bucket public.

AWS Firewall Manager centralizes WAF, Shield Advanced, security group and network firewall policies across accounts. Prerequisites from the docs: the organization must have all features enabled; you designate a Firewall Manager administrator account (a delegated administrator can be set only from the management account); and AWS Config must be enabled in the accounts so Firewall Manager can detect new resources. Policies scope to OUs or accounts, so adding or removing accounts needs no custom automation, which is why it beats a hand-built Lambda and Parameter Store design.

items: Route tables are also a control: no route to an internet gateway or NAT keeps a subnet private; endpoint policies filter what a gateway or interface endpoint will carry.
Common mistake: expecting a network ACL deny to be bypassed by a security group allow; they are independent layers and both must permit.

Common mistake: using a bucket policy with `aws:SourceIp` for traffic coming through a VPC endpoint; the `aws:SourceIp` key is not included in requests that use a VPC endpoint (use `aws:SourceVpce` or `aws:SourceVpc`).
Shield, WAF and edge protections for task 2.3 are covered in the security-requirements lesson.

'Hundreds of apps, one bucket, each least privilege, VPC only' means S3 access points with VPC network origin. topics.title: Detection, auditing and central security events

blocks.body: The fourth skill asks you to design a strategy for centralized security event notifications and auditing. Think in layers: a log of API activity (CloudTrail), a continuous configuration record (Config), threat and vulnerability detection (GuardDuty, Inspector), external-access analysis (Access Analyzer), a place to aggregate findings (Security Hub) and a notification path (EventBridge to SNS, or Firehose to a log archive).

blocks.body: CloudTrail design. A trail records management events by default; data events (S3 object access, Lambda invoke and others) must be enabled explicitly and are billed. The storage blog warns that CloudTrail charges for management events from the second copy of a trail onward per Region, only the first copy being free, so avoid duplicate management-event trails. To audit every S3 GET on selected buckets, enable S3 data events (read) on a trail, not S3 event notifications or server access logs, which are not equivalent audit records for the exam. An organization trail applies to all accounts automatically and is the right answer to 'log all accounts to a central bucket with no per-account setup'. Deliver logs to a bucket in a dedicated log archive account with a bucket policy that grants `cloudtrail.amazonaws.com` write access conditioned on `aws:SourceArn` (and `aws:SourceAccount`), the confused-deputy protection pattern in the IAM docs. Log file integrity validation produces hourly digest files in a different folder of the same bucket, so you can grant separate access and detect modification or deletion. Encrypt with SSE-KMS and make sure the key policy allows CloudTrail.

Event-driven reaction. IAM API activity is delivered to EventBridge via CloudTrail and the Knowledge Center says IAM service events are available only in US East (N. Virginia), so the EventBridge rule for IAM changes (for example CreateUser) must be in us-east-1 and a trail with management events must exist. A rule can invoke Lambda to remediate (for example attach a deny-all policy) and publish to SNS to notify. For 'immediate notification of manual access to production', combine CloudTrail with a metric filter and CloudWatch alarm, or an EventBridge rule on the relevant sign-in or API events; the exact event shapes depend on how access happens and were not detailed in the pages read.

Access Analyzer details. An external access analyzer produces a finding for each resource policy that grants access to a principal outside the zone of trust; if the zone is the organization, sharing between member accounts produces no finding but sharing with an outside account does. Roles are global, so a finding appears in each Region where an analyzer is enabled. Archive intended findings, remediate unintended ones. Unused access is a separate analyzer type that must be created in addition to an external access analyzer, and can be created at the organization level to view findings centrally. External access analyzers are Regional, so create one per Region you use; an unused access analyzer is not Regional, and one analyzer covers all Regions. Access Analyzer detects public exposure of S3 buckets and publishes an event to EventBridge for each finding on supported resources (source `aws.access-analyzer`), so you can route findings to SNS or Lambda. Findings can take up to 30 minutes to appear after a policy change, so this is not real-time detection.

Security Hub. The service has evolved: AWS now describes Security Hub as a unified cloud security solution that correlates signals from GuardDuty, Inspector and the posture (CSPM) checks, with near real-time risk analytics, and the posture product is documented as 'Security Hub CSPM'. Documentation read for CSPM says it is Regional, and recommends: designate the delegated administrator (in the security tooling account), enable central configuration, create configuration policies, and configure cross-Region aggregation with a home Region so findings from all linked Regions and member accounts flow into the administrator's home Region. A single EventBridge rule in the home Region can then send all aggregated findings to Firehose and the central logging bucket. Member accounts must be signed in to the home Region to see aggregated data from their own account, and removing the administrator stops aggregation for members.

Config and compliance reporting. Config aggregators with organization sources collect compliance data without per-account authorization. AWS Audit Manager automates evidence collection for audits, but its documentation now states it is no longer open to new customers; existing customers continue as normal. In a design answer today, prefer Config conformance packs and Security Hub standards for continuous control evidence unless the stem says Audit Manager is already in use.

items: Separate duties: security tooling account as delegated administrator for Security Hub, GuardDuty, Inspector and Access Analyzer; log archive account for CloudTrail and Config logs; keep both separate from the management account.
Detective is not preventive: Access Analyzer, GuardDuty and Config tell you after the policy exists; use SCPs, Block Public Access and boundaries to prevent.
Regional gaps: GuardDuty and Security Hub CSPM are Regional, so enable them in every Region you use or deny unused Regions with an SCP.
Pricing dimension note: CloudTrail data events and additional management-event copies are billed; other service pricing was not retrieved in this build.

blocks.body: 'Central', 'all accounts', 'automatically include new accounts' push you to delegated administrator plus organization-level enablement. 'Only notify when a bucket becomes public' targets Access Analyzer (or Config rule) plus EventBridge to SNS, not CloudTrail alone. 'Object-level reads audit' means CloudTrail S3 data events. 'Vulnerabilities in Lambda or ECR' means Inspector. 'Aggregate findings from many services and Regions' means Security Hub with cross-Region aggregation.

blocks.title: Scenario 1: Central logging and a shared analytics bucket
blocks.body: Requirements: a company with 40 accounts in AWS Organizations must keep an immutable-style audit trail of all API activity and object-level reads on regulated buckets, deliver it to one location, and alert the security team within minutes when any bucket is exposed publicly. Constraints: no per-account manual setup, new accounts must be covered automatically, the logging account must not be the management account. Existing environment: Control Tower is not used; accounts joined over time; a security tooling account exists. Architecture: an organization trail created from the management account with management events and S3 data events for regulated buckets, delivered to an S3 bucket in a dedicated log archive account with SSE-KMS and log file validation; the bucket policy lets `cloudtrail.amazonaws.com` write with `aws:SourceArn` conditions. An organization-level IAM Access Analyzer plus Security Hub with a delegated administrator in the security tooling account; an EventBridge rule on the aggregated findings publishes to SNS. Security: log bucket writable only by the CloudTrail service, readable by a security role; MFA delete and S3 Object Lock considerations are outside the scope of this lesson. Cost: data events are billed per event, so scope them to regulated buckets; avoid second management-event trails. Alternatives rejected: per-account trails (setup effort, drift), S3 server access logging (best effort, not equivalent to API audit; not verified in docs), S3 event notifications (not an audit log), CloudTrail in each account with replication (more moving parts).

blocks.title: Scenario 2: Cross-account encrypted data for another team
blocks.body: Requirements: the sales account owns a large SSE-KMS encrypted S3 bucket; the marketing account's analytics service role must read it read-only. Constraints: least privilege, no copying of petabytes, key rotation owned by the sales team. Architecture: keep the data in place. In the sales account: bucket policy (or an access point policy) allowing the marketing role `s3:GetObject` and `s3:ListBucket`; KMS key policy allowing the marketing role (or account) `kms:Decrypt` and `kms:DescribeKey`; confirm the key policy still has the account-root enabling statement. In the marketing account: identity policy on the role allowing the same S3 actions on the bucket and `kms:Decrypt` on the key ARN. Rationale: both accounts must grant; the key is a customer managed key that the sales team can share. Alternatives: replicate the data (cost, delay), make the bucket public (violates requirement), share an IAM user (long-lived credentials). A role in the sales account that marketing assumes is also valid and moves all permissions to the sales account, at the price of a role-assumption step in the analytics tool; pick it when the consuming service supports role assumption.

blocks.title: Scenario 3: Workforce SSO for a multi-account landing zone
blocks.body: Requirements: hundreds of employees sign in with on-premises Active Directory credentials to the console and CLI of many accounts, with permissions based on AD groups; SCIM is not available on-premises. Constraints: minimum change, existing Direct Connect or VPN to AWS, one place to manage access. Architecture: enable an organization instance of IAM Identity Center in the management account (or delegate administration), choose Active Directory as the identity source using AD Connector or AWS Managed Microsoft AD with a trust, create permission sets for job functions, assign AD groups to accounts, and optionally use ABAC attributes. Security: MFA through Identity Center, session duration set per permission set, SCPs to stop creation of new IAM users, break-glass IAM role with alarms. Cost: the documents reviewed for this lesson do not show a charge for Identity Center itself; Managed AD is billed (not verified here). Alternatives: per-account IAM users (does not scale, long-lived keys), per-account SAML providers (trust policy and provider sprawl, since SAML IdPs must be in the same account as the role), a custom broker (unneeded).

blocks.body: Service-distinction rules to memorize:

items: SCP caps permissions for member-account principals; permissions boundary caps one identity; session policy caps one session; none of them grant.
Resource-based policy plus identity policy for cross-account; role assumption moves permissions to the resource account.
Security group allow-only and stateful; NACL allow/deny and stateless.

Access Analyzer finds external, internal or unused access; GuardDuty detects threats from logs; Inspector finds vulnerabilities; Config tracks configuration and compliance; CloudTrail records API calls; Security Hub aggregates.

blocks.body: Watch for traps: an option that says 'create a new role in the caller account' when the permission must live in the resource account; an option that edits a bucket policy in the wrong account; options with SCPs that attempt to grant access; options that use `Bool` for MFA instead of `BoolIfExists`; options that rely on the AWS managed key for cross-account encryption; options naming the former 'AWS SSO' (the same capability, now called IAM Identity Center); options requiring Audit Manager or other services that are closed to new customers. Also remember several exam answers are 'best among the options' even when a newer feature (for example resource-based policies on more services) would also work; choose the option that best fits the stem's constraints, not the one you would design today.

blocks.title: Key concepts
blocks.body: Policy evaluation: explicit deny wins; same-account union of identity and resource policies; cross-account needs both sides. Guardrails (SCP, boundary, session policy) never grant. Identity: Identity Center for workforce multi-account; SAML/OIDC federation to roles; roles over users. Encryption: key policy decides; cross-account KMS needs key policy plus IAM; ACM is Regional. Network: SG stateful allow, NACL stateless allow/deny; prefix lists, access points, endpoints for perimeter. Detection: organization trail, Config aggregator, Access Analyzer, GuardDuty, Inspector, Security Hub with delegated administrators and EventBridge.

items: Decision rule: sharing with many accounts means avoid enumerating principals; use access points, ABAC, brokers or organization conditions.
Decision rule: if the caller is outside your organization, SCPs do not apply to it; use resource and identity policies.

blocks.body: This lesson covers SAP-C02 task 1.3, designing reliable and resilient architectures. The exam objectives for this task are: designing disaster recovery solutions based on RTO and RPO requirements; implementing architectures that automatically recover from failure; developing the optimal architecture by considering scale-up and scale-out options; and designing an effective backup and restoration strategy. The knowledge areas are RTO and RPO, disaster recovery (DR) strategies (including AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery, pilot light, warm standby and multi-site), and data backup and restoration. Domain 1 (Design Solutions for Organizational Complexity) is one of the four exam domains, and DR/resilience scenarios also reappear under business continuity (task 2.2) and improving reliability (task 3.4), so the reasoning here pays off in several places.

Prerequisites: you should know what an AWS Region and Availability Zone (AZ) are, basic VPC networking, EC2/EBS, RDS, S3, IAM and KMS, and DNS basics (TTL, alias records). Terms used throughout: RTO is how long you can be down; RPO is how much recent data you can lose; failover is switching production to the recovery environment; failback is returning to the original environment afterwards; a drill is a non-production test of recovery.

items: You will be able to translate a business RTO and RPO into one of the four DR strategies (backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site active/active) and justify it on cost.
You will be able to design an AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) deployment, including staging area, agent requirements, point-in-time recovery, drills, failover and failback.
You will be able to choose a database DR mechanism (Multi-AZ, cross-Region read replica, Aurora global database, DynamoDB global tables, backup copy) for a stated RPO.
You will be able to design a centralized, cross-Region, cross-account and immutable backup strategy with AWS Backup, and explain the encryption constraints.
You will be able to select and configure the traffic-redirection layer (Route 53 failover, Route 53 ARC, WorkSpaces cross-Region redirection, Amazon Connect Global Resiliency).
You will be able to design automatic in-Region recovery (Auto Scaling health checks, EC2 auto recovery, Multi-AZ) and decide between scale-up and scale-out.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.body: Almost every DR question gives you an RTO, an RPO and a cost or operational-overhead constraint, then offers four architectures that each satisfy a different pair of values. The skill being tested is matching the objectives to the cheapest strategy that still meets them, and spotting services whose behavior (asynchronous replication, DNS TTL, key policies) quietly breaks the requirement.

links.label: AWS Well-Architected: Use defined recovery strategies

topics.title: RTO, RPO and the four DR strategies

blocks.body: Recovery time objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable delay between the interruption of service and restoration of service. Recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable amount of time since the last data recovery point, that is, how much data you can afford to lose. Both are set by the business and then used by technical teams to choose a DR strategy; cost constraints, workload dependencies and operational requirements are further inputs. Well-Architected lists the following anti-patterns: choosing arbitrary objectives; setting objectives more stringent than the business needs (which forces costlier and more complex recovery than necessary); setting unrealistic objectives such as zero time or zero data loss; and setting objectives incompatible with those of a dependent workload.

A DR strategy across multiple AZs in one Region mitigates events such as fires, floods and major power outages. If you must also protect against an event that prevents the workload from running in a whole Region, use a multi-Region strategy. Well-Architected lists the multi-Region strategies in increasing order of cost and complexity and decreasing order of RTO and RPO.

headers: What runs in the recovery Region
rows: RPO in hours, RTO 24 hours or less
Continuous/automated backups give point-in-time recovery, which can lower RPO to as low as 5 minutes in some cases. You redeploy infrastructure, code and data at recovery time.
Core infrastructure copy; data replication and backup resources (databases, object storage) always on; app servers/serverless not deployed
RPO in minutes, RTO in tens of minutes
Compute is created only when needed.
Scaled-down but fully functional copy always running

Business-critical systems fully duplicated and always on, but scaled down; scale out on failover.
Full workload serving traffic in more than one place
Highest cost and complexity; data conflict handling becomes a design concern.

blocks.body: Another AWS page gives RTO bands of hours to days for backup and restore, hours for pilot light, minutes to hours for warm standby and seconds to minutes for active-active. The two sources are not identical, so on the exam treat the ordering (backup and restore, then pilot light, then warm standby, then active/active) as the reliable part and the exact numbers as approximate. Stated objectives also differ by workload tier: the AWS DRS whitepaper gives common figures of an RTO of 15 minutes and near-zero RPO for tier-1 applications, RTO of four hours and RPO of two hours for tier-2, and RTO of 8 to 24 hours with RPO of four hours for tier-3.

blocks.title: How failover time is actually composed
blocks.body: For active/passive DNS-based failover, total failover time is DNS TTL plus (health check interval times failure threshold). Route 53 health checks default to a 30 second interval (configurable as low as 10 seconds) and a failure threshold of 3 (configurable 1 to 10), per the AWS News Blog post on Route 53 health check improvements (failover = TTL + interval x threshold). A 300 second TTL therefore adds minutes that no amount of fast infrastructure can remove, which matters when the stem says RTO of 5 minutes.

items: Pick the least expensive strategy whose RTO and RPO both meet the requirement; the one that meets only one of them fails.
If the stem says data can be restored from backups and hours of downtime are fine, backup and restore is the answer and anything with always-on compute is over-engineered.
Pilot light keeps the data layer live but has no application compute, so recovery involves launching and scaling compute; warm standby already runs a scaled-down compute tier and only needs scaling.
A near-zero RTO and RPO combined with 'users in several Regions' points to active/active.
Replication is the RPO driver; automation and pre-provisioned capacity are the RTO drivers.

blocks.body: Do not assume warm standby always meets a very short RTO. Documentation describes warm standby as RTO in minutes (or minutes to hours); if all four options fail an aggressive RTO, choose the best available and note the keyword 'cost-efficient' or 'LOWEST RTO' in the stem. Asynchronous replication (read replicas, Aurora global database, S3 replication) never guarantees a zero RPO; only synchronous mechanisms (Multi-AZ within a Region) do.

blocks.body: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (AWS DRS) replicates on-premises and cloud-based servers into your AWS account so that you can launch recovery instances on AWS in minutes, using the most recent state or a previous point in time. This is the service to choose when the stem describes servers (physical, VMware, Hyper-V, other cloud, or EC2 in another Region/AZ) that need DR to AWS without re-architecting. Note the naming history: it is the successor to CloudEndure Disaster Recovery, and the CloudEndure-era vCenter-appliance failback is no longer the mechanism; failback now uses the DRS Failback Client or DRS Failback Automation.

How it works: you install the AWS Replication Agent on each source server. The agent performs continuous block-level replication to a staging area subnet in your account in the target Region. The staging area uses low-cost storage and minimal compute: by default DRS provisions a t3.small replication server and the typical ratio is 15 volumes per replication server. During normal operation you monitor replication and run non-disruptive drills. When recovering, DRS launches a conversion step and then EC2 recovery instances from a launch template you can customize. Documentation states that DRS achieves a crash-consistent RPO of seconds (typically sub-second) and an RTO typically ranging between 5 and 20 minutes, with the caveat that environment conditions affect both.

rows: 64-bit only. Agent supports x86_64 servers, and arm64 Linux servers running on EC2; no 32-bit and no Windows on arm64. Windows Server 2003 is no longer supported.
IAM user or role with the AWSElasticDisasterRecoveryAgentInstallationPolicy managed policy attached.
Outbound TCP 443 to the DRS, Amazon S3 and Amazon EC2 endpoints in the target Region; DRS must be initialized in the target Region before agent install.
Each volume max 16 TiB; each source server max 63 volumes; volumes beyond these limits are not replicated.

Dedicated subnet recommended. Unless 'Use private IP' is enabled and routing exists, replication servers must be in a public subnet (they get a public IPv4 by default). Private IP replication works over VPN, Direct Connect or VPC peering.

Default schedule per the DRS documentation: every 10 minutes for the last hour, hourly for the last 24 hours, and daily for 7 days by default; only the daily retention is configurable, from 1 to 365 days.

Hourly rate per source server (listed at $0.028 per server-hour on the pricing page at time of reading), plus the AWS resources used: staging EBS volumes, replication server EC2, snapshots, and (after failover) conversion servers and recovery instances. Verify current prices before relying on them.

blocks.body: Quotas: AWS DRS limits seen in documentation include a maximum of 300 concurrently replicating source servers per account, 100 source servers per recovery job, 500 source servers across all active jobs and 20 concurrent jobs (Disaster recovery at scale guide). The FAQ states that up to 3,000 servers can be recovered into a single target account by using multiple staging accounts, with up to 300 servers replicating into any one staging account. Recovery plans: 1,000 per account per Region, 20 steps per plan, 100 source servers per plan across all steps, 1 concurrent execution per plan, wait steps of 1 to 120 minutes and a 24 hour maximum execution. The AWS General Reference lists the 300 replicating source servers, 100 source servers per job, 500 source servers across all jobs, and 20 concurrent jobs as not adjustable. The recovery plan quotas did not state adjustability on the page read, so check Service Quotas for those.

blocks.title: Failback
blocks.body: Failback returns operations to the source. Per documentation it is only supported to AWS and to non-AWS environments that can boot from an ISO; the Failback Client supports x86_64 servers only, and arm64 servers fail back within AWS only. For on-premises sources you use the Failback Client ISO or DRS Failback Automation; for AWS sources you start reverse replication on the recovery instance. Redirecting user traffic is performed outside DRS. In a cross-Region AWS failback you should start reversed replication immediately after recovery because the recovered instances are not protected; the reverse replication copies the full data set (new staging resources are created) and incurs cross-Region data transfer cost. Initialize DRS in both Regions in advance and drill regularly.

items: Drill instances and recovery instances launch the same way but serve different purposes; use drills during normal operations to prove recoverability without disrupting replication.
Use recovery plans to launch interdependent servers in a defined order with waits between groups.

DRS protects servers, not application data semantics: for a database with a stricter RPO or cross-Region read scaling, pair DRS for the compute tier with a native database replica (see the next topic).
Do not choose DRS for managed services (RDS, DynamoDB, S3); it needs an agent on an operating system.
Common mistake: forgetting that replication servers in a public subnet need internet reachability unless private IP data routing is enabled.

blocks.body: Keywords that select DRS: 'physical servers', 'VMware', 'on-premises application', 'minimal changes', 'RPO of seconds', 'RTO of minutes', 'failback', 'non-disruptive drills', 'least operational overhead'. Older answer choices mentioning CloudEndure or a vCenter appliance for failback are dated; the service name is AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery.
The data tier usually determines RPO. Choose the mechanism by the failure you must survive (instance, AZ, Region, logical corruption) and by whether replication is synchronous or asynchronous.

rows: RPO zero on failover; failover usually 1 to 2 minutes. Standby does not serve reads. Backups and snapshots are taken from the standby.
Not a Region-level DR solution. Failover terminates in-flight queries; long recovery can extend failover.
Standbys provide failover and can serve read traffic.
RDS cross-Region read replica (Db2, MariaDB, MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server)
Promote the replica to a standalone instance on disaster. Lag varies and can be significant; monitor the ReplicaLag CloudWatch metric.
RPO is not guaranteed, promotion breaks replication, application must be repointed. PostgreSQL long-running replica queries can conflict with replay.
RDS automated backups with cross-Region replication
Daily snapshots plus transaction logs copied
Point-in-time restore to any second within retention, up to the last 5 minutes; retention 1 to 35 days.
Restore creates a new instance, so RTO is hours-scale for big databases.

Typical cross-Region lag under one second. Switchover (planned) has RPO 0; failover (unplanned) RPO is non-zero, measured in seconds, depending on lag. Secondary promotion typically within about a minute (Global Database Failover announcement).

Engine/version/Region support; matching engine version needed for managed failover (patch level too, except for newer Aurora PostgreSQL versions); no Backtrack; Aurora Auto Scaling not supported for secondary clusters.
Asynchronous (eventual) typically within about a second; optional multi-Region strong consistency
Any replica serves reads and writes; low or zero RPO by shifting traffic. Conflicts resolved last-writer-wins in eventual-consistency mode.
Application or Route 53 must redirect traffic; cross-Region reads of replicated data are eventually consistent.

blocks.body: Aurora global database in detail: it consists of one primary cluster (the only writer) and up to 10 read-only secondary clusters in other Regions. Replication uses the cluster storage volume and dedicated infrastructure, not the database engine, which has less impact on the primary and lower lag than logical replication. There are two failover methods for DR: managed failover (recommended; Aurora re-adds the old primary as a secondary when it returns, maintaining the topology) and manual failover (when managed is not possible, e.g. incompatible engine versions). Both can lose writes not yet replicated, and both are exposed to split-brain, although the promotion guarantees transactional consistency. For Aurora PostgreSQL you can enforce a maximum RPO with the rds.global_db_rpo parameter, which blocks commits on the primary when all secondaries lag beyond the target; in a two-Region database AWS recommends leaving the default in the secondary Region's parameter group so a failover does not stall transactions.

Cost lever: a headless secondary cluster has no DB instance, so you pay for storage but not compute, while Aurora keeps its storage volume in sync with the primary. Compute must be added during recovery, so RTO is longer than with a running reader. This is the pattern behind 'lowest cost cross-Region DR for a large relational database with RPO under 5 minutes'.

blocks.title: RDS cross-Region replica versus Aurora global database
blocks.body: Both are asynchronous and neither guarantees a number for RPO. The Aurora global database replicates at the storage layer with typical lag under a second and offers managed failover/switchover; an RDS read replica replays engine logs, can lag under heavy writes, and requires a manual promote step. If Aurora is allowed, global database is the stronger answer for sub-minute RPO and RTO of minutes; if the stem fixes the engine as RDS MySQL/PostgreSQL, the cross-Region read replica is the native low-RPO option.

items: Multi-AZ is for AZ and instance failures; it is never the answer to 'survive a Region outage'.
A read replica is not a backup: a destructive statement replicates. Add point-in-time recovery or snapshots for logical corruption.
After promoting a cross-Region replica, change the connection string or DNS, and rebuild replication in the other direction for failback.

For managed cross-Region switchover or failover, Aurora MySQL requires the primary and secondary clusters to run identical major, minor and patch levels. Aurora PostgreSQL tolerates differing patch levels only on the documented minor versions (for example 14.5 or higher, 13.8 or higher); older versions need matching patch levels. A manual failover needs only the same major and minor version.

blocks.body: RPO under 5 minutes plus a single engine usually means cross-Region read replica or Aurora global database; 'continuous' and 'any second' language means point-in-time recovery from automated backups. A synchronous guarantee of zero data loss across Regions is not offered by these services, so beware options that promise it.

links.label: Using switchover or failover in Aurora Global Database

blocks.body: Backup and restore is both a DR strategy of its own and the safety net under every other strategy, because replication copies corruption and deletion as faithfully as good data. A sound design answers: what is backed up (and how consistently), how often (RPO), how long it is kept (retention/compliance), where copies live (another Region for Region loss, another account for account compromise), who may delete them (immutability), and how fast you can restore (RTO, which must be tested).

AWS Backup is the centralized service. A backup plan defines schedule, window, lifecycle and copy rules; recovery points are stored in backup vaults. Key capabilities seen in documentation: scheduled cross-Region and cross-account copy (the wizard offers a destination Region and 'copy to another account's vault' with an external vault ARN, and requires the destination vault access policy to allow the source), organization-wide backup policies that create backup plans in all member accounts of an OU, SCPs that protect backup resources from modification or deletion, and EventBridge forwarding of backup events to a central bus for monitoring. For cross-account copies the source and destination accounts must be in the same organization, the resource type must support cross-account copy, and the source KMS key policy and destination vault policy must allow the other account.

rows: The first copy to a new Region or account is a full copy; later copies are incremental where the service supports incremental backups.

Copies are encrypted with the destination vault's KMS key, even if the source backup is unencrypted. For resources not fully managed by AWS Backup, cross-account copy with AWS managed keys is not supported because the key policy of an AWS managed key is immutable; use a customer managed key (CMK).
Copies of unencrypted clusters are also unencrypted.

Optional, one lock per vault. Governance mode: users with sufficient IAM permissions can manage or remove it. Compliance mode: after a grace period of at least 72 hours (3 days, ChangeableForDays 3 or more) the lock becomes immutable and cannot be altered or deleted by any user or by AWS. An empty vault can still be deleted.
MaxRetentionDays, if set, makes any backup or copy job with longer retention fail; recovery points already in the vault are unaffected.

Enabled by default; retention 1 to 35 days; point-in-time restore to any second in the retention period, up to the last 5 minutes. For retention beyond 35 days or a 6-hourly schedule, use AWS Backup or manual snapshots.
In the CloudFormation lifecycle type, DeleteAfterDays must be at least 90 days after MoveToColdStorageAfterDays.

blocks.body: Object and file data: Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication (CRR) is asynchronous and requires versioning to be enabled on both the source and destination buckets. Most objects replicate within 15 minutes but replication can sometimes take much longer (a Knowledge Center article states up to 48 hours), influenced by Region pair, object size, object count and AWS KMS throttling. S3 Replication Time Control (RTC) replicates most objects in seconds and 99.99 percent within 15 minutes, backed by an SLA on 99.9 percent of objects within 15 minutes per billing month; only a value of 15 minutes is accepted in the configuration, and RTC includes replication metrics and event notifications. Amazon FSx for Windows File Server stores daily backups in S3 automatically (using Windows Volume Shadow Copy Service) and allows additional backups at any time; a Multi-AZ file system protects against AZ loss but not Region loss, so cross-Region DR needs backup copies or replication. A separate AWS Storage Blog describes replicating FSx for Windows data across Regions; the exact native cross-Region backup-copy and DataSync behaviors were not verified against reference docs in this build.

items: Define RPO/RTO and retention per workload tier (WA REL13-BP01).
Tag resources by tier so an AWS Backup policy assigns them to the right plan automatically.
Create a plan with the schedule that meets the RPO (for example every 6 hours), a lifecycle that meets retention (for example 30 days) and a copy rule to a vault in another Region (and account).
Use customer managed KMS keys where cross-account copies are required, and grant the destination account on the key and the vault policy.
Lock the destination vault (start with governance mode, move to compliance mode after the grace period) and protect backup resources with SCPs.
Schedule restore tests and measure RTO; send backup job events to central monitoring.

Common mistake: relying on the default RDS 7-day automated backups when the requirement is 30-day retention or a 6-hour schedule. Use AWS Backup (via Organizations backup policies for multi-account) or manual snapshot automation.
Common mistake: single-account backups. Account compromise or deletion by an attacker removes everything; cross-account plus Vault Lock addresses it.
Common mistake: encrypting with the service default key and then expecting to share or copy across accounts.
Best practice: treat the backup vault in the recovery account/Region as the DR 'pilot light' for data.

blocks.body: 'Centrally manage', 'across all accounts in the organization', 'least operational overhead' for backup schedules points to AWS Backup with an Organizations backup policy, not per-account Lambda snapshot scripts. 'Cannot be deleted even by the root user' points to Vault Lock in compliance mode.

blocks.body: Recovering the data and compute is only half of failover: clients must be sent to the recovery environment. Application Load Balancers are Regional, so a single ALB cannot span Regions (the documentation reads for this build show ALB nodes and targets are within a Region but do not state this exact sentence). Multi-Region designs therefore place a DNS or global routing layer in front of one load balancer per Region.

Route 53 DNS failover: in an active-passive configuration you create a primary and a secondary failover record, each tied to a health check. Route 53 returns the primary while it is healthy; if the primary is unhealthy and the secondary is healthy it returns the secondary; if the secondary is unhealthy it returns the primary regardless; and if both are unhealthy it returns the primary. Without a health check on the secondary record, an unhealthy primary always sends traffic to the secondary. For alias failover records you must set EvaluateTargetHealth to true. Health checks run from multiple Regions; a health check can monitor an endpoint, other health checks, a CloudWatch alarm, or a Route 53 ARC routing control. By default, Route 53 considers an endpoint healthy only if more than 18 percent of health checkers report it healthy (the value might change in a future release). When the primary recovers Route 53 fails back automatically; to prevent that, change the health check configuration or use weighted routing. Active-active failover uses any non-failover routing policy with health checks.

Route 53 Application Recovery Controller (ARC): health-check-driven failover is automatic and has no control plane dependency, but you cannot force a failover during intermittent problems and you should not rely on the Route 53 health check APIs to force one. ARC routing controls are on/off switches that flip a health check and therefore a DNS record. They are hosted on a dedicated cluster across five Regions with quorum (works with up to two Regional endpoints unavailable), and safety rules (assertion rules and gating rules) prevent unsafe states such as turning all cells off. ARC also provides readiness checks to confirm the standby is ready.

rows: Use an FQDN as the registration code (a connection alias); associate aliases with directories in two Regions as an association pair; Route 53 failover records (TXT type in the AWS blog walkthrough) decide which Region users reach; Route 53 health checks can monitor CloudWatch alarms. Requires WorkSpaces provisioned in both Regions.

Replicate the instance (ReplicateInstance), create a traffic distribution group, claim phone numbers into it, and shift telephony and agents between Regions in 10 percent increments. Available only for instances in specified Regions and only for specific Region pairs (e.g. N. Virginia with Oregon, Frankfurt with London, Osaka with Tokyo); access is by contacting your AWS team. AWS states it is the only supported multi-Region resiliency solution for Connect; custom-built alternatives are unsupported.
Cross-zone load balancing is always on at the load balancer level for ALB and cannot be turned off there (it can be overridden at target-group level). With it off, an empty AZ returns 503 errors.

blocks.title: DNS TTL and caching
blocks.body: Failover is only as fast as clients re-resolve. Low TTLs shorten recovery but raise query volume; resolvers that ignore TTL can prolong it. Alias records pointing to ALBs are the usual pattern because the alias target health can be evaluated.

items: Use Route 53 failover with health checks for simple automatic active-passive; add ARC when you need controlled, safe, data-plane-only failover for a critical application.
Avoid a design that requires changing DNS through the control plane during a Regional impairment if an alternative with health checks or ARC exists.
Managed services with a built-in feature (Connect Global Resiliency, WorkSpaces cross-Region redirection) beat hand-built solutions on operational overhead and support.

blocks.body: In Connect questions, the dated option is a hand-built replica; the modern answer is Global Resiliency with traffic distribution groups, constrained to supported Region pairs. In WorkSpaces questions, the answer combines a connection alias (FQDN) with a Route 53 failover policy, not Region-specific registration codes.

topics.title: Designing for automatic recovery from failure

blocks.body: Resilient designs remove people from the first line of recovery. Layer the mechanisms: component replacement (Auto Scaling), host recovery (EC2 auto recovery), AZ failover (Multi-AZ databases, Multi-AZ file systems, load balancers across subnets) and Region failover (DNS plus replicated data).

EC2 Auto Scaling health checks: Auto Scaling monitors instances using EC2 status checks and, if enabled, Elastic Load Balancing health checks, VPC Lattice, EBS volume checks and custom health checks. When an in-service instance is unhealthy, Auto Scaling terminates it and launches a replacement using the group's current launch template, and with a load balancer it gracefully detaches the impaired instance and attaches the new one. EC2 status checks alone will not replace an instance whose application is down; enable ELB health checks so that the load balancer's view drives replacement. Instances that terminate unexpectedly (e.g. Spot interruption) are replaced to maintain desired capacity. A health check grace period gives new instances time to start before checks count.

EC2 automatic instance recovery: if a system status check fails because of an underlying hardware or software issue, simplified automatic recovery (enabled by default on supported instances at launch) or CloudWatch action based recovery (alarm on StatusCheckFailed_System with the Recover action) moves the instance to another host. The recovered instance keeps its instance ID and IP addresses, but RAM contents are lost and the OS uptime restarts; with CloudWatch action based recovery instance store data is also lost. It cannot recover a failed instance status check (an OS-level problem), only works for supported instance types, requires the instance to be running, and can fail if there is no capacity. AWS notes it is for individual instances; for a resilient system use multiple instances behind Auto Scaling and load balancing.

items: Stateful single instance that cannot be scaled out: EC2 auto recovery plus EBS backups is the minimum, but it is still one AZ at a time. Prefer a design that tolerates AZ loss.
Databases: Multi-AZ gives automatic failover with a stable DNS name so the application reconnects without manual change.

File storage: FSx for Windows Multi-AZ keeps an active and standby file server in separate AZs with synchronous replication and fails over automatically, typically in under 30 seconds; the DNS name stays the same and failback to the preferred subnet also occurs automatically.
ALB: register targets in every enabled AZ; leave cross-zone load balancing on unless you can guarantee capacity per AZ.
Make bootstrapping automatic (launch templates, user data or baked AMIs) so a replacement is production-ready without manual steps.

blocks.body: 'Automatically recover' and 'no manual intervention' suggest Auto Scaling with ELB health checks, Multi-AZ, or EC2 recovery. If the failing component is the whole Region, those do not help; look for replicated data and DNS failover instead.

links.label: Health checks for Auto Scaling instances

blocks.body: Scaling up (vertical) means moving to a bigger instance type or class; scaling out (horizontal) means adding more instances or replicas. They interact with resilience: horizontal scaling across AZs removes single points of failure and lets Auto Scaling replace failed nodes, whereas vertical scaling leaves a single node as the failure domain.

rows: Change instance type (EC2) or DB instance class
Auto Scaling group adds instances; read replicas or more shards/partitions
Resizing an EC2 instance involves stopping it if running; instance-store data is lost on stop and a public IP not backed by an Elastic IP is released
None for the existing nodes; new nodes join the load balancer
Largest available instance size; single point of failure
Needs stateless or shared-state design; licensing and coordination overhead
Spreads load over AZs; replacement on failure
Legacy single-node or memory-bound databases that cannot shard
Web/application tiers, queue workers, read-heavy databases (replicas)

blocks.body: Auto Scaling policy types: target tracking keeps a metric near a target value and scales proportionally; step scaling responds to alarm breach size; scheduled scaling changes minimum and maximum capacity on a schedule for cyclical load, and combining scheduled with target tracking reduces the impact of sharp increases. When several target tracking policies exist, Application Auto Scaling scales out if any is ready to scale out and scales in only if all are ready; if several policies conflict it uses the one giving the largest capacity. Be cautious mixing target tracking with step scaling on the same target because conflicts can cause flapping.

Disaster recovery implication: in pilot light, the Auto Scaling group in the recovery Region typically exists with minimum capacity zero or very low and is scaled out during failover; in warm standby it runs at reduced size and is scaled to full production size. Remember to confirm that EC2 quotas and capacity in the recovery Region are sufficient for the scaled-out size, and that scaling up the database (a larger instance class, or a Multi-AZ conversion) is part of the runbook if the standby database is smaller than production.

If a question says 'dynamically scale to meet user traffic' and 'highly available', the answer scales out across at least two AZs behind an ALB with Auto Scaling. If a workload is a single database that is hitting memory limits and cannot be sharded, scale up is the answer, but note it does not give HA; pair with Multi-AZ.

Scenario 1: on-premises Windows application, 15-minute RTO, 5-minute RPO. A company runs hundreds of Windows Server VMs on VMware plus a shared file share. Requirements: RTO 15 minutes, RPO 5 minutes, native failover and fallback, minimal re-architecture, existing Direct Connect. Chosen architecture: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery for all servers with the agent installed on each VM, staging subnet using private IP replication over Direct Connect, launch templates sized for production, recovery plans that start domain services and file servers first. The shared file share data is moved to or replicated into Amazon FSx for Windows File Server so it is available when servers launch (the exact replication tool, e.g. DataSync, was not verified against reference docs in this build). Rationale: DRS gives a documented RPO of seconds and a typical RTO of 5 to 20 minutes (which brackets the 15-minute target, so drills must prove it) and has a supported failback path. Security: least-privilege agent role (AWSElasticDisasterRecoveryAgentInstallationPolicy), outbound TCP 443 only, encryption settings reviewed, drill instances isolated. Cost: low compute during steady state (t3.small replication servers, staging EBS), full price only after failover. Alternatives rejected: AMI-based backup and restore (RTO hours), a hand-built replica site (high operational overhead, no orchestrated failback).

Scenario 2: three-tier web application in us-east-1, RDS MySQL, RPO 5 minutes, cost-sensitive. Requirements: survive loss of a Region, RTO under an hour, minimal ongoing cost. Chosen: pilot light in a second Region. A cross-Region RDS read replica (monitored on ReplicaLag with a CloudWatch alarm), AMIs copied to the DR Region, infrastructure defined in CloudFormation so the web and app tiers can be launched on demand, and a Route 53 failover record pair with health checks. On disaster: promote the replica, launch the stacks, scale the Auto Scaling group, and DNS fails over. Rationale: replica lag is typically small enough for a 5-minute RPO but is not guaranteed, hence the alarm; compute cost is near zero until failover. Security: replica encrypted with a KMS key in the DR Region, separate IAM roles. Alternatives rejected: Multi-AZ only (does not survive Region loss), backup and restore (RPO and RTO too long unless PITR plus slow restores are acceptable), warm standby (meets targets but costs more than needed), active/active (excess).

Scenario 3: multi-account organization needs 6-hourly RDS snapshots kept 30 days, with a copy in another Region and tamper protection. Existing: daily RDS automated snapshots with 7-day retention in about forty accounts. Chosen: an AWS Organizations backup policy attached to the OU that creates a plan in every member account (tag-based resource assignment, every 6 hours, 30-day lifecycle, copy rule to a vault in a dedicated backup account in the DR Region), customer managed KMS keys, Vault Lock on the destination vaults, SCPs that deny deleting the vaults and plans, and an EventBridge rule forwarding backup events to a central bus. Rationale: centrally managed, no per-account scripts, satisfies RPO/retention and ransomware or insider scenarios. Cost: storage for 30 days of snapshots in two Regions plus cross-Region transfer; the first copy is full, later ones incremental. Alternatives rejected: modifying each instance's automated backup retention (cannot reach a 6-hour schedule or central control), Lambda cron scripts in each account (operational overhead).

This topic gives console steps, CLI, policy JSON and IaC for the main patterns. Replace placeholders in angle brackets. Command and template syntax shown was cross-checked against AWS pages where noted; run each against current CLI/CloudFormation references before production use, and no command output is shown because none was produced in this build.
A. Elastic Disaster Recovery setup (console)

items: In the target Region open the AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery console and initialize the service; create a dedicated staging area subnet and set it in the default replication settings (replication server type defaults to t3.small).
Decide data routing: enable 'Use private IP for data replication' if you have VPN, Direct Connect or VPC peering, otherwise replication servers need a public subnet.

Create an IAM user or role with the AWSElasticDisasterRecoveryAgentInstallationPolicy managed policy, download the agent installer for the target Region and run it on each source server (Windows or Linux, 64-bit). Ensure outbound TCP 443 to DRS, S3 and EC2 endpoints.
Wait for initial sync; the server must reach Continuous Data Protection before drills and recovery are available.
Edit the EC2 launch template and launch settings (subnet, security groups, instance type) and set PIT retention.
Run a drill, validate the application, then terminate drill instances. Group servers into a recovery plan with ordered steps.
On disaster, launch recovery instances; for failback, start reverse replication (AWS sources) or use the Failback Client/Automation (on-premises), then redirect traffic outside DRS.

blocks.label: CLI (verify syntax)
blocks.body:
# DRS: list source servers and replication state in the target Region (syntax not verified in this build)
aws drs describe-source-servers --region <dr-region>

# RDS cross-Region replica promotion and lag check (promote-read-replica and ReplicaLag metric appear in AWS docs read)
aws rds promote-read-replica --db-instance-identifier <replica-id> --region <dr-region>
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/RDS --metric-name ReplicaLag \
  --start-time <iso-start> --end-time <iso-end> --period 60 --statistics Maximum \
  --dimensions Name=DBInstanceIdentifier,Value=<replica-id> --region <dr-region>
B. AWS Backup: copy and lock

blocks.label: CloudFormation (YAML)
blocks.body:
Resources:
  DrVault:
    Type: AWS::Backup::BackupVault
    Properties:
      BackupVaultName: dr-vault
      EncryptionKeyArn: <cmk-arn-in-this-region>
  Plan:
    Type: AWS::Backup::BackupPlan
    Properties:
      BackupPlan:
        BackupPlanName: tier2-six-hourly
        BackupPlanRule:
          - RuleName: every-6h-keep-30d
            TargetBackupVault: <source-vault-name>
            ScheduleExpression: cron(0 0/6 * * ? *)
            Lifecycle:
              DeleteAfterDays: 30
            CopyActions:
              - DestinationBackupVaultArn: arn:aws:backup:<dr-region>:<dr-account-id>:backup-vault:dr-vault
                Lifecycle:
                  DeleteAfterDays: 30

blocks.label: CLI
blocks.body:
aws backup put-backup-vault-lock-configuration --backup-vault-name dr-vault \
  --min-retention-days 7 --max-retention-days 30 --changeable-for-days 3
# Omitting --changeable-for-days creates a governance-mode lock; including it creates compliance mode
# (3 day minimum cooling-off before the lock becomes immutable).

blocks.label: IAM / vault access policy (JSON)

blocks.body: The vault access policy above lets principals in your organization copy into the destination vault; backup:CopyIntoBackupVault is the action that AWS Backup documents for allowing cross-account copies into a destination vault; AWS Backup also documents account-level, organization-level and role-level variants of this policy. The source side also needs a KMS key policy that allows the destination account when a customer managed key is used.
C. Route 53 active-passive failover

blocks.label: CloudFormation (YAML)
blocks.body:
Resources:
  PrimaryHealthCheck:
    Type: AWS::Route53::HealthCheck
    Properties:
      HealthCheckConfig:
        Type: HTTPS
        FullyQualifiedDomainName: <primary-alb-dns-name>
        ResourcePath: /health
        RequestInterval: 10
        FailureThreshold: 3
  PrimaryRecord:
    Type: AWS::Route53::RecordSet
    Properties:
      HostedZoneId: <hosted-zone-id>
      Name: app.example.com
      Type: A
      SetIdentifier: primary
      Failover: PRIMARY
      HealthCheckId: !Ref PrimaryHealthCheck
      AliasTarget:
        DNSName: <primary-alb-dns-name>
        HostedZoneId: <primary-alb-hosted-zone-id>
        EvaluateTargetHealth: true
  SecondaryRecord:
    Type: AWS::Route53::RecordSet
    Properties:
      HostedZoneId: <hosted-zone-id>
      Name: app.example.com
      Type: A
      SetIdentifier: secondary
      Failover: SECONDARY
      AliasTarget:
        DNSName: <secondary-alb-dns-name>
        HostedZoneId: <secondary-alb-hosted-zone-id>
        EvaluateTargetHealth: true

Per the CloudFormation reference for AWS::Route53::RecordSet: set Failover to PRIMARY on one record and SECONDARY on the other, attach HealthCheckId, and for alias records set EvaluateTargetHealth true. Health check interval (10 or 30 seconds) and failure threshold are tunable; lower values speed detection, and the 10-second (fast) interval carries an additional charge (see Route 53 pricing). The request interval cannot be changed after the health check is created.
D. Verification and troubleshooting

items: DRS: confirm source server status and lag in the console; if initial sync stalls check outbound TCP 443, DNS resolution of the regional DRS endpoint, and that the staging subnet is reachable. For failback from a recovered EC2 instance, ensure instance metadata access and DNS resolution of the DRS endpoint in the failback Region.

RDS replica: watch ReplicaLag before promotion; for MySQL/MariaDB stop writes at the source and wait for lag to reach zero when you need a clean cut-over; test the application connection string change.

AWS Backup cross-account copy fails: check same organization, resource type supports cross-account copy in those Regions, source KMS key policy allows destination, destination vault access policy allows source, and tag policy configuration.

Route 53: query the record from outside (dig or Resolve-DnsName) and force the health check unhealthy in a test (for example by putting the primary target into maintenance or tripping the monitored CloudWatch alarm) to confirm the secondary is returned; remember resolver caching up to the TTL.

Aurora global database: check replication lag metrics before planned switchover (RPO 0 for switchover); after failover reconfigure application endpoints, as the writer endpoint in the new primary Region becomes the active one.

blocks.body: Step 1: find the primary requirement. It is usually one of: meet a specific RTO/RPO, minimize cost, minimize operational overhead, or minimal changes to the existing application. Step 2: list mandatory constraints such as 'Region failure', 'on-premises physical servers', 'must support failback', 'Windows file share', 'retain 30 days', 'managed across accounts'. Step 3: eliminate distractors that miss any constraint, then rank the survivors by the primary requirement.

Avoids custom scripts and hand-built replicas
