items: Distinguish replication from backup: replicas protect availability, backups protect against corruption and deletion.
Distinguish Multi-AZ (HA, synchronous, same Region) from cross-Region replicas (DR, asynchronous).
Distinguish DRS (server replication, drill and failback) from AWS Backup (point-in-time copies) and from AMI copies (backup and restore RTO).
Distinguish Route 53 health-check failover (automatic) from ARC routing controls (deliberate, safe, data-plane controlled).
Distinguish governance vs compliance Vault Lock, and AWS managed vs customer managed KMS keys for cross-account copies.
Distinguish switchover (planned, RPO 0) from failover (unplanned, non-zero RPO) in Aurora global database.
Watch for dated options: CloudEndure-era names and vCenter-appliance failback; hand-built Connect replicas; 'Elastic Disaster Recovery' is the current name.
If every option fails a strict number, choose the one that best meets the objectives and does not violate a hard constraint; stems with aggressive RTOs can still have a 'best available' answer.

blocks.body: A frequent trap is an answer that satisfies RTO with warm standby but uses a smaller database instance than the data requires, or an answer whose replication is asynchronous yet claims zero data loss. Check that the standby can actually hold the workload (for example memory-bound databases) and that the replication mode supports the stated RPO.

items: RTO is time to restore service; RPO is acceptable data-loss window. Strategies in rising cost and falling RTO/RPO: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, active/active.
Failover time for DNS-based designs is TTL plus health check interval times failure threshold.

Elastic Disaster Recovery: agent-based continuous block-level replication into a staging area, RPO of seconds, RTO typically 5 to 20 minutes, drills, recovery plans, Failback Client or reverse replication; TCP 443; 16 TiB per volume and 63 volumes per server; 300 concurrently replicating servers per account (not adjustable).

Multi-AZ RDS: synchronous, RPO 0, same Region, standby not readable. Cross-Region read replica and Aurora global database: asynchronous; Aurora global database up to 10 secondary Regions with lag typically under a second; switchover RPO 0, failover non-zero.
DynamoDB global tables: multi-active, low or zero RPO by shifting traffic; eventual consistency with last-writer-wins unless multi-Region strong consistency is chosen.

AWS Backup: centralized plans, cross-Region and cross-account copies encrypted with the destination vault key; use customer managed keys for cross-account; Vault Lock governance versus compliance (72 hour minimum grace); organization backup policies for multi-account.
RDS automated backups: 1 to 35 days, restore to any second up to last 5 minutes, new instance on restore.
S3: CRR is asynchronous; RTC targets 99.99 percent of objects within 15 minutes with an SLA on 99.9 percent.
Route 53 failover returns the primary if both records are unhealthy; ARC routing controls give safe, data-plane failover with safety rules.
Auto Scaling replaces unhealthy instances (enable ELB health checks); EC2 auto recovery fixes host problems for supported instance types but loses RAM and cannot fix instance status check failures.
Scale out for HA and elasticity; scale up for non-shardable single nodes, with downtime and no HA improvement.

blocks.title: Misconceptions to avoid
blocks.body: Multi-AZ is not DR for a Region. A read replica is not a backup. Cross-Region replication is not zero RPO. Backups in the same account are not safe from account compromise. Auto recovery is not high availability. A DR plan that has not been drilled is not a plan.

rows: Per account and Region (and per staging account); not adjustable
DRS source servers per recovery job / active jobs / concurrent jobs
Per account and Region; not adjustable
1,000 per account per Region; 20 steps; 100 servers; 1 concurrent execution
16 TiB per volume, 63 volumes per server
Per source server; volumes beyond are not replicated

items: Takeaways: start from RTO/RPO, pick the cheapest strategy that meets both, protect data with backups as well as replicas, automate recovery, and drill it.

blocks.body: This lesson covers SAP-C02 Task 1.4: designing a multi-account AWS environment. Domain 1 (Design Solutions for Organizational Complexity) accounts for 26% of scored content in the SAP-C02 exam guide, second to Domain 2 (29%). Prerequisites: IAM policy evaluation (identity policies, resource policies, explicit deny), basic VPC and Transit Gateway concepts, CloudTrail and CloudWatch Logs basics, and CloudFormation.

A multi-account design uses the AWS account as the hard boundary for permissions, billing, and blast radius, then adds central governance on top. Three pillars are tested: (1) AWS Organizations and AWS Control Tower for account structure and guardrails, (2) multi-account event notification and logging, and (3) resource sharing across accounts (AWS RAM, Service Catalog, AWS Backup).

blocks.title: Objectives
blocks.body: You will be able to: (1) choose an OU and account structure from requirements; (2) predict the effective permissions of a principal under SCPs, IAM policies and resource policies, including the management-account exception; (3) pick between SCPs, RCPs, declarative policies, tag policies and Control Tower controls; (4) design central logging and event routing with organization trails, CloudWatch Logs destinations, EventBridge buses and Config aggregators; (5) share VPC subnets and other resources with AWS RAM and know what participants can and cannot do; (6) automate account baselines with StackSets, Account Factory customization and Service Quotas templates.

items: Services and patterns: Organizations, SCP/RCP/declarative/tag/backup policies, Control Tower, IAM Identity Center (access), CloudTrail organization trails, CloudWatch Logs cross-account subscriptions, EventBridge cross-account buses, AWS Config aggregators, AWS RAM, Service Catalog, AWS Backup, StackSets, Service Quotas, Firewall Manager.
Why it matters: the question bank maps roughly eighty items to this lesson, mostly SCP semantics, Control Tower controls, central logging, RAM sharing and account-onboarding automation.

blocks.body: AWS Organizations groups accounts under a single root, optionally in organizational units (OUs). The management account pays for all accounts (consolidated billing) and administers the organization. Member accounts are either created through Organizations or invited. Organizations can run with consolidated billing features only or with all features; organization policies such as SCPs require all features to be enabled.

rows: An organization with only consolidated billing features cannot use advanced features such as organization policies; enabling all features sends a handshake to every invited account, and each must approve. Created accounts need no approval.
Organizations automatically creates `OrganizationAccountAccessRole` with full administrator permissions, trusting the management account.
No role is created automatically; you create it manually, ideally with the same name `OrganizationAccountAccessRole`.
A created account must exist for at least 4 days before it can be removed from the organization.
Keep workloads out of the management account because SCPs do not restrict its users or roles; delegate service administration to member accounts.
Per organization (Organizations is a global service hosted in us-east-1; use us-east-1 in Service Quotas)
10 by default; increases up to 50,000 can be granted based on qualifications and requirements (new accounts and organizations might see a lower quota)
Yes, request from the management account
Not specified on the quotas page
Not specified on the quotas page
5 levels of OUs under the root
Not specified on the quotas page

blocks.body: An invitation counts against the account quota even if declined, canceled, or expired, and a closed account keeps counting until it is permanently closed.

Design guidance: base OUs on function or a common set of controls rather than on your reporting chart. AWS recommends foundational Security and Infrastructure OUs, with Prod and SDLC nested OUs where policies differ, and attaching policies at OUs rather than individual accounts for easier troubleshooting. Separate accounts per business unit or workload give isolation, a minimal blast radius, and per-team billing; consolidated billing still yields one invoice with per-account breakdown.

Delegated administrators let a member account administer an integrated service (for example StackSets, Config, Firewall Manager, Identity Center) for the whole organization. Before registering a delegated administrator, confirm that the service supports delegation and enable trusted access for that service.

Moving accounts: to bring an existing company's account into your organization, send an invitation from the management account and have the account accept it. For moving many accounts between organizations, current guidance reportedly allows migrating directly without first making the accounts standalone; this has not been confirmed against AWS documentation.

items: Common mistake: assuming an invited account gets `OrganizationAccountAccessRole`. It does not; create it.
Common mistake: putting shared tooling or workloads in the management account, where SCPs cannot protect them.
Best practice: one account per workload/environment, centralized security and log-archive accounts, SCPs on OUs.

blocks.body: If the stem says 'access a newly created member account', the answer is assuming `OrganizationAccountAccessRole` from the management account, not signing in as the new account's root user. For an invited account, the role must be created first.

links.label: Accessing a member account with OrganizationAccountAccessRole
Creating the role in an invited account

topics.title: SCPs and other organization policy types

blocks.body: A service control policy (SCP) defines the maximum permissions for IAM users and roles in member accounts. An SCP never grants permissions. Effective permissions are the intersection of what the SCPs allow, what the IAM identity policies allow and what any resource policies allow.

items: SCPs affect only IAM principals in member accounts, including a member account's root user. They have no effect on the management account or on service-linked roles, and they do not directly affect resource-based policies or principals from outside the organization.
An account has only the permissions permitted by every parent: a block at the root, OU or account level (implicit or explicit) cannot be undone lower down, even with AdministratorAccess.
SCPs also apply to member accounts that are delegated administrators.
Users still need IAM permission policies; an SCP allowing everything gives no access by itself.
Every root, OU and account must keep at least one SCP attached while SCPs are enabled.

rows: Keep the default `FullAWSAccess` SCP attached everywhere and add explicit Deny SCPs
Simplest; explicit Deny overrides every Allow; new services stay allowed
Detach `FullAWSAccess` and attach SCPs that Allow only listed services
Attach the replacement SCP before detaching FullAWSAccess; new services stay blocked until explicitly allowed
10,240 characters (whitespace counts when you save through the CLI or an SDK; the console removes extra white space between JSON elements)
SCPs you can define in an organization

10 per root, OU, or account (hard limit; only directly attached SCPs count, not inherited ones), per the Organizations quotas page. An older Knowledge Center article that states five conflicts with the quotas page.

blocks.body: Other policy types: Resource control policies (RCPs) set maximum permissions on resources (for example Amazon S3 buckets, AWS KMS keys, Amazon SQS queues, AWS Secrets Manager secrets, AWS STS, Amazon ECR, and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless) and are used for data perimeters such as 'only principals from my organization'; they also grant nothing and, like SCPs, do not affect resources in the management account. Each RCP document is limited to 5,120 characters. Declarative policies enforce a service configuration in the service control plane (for example the EC2 Allowed Images setting, which has an audit mode) and, unlike SCPs and RCPs, also govern service-linked roles. Tag policies standardize tag keys and values; backup policies manage AWS Backup plans organization-wide.

rows: Block principals from an action or Region
Ensure only org principals can reach buckets/keys/queues
Force a service setting such as allowed AMI publishers
Durable even when new APIs appear
Reporting by default; enforcement only for supported resource types via `enforced_for`
Require a tag at launch (deny if missing)
Tag policies alone do not block untagged creation

blocks.body: Tag policy reality check: reporting mode evaluates compliance, but the report includes only resources that have had at least one user-defined tag at any point in their lifecycle, so untagged resources do not appear as noncompliant. The `report_required_tag_for` field marks required keys for reports and CloudFormation validation. To find untagged resources use Resource Explorer. Preventing creation without a tag therefore needs an SCP (deny when the request tag is absent), possibly paired with an OU-specific tag policy for allowed values.

Region restriction is the classic SCP: deny when `aws:RequestedRegion` is not in the approved list, with a NotAction exemption for global services such as IAM and Organizations. Control Tower provides the same capability through its Region deny controls.
Data residency note: an SCP prevents resource creation or API calls outside approved Regions, but routing mechanisms such as Route 53 geolocation only steer traffic and do not enforce residency.

blocks.title: Management account exception
blocks.body: Questions that require an SCP to restrict the management account (the account that created the organization) are traps. Move the workload or principal to a member account, or accept that the management account cannot be constrained.

'Least operational overhead' with hundreds of accounts: attach one SCP to an OU or the root rather than per-account IAM changes. 'Prevent' needs SCP/RCP/declarative; 'detect' or 'report' means Config rules, tag policy reports or Control Tower detective controls.

Control Tower orchestrates Organizations, CloudFormation StackSets, IAM Identity Center, AWS Config and CloudTrail into a landing zone: a governed multi-account baseline. It creates two shared accounts alongside the management account: Log Archive (central store of CloudTrail and Config logs) and Audit (access for security and compliance teams). You may reuse existing security and logging accounts at initial setup; existing AWS Config recorders, delivery channels, or aggregation setups in accounts you enroll must be modified or removed before enrollment.

The landing zone creates an organization-level CloudTrail trail that logs the management account and all member accounts (it relies on trusted access). Enrolling an account that already has its own trail can produce duplicate charges unless you delete the old trail.

rows: Do not affect the management account; supported in all Regions
Only in Control Tower supported Regions; detect, do not block

blocks.body: Control behavior (preventive/detective/proactive) is independent of guidance (mandatory, strongly recommended, elective). The console and docs now say 'controls'; older material and exam stems say 'guardrails'.

Region deny: `AWS-GR_REGION_DENY` applies to the whole landing zone (set in Landing zone settings, applies to OUs with `AWSControlTowerBaseline`, cannot be configured per OU, cannot deny the home Region, global services such as IAM and Organizations are exempt). `CT.MULTISERVICE.PV.1` applies per OU and must always include the home Region. Warning: enabling a Region deny control blocks access to resources in denied Regions, and the two controls can conflict.

Account Factory provisions accounts. Account Factory Customization (AFC) applies blueprints (CloudFormation templates published as Service Catalog products in a hub account) when you create, enroll or update an account; Control Tower creates a role in the member account for CloudFormation to assume; an allow-all policy is simplest and works with any blueprint, but best practice is to supply a narrower custom policy. OUs must have `AWSControlTowerBaseline` enabled. Customizations beyond this (pipelines, custom SCP sets) are covered by the separate Customizations for AWS Control Tower solution, which is not covered by the documentation reviewed for this lesson.

items: Use Control Tower when you want an opinionated, managed landing zone with a dashboard and built-in controls; use plain Organizations plus StackSets when you need a bespoke structure and accept more operational work.
Control Tower does not create custom controls inside the service; custom SCPs are applied through Organizations (not verified against AWS documentation).
Identity: Control Tower integrates with IAM Identity Center for workforce access; the external IdP choice (for example an SAML 2.0 IdP) is configured in Identity Center.

blocks.body: A stem asking for 'built-in blueprints and guardrails' for production accounts only points to Control Tower with controls enabled on the production OU, not on the landing zone as a whole.

links.label: Best practices for Control Tower administrators

topics.title: Multi-account events, logging and compliance data

blocks.body: Central logging separates the people who generate logs from the people who can alter them. Pattern: workload accounts emit, a dedicated log-archive account stores, a security account analyzes.

rows: CloudTrail organization trail created in the management account (or a delegated administrator)
Applied automatically to all member accounts and Regions chosen; members can see it but cannot modify or delete it; by default members cannot read the log bucket
Application/VPC/CloudTrail logs near real time to one account
CloudWatch Logs subscription filter to a cross-account destination (Kinesis Data Streams or Firehose)

Recipient creates a destination (name, target ARN, role ARN, access policy); log group and destination must be in the same Region, target may be in another Region; an organization can be named as sender, but each sender account still creates its own subscription filter
EventBridge rule targeting a bus in another account

Receiver bus resource policy allows accounts or an organization (`aws:PrincipalOrgID`); sender needs an IAM role when permission comes from an organization; sending account is charged custom-event rates
AWS Config aggregator (organization aggregator, can run from a delegated administrator)
Collects configuration and compliance only, read-only view; rules still evaluate in each account

blocks.body: Granting member accounts access to the central CloudTrail bucket: the preferred approach is a short bucket policy scoped to accounts, which scales without per-account edits; per-account roles are heavy, and ACLs are legacy. If the logs use SSE-KMS, use a customer managed key and grant `kms:Decrypt`, because the key policy of an AWS managed key such as `aws/s3` cannot be edited to allow cross-account access.

Plan log destinations by Region: if logs must remain in the Region of creation, create a destination and stream in each Region of the central account. Kinesis-based destinations suit near-real-time analytics; the documentation describes the same pattern with Firehose delivering to S3.

Analytics storage: CloudTrail Lake can query organization events with SQL, but it has not been open to new customers since 31 May 2026 (existing customers continue). A design today should consider Athena over the organization-trail S3 data or CloudWatch-based alternatives.
Older exam stems may refer to Amazon Elasticsearch Service, which is now Amazon OpenSearch Service.

items: EventBridge pattern: for security events such as an EC2 security group change, each account forwards matching events to a central bus, then a rule fans out to SNS.

Preventive versus detective: Config and EventBridge detect and notify; auto-remediation reacts after the fact. Only preventive controls (SCPs, RCPs, declarative policies, and IAM or resource policies) stop an action before it happens.
Config rules and conformance packs can be deployed organization-wide so member accounts cannot edit them (reference: Config and Organizations page).

blocks.body: 'Near-real-time, all accounts, central analysis' means CloudWatch Logs subscription to Kinesis/Firehose in the logging account. 'Audit all API calls, tamper-resistant, new accounts included' means an organization trail.

AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) shares resources you own with accounts, OUs, an entire organization and, for some types, individual IAM roles and users. It can share resources that have no resource-based policy, such as VPC subnets and Route 53 Resolver rules. In an organization, enable sharing with AWS Organizations from the management account (RAM Settings) first; shares to an organization or OU need no invitation acceptance, whereas shares to outside accounts require accepting an invitation.

A resource share contains resources, principals and one managed permission per resource type. AWS managed permissions exist for every type; customer managed permissions (Region specific) offer least privilege where supported. Scope shares to the minimum set of OUs or accounts.

rows: Owner shares subnets; subnets in a default VPC cannot be shared
Transit gateways, Route 53 Resolver rules, prefix lists
Prefix lists let many accounts reuse one CIDR allow list
Principals are an organization or account; organization shares skip acceptance; certificates are issued in the consumer account
Needs customer managed KMS key for services without full AWS Backup management
S3 Access Grants or resource policies
Cross-account Access Grants use an instance resource policy in the docs reviewed, not RAM

blocks.body: VPC sharing details. The VPC owner shares subnets with participants. Participants can view, create, modify and delete their own resources in shared subnets (for example EC2, RDS, Redshift, Lambda) but not those of others or the owner. Participants cannot create, attach or delete internet gateways, NAT gateways or route tables, cannot create or replace NACLs, and cannot use the VPC default security group (it belongs to the owner); security groups are controlled separately in each account. The owner can describe participant network interfaces but cannot modify them. Use it when applications sit in one trust boundary and need implicit routing; use PrivateLink, transit gateway or peering to connect shared subnets to others.

Typical design: a Network account owns the VPC and Transit Gateway, shares subnets with the organization, and workload accounts deploy their own resources, such as databases, in the same subnets. This decouples network administration from application teams while keeping separate billing and access.

Service Catalog launch constraints: the product launches with an IAM role that Service Catalog assumes, so end users need only Service Catalog access, not CloudFormation or service permissions. Constraints attach per product within a portfolio, not to the portfolio as a whole. Pair with a share of the portfolio to the organization and a StackSet that deploys the launch role to every account.

AWS Backup: copies are encrypted with the destination vault key. Cross-account copy of resources not fully managed by AWS Backup (for example RDS, EBS) cannot use AWS managed keys because their key policy is immutable; encrypt with a customer managed key and share it, and use a vault with a customer managed key (the default vault uses an AWS managed key). The destination account uses the service-linked role `AWSServiceRoleForBackup`. Ransomware-resilience patterns add Vault Lock and organization backup policies; Vault Lock details are not covered by the documentation reviewed for this lesson.

blocks.body: CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions deploy a template to every account in an organization or chosen OUs. CloudFormation creates the required IAM roles on your behalf, so you do not create them in each target account. Prerequisites: Organizations with all features and trusted access. The exact capability name has not been verified against a retrieved page (listed as unverified).

A Service Quotas request template can include up to 10 quotas; once template association is enabled, it automatically requests those increases for newly created accounts. Constraints: organization must have all features; commercial Regions only; opt-in Regions and China Regions unsupported; changing the template does not affect existing accounts; only for adjustable quotas.

blocks.title: Scenario 2: Central network and logging after an acquisition
blocks.body: Requirements: unify an acquired account, share one VPC and on-premises connectivity, centralize logs. Design: invite the acquired account, create `OrganizationAccountAccessRole` in it, move it to the right OU under SCPs. Network account owns the VPC and Transit Gateway and shares subnets via RAM to the organization. An organization trail writes to a log-archive bucket; CloudWatch Logs destinations (Kinesis) in a security account receive application logs; an organization Config aggregator in a delegated administrator gives compliance view. Rationale: separation of duties, one invoice. Rejected: VPC peering mesh (operational overhead), per-account trails (members could alter them), sharing log bucket via ACLs.

blocks.title: Scenario 3: Immutable backups in an isolated account
blocks.body: Requirements: 40 RDS databases encrypted with the default aws/rds key in production must be copied to a write-once backup account. Design: re-encrypt with a customer managed key (snapshot copy with new key), share the key with the backup account, create a destination vault with a customer managed key in the isolated account, run cross-account copy via a backup plan, and enable Vault Lock there. Rationale: AWS managed key policies are immutable so cannot be shared. Rejected: sharing the default key; copying into the default vault.

This lesson covers SAP-C02 Task 1.5, determining cost optimization and visibility strategies for organizations that run many AWS accounts. It splits into three skills: monitoring cost and usage with AWS tools, building a tagging strategy that maps spend to business units, and understanding how purchasing options change both cost and performance. Domain 1 (Design Solutions for Organizational Complexity) is one of the heaviest domains on the exam, and cost questions in it are usually multi-account questions: who can see what, who pays, and which control stops overspend.

Prerequisites: AWS Organizations basics (management account, member accounts, OUs, all features versus consolidated billing only), IAM roles and policies, and a working idea of EC2, Fargate, Lambda, S3 and NAT gateways as cost drivers. Jargon used throughout: the payer or management account is the account that receives the consolidated bill; a cost allocation tag is a tag you activate in Billing so that it appears in cost reports; an hourly commitment is the dollars-per-hour you promise to spend under a Savings Plan.
Objectives. You will be able to:

items: Choose between AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR) or AWS Data Exports with Amazon Athena and Amazon QuickSight, AWS Budgets, AWS Cost Anomaly Detection, and the AWS Pricing Calculator for a stated visibility requirement.
Design a tagging strategy: user-defined tags, AWS-generated tags, account tags, Cost Categories, tag policies and SCP enforcement, and explain why activation in the management account is required.
Select among On-Demand, Reserved Instances, Compute, EC2 Instance and other Savings Plans, and Spot, and explain how each behaves across a consolidated billing family.
Control sharing of RI and Savings Plans discounts per account, and place commitments in the right account.
Use Compute Optimizer, Trusted Advisor and S3 Storage Lens to find rightsizing and storage-class savings, including their data-retention and support-plan limits.
Allocate shared container and network costs (ECS split cost allocation data, ECS managed tags, centralized NAT egress) and apply Budgets actions and Athena workgroup limits as guardrails.

topics.title: Cost Explorer, CUR and billing access

blocks.body: Cost Explorer is the interactive analysis tool in the Billing and Cost Management console. You enable it by opening it for the first time in the console; it cannot be enabled through the API. After enabling, AWS prepares data for the current month and the previous months and forecasts the next 12 months; current-month data appears in about 24 hours and the rest takes a few days, and data is refreshed at least once every 24 hours. Enabling Cost Explorer also sets up Cost Anomaly Detection with an AWS services monitor and a daily summary subscription. Cost Explorer API requests are charged $0.01 per request, and each page of a paginated result counts as a separate request.

By default Cost Explorer shows daily and monthly granularity. From the management account, Cost Management preferences let you turn on multi-year data at monthly granularity (up to 38 months, with data beyond the first 14 months monthly only), hourly data for all services, EC2 resource-level hourly data, and daily resource-level data for selected services (hourly and resource-level data cover the last 14 days). Changes can take up to 48 hours to apply and you cannot change the preferences again for 48 hours.

Cost and Usage Reports (CUR), and its successor CUR 2.0 delivered through Data Exports, are the most detailed billing dataset: line items with resource IDs and tags, delivered to S3, queryable with Athena and visualized with QuickSight. AWS Organizations behavior matters: a CUR created in the management account contains cost and usage for the management account and all member accounts; a CUR created in a member account contains only that account's data, from the time it joined the current organization. After a member account leaves the organization, it can still read earlier reports if it has permissions to the S3 bucket.

blocks.body: Access to billing data takes two steps. First, member-account visibility into Cost Explorer is controlled from the management account: activating at the management level grants access to all member accounts, and individual member accounts cannot be selected. Second, IAM users and roles reach the Billing console only if the account's Activate IAM Access setting is on and they have IAM permissions; that setting is off by default. The Activate IAM Access setting does not control the Cost Explorer, Budgets and CUR SDK APIs, which are governed by their own IAM permissions. Member-account owners cannot see other accounts' Cost Explorer data.

blocks.title: Management account is not a skeleton key
blocks.body: Being the management (payer) account gives billing and policy control, not implicit access to resources inside member accounts. Reaching resources in a member account still requires role assumption through a trust policy, for example the OrganizationAccountAccessRole that Organizations creates, or another cross-account role you define. Billing visibility and resource access are separate permissions.

Common mistakes: expecting a member-account CUR to include the whole organization; forgetting to enable IAM access to billing; assuming Cost Explorer data exists before it is enabled; and using account-level CUR when the requirement is one organization-wide report (create it in the management account). Terminology note: older material says master account; the current term is management account.

Org-wide, detailed, long-retention, custom grouping means CUR (or Data Exports) in the management account with Athena and QuickSight. A single quick chart with forecast means Cost Explorer. Per-OU views need a way to map accounts to OUs, typically a Cost Category, account tag, or an account list filter; the raw CUR has account IDs, not OU names.

blocks.body: Cost allocation on AWS is a three-step process: attach tags to resources, activate them as cost allocation tags in the Billing console, then use them to filter and group in Cost Explorer, Budgets and CUR. A tag that is never activated does not appear in cost reports. After you create user-defined tags it can take up to 24 hours for the keys to show on the Cost allocation tags page, and up to another 24 hours to activate. In an organization, tags are activated in the management (payer) account, not in member accounts.

blocks.body: Backfill: a backfill tags request lets you retroactively view costs for tags from a previous month, applying the tag's current active status to that month. You can submit one request every 24 hours once the previous request completes. Without backfill, a newly activated tag shows costs only from activation forward.

AWS Cost Categories group costs into business-meaningful values using rules over dimensions such as linked account, service, region, charge type, cost allocation tags and other cost categories. Rules are evaluated in order, and the first match wins; an optional default value catches the remainder. Only active cost allocation tags are visible in rules. Changes can be applied retroactively for up to a year in Cost Explorer and Budgets, but CUR data must be backfilled (a support case is needed). Cost Categories can group accounts so that, for instance, Savings Plans can be purchased at group level.

Enforcement. Tagging only works if it is consistent, and the preventive controls split in two. Tag policies (an Organizations policy type, requiring all features) standardize tag keys, capitalization and allowed values; with enforcement on, noncompliant tagging operations on supported resource types are blocked. But tag policies do not evaluate untagged resources or tags not in the policy, so they cannot make a tag mandatory. To require a tag at creation, use an SCP that denies the create action when `aws:RequestTag/<key>` is null. Compliance reporting for tag policies is viewed through Resource Groups, organization-wide from the management account.

items: Standardize a small set of keys (for example CostCenter, BusinessUnit, Application, Environment) and enforce values with a tag policy.

Add an SCP that denies resource creation when the required request tag is missing, and test per service: tag-based conditions are supported only for some actions and resources (check ABAC support for the service).
Activate the keys in the management account and, if history matters, run backfill.
Use Cost Categories to roll up keys and accounts into business units, and Cost Anomaly Detection monitors keyed to the same tag or category.
Use account-level tags when the account maps cleanly to a team; they cost nothing to maintain per resource.

blocks.title: Tag policy versus SCP
blocks.body: Tag policy: what a tag may look like (keys, case, values). SCP: whether the action is allowed at all without the tag. Mandatory tags need the SCP. Standardized values need the tag policy. Exam answers that combine both are usually right; answers that rely on the tag policy alone for mandatory tags are not.

Common mistakes: activating tags in a member account and wondering why the organization report lacks them; expecting past months to populate automatically; relying on AWS-generated tags in unsupported Regions; and building rules in Cost Categories on tags that were never activated. Data that has no tag (some shared and untagged charges) stays in an untagged bucket, so pair tags with account structure.
Words to watch: activated from the management account, backfill, enforce mandatory tags at creation (SCP), consistent values (tag policy), group by business unit (Cost Categories).

topics.title: Budgets, anomaly detection and spend guardrails

blocks.body: AWS Budgets tracks cost, usage, and Reserved Instance or Savings Plans utilization and coverage against targets. Budget types include cost budgets, usage budgets, and Reserved Instance (RI) and Savings Plans utilization and coverage budgets. Budgets data is refreshed up to three times a day (typically 8 to 12 hours apart). Budgets can use blended, unblended, net unblended, amortized or net amortized costs, and can include or exclude credits, refunds, support fees and taxes. Monitoring and notifications are free; the first two action-enabled budgets per month are free, and each additional action-enabled budget incurs a $0.10 daily charge.

Can fire more than once in a period; need about 5 weeks of usage history

Apply an IAM policy, apply an SCP, or target EC2/RDS instances; automatic or with approval; need a notification recipient; the multi-account guidance describes them for monthly, quarterly or annual budgets
Service, Region, tag, Cost Category, linked account

blocks.body: In an organization, create the budget in the management account and filter by linked account, tag, or Cost Category to scope it to an OU or business unit; a member account can also set its own budget. Billing views allow decentralized budget management without access to the management account. A budget action that attaches a restrictive SCP to an OU affects every account in it, so AWS guidance is to create separate budgets for individual linked accounts or group accounts of one OU through filters; the SCP is detached automatically at the start of the next budget period if not reversed manually.

Notify or enforce? A threshold with an email or SNS alert only informs. To stop spend, use a Budgets action (apply a deny-style IAM policy or SCP, or stop targeted instances) or an alert wired to Lambda or Systems Manager. Budgets are driven by billing data that lags, so they limit but do not hard-cap spend.

AWS Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to flag unusual spend. Monitors can be built on four dimensions: AWS services, linked accounts, cost categories and cost allocation tags. AWS managed monitors track up to the top 5,000 values of a dimension each on their own; customer managed monitors evaluate chosen values in aggregate (up to 10 accounts or tag values). Linked-account managed monitors are available only in the management account. Use Budgets for known limits and Anomaly Detection for unknown spikes.

Service-specific guardrails: Amazon Athena workgroups can carry data usage controls. A per-query limit cancels any query that scans more than the limit (you pay for what was scanned up to cancellation); a workgroup-wide limit sums data scanned over an hourly or daily period and can trigger an SNS notification, a Lambda function, or disabling the workgroup. The two limits are independent. A workgroup has one per-query limit and may have several workgroup limits. A per-query cap alone does not bound a month's total, so to translate a budget into a ceiling you need the periodic workgroup limit with a disable action. Up to 1000 workgroups per Region per account can be created, and a disabled workgroup runs no queries until re-enabled.

Notify only: Budgets alert (SNS or email). Stop: Budgets action or an automated response. Unknown spike: Anomaly Detection. Query scan cost: Athena workgroup limits. Daily budget with 80 percent alert: actual-spend alert only, since daily budgets lack forecasts.

topics.title: Purchasing options: On-Demand, Reserved Instances, Savings Plans, Spot

blocks.body: AWS separates how you pay for compute (purchasing options) from whether capacity is held for you (Capacity Reservations). The two are independent and are often layered: a Capacity Reservation is billed at the On-Demand rate whether or not it is used, and can then be discounted with a Savings Plan or a Regional Reserved Instance. Exam options frequently confuse the two.

rows: None; pay per use (per-second billing for Linux, RHEL, Windows)

blocks.body: Reserved Instances are a billing discount, not a running instance: any matching On-Demand usage is charged at the RI rate, and you receive no discount until a matching instance runs. Scope matters. A Regional RI discounts matching usage anywhere in the Region (and does not reserve capacity); a zonal RI reserves capacity in one Availability Zone and discounts usage there. Standard RIs cannot be exchanged, so they lock you to a configuration; Convertible RIs trade discount depth for the ability to change.

Savings Plans commit you to a dollars-per-hour amount (the commitment is expressed at the Savings Plans rate, not the On-Demand price). Payment options are No Upfront, Partial Upfront (at least half up front) and All Upfront, which has the lowest price. Unused hourly commitment does not roll over; utilization is the percentage of the commitment you consume each hour. Compute Savings Plans cover EC2, Fargate and Lambda automatically, and let you move a workload between instance families, Regions, or from EC2 to Fargate without losing the discount. Recommendations in Cost Explorer use a 7-, 30- or 60-day lookback of past usage; they do not forecast, and are generated when average On-Demand spend is at least $0.10 per hour. Purchase Analyzer lets you test a custom commitment against history.

Spot Instances are spare capacity. An interruption notice arrives two minutes before reclaim as an EventBridge event and instance metadata item; a rebalance recommendation signals elevated risk earlier. Architect for it: stateless or checkpointed work, diversified instance types and AZs, Auto Scaling Capacity Rebalancing. For time-flexible workloads, Spot can stop or hibernate instead of terminating.

items: Steady baseline: commit (Savings Plans first, RIs where you need a zonal capacity reservation or need a service that Savings Plans do not cover).
Variable layer: On-Demand, optionally Spot for interruptible parts.
Unknown future shape: prefer the more flexible commitment (Compute Savings Plan or Convertible RI) and accept a lower discount.
Commit to what you are sure of, using Purchase Analyzer or recommendations, not to peak usage.

blocks.title: Performance versus cost
blocks.body: Pricing models do not change instance performance; Spot adds interruption risk, zonal RIs and Capacity Reservations add capacity assurance, and Savings Plans or Regional RIs add neither. If the requirement is guaranteed capacity, a discount-only option does not satisfy it.

Mixed EC2 + Fargate + Lambda, unpredictable per-account demand, 3 years: Compute Savings Plan. One instance family in one Region, maximum discount, no change expected: EC2 Instance Savings Plan or Standard RI. Instance family expected to change but you want an RI: Convertible RI. Fault tolerant batch: Spot. Expired Standard RIs cannot be exchanged to renew; you buy new commitments.

links.label: Choosing a purchasing option for Amazon EC2

blocks.body: In a consolidated billing family, commitments are pooled by default. Savings Plans can be purchased in any account of the family, and by default the benefit applies to usage across all accounts. Order of application: first to usage in the purchasing account, then any unused hourly commitment flows to other accounts that have sharing turned on, applied to the usage with the largest calculated savings. At least one account in the family needs eligible usage for the plan type for the benefit to apply.

Reserved Instances behave the same way. The account that bought the RI receives the discount first; if it has no matching instance, the discount goes to matching usage in another account. The RI discount continues to apply for the full term even if the purchasing member account is closed, but not if that account leaves or is removed from the organization.

Sharing preference. The management account can turn off RI and Savings Plans discount sharing for individual member accounts in Billing preferences. When sharing is off for an account, its RIs and Savings Plans apply only to its own usage, and it also receives no discount from commitments bought elsewhere; its charges still roll up to the consolidated bill paid by the management account. Turning sharing off can raise the organization's bill because unused commitment in one account can no longer cover usage in another. The console shows Reserved Instances and Savings Plans sharing in one preference, with an option to default new member accounts to sharing and to download the preference history.

rows: Keep sharing on; buy at the management account or a central cloud-finance account
Keep a business unit's commitments and discounts separate (for example HR must not benefit from, or fund, other departments)
Deactivate sharing for that account (and for the others it should be isolated from); accept that it loses others' discounts
Restrict or prioritize Savings Plans benefits by group
Group accounts with Cost Categories and buy at group level (Savings Plans FAQ)
Management-account recommendations consider usage of all accounts with sharing enabled; member-account recommendations consider only that account

blocks.title: Where to buy
blocks.body: Buying in the management account (or one central account) pools demand and gives the best utilization; AWS notes Convertible RIs are easier to modify when bought in the payer account. Buying in each member account fragments commitments and risks wasted hours, unless isolation is a requirement.

Recommendations and reporting. Recommendations at the management-account level are computed from the combined usage of accounts that have sharing enabled, so changing sharing preferences changes the numbers. Use the Savings Plans utilization and coverage reports, and Budgets for utilization or coverage thresholds (for example alert when utilization falls below 80 percent for a day) to catch under-use early. Capacity Reservations can be shared within an organization at no additional cost.

Common mistakes: believing that sharing off for an account only stops others from using its commitment (it also stops it receiving others'); assuming an RI purchased by an account that later leaves the organization keeps discounting the family; and sizing a Savings Plan to peak instead of steady baseline.

Business unit wants no cross-subsidy: sharing preferences per account. Company wants maximum savings and simple management: purchase centrally, sharing on. Keep in mind the management account can change preferences, member accounts cannot.

topics.title: Rightsizing visibility: Compute Optimizer, Trusted Advisor, Storage Lens

blocks.body: AWS Compute Optimizer uses machine learning on historical utilization metrics to recommend better configurations. It supports EC2 instances, EC2 Auto Scaling groups, EBS volumes, Lambda functions (memory size), ECS services on Fargate, commercial software licenses (SQL Server on EC2), Aurora and RDS databases, and idle-resource recommendations for NAT gateways, DynamoDB provisioned tables, ElastiCache and others. By default EC2 analysis looks at the past 14 days of CloudWatch metrics; the paid enhanced infrastructure metrics preference extends the lookback to up to 93 days, for EC2 instances, Auto Scaling group instances and RDS DB instances, and can be activated at resource, account or organization level. You must opt in (including organization-wide from the management account) before recommendations appear.

AWS Trusted Advisor runs automated checks in cost optimization, security, performance, fault tolerance, service quotas and more. Core security checks and service quota checks are available to all accounts; the full set of checks, including cost optimization, requires Business or Enterprise Support. Trusted Advisor flags service quotas when usage reaches 80 percent or more of the quota. An Organizational View (for Business and Enterprise Support customers) gives a consolidated report of recommendations for all accounts in the organization, in JSON or CSV. Trusted Advisor's former service limits checks are now called service quotas, and Service Quotas with CloudWatch alarms is another way to track utilization.

Amazon S3 Storage Lens provides organization-wide storage visibility. It has two tiers. Free metrics: 62 metrics at bucket level, collected daily, queryable for 14 days. Advanced metrics and recommendations: additional metrics (activity, detailed status codes, advanced cost optimization and data protection), prefix aggregation, CloudWatch publishing, Storage Lens groups, with 15 months of queryable data; additional charges apply. Metrics can take up to 48 hours to appear after creating a dashboard. Prefix-level metrics are not published to CloudWatch, and Storage Lens groups expose only free-tier metrics.

topics.title: Allocating shared container and network costs

blocks.body: Some of the largest cost-allocation gaps are shared infrastructure. Two patterns recur: containers sharing compute, and many VPCs each running NAT gateways.

ECS on EC2: the EC2 bill is for instances, not tasks. Split Cost Allocation Data adds task-level CPU and memory cost to the CUR (and CUR 2.0) so shared instances can be apportioned to business groups using tags and Cost Categories. You opt in from the Cost Management preferences in the payer or regular account, then enable 'split cost allocation data' on a new or existing report; only regular and payer accounts can opt in, member accounts then see the data in CUR, and data can take up to 24 hours to appear. It is not available in Cost Explorer. For ECS on EC2 the agent must send metrics (ECS_DISABLE_METRICS=false; this is the default on Linux and true by default on Windows) and Docker v20.10.13 or later is recommended for reliable metrics. Allocation uses the task's resource usage or reservation, and the remaining unused instance capacity is also allocated.

ECS on Fargate: tag at the task level. With ECS managed tags enabled (enableECSManagedTags) ECS tags new tasks with cluster information and the task definition or service tags, and also tags EBS volumes attached to tasks; the propagate-tags setting is not on by default and must be set to copy tags from the task definition or service to the task. Tags then need to be activated as cost allocation tags in the management account. For one-off tasks, pass `--tags` and `--enable-ecs-managed-tags` to `aws ecs run-task`. To split Fargate per delivery section, team or tenant, run one service or task set per unit with its own tag value, or tag at launch.

blocks.body: NAT gateway cost. Each NAT gateway has an hourly charge, plus data processing, so one template that deploys three NAT gateways into every account and VPC multiplies fixed cost as teams are added. Centralizing egress places NAT gateways in an egress VPC in a network services account and routes spoke VPC traffic there through AWS Transit Gateway (or AWS Cloud WAN). Trade-offs from the documentation: you pay an extra Transit Gateway data processing charge versus a NAT gateway per VPC; for very high-volume VPCs a local NAT can be cheaper; the account owning the egress VPC pays the NAT gateway charges; and to cut both Transit Gateway and NAT gateway data processing costs, use gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB in each VPC that needs them. For resilience, also use one NAT gateway per AZ in the egress VPC, and a Transit Gateway attachment spanning all the workload's AZs so traffic stays within an AZ.

blocks.body: Scenario 1: chargeback across 300 accounts. Requirements: finance wants monthly cost by business unit and application, 12-month history, and engineers must not need management-account access. Constraints: some resources are untagged, accounts are grouped by OU, and tags are inconsistent. Chosen architecture: define a small tag standard (BusinessUnit, Application, CostCenter); a tag policy for allowed values; an SCP that denies creation of key resource types when the request tag is missing; activate the keys in the management account and backfill; create a Cost Category that maps accounts and tags to business units; create CUR 2.0 in the management account into S3 with Athena and a QuickSight dashboard, sharing dashboards per business unit. Rationale: CUR from the management account covers all members, Cost Categories supply the OU-like grouping that raw CUR lacks. Security: restrict the S3 bucket and QuickSight access by business unit. Cost: S3, Athena and QuickSight charges are small compared with the spend analysed. Rejected: per-account CUR (fragmented, N reports), Cost Explorer only (no custom resource-level history beyond its retention, harder to share), tag policy alone (does not force a tag to exist).

Scenario 2: runaway development spend. Requirements: 20 accounts in Dev and Prod OUs; notify when forecasted monthly dev cost exceeds budget; automatically stop provisioning when actual spend passes 100 percent. Constraint: production must be untouched. Chosen architecture: in the management account, a monthly cost budget filtered to the development accounts (linked account or Cost Category filter) with a forecasted alert at 100 percent to an SNS topic, and a Budgets action that applies a restrictive SCP to the Dev OU on the actual threshold, with an approval workflow if desired; a Cost Anomaly Detection monitor on linked accounts for unknown spikes. Rationale: forecast alerts give early warning (they need about 5 weeks of history), an action stops the spend. Security: the Budgets role needs permission to attach policies; scope the SCP to avoid blocking budget and billing actions. Cost: the first two action-enabled budgets per month are free per the pricing page. Rejected: daily budget with forecasts (not supported), email-only alerts (do not stop spend), SCP attached at the root (hits Prod).

Scenario 3: three-year compute commitment with mixed services. Requirements: workloads on EC2, Fargate and Lambda, demand varies by month and by account; the company will migrate some EC2 to Fargate; minimize cost for 3 years with low management effort. Chosen architecture: purchase a Compute Savings Plan in the management account sized to the steady hourly baseline, validated with Purchase Analyzer and the 30- or 60-day recommendation; keep sharing on so unused commitment in one account covers others; use Budgets utilization and coverage alerts; cover any remaining steady, single-family EC2 with an EC2 Instance Savings Plan only if that family is stable. Rationale: Compute Savings Plans cover EC2, Fargate, Lambda across Regions and families. Alternatives rejected: Standard RIs (EC2 only and no exchange, so a migration to Fargate would strand them), Spot for the baseline (interruptions), On-Demand only (no discount).

In scenarios, check the alternatives against the one constraint they violate: cannot stop spend, wrong scope (member versus organization), cannot cover serverless, requires a support plan that is not mentioned, or cannot go back far enough in time.

blocks.body: Takeaways: decide whether the requirement is to see, allocate, notify, stop or commit; check the account that owns the action; pick the managed feature; and mind retention windows. Items marked unverified in this lesson should be confirmed against current AWS documentation before relying on them.

Task 2.1 asks you to design a deployment strategy that meets business requirements. The verbatim exam knowledge areas are: infrastructure as code (IaC, for example AWS CloudFormation); continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD); change management processes; and configuration management tools (for example AWS Systems Manager). The skills are: determining an application or upgrade path for new services and features; selecting services to develop deployment strategies and implement appropriate rollback mechanisms; adopting managed services as needed to reduce infrastructure provisioning and patching overhead; and making advanced technologies accessible by delegating complex development and deployment tasks to AWS.

Terms used throughout: infrastructure as code means describing infrastructure in a template or program so it can be versioned, reviewed and recreated; a stack is the set of resources CloudFormation manages as one unit; CI/CD is the automated path from a code commit through build and test to release; a deployment strategy is the way a new version replaces the old one (in place, rolling, immutable, blue/green, canary, linear); rollback is returning to the last known good state.

items: Prerequisites: basic Amazon EC2, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling groups, Elastic Load Balancing, AWS Lambda versions and aliases, IAM roles and iam:PassRole, and Amazon CloudWatch alarms.

Services and patterns covered: AWS CloudFormation (change sets, rollback triggers, policies, import, drift, quotas, StackSets); AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) and AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM); AWS Service Catalog; AWS CodePipeline; AWS CodeDeploy (EC2/Auto Scaling, Amazon ECS, Lambda); Lambda weighted aliases; AWS Elastic Beanstalk deployment policies and URL swap; Amazon CloudFront continuous deployment; and AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager, Automation, and State Manager.

blocks.body: Objectives. You will be able to:

items: choose between in-place, rolling, immutable, blue/green, canary and linear strategies from stated downtime, blast-radius and rollback-speed requirements;
protect stateful resources and preview risky changes using DeletionPolicy, UpdateReplacePolicy, change sets, termination protection and rollback triggers;
design a multi-account, multi-Region IaC rollout with StackSets, and a self-service model with Service Catalog;
assemble a CodePipeline-based CI/CD flow with build, test, manual approval and CloudFormation or CodeDeploy deploy actions;
configure automatic rollback with CloudWatch alarms for CodeDeploy and SAM Lambda deployments;
select Systems Manager capabilities or managed services to remove patching and provisioning effort.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.body: Domain 2 (Design for New Solutions) carries the largest share of the SAP-C02 exam, and deployment questions appear in the operational-excellence and reliability scenarios across domains. According to the official SAP-C02 exam guide, Domain 2 accounts for 29 percent of scored content. Expect scenario questions where the deciding words are zero downtime, fast rollback, least operational overhead, or minimal code change.

CloudFormation turns a template into a stack. For production, the question is rarely how to create resources; it is how to change them safely and recover when a change goes wrong. The mechanisms are previews (change sets), automatic recovery (stack rollback and rollback triggers), data protection (DeletionPolicy, UpdateReplacePolicy, termination protection) and detection of out-of-band edits (drift).

blocks.title: Change sets
blocks.body: A change set previews how proposed changes will affect running resources, including whether critical resources will be deleted or replaced. CloudFormation changes the stack only when you execute the change set, so you can review, then execute or create another change set. They work from the console, CLI and API. In pipelines, the usual pattern is create change set, manual approval, execute change set.

Rollback triggers: you name CloudWatch alarms (or composite alarms, up to a maximum of 5 triggers) and CloudFormation monitors them during a stack create or update and for a monitoring period afterward (default 0, up to 180 minutes). If any alarm enters the ALARM state, CloudFormation rolls back the entire operation. By default only ALARM triggers rollback, not INSUFFICIENT_DATA; to roll back on missing data, configure the alarm to treat missing data as breaching. If you set a monitoring time but no triggers, CloudFormation still waits before cleaning up old resources, giving you time for manual validation and cancellation.

DeletionPolicy controls what happens to a resource when it is removed from the stack or the stack is deleted. Without a DeletionPolicy, CloudFormation deletes the resource (an Amazon S3 bucket must be empty for deletion to succeed). Exceptions: the default is Snapshot for AWS::RDS::DBCluster resources and for AWS::RDS::DBInstance resources that do not specify DBClusterIdentifier. Retain keeps the resource (works for any resource type, including nested stacks, S3 buckets, EC2 instances). Snapshot creates a snapshot before deletion for resources that support it, such as AWS::EC2::Volume. Retained resources and snapshots continue to incur charges until you delete them. DeletionPolicy also applies to stack updates that remove a resource from the template, but not to resources replaced during an update.

UpdateReplacePolicy covers that replacement case: when a property change forces CloudFormation to replace a resource, the old physical resource is deleted by default. Set Retain or Snapshot to keep it; with Retain the old resource is removed from CloudFormation's scope. If you specify Snapshot on a type that does not support snapshots, CloudFormation falls back to Delete. For S3 buckets, Delete only succeeds if the bucket is empty.

blocks.body: Service role. A stack can run with a CloudFormation service role, an IAM role CloudFormation assumes for all operations on that stack. This lets you give users permission to manage stacks without giving them direct permission to create the underlying resources. Users need iam:PassRole for the role. Important documented caveat: CloudFormation always uses the service role for operations on that stack, you cannot remove the role after the stack is created, and other users who can operate on the stack can use it even without iam:PassRole, so keep the role least privilege or you create a privilege-escalation path.

Resource import brings existing, manually created resources under CloudFormation without recreating them. You supply a template describing the whole stack including the imported resources, each imported resource needs a DeletionPolicy attribute, and you give identifiers so CloudFormation maps logical IDs to physical resources. You cannot import the same resource into multiple stacks in the same Region, and only one level of nesting is supported (cannot import a stack into a child stack or one that has children). Import runs as a change set. This is the lowest-effort way to adopt a hand-built VPC into IaC.

Drift detection compares actual resource configuration with the template and reports unmanaged changes made outside CloudFormation; it runs per stack and per StackSet (stack instance by instance). Detecting drift does not fix it: you re-apply, revert the manual change, or import to resolve.

Wait signals: CreationPolicy with ResourceSignal waits for a count of cfn-signal success signals (default 1) before marking the resource CREATE_COMPLETE; failure or timeout fails creation and rolls the stack back. The maximum timeout is 12 hours. UpdatePolicy applies to Auto Scaling groups (AutoScalingRollingUpdate replaces instances in batches without replacing the group; AutoScalingReplacingUpdate replaces the whole group; AutoScalingScheduledAction guards scheduled-action changes). The documented warning for rolling updates: they do not honor the group's instance maintenance policy, healthy capacity can fall below MinHealthyPercentage, and new instances are not launched before old ones are terminated. To preserve the instance maintenance policy during stack updates, use the AutoScalingInstanceRefresh policy instead.

blocks.body: DeletionPolicy answers 'prevent data loss when the stack or resource is deleted'. Termination protection answers 'prevent anyone deleting the stack'. The best answer for RDS and EBS under accidental stack deletion is Snapshot or Retain on those resources; if an option offers only termination protection and another offers DeletionPolicy for data, check which control the wording targets. Change sets preview; they do not roll back.

items: Termination protection: the documented rule is that deletion fails and the stack, including status, is unchanged. Enabling or disabling it on a stack passes the same choice to its nested stacks; you cannot toggle it on a nested stack directly. A stack update that removes the nested stack still deletes it. It is different from disabling rollback.

Service role enforcement pattern: give engineers cloudformation permissions and iam:PassRole on one named service role, and give the service role the permissions to create only approved resource types. Engineers can then provision only through CloudFormation, within the role's limits.
Import prerequisite: a DeletionPolicy on every imported resource. The cloudformation:ImportResourceTypes condition key controls which resource types a user may import.
Stack policies and IAM policies protect specific resources from updates; this lesson does not cover detailed stack policy behavior.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Assuming DeletionPolicy: Retain is free safety. Retained buckets, volumes and databases keep billing and fall outside the stack, so deleting the stack does not clean them up, and a later stack that reuses fixed names will collide with them.

topics.title: Organizing IaC: nested stacks, StackSets, Service Catalog and CDK

blocks.body: Large environments are split into stacks by lifecycle and ownership (network, data, application). The tools differ in what they solve: reuse inside one account and Region, fan-out across accounts and Regions, governed self-service, or developer-friendly authoring.

Cross-stack references: Fn::ImportValue imports a value another stack explicitly exports; it is a strong reference within the same account and Region and CloudFormation blocks deleting the exporting stack while it is in use. Fn::GetStackOutput references an output directly, including from other accounts or Regions, without an export; it is a weak reference resolved at create or update time. Nested stacks are child stacks declared as resources in a parent template; they help when a template nears the 500-resource limit and when a pattern (for example a VPC) is reused. The documented nested-stack limit is 2,500 resources created, updated or deleted per operation.

StackSets create, update or delete stacks across multiple accounts and Regions with one operation. Permission models: self-managed (you create IAM roles in the administrator and each target account) or service-managed (AWS Organizations trusted access; CloudFormation creates the roles). With service-managed permissions you target the organization or OUs, and can enable automatic deployment so accounts added to a target OU later receive the stack automatically; on account removal you choose to retain or delete the stacks. Automatic deployment settings can be changed any time for service-managed StackSets. Deployment options: Maximum concurrent accounts, Failure tolerance (per Region; when reached, the operation stops and does not proceed to other Regions), Region concurrency (sequential or parallel), and concurrency mode. Strict failure tolerance (the default) reduces concurrency after failures (effective concurrency is limited to failure tolerance + 1, for example tolerance 5 and max 10 gives 6), while Soft keeps the configured concurrency. A StackSet can define up to 10 dependencies (up to 100 per account). Service-managed StackSets cannot be created or updated from templates containing macros or transforms.

blocks.body: Service Catalog lets administrators publish approved CloudFormation-based products in portfolios. Constraints control how products are deployed: launch constraints specify the role used to provision (users need no direct permission on the underlying resources), notification constraints send stack events to an SNS topic, and template constraints limit parameter values such as instance types. The most restrictive applicable constraint is applied. Template constraints are not supported for Terraform configurations per the FAQ. This is the answer when many teams repeatedly fill in many parameters or must stay within guardrails: wrap the nested templates in one product.

AWS CDK lets developers define infrastructure in a programming language. cdk synth runs the app and produces a CloudFormation template; cdk deploy synthesizes automatically if you have not. CDK apps deploy through CloudFormation, so change sets, rollback and policies still apply. Bootstrapping creates resources in the environment that CDK uses for deployments and assets, and synthesized templates reference those bootstrap resources. When a team knows Python or TypeScript and is reluctant to adopt raw YAML, CDK is the lowest-friction path that keeps CloudFormation as the engine.

blocks.title: StackSets vs per-account pipelines
blocks.body: If the requirement is 'deploy the same baseline to every current and future account in an OU', service-managed StackSets with automatic deployment is the managed answer. If each account needs different code released through different approval gates, use pipelines per account.

CodePipeline models a release as stages containing actions: source, build and test (commonly CodeBuild), approval, and deploy. It is the orchestrator; CloudFormation, CodeDeploy and others perform the deployment.

Manual approval: an approval action pauses the pipeline until someone with IAM permission approves or rejects. Rejection, or no response within seven days of the pipeline stopping at the action, counts as an action failure and the execution does not continue. Approval actions cannot be added to source stages. To send Amazon SNS notifications, the pipeline service role needs SNS permission and approvers need permission to update the approval status. Use it for change-management review, manual QA, or integrity confirmation before release.

CloudFormation deploy action modes: CHANGE_SET_REPLACE (create the change set, replacing an existing one), CHANGE_SET_EXECUTE, CREATE_UPDATE (create or update the stack; does not replace a failed stack), REPLACE_ON_FAILURE (delete and recreate a failed stack; recommended for testing only), and DELETE_ONLY. Capabilities such as CAPABILITY_IAM must be acknowledged when templates contain IAM resources. The reference walkthrough builds test and production stacks where the production stage creates a change set, waits for approval, then executes it.

CDK Pipelines is a CDK construct that creates a CodePipeline. It is self-mutating by default: the pipeline updates itself before deploying application stages, so changes to the pipeline definition flow through git. Administrative permissions are needed only for the first cdk deploy of the pipeline stack, after which the documentation recommends removing those credentials. Self-mutation can be turned off temporarily during pipeline development.

items: Feature-branch pipelines: create a pipeline (or CodeBuild project) per feature branch or pull request, build and test in an isolated or separate account, and tear it down on merge; keep infrastructure in IaC so environments are cheap to create and delete.

topics.title: CodeDeploy for EC2, Auto Scaling and ECS

blocks.body: CodeDeploy automates application deployment to three compute platforms: EC2/on-premises, Lambda and ECS. Deployment types: in place (replace the revision on existing instances) and blue/green (shift traffic to a separate set).

EC2/on-premises: instances need the CodeDeploy agent running, a connection to CodeDeploy, tags or an Auto Scaling group to select them, and for EC2 an IAM instance profile. If no deployment configuration is set, CodeDeploy deploys to one instance at a time by default. A deployment configuration can require minimum healthy hosts (fleet percent or count), which is how in-place deployments avoid downtime on multi-instance groups. With Elastic Load Balancing, CodeDeploy deregisters instances from the load balancer, deploys, then re-registers them. Blue/green on EC2 requires EC2 instances (on-premises instances are not supported for blue/green). You specify the replacement environment by copying an existing Auto Scaling group as a template (CodeDeploy launches the new instances) or by choosing instances manually by tags or ASG names. You also pick the load balancers (Classic, ALB target groups or NLB target groups), whether to reroute immediately or wait, and the rate of rerouting. After replacement instances are registered the original instances are deregistered and, if configured, terminated.

Auto Scaling integration: when a deployment group includes an Auto Scaling group, CodeDeploy installs a launch lifecycle hook. On scale-out the new instance waits in Pending:Wait while CodeDeploy deploys the latest successful revision; CodeDeploy sends heartbeats every five minutes and then signals CONTINUE or ABANDON. On ABANDON the instance is terminated and Auto Scaling retries to reach desired capacity. This is how instances that constantly change due to scaling events still receive the application: the agent must be present on the instance image or installed at launch, and the ASG must be part of the deployment group. Problems arise with leftover hooks from deleted deployment groups, too many concurrent deployments, or throttling.

ECS: CodeDeploy blue/green creates a replacement task set, registers it with a second target group, optionally serves test traffic on a test listener, then shifts production traffic using canary, linear or all-at-once. With a Network Load Balancer, only the predefined CodeDeployDefault.ECSAllAtOnce configuration is supported. Lifecycle hooks (BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, AfterAllowTestTraffic, BeforeAllowTraffic, AfterAllowTraffic) run Lambda validation functions; from AfterInstall onward their failure can trigger rollback, while a rollback is not possible at BeforeInstall. Rollback is achieved by pointing the production listener rule back at the original target group. Per AWS guidance, Amazon ECS now also offers built-in blue/green deployments that use service revisions, and AWS publishes a migration guide away from CodeDeploy. Both approaches are documented, and the exam may still reference CodeDeploy.

Rollback: you can configure a deployment group or a single deployment to roll back automatically when a deployment fails or a monitoring threshold (CloudWatch alarm) is met. CodeDeploy then redeploys the last known good revision; this is a new deployment, not an undo. SNS notifications can report automatic rollbacks.

Pricing (from the CodeDeploy FAQ): no additional charge for deployments to EC2 instances through CodeDeploy; $0.02 per on-premises instance update. Lambda and ECS pricing were not shown on the pages retrieved and are not verified.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Treating an in-place rolling deployment as a rollback-friendly strategy. Rollback means another deployment of the old revision on the same instances. If the requirement says 'rapid rollback' or 'zero downtime with instant switch back', blue/green keeps the old fleet intact.

topics.title: Serverless releases: Lambda aliases, SAM and CodeDeploy

blocks.body: A Lambda version is an immutable snapshot of function code and configuration; an alias is a named pointer to a version. Invoking the alias lets you change what runs without changing callers. A weighted alias points to two versions: you give the additional version a weight and the first version receives the residual. For example, 10 percent to the additional version leaves 90 percent on the first. You set it with the routing configuration on create-alias or update-alias (AdditionalVersionWeights). To promote, point the alias at the new version and clear the routing configuration; to abort, remove the additional weight.

CodeDeploy automates this shifting for Lambda. Predefined configurations: LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes, 10Minutes, 15Minutes and 30Minutes (10 percent first, the remaining 90 percent after the interval); LambdaLinear10PercentEvery1Minute, 2Minutes, 3Minutes and 10Minutes (10 percent increments until complete); and LambdaAllAtOnce. You can also create custom canary or linear configurations. Trusted Advisor flags Lambda deployment groups using all-at-once as a yellow finding and recommends canary or linear.

AWS SAM wraps this. Add AutoPublishAlias to an AWS::Serverless::Function and a DeploymentPreference with a Type (for example Canary10Percent10Minutes), optional Alarms and Hooks. SAM then publishes a new version on code change, updates the alias, creates the CodeDeploy application and deployment group for you, shifts traffic gradually, runs PreTraffic and PostTraffic validation functions, and rolls back automatically if the listed CloudWatch alarms fire. DeploymentPreference requires AutoPublishAlias, otherwise an error results. Function invocations (API Gateway integration, event source mappings) must use the alias qualifier to benefit.

rows: Automatic on alarms or failed hooks
New CloudFormation stack + Route 53 weighted records

blocks.body: Shared code. Lambda functions deployed as container images do not support adding Lambda layers; you include shared libraries in the image at build time. Container images support up to 10 GB (the 250 MB unzipped limit applies to zip packages). For shared libraries across many zip functions, layers remain the packaging mechanism; for container functions the shared code must be built into each image, ideally from a common base image. The scale and price of ECR storage were not verified.

'Canary release for a Lambda-based application deployed through CloudFormation, with rollback on errors' maps to SAM AutoPublishAlias plus DeploymentPreference with a canary type and alarms. If it also says 'abort', 'subset of users first', that is canary or linear; canary fits 'small percentage then everyone', linear fits 'ramp up gradually'.

topics.title: Elastic Beanstalk and CloudFront release options

blocks.body: Elastic Beanstalk is the managed platform choice when a team wants to upload code and let AWS provision and manage the EC2, Auto Scaling and load balancing, which satisfies the skill of adopting managed services to cut provisioning and patching effort. Its deployment options range from in-place policies to separate-environment blue/green.

Batches, each batch out of service; reduced capacity
