blocks.body: Blue/green with Elastic Beanstalk: because normal updates are in place and may briefly make the app unavailable, deploy the new version to a separate environment (clone the current one or launch a new one), test, then use Swap environment URLs, which swaps the CNAME records of the two environments. Rollback is another swap. Do not terminate the old environment until DNS changes propagate and old records expire. Blue/green is also required to move to an incompatible platform version. The environment should run independently of the production database: a database created by Elastic Beanstalk inside the environment is not preserved unless you use the Retain database lifecycle option, so use an external RDS instance for blue/green.

CloudFront continuous deployment is the native canary for CDN or static-site changes. You associate a staging distribution with a primary distribution through a continuous deployment policy, update the staging configuration, then route a subset of production traffic either by a header (known testers) or by weight (a percentage that you raise over time). With weight-based routing, session stickiness keeps a viewer on the same distribution until the session closes or the staging distribution is removed or promoted. CloudFront provides analytics; when satisfied you promote the staging configuration. It is configurable by console, SDK, CLI or CloudFormation (AWS::CloudFront::ContinuousDeploymentPolicy). Older patterns use Route 53 weighted records across two distributions; continuous deployment avoids DNS TTL effects and extra distributions.

blocks.title: Choosing within Beanstalk
blocks.body: Need minimal capacity loss and easy rollback in place: immutable. Need to test with a slice of real users: traffic splitting. Need to change platform or have the instantaneous switch and instant swap-back: blue/green URL swap.
Pick the pattern from the requirement, then pick the AWS service that implements it for the compute type.

blocks.body: Rollback options: CloudFormation rolls back failed updates automatically and can use rollback triggers; CodeDeploy redeploys the last known good revision or re-routes traffic; Lambda and ECS blue/green revert by routing back to the original version or task set; Beanstalk reverts by swapping URLs again or deploying the previous application version; pipelines can halt at approval. Design rollback before release: alarms on error rate and latency, hooks that test before traffic arrives, and data-layer compatibility.

blocks.title: Database changes
blocks.body: Blue/green and canary assume the old and new application versions can both use the data store at once. Use backward-compatible schema changes (expand, migrate, contract) or the old version breaks on rollback. The environment-specific database should be external to the swapped environments.

items: Mixed versions during rolling or canary: ensure API and message compatibility.
Cost: blue/green and immutable temporarily double compute; the old environment should be terminated after the observation period.
DNS-based switches (Route 53 weights, Beanstalk CNAME swap) are subject to caching, so clients can keep hitting the old environment for a while; load balancer or alias level switching avoids this.

blocks.body: Keyword map: 'zero downtime and fast rollback' = blue/green; 'expose to a small subset of users first' = canary; 'gradual increase' = linear; 'avoid impact on capacity' = immutable or rolling with additional batch; 'minimal change to existing process' = in-place policy on the existing platform.

blocks.body: Systems Manager provides configuration management and operational automation across instances without bastions or SSH. Patch Manager applies patches according to a patch baseline (approved and rejected patches). Instances are grouped with a Patch Group tag (use PatchGroup, without a space, if tags in EC2 instance metadata are allowed); a maintenance window defines a schedule, targets (by Patch Group tag) and a task running the AWS-RunPatchBaseline document in scan or install mode. After installation Systems Manager reboots the node unless the RebootOption parameter is NoReboot. For one-off fixes call AWS-RunPatchBaseline through Run Command. State Manager associations (document + targets + schedule) enforce a desired state, for example daily patch scans; maintenance windows give tighter control over reboot timing.

Automation runs runbooks (multi-step workflows) and can run across multiple Regions, accounts or OUs from a central account. For OU targets the central account must be the Organizations management account or, recommended, a delegated administrator; the administrator needs an assumable role and targets must trust it. Typical uses: central patching, remediating configuration drift such as S3 bucket policies or VPC settings, and fleet-wide operations.

Managed services reduce provisioning and patching overhead: Elastic Beanstalk (platform handles instances), Lambda and Fargate (no instances to patch), RDS, and CodeDeploy/CodePipeline/CodeBuild (no CI servers). Making advanced technology accessible by delegating to AWS means preferring SAM or CDK over hand-built deployment scripts, Service Catalog over custom portals, and managed pipelines over self-run Jenkins when the requirement is least operational overhead. Costs and exact managed-service patching responsibilities were not verified in this build.

rows: Scheduled patching with controlled reboot window

blocks.body: Three scenarios show how requirements steer the choice. None repeats a practice question; they use the same reasoning.

blocks.title: Scenario 1: retail API on Lambda, weekly releases, outage-averse
blocks.body: Requirements: serverless API behind API Gateway, each release exposed to about 10 percent of traffic for 10 minutes, automatic rollback if errors rise, minimal new tooling. Existing: CloudFormation stacks, CLI scripts that repoint a function. Chosen: convert to SAM; add AutoPublishAlias and DeploymentPreference Canary10Percent10Minutes with a CloudWatch alarm on alias errors and a PreTraffic hook; invoke through the alias. Security: CodeDeploy service role scoped to the function; pipeline role cannot edit production IAM. Cost: CodeDeploy for Lambda adds no instance fleet; the extra cost is the alarms. Rejected: second CloudFormation stack plus Route 53 weighted records (duplicate stacks, DNS caching, slower rollback); hand scripts around update-alias (no automatic rollback unless you build it); all-at-once (no blast-radius control).

blocks.title: Scenario 2: EC2 Auto Scaling fleet, zero downtime, instant rollback
blocks.body: Requirements: web tier in an ASG behind an ALB, deployments several times a day, switch back in under a minute, instances come and go with scaling. Chosen: CodePipeline with CodeBuild tests and CodeDeploy blue/green copying the existing ASG, reroute through the ALB target group; CodeDeploy agent baked into the AMI; automatic rollback on a CloudWatch alarm. Security: instance profile for CodeDeploy artifact access, service role for ASG and ELB permissions. Cost: double capacity during the shift; configure termination of the original instances after a wait. Rejected: in-place one-at-a-time (rollback is another deployment, capacity reduced); Beanstalk URL swap (would require re-platforming and relies on DNS caching); user data scripts pulling from S3 (no health gates, no managed rollback).

blocks.title: Scenario 3: baseline controls across 80 accounts
blocks.body: Requirements: every current and future account in two OUs gets a logging role and a config recorder stack in two Regions; failures in a few accounts must not halt everything; no engineer may be given direct IAM rights to create the resources. Chosen: service-managed StackSets targeting the OUs with automatic deployment, Regions deployed in parallel, failure tolerance and maximum concurrent accounts set to a safe percentage; a CloudFormation service role pattern that separates human users from permission to create the resources. Alternatives rejected: per-account pipelines (operational overhead scales with accounts), self-managed StackSets (need IAM roles in every account), a custom Lambda looping over accounts (reinvents StackSets).

Console path for a safe update: CloudFormation, choose the stack, Update, supply the template, then at Review choose to create a change set instead of updating directly; inspect Replacement and Action columns; Execute only after review. The command forms below follow the documented operations, and the update-stack rollback configuration, termination protection, create-stack-set (service-managed permissions and automatic deployment) and create-stack-instances (deployment targets and operation preferences) options match the AWS documentation reviewed for this lesson. Other flag spellings were not individually verified against the CLI reference, so run --help before use.

blocks.label: SAM template: canary with alarm and pre-traffic hook
blocks.body:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31
Resources:
  OrdersFunction:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::Function
    Properties:
      Handler: app.handler
      Runtime: python3.12
      CodeUri: src/
      AutoPublishAlias: live
      DeploymentPreference:
        Type: Canary10Percent10Minutes
        Alarms:
          - !Ref AliasErrorsAlarm
        Hooks:
          PreTraffic: !Ref PreTrafficFunction
  PreTrafficFunction:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::Function
    Properties:
      Handler: pretraffic.handler
      Runtime: python3.12
      CodeUri: src/
  AliasErrorsAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Properties:
      Namespace: AWS/Lambda
      MetricName: Errors
      Statistic: Sum
      Period: 60
      EvaluationPeriods: 1
      Threshold: 1
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold
      Dimensions:
        - Name: FunctionName
          Value: !Ref OrdersFunction

blocks.title: Takeaway
blocks.body: Match the strategy to the requirement, then choose the managed AWS feature that implements it with automatic rollback and the fewest custom parts.

Business continuity (task 2.2 of Domain 2, Design for New Solutions) asks you to design so that a workload keeps serving, or can be brought back, after a disruption: a failed instance, a lost Availability Zone, a lost Region, a deleted database, or a compromised account. This lesson is about choosing and combining services to meet stated recovery targets at the lowest justified cost. Pure Multi-AZ high availability and quotas are covered in the reliability lesson (2.4); here the emphasis is on Regional disaster recovery (DR), backup, replication, failover mechanics and testing.

items: Prerequisites: VPC and Regions/Availability Zones basics; Route 53 record types; RDS/Aurora, DynamoDB and S3 fundamentals; IAM roles and KMS keys at the associate level.

Official 'Skills in' objectives for 2.2: configure disaster recovery solutions; configure data and database replication; perform disaster recovery testing; architect a backup solution that is automated, cost-effective and supports continuity across multiple Availability Zones or Regions; design an architecture that provides application and infrastructure availability in the event of a disruption; use processes and components for centralized monitoring to proactively recover from system failures.

Official knowledge areas: AWS Global Infrastructure; AWS networking concepts (for example Route 53 routing methods); RTOs and RPOs; DR scenarios (backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site); DR solutions on AWS.

blocks.title: Objectives
blocks.body: You will be able to: (1) derive an RTO and RPO from requirements and pick between backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby and multi-site active/active; (2) choose the right failover mechanism (Route 53 failover/latency/weighted, ARC routing controls, Global Accelerator, CloudFront origin groups) and compute approximate DNS failover time; (3) select the correct cross-Region replication feature for each data store (Aurora Global Database, RDS cross-Region read replicas, DynamoDB global tables, ElastiCache Global Datastore, S3 replication and S3 RTC, EFS replication); (4) design an automated, centralized, cross-Region and cross-account backup architecture with AWS Backup, Data Lifecycle Manager and Vault Lock; (5) use AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery for server-based workloads; (6) plan DR tests and centralized monitoring that detect failure early.

Services and patterns covered: Route 53 (routing policies, health checks), AWS Application Recovery Controller (ARC), AWS Global Accelerator, CloudFront origin failover, Aurora Global Database, RDS cross-Region read replicas, DynamoDB global tables, ElastiCache Global Datastore, S3 Cross-Region Replication and Replication Time Control, EFS replication, AWS Backup (cross-Region, cross-account, Vault Lock, restore testing), Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM), AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS), ECR/Secrets Manager/KMS multi-Region components, WorkSpaces cross-Region redirection, AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS), AWS Resilience Hub and CloudWatch cross-account observability.

Task 2.2 sits in the 'Design for New Solutions' domain, and DR questions also appear in other domains (reliability, organizational complexity, migration). The practice questions mapped to this lesson are dominated by three patterns: Route 53 failover plus a replicated data tier, pilot light/warm standby with cross-Region database replicas, and AWS Backup/DLM cross-Region copies. The exact domain weighting percentage was not verified against AWS documentation here.

links.label: Disaster recovery options in the cloud (AWS whitepaper)

topics.title: RTO, RPO and the four DR strategies

blocks.body: Two numbers drive every DR design. The recovery time objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable delay between the interruption of service and restoration of service. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable amount of time since the last data recovery point, which sets how much data loss is acceptable between the last recovery point and the interruption. Both are defined by the organization per application. The Reliability Pillar also distinguishes RTO from mean time to recovery (MTTR): RTO is a target for a single event, MTTR is a mean over several events.

The AWS DR whitepaper groups strategies from cheap and slow to expensive and fast. Active/passive strategies use one active site (for example one Region) and keep a passive site for recovery that does not serve traffic until failover. Backup and restore is enough for loss of one data center for a well-architected multi-AZ workload; if your definition of disaster is a whole Region, or regulation demands it, consider pilot light, warm standby or multi-site.

Full stacks in several Regions serving traffic (or a full-size standby)
Continuous replication, with a write strategy (write global, write local, write partitioned)
No failover as such: traffic is routed away from the failed Region
Near-zero RTO and RPO for most disasters, highest cost and complexity

blocks.title: Pilot light vs warm standby
blocks.body: Both keep a copy of the primary Region's assets in the DR Region. Pilot light cannot process requests until you take action first (turn on servers, perhaps deploy extra infrastructure, scale up). Warm standby can handle traffic immediately at reduced capacity and only requires scaling up. A passive stack at full capacity is hot standby. Because warm standby has a working endpoint, you can test it continuously with synthetic transactions.

Design rules from the whitepaper worth memorizing. (1) Use data plane operations for failover where possible: data planes have higher availability design goals than control planes, so failover that depends on creating or changing resources (Auto Scaling scale-out, restore from backup, changing Route 53 weights) is less resilient than failover through health checks or ARC routing controls. Hence the advice to run periodic restores so you hold operable data stores before a disaster. (2) Use infrastructure as code so the DR Region can be deployed consistently; condition logic on CloudFormation pseudo parameters can deploy only the scaled-down version in the DR Region, and StackSets deploy across accounts and Regions in one operation. (3) Copy golden AMIs (for example built by an Image Builder pipeline) to both Regions. (4) Make sure service quotas in the DR Region are high enough to scale to production capacity. (5) The whitepaper recommends a different account per Region for the strongest isolation when compromised credentials are part of the DR threat model.

Automatic versus manual failover: the whitepaper cautions that automatically initiated failover based on health checks or alarms should be used with caution because recovery time and recovery point are greater than zero and a false alarm incurs those losses. Manually initiated failover is therefore common, but the steps should still be automated so the manual step is like pushing a button.

Continuous replication does not protect against corruption or deletion: a bad write or a malicious delete is replicated too. Pair replication with versioning or point-in-time backups. For S3 replication, by default a delete in the source bucket adds a delete marker in the source only, which protects the DR copy from malicious deletions in the source Region (delete marker replication is a configurable option).

Map the numbers to the strategy: RTO/RPO of hours with a cost constraint points to backup and restore or pilot light; minutes of RTO with seconds of RPO points to warm standby or active/active; 'minimize cost' with a relaxed RTO (for example several hours) points to pilot light with Auto Scaling groups at zero and a replicated database. 'Near-zero RTO' means no failover step: active/active. A warm or hot copy still needs data replication; an RPO of 24 hours is satisfied by daily snapshot copies, not necessarily by a replica.

Pilot light and warm standby (AWS Architecture Blog)

blocks.body: Failing over compute means getting users to the DR endpoint. The DR whitepaper lists four AWS options: Route 53, Application Recovery Controller (ARC), Global Accelerator and CloudFront origin failover.

Amazon Route 53 routing policies. Simple: a single resource, standard DNS; you cannot attach a health check to a simple record, and all values are returned regardless of status. Failover: active-passive with a PRIMARY and SECONDARY record. Latency: route to the AWS Region with the lowest latency; all resources must be in AWS Regions. Weighted: route proportions of traffic. Geolocation: by user location. Geoproximity: by location of users and resources with an optional bias. IP-based: by client IP ranges you know. Multivalue answer: up to eight healthy records chosen at random per query. Active-active failover is achieved with any policy other than failover (for example latency or weighted records with health checks), and combinations can be nested in a tree (traffic policies).

items: Failover record behavior: if the primary is healthy Route 53 answers with the primary regardless of the secondary; if the primary is unhealthy and the secondary healthy it answers with the secondary; if both are unhealthy it returns the primary. If you omit HealthCheckId on the secondary and the primary is unhealthy, Route 53 always answers with the secondary.

Health checks: checkers in locations worldwide send requests at a 30 second default interval or an optional fast 10 second interval; the interval cannot be changed after creation. The failure threshold (consecutive observations) is 1 to 10, default 3. An endpoint is healthy if more than 18% of checkers report healthy. HTTP/HTTPS checks must connect within four seconds and get a 2xx or 3xx within two seconds; HTTPS checks do not validate certificates.

A health check can monitor an endpoint, other health checks (calculated), a CloudWatch alarm (CLOUDWATCH_METRIC type) or an ARC routing control. CloudWatch-alarm health checks let you fail over on real application signals (5xx rate, latency, DynamoDB errors, composite alarms) instead of simple reachability; the behaviour for insufficient data can be set to Healthy, Unhealthy or LastKnownStatus.

Alias records with Evaluate Target Health inherit the health of the target (for example an ALB). This detects only service-level unavailability of the AWS resource; the DynamoDB global tables failover guidance recommends health checks on real application signals for better coverage. If your endpoint does not receive traffic through an alias record, clear Evaluate Target Health and create a health check.

Failback is automatic: when the primary health check returns to healthy Route 53 returns to the primary record. To prevent automatic failback, change the health check configuration or use weighted routing.

blocks.title: DNS failover time
blocks.body: Failover time is approximately TTL + (health check interval x failure threshold). Example from AWS: TTL 60 s, 10 s interval and threshold 5 gives 110 s. With the defaults (30 s interval, threshold 3, TTL 60 s) detection alone takes about 90 s plus the TTL, so a '1 minute failover' requirement means fast 10 s checks, a low threshold and a short TTL. DNS caching in clients and resolvers still limits how fast users move; Global Accelerator avoids DNS caching issues.

Manual versus automatic failover with Route 53. Automatic health-check failover is a data plane operation with no dependency on the Route 53 control plane, but you cannot force a failover during intermittent problems, and you should not depend on the health check APIs to force one. For controlled failover use ARC routing controls: these are on/off switches hosted on a highly available ARC cluster; you integrate them with Route 53 health checks attached to DNS records, then turn one control on and another off to move traffic between Regions or AZs. Safety rules prevent mistakes: an assertion rule enforces criteria such as 'at least one routing control must stay On' (avoiding a fail-open or a blackhole), and a gating rule is an overall on/off switch over a set of target routing controls. ARC is global; configuration resources are created via the US West (Oregon) Region, and state changes should use the regional cluster endpoints through the CLI/SDK (hard-code the five cluster endpoints; do not depend on DescribeCluster or the console in the recovery path). Routing control and Region switch carry separate charges; zonal shift (moving traffic away from one AZ for supported resources) is included with services at no extra charge, and zonal autoshift is AWS-initiated.

AWS Global Accelerator gives static anycast IP addresses and routes users onto the AWS network at the nearest edge location, to endpoint groups (one per Region) holding ALBs, NLBs, EC2 instances or Elastic IPs. It health-checks endpoints (for ALB/NLB endpoints it reuses the load balancer's own health checks) and spreads traffic by traffic dial (percentage per endpoint group) and endpoint weight. If no healthy endpoint with weight greater than zero exists in a group, it fails over to another group ignoring the traffic dial, and if nothing healthy is found after trying the three closest groups it fails open to a random endpoint in the closest group. Return to regular routing typically takes about 30 seconds, but established connections are not moved until reset. Changing the traffic dial is a control plane operation. Use it when clients cannot be trusted to honor DNS TTLs, when you need static IPs (for example IP allow lists, or an apex domain on external DNS), or for lower latency.

CloudFront origin failover uses an origin group with a primary and secondary origin and the HTTP status codes that trigger failover. It is stateless and per request: every request first goes to the primary, and only if it times out, fails to connect or returns a configured error code does CloudFront retry on the secondary. It applies only when the viewer request method is GET, HEAD or OPTIONS. Timeouts are tunable: connection attempts 1 to 3, connection timeout 1 to 10 s, response timeout 1 to 60 s (custom origins). It is the fastest way to hide a primary backend failure for cacheable web content, and can be combined with Route 53 failover (hybrid).

blocks.body: Keywords: 'static IP addresses' or 'clients cache DNS' -> Global Accelerator. 'Active-passive' -> Route 53 failover records. 'Users in two continents, both Regions serve traffic' -> latency (or geolocation) routing with health checks so an unhealthy Region is dropped. 'Controlled/manual failover without depending on the control plane' -> ARC routing controls. 'Fail over per request for a website with two origins' -> CloudFront origin groups. An ALB is Regional, so a single ALB cannot span Regions: multi-Region needs one load balancer per Region (reasoning, not quoted from a retrieved page).

topics.title: Database and data replication across Regions

blocks.body: Choose the replication feature by data store, direction of writes and RPO/RTO. All the cross-Region features below replicate asynchronously except DynamoDB multi-Region strong consistency (MRSC), so RPO is small but not strictly zero for unplanned failover (the one exception noted in the docs is an Aurora switchover, which synchronizes first and has RPO 0).

Aurora Global Database. One primary Region takes writes; secondary Regions are read-only. Replication is storage-level, uses dedicated infrastructure outside the DB instances and has typical latency under a second. The current user guide says up to 10 secondary Regions (older whitepaper text and blogs say five; see discrepancies). Each secondary can have up to 16 read-only instances, and the global writer endpoint always points to the primary after a switchover or failover. Two operations change the primary: switchover (formerly managed planned failover) for healthy, planned moves such as Region rotation or DR drills, which synchronizes secondaries first so RPO is 0; and failover for unplanned outages, run with `--allow-data-loss` on `failover-global-cluster`, which can lose transactions not yet replicated (RPO is typically a non-zero value in seconds, depending on replication lag) and is susceptible to split-brain, though the promoted cluster is transactionally consistent. Managed failover is recommended for DR because Aurora re-adds the old primary Region as a secondary later; manual failover (detach and promote) is the fallback, for example when Regions run incompatible engine versions. Promoting a secondary by removing it from the global database takes typically under a minute (the AWS whitepaper states promotion in less than one minute) but permanently stops replication into that cluster and it cannot be reattached to the old global database.

items: Aurora PostgreSQL RPO management: set `rds.global_db_rpo` (valid values start from 20 seconds per AWS blog); Aurora then blocks commits on the primary if all secondaries lag more than the RPO. With only two Regions, keep the default in the secondary Region's parameter group, or a failover could pause transactions.

Headless secondary: a secondary cluster with no DB instance. Compute and storage are decoupled, so you pay only for storage while the volume stays in sync. It lowers cost but raises RTO because you must add an instance after promotion. For Aurora PostgreSQL create it with the CLI/API (not supported in the console).

Requirements and limits: same major and minor engine version for managed switchover/failover (patch level rules depend on engine), no backtracking, no Aurora Auto Scaling for secondary clusters, specific engine versions and Regions, automatic minor version upgrade does not apply.
Write forwarding lets secondary clusters send writes to the primary. Applications switch connection strings if they use cluster endpoints rather than the global writer endpoint.

blocks.body: RDS cross-Region read replicas (RDS for MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, Db2). The replica is created from the destination Region, referencing the source ARN, and uses the engine's native asynchronous replication. Use for DR, local read scaling and Region migration. To create an encrypted replica in another Region the source must be encrypted and you pass a KMS key from the destination Region. In a disaster you promote the replica manually; for non-Aurora instances the whole process takes a few minutes and includes a reboot. A promoted replica is a standalone instance and cannot become a replica again; you re-establish replication by creating new replicas from it. You pay for the replica instance, storage and cross-Region data transfer. Monitor replication lag with CloudWatch and alarm on it. Compared with Aurora Global Database it has higher lag, slower promotion and fewer managed failover features, so choose it when the engine is RDS (not Aurora) or cost is the priority.

DynamoDB global tables are multi-active: every replica accepts reads and writes (write local). Default mode is multi-Region eventual consistency (MREC): asynchronous replication, typically within a second or so; conflicts on the same item are resolved by last writer wins at item level; transactions are not supported across Regions (readers in another Region can see partial transaction results); strongly consistent reads are strongly consistent only for items last written in that Region; conditional writes evaluate against the local version. Multi-Region strong consistency (MRSC) replicates synchronously to at least one other Region before acknowledging, supports strongly consistent reads from any replica, and a concurrent conflicting write fails with a retryable exception instead of last-writer-wins. An MRSC global table must be deployed in exactly three Regions (three replicas, or two replicas and a witness) and does not support the transaction APIs. Global tables offer a 99.999% availability SLA (compared with 99.99% for single-Region tables), a replica can be in any Region where DynamoDB is available, adding a replica has no performance impact on existing replicas, and a replica can be disassociated to become a standalone table. Failover is an application/DNS decision since both replicas already accept writes: typical designs use Route 53 failover or latency records, with CloudWatch-alarm health checks (for example API 5xx or DynamoDB SystemErrors).

Other stores. ElastiCache Global Datastore: a primary cluster takes writes and replicates asynchronously to secondary clusters in other Regions (read-only); you promote a secondary during Regional degradation, promotion typically takes under a minute per the ElastiCache FAQ, which states there is no RPO/RTO SLA; each cluster may use its own customer managed KMS key. Amazon EFS replication: copies a file system to another Region (or AZ); most changes replicate within a minute and the overall RPO is 15 minutes for most file systems (replication can take longer for frequently changing file systems with more than 100 million files or files larger than 100 GB); the destination is read-only until you fail over, then it becomes writable. S3 replication: cross-Region (CRR) or same-Region (SRR); requires versioning on both buckets and an IAM role that S3 can assume; new objects replicate by default only after the rule exists, so use S3 Batch Replication for existing objects (the bucket needs a replication configuration first). S3 Replication Time Control (RTC) adds an SLA: designed to replicate most objects in seconds and 99.99% within 15 minutes, backed by an SLA that 99.9% of objects replicate within 15 minutes in a billing month; it includes replication metrics and event notifications, and the only accepted value for the threshold/time minutes is 15. RTC is enabled in the replication rule (also with prefix filters), and costs extra (pricing dimensions not verified in this build).

blocks.body: If the stem says Aurora and RPO in seconds / RTO under a minute or a few minutes -> Aurora Global Database (not a snapshot copy, not binlog replica). If it says 'RDS for MySQL' and Multi-Region DR -> cross-Region read replica promoted on failover. If it says 'both Regions must accept writes' on a NoSQL table -> DynamoDB global tables. 'Predictable replication, compliance, 15 minutes' -> S3 RTC. 'Lowest cost secondary database' with relaxed RTO -> headless Aurora secondary or pilot light replica. Replication never replaces backups for corruption or deletion events.

topics.title: Backup architecture: AWS Backup, DLM and data protection

blocks.body: A backup solution that supports business continuity must be automated, policy-driven, cross-Region (and ideally cross-account), tamper-resistant and tested. AWS offers a centralized service (AWS Backup) and service-native options (EBS/AMI snapshots via DLM, RDS automated backups, DynamoDB backups).

AWS Backup is a centralized place to configure, schedule and monitor backups for EBS volumes, EC2 instances, RDS (including Aurora), DynamoDB, EFS, Storage Gateway volumes, FSx file systems and more. A backup plan holds rules (schedule, vault, lifecycle, copy actions); resources are assigned by tag or ARN. A copy action in a rule copies each recovery point to a destination vault ARN in another Region and/or account; if you do not specify a lifecycle for the copy, the source lifecycle applies, and data moved to cold storage must stay there for at least 90 days. Continuous backups give point-in-time recovery, with retention of 1 to 35 days; AWS Backup documents continuous backup support for resources such as Amazon RDS, Aurora and Amazon S3 (check the point-in-time recovery page for the current list), and continuous backups cannot transition to cold storage. For EC2 instance backups AWS Backup also records instance type, VPC, security groups, IAM role, monitoring configuration and tags, but this metadata is used only when restoring in the same Region. AWS Backup can restore but does not schedule restores itself; the whitepaper suggests an SNS + Lambda pattern to restore automatically in the DR Region and recommends periodic restores because restore is a control plane operation.

items: Cross-account copy: the destination vault needs a resource-based access policy permitting `backup:CopyIntoBackupVault` for the source account, role or organization/OU. The vault name is case sensitive and AWS Backup does not validate that the destination vault exists. With AWS Organizations you can allow the whole organization or OUs by PrincipalOrgPaths.

Encryption of copies: AWS Backup encrypts the copy with the destination vault's KMS key, even if the source is unencrypted. For resource types not fully managed by AWS Backup (for example EC2/EBS), the destination vault key must be a customer managed key or the owning service's managed key (aws/ebs); the AWS Backup managed key causes copy job failure. Cross-account copy of resources encrypted with AWS managed keys is not supported for those types because the key policy of an AWS managed key is immutable; use a customer managed key. Unencrypted Aurora, DocumentDB and Neptune clusters stay unencrypted in the copy.

Vault Lock: governance mode lets users with sufficient IAM permissions manage or delete the lock; compliance mode becomes immutable after a grace (cooling-off) time of at least 3 days (72 hours), and no one, including AWS, can alter the lock or delete backups before retention ends. Including ChangeableForDays (minimum 3) on the API creates compliance mode. Pair a compliance-locked vault in a separate account with cross-account copy to protect against ransomware, insider threats and account compromise.

Restore testing: define a restore testing plan (frequency, start time), assign protected resources and choose latest or random recovery points; AWS Backup runs the restore, measures completion time, optionally runs your validation (for example Lambda triggered by EventBridge), then deletes the restored resources. Results feed compliance evidence (Backup Audit Manager reports).
Notifications and monitoring: use vault notifications/EventBridge for job failures and CloudWatch alarms; the whitepaper and the mapped scenarios stress alerting on failed backup and copy jobs.

blocks.body: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) automates EBS snapshot and AMI creation, retention and deletion by policy keyed on tags. A schedule can enable cross-Region copy: copies can be scheduled to up to three Regions from a single policy, with retention set per destination Region, copies are incremental, and you can choose encryption and a KMS key for the copy. Cross-account snapshot copy uses two policies: a source-account snapshot policy that shares snapshots, and a target-account cross-account copy event policy (both created in the same Region; the target account can then copy onward to other Regions), protecting against loss if the source account is compromised. DLM is the lowest-overhead answer when the requirement is only EBS snapshots in additional Regions; AWS Backup is the answer for multiple resource types, central governance, vault lock or cross-account vaults.

topics.title: Elastic Disaster Recovery and multi-Region supporting services

blocks.body: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) provides block-level continuous replication of physical, virtual and cloud servers (and the databases running on them) into a staging area subnet in your AWS account and Region. The staging area uses low-cost storage and minimal compute (replication servers, which the service provisions, manages and recycles every 14 days). On a drill or recovery, DRS converts the servers to boot natively on AWS and launches full-capacity recovery instances in the target VPC within minutes, from the latest state or a point in time; afterwards you can fail back. The whitepaper classifies it as a pilot light implementation, and says it can protect AWS-hosted workloads only if they consist of applications and databases on EC2 (not RDS).

items: Point in time (PIT): EBS snapshots of staging volumes give sub-second (latest) recovery, every 10 minutes for the last hour, hourly for 24 hours, then daily for 1 to 365 days (default 7). Only the DAY rule's retention is configurable; more days means more recovery options and more cost.

Network: replication can use public internet or private connectivity. Enabling 'Use private IP for data replication (VPN, Direct Connect, VPC peering)' keeps replication traffic on private paths; combine with VPC interface endpoints and a staging subnet without an internet gateway when the application must not be reachable publicly. Replication bandwidth can be throttled per source server.
Testing: launch non-disruptive drill instances regularly, monitor replication health, and run failback drills.

blocks.body: Multi-Region building blocks that recurring DR designs depend on. These are easy to forget and exam stems often hinge on them.

items: ECR private image replication: configure replication rules in the registry for cross-Region and cross-account replication; for cross-account replication the destination account must set a registry permissions policy allowing the source account (actions such as ecr:CreateRepository and ecr:ReplicateImage). Container tasks in the DR Region then pull from a local repository.

KMS multi-Region keys: a primary key and its replicas in other Regions share key ID and key material, so you can encrypt in one Region and decrypt in another without re-encrypting or making a cross-Region call. Replicas are independent: key policy, tags, aliases and key state can differ, and pricing and quotas apply to each key. A replica is in the Creating state for a few seconds before use. Each Region can hold only one replica of a given primary key.

Secrets Manager replication: secrets (value and metadata such as tags and resource policies) replicate to selected Regions; replicas share the ARN except for the Region; rotation of the primary propagates to replicas; each replica is billed as a separate secret; you can promote a replica to a standalone secret. Replicated database credentials still point to the source database, so add Region-specific connection info.
ACM certificates are Regional, so the DR Region needs its own certificate for its load balancer (stated here as a general fact; not confirmed on a page retrieved in this build).
AWS CloudFormation / StackSets and Image Builder: deploy identical (or conditionally scaled-down) stacks and AMIs to multiple Regions and accounts.

Amazon WorkSpaces cross-Region redirection: users register with a fully qualified domain name (connection alias) instead of a Region-specific registration code; you associate connection aliases with directories in two Regions and use DNS failover routing (Route 53 with a health check, which can monitor a CloudWatch alarm) to redirect users to the failover Region's WorkSpaces. WorkSpaces must exist in both Regions and the domain must be registered; use of a CloudWatch-alarm health check fails over all users, so omit automated failover if you want a manual decision.

blocks.body: Servers in a data center, a private connection and 'not accessible from the internet' -> Elastic Disaster Recovery with private IP replication over Direct Connect/VPN. Containerized active-active across Regions -> ECR replication + Aurora global database/DynamoDB global tables + per-Region certificates + a latency/failover DNS layer. Encrypted data replicated to another Region -> multi-Region KMS keys or per-Region keys on the destination (RDS replicas and AWS Backup copies re-encrypt with a destination key). DRS is for servers; it does not replicate RDS.

links.label: Replicate Secrets Manager secrets across Regions

blocks.body: A recovery path that is not exercised is assumed broken. The Reliability Pillar says test DR to validate the implementation and regularly test failover to the DR Region to ensure RTO and RPO are met; avoid rarely exercised recovery paths because capacity, quotas and assumptions drift (a read-only secondary that handled queries may not handle writes and production load, and service quotas in the secondary Region may be too low). Prefer a small number of recovery paths and test them frequently. For complex or critical paths, exercise them in production.

items: Backup restore tests: run periodic restores; AWS Backup restore testing automates this and reports restore duration. Restore time measured in a test is your real RTO for that data store.

Failover drills by strategy: pilot light/warm standby - scale the DR Region and send test or real traffic; Aurora - use switchover (RPO 0) for drills and rotation; DRS - launch drill instances without disrupting the source; active/active - test how the workload reacts to loss of a Region (traffic routed away? can remaining Regions take all traffic?), and still test backup recovery for data disasters.

Chaos / fault injection: AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) runs experiments from templates containing actions, targets and stop conditions; a stop condition is a CloudWatch alarm that halts the experiment; a safety lever stops all running experiments and blocks new ones. Choose stop-condition alarms on customer impact, not on the effect you are injecting.

Validation tooling: AWS Resilience Hub lets you define resilience policies with RTO/RPO targets for application, infrastructure, AZ and Region disruptions, assesses components against Well-Architected practices and tells you whether targets are likely to be met. The whitepaper recommends it to continuously validate and track resilience.

Drift: AWS Config can detect configuration drift in the DR Region and trigger Systems Manager Automation to remediate; CloudFormation drift detection covers stacks. Check AMIs and service quotas stay current in the DR Region.

blocks.body: Centralized monitoring to recover proactively. CloudWatch cross-account observability links monitoring accounts to source accounts (within a Region) using Observability Access Manager: a sink in the monitoring account (one sink per Region per account) and a link created from each source account, sharing metrics, log groups, X-Ray traces and more; you can use AWS Organizations to link source accounts. The cross-account cross-Region CloudWatch console lets you view dashboards, metrics and alarms of other accounts and Regions, and cross-account cross-Region centralization copies logs and metrics to a destination using centralization rules. These features are complementary. Alarms drive automation: Route 53 health checks can read CloudWatch alarms (failover on an application signal), alarms can invoke SNS/EventBridge/Lambda/Systems Manager for remediation, and DRS/Backup/Aurora replication-lag metrics should have alarms so that an RPO breach is noticed before a disaster.

Operational habits that exam answers reward: alarm on replication lag (Aurora global replication lag, S3 RTC replication metrics and event notifications, EFS TimeSinceLastSync), alarm on failed backup and copy jobs, run health checks on a real dependency chain (a deep health endpoint or CloudWatch composite alarm) instead of a static page, and keep runbooks automated so manual failover is a single action.

Questions about 'proactively recover' or 'detect failure early' usually want CloudWatch alarms/composite alarms feeding Route 53 health checks, EventBridge or Systems Manager Automation, plus cross-account observability when many accounts are involved. 'Validate that DR meets RTO' -> run a real failover or restore test (FIS/Resilience Hub for assessment); 'without affecting production' -> DRS drills or AWS Backup restore testing in an isolated environment.

links.label: What is AWS Fault Injection Service?

blocks.body: Scenario 1 - Cost-sensitive pilot light for an RDS-backed web application. Requirements: web tier on EC2 behind an ALB in an Auto Scaling group, RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ, RTO 6 hours, RPO 15 minutes, minimal cost, Region-level protection. Constraints: stateless web tier, AMIs already built. Chosen architecture: a cross-Region read replica of the database (continuous asynchronous replication meets the RPO), AMIs copied to the DR Region (or built there by Image Builder), an ALB and an Auto Scaling group with minimum, maximum and desired set to zero, and the same stack defined in CloudFormation so it can be deployed with a scaled-down condition. A Route 53 failover record set (primary alias to the primary ALB, secondary to the DR ALB) uses a health check that watches a CloudWatch alarm; failover triggers automation (Lambda or runbook) that promotes the replica and raises the Auto Scaling group capacity. Rationale: pilot light keeps only the replica running, which is the minimal cost option that still meets a 6 hour RTO; promotion of a non-Aurora replica takes minutes plus scale-out time. Security: encrypted replica using a KMS key in the DR Region, IAM role for the automation limited to rds:PromoteReadReplica and autoscaling:UpdateAutoScalingGroup on named resources. Cost: replica instance, storage and cross-Region transfer; no web fleet. Alternatives rejected: backup and restore (a snapshot restore can miss the 15 minute RPO and takes longer), warm standby (pays for running servers not needed for a 6 hour RTO), multi-site (cost and complexity far above the requirement). Caveat: the automation depends on control plane calls in the DR Region and on quotas there.

Scenario 2 - Active-active API with near-zero RTO. Requirements: global API on API Gateway Regional endpoints and Lambda in two Regions, data in DynamoDB, a third-party API key in Secrets Manager, RTO under one minute, RPO seconds, data encrypted with customer managed keys. Constraints: users on two continents, both Regions should serve traffic. Chosen architecture: a DynamoDB global table with replicas in both Regions; the API deployed identically in both Regions with a custom domain; Route 53 latency records (one per Region) each tied to a health check on a CloudWatch alarm (API 5xx rate or DynamoDB system errors) so an unhealthy Region is removed; the secret replicated with Secrets Manager replication; the secret and data protected with customer managed KMS keys in each Region (multi-Region keys let a Region use its local replica key; the exact key setup for DynamoDB replicas was not verified in this build); certificates created in each Region. TTL kept short (for example 60 s and below) and fast 10 second health checks to meet the target (about TTL + interval x threshold). Rationale: with multi-active data there is nothing to promote, so failover is only a DNS decision. Security: IAM roles per Region scoped to the local table, key and secret; key policies on each replica key. Cost: two full stacks plus global table replicated writes and data transfer. Alternatives rejected: Aurora global database (single writer, wrong data model), CloudFront origin failover (APIs with POST are not covered since failover applies only to GET, HEAD, OPTIONS), pilot light (RTO too long). Trade-offs: last-writer-wins conflict resolution means the application must tolerate or partition writes; transactions and strongly consistent reads do not span Regions in MREC mode.

Scenario 3 - Ransomware-resistant centralized backups across accounts. Requirements: EC2/EBS, RDS and EFS in many accounts of an AWS Organization, backups retained 35 days and monthly for a year, a copy in a second Region, no one able to delete backups early, alerts when a job fails, lowest operational overhead. Chosen architecture: AWS Backup plans with a daily rule and a monthly rule, each with a copy action to a vault in the DR Region of a dedicated backup account; destination vault access policy allowing the organization to copy in (`backup:CopyIntoBackupVault`); customer managed KMS keys on destination vaults (required for resource types not fully managed by AWS Backup such as EC2); Vault Lock in compliance mode on the destination vault with a grace period for validation; vault notifications to SNS for failed jobs; restore testing plans against the destination vault. Rationale: cross-account plus compliance lock protects against account compromise and insiders; restore testing proves the RTO. Cost: storage in both Regions, cross-Region transfer, restore tests; use lifecycle rules (cold storage requires at least 90 days of retention there). Alternatives rejected: custom Lambda snapshot copy scripts (operational overhead), DLM only (EBS only, no central governance for RDS/EFS), governance mode lock (IAM principals can still remove it).

blocks.body: Create the destination vault (with a customer managed KMS key in the DR Region) in the backup account, attach the access policy below, then add a copy action to the plan. Optionally configure Vault Lock (governance first, compliance after validation).

CloudFormation - plan with cross-Region copy

AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Resources:

    Type: AWS::Backup::BackupPlan
    Properties:
      BackupPlan:
        BackupPlanName: dr-daily

blocks.title: F. Verification and troubleshooting checklist
blocks.body: Check: health check status and failover record answer; replication lag metrics; backup copy job status (a copy job fails if the destination key is the AWS Backup managed key for EC2/EBS); destination vault policy and KMS key policy allow the source; DR Region quotas and AMIs exist; promoted replicas have security groups, parameter groups and subnet groups equivalent to the primary; application connection strings or DNS CNAMEs point at the new writer.

Method: (1) underline the primary requirement (RTO, RPO, cost, operational overhead, isolation from account compromise); (2) list mandatory constraints (existing engine, 'no changes to the application', data residency, 'must not be reachable from the internet'); (3) eliminate options that do not span Regions, do not replicate data, depend on manual steps where automation is required, or use the wrong data model; (4) among the remaining options choose the one that matches the keyword (cost, overhead, speed).

items: Replication vs backup: replication copies mistakes; backups (and versioning) restore to a point in time. Questions about corruption, accidental deletion or ransomware need a backup/versioning/lock answer, not just a replica.

Aurora vs RDS: 'Aurora' + minimal RPO/RTO -> Global Database; promotion of a standard RDS replica is slower and manual. Binlog-based Aurora MySQL replicas across Regions are slower and less managed than Global Database.
Switchover vs failover: planned, healthy, zero data loss -> switchover; outage -> failover with possible data loss.

DynamoDB global tables are multi-active: 'fail over' means redirect traffic, not promote. They do not give cross-Region transactions or strongly consistent reads of other Regions' writes in the default mode.

Traffic: Route 53 failover = active-passive; latency/weighted/geolocation with health checks = active-active; CloudFront origin groups = per-request, GET/HEAD/OPTIONS only; Global Accelerator = static anycast IPs and edge failover.
Evaluate Target Health is not a deep health check; if the stem talks about application-level failure signals, think health check on a CloudWatch alarm.

Distractor patterns: an ALB or Auto Scaling group 'spanning Regions' (they are Regional); copying snapshots manually; S3 buckets 'in another Region' without replication; relying on Multi-AZ to satisfy a Region-failure requirement; read replica in the same Region for a Regional DR requirement; a DR design whose recovery steps require control plane APIs that may be impaired.

blocks.body: Check that every layer of the stack is covered: DNS/traffic, compute and images (AMIs/ECR), data stores, secrets and keys, certificates, quotas and the monitoring that triggers failover. An answer that replicates the database but leaves the DR Region with no capacity, no image or no certificate is incomplete.

blocks.title: Key concepts
blocks.body: RTO = how long to restore; RPO = how much data you can lose. Strategy ladder: backup and restore < pilot light < warm standby < multi-site active/active in cost and speed. Replication gives low RPO; backups give point-in-time protection; both are needed. Failover is DNS, anycast or per-request routing driven by health checks or manual switches. Test and monitor continuously.

items: Decision rules: pick the cheapest strategy that meets both RTO and RPO; use data plane failover (health checks, ARC) over control plane (scale-out, restore, weight changes) where RTO is tight; use Aurora Global Database for Aurora, read replicas for RDS, global tables for multi-active NoSQL; use DLM for EBS-only snapshot copies and AWS Backup for everything else, with Vault Lock compliance in a separate account for immutability.

Misconceptions: Multi-AZ is not Regional DR; read replicas in the same Region are not DR; replication is not a backup; Evaluate Target Health is not a deep application check; an Auto Scaling group at zero is not a running warm standby; a promoted read replica cannot be a replica again; Aurora failover with --allow-data-loss can lose data, switchover cannot; CloudFront origin failover does not cover POST.

Service distinctions: pilot light (cannot serve until switched on) vs warm standby (serves at reduced capacity); Route 53 (DNS, TTL-bound) vs Global Accelerator (static IPs, no DNS cache dependence) vs CloudFront origin group (per request); ARC routing control (on/off health checks) vs zonal shift (AZ only); AWS Backup vs DLM; DRS (servers) vs Aurora Global Database (database storage replication).

Numbers to remember (all from retrieved AWS pages): Route 53 health check interval 30 s default or 10 s, threshold 1 to 10 default 3, healthy if more than 18% of checkers agree, failover time about TTL + interval x threshold; multivalue answer returns up to eight healthy records; S3 RTC 99.99% within 15 min with SLA 99.9% in 15 min and only 15 as an accepted minutes value; EFS replication RPO 15 min for most file systems; DLM cross-Region copies up to three Regions per policy; AWS Backup continuous backup retention up to 35 days; cold storage minimum 90 days; DRS PIT retention 1 to 365 days default 7, replication servers recycled every 14 days; Aurora Global Database up to 10 secondary Regions per current guide (older sources say five) and up to 16 readers per secondary; CloudFront origin failover timeouts 1 to 3 attempts, 1 to 10 s connect, 1 to 60 s response.

Takeaways: translate each requirement into RTO/RPO first; always cover data, traffic, compute, keys and quotas in the DR Region; automate and test; centralize monitoring so failure is detected before users report it.

blocks.body: Task 2.3 of the SAP-C02 blueprint, 'Determine security controls based on requirements', sits in Domain 2 (Design for New Solutions). The exam does not ask you to recite console steps. It gives you a business requirement (for example 'credentials must rotate automatically', 'traffic must never cross the internet', 'records must be immutable for a year') plus constraints (least operational overhead, minimal change, lowest cost) and asks you to pick the control that satisfies the requirement exactly. This lesson builds the vocabulary and decision rules to do that quickly.

Prerequisites: you should already know what an IAM role, a VPC, a subnet, an Availability Zone and an S3 bucket are, and have used AWS Organizations at a basic level. Jargon is defined on first use. A 'control' is any mechanism that prevents, detects, or corrects a security problem. 'Data at rest' is data stored on disk or in an object store; 'data in transit' is data moving across a network. 'Least privilege' means granting only the permissions needed for a task and nothing more.

blocks.title: Objectives
blocks.body: By the end of this lesson you will be able to: (1) predict whether a request is allowed by walking IAM policy evaluation, including SCPs, permissions boundaries and resource policies; (2) specify security group and network ACL rules for a multi-tier flow and explain why return traffic behaves differently for each; (3) choose between gateway endpoints, interface endpoints and endpoint/resource policies to keep service traffic private; (4) design an encryption strategy (S3, EBS, RDS, KMS key types, TLS and ACM) that satisfies a stated compliance requirement; (5) select the right credential-management service (AWS Secrets Manager, AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, IAM database authentication, AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, Amazon EC2 Instance Connect) for a scenario; (6) assemble a layered attack-mitigation and patching strategy using Amazon CloudFront, AWS WAF, AWS Shield, Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Security Hub, Amazon Inspector, Amazon Macie and AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager.

The official 'Skills in' statements for this task are: specifying IAM users and roles that adhere to least privilege; specifying inbound and outbound flows with security group and network ACL rules; developing attack mitigation strategies for large-scale web applications; developing encryption strategies for data at rest and in transit; specifying service endpoints for service integrations; and developing patch management strategies to remain compliant with organizational standards. The knowledge areas are IAM, route tables/security groups/network ACLs, encryption options, AWS service endpoints, credential management services, and AWS managed security services (Shield, WAF, GuardDuty, Security Hub).

blocks.body: This task belongs to Domain 2 (Design for New Solutions). The exact domain weighting percentage is not verified against an AWS page in this build; consult the official exam guide on AWS Training and Certification. What the question bank shows is that 104 practice questions in this app map to this lesson, and security requirements are embedded in many architecture questions that are not obviously about security, so treat this lesson as cross-cutting.

topics.title: IAM, least privilege and policy evaluation

blocks.body: Every AWS request is evaluated by the AWS enforcement code against all applicable policies. The documented rules are: by default all requests are implicitly denied (the account root user is the exception); a request must be explicitly allowed by a policy or set of policies; and an explicit deny overrides any allow. Evaluation first looks for an explicit Deny in any applicable policy (Organizations SCPs and RCPs, resource-based policies, identity-based policies, permissions boundaries and session policies). If it finds one, the decision is final. If not, it continues to check that the guardrail layers allow the action and that an allow exists in an identity-based or resource-based policy.

rows: Defines what the principal may do; must be present unless a resource policy grants access in the same account
Resource-based policy (bucket policy, key policy, secret policy, API resource policy)
Can grant cross-account access; has a Principal element
Member-account principals need an Allow in the SCP chain AND in IAM; an explicit Deny in either wins
No - sets a ceiling on resources
Applies to resources in the accounts where it is attached; a managed policy RCPFullAWSAccess is attached by default when RCPs are enabled
Effective permissions are the intersection of the boundary and the identity policy
A role session or federated session

blocks.body: Two points are tested repeatedly. First, SCPs and permissions boundaries never grant anything; they only limit what other policies can grant. An SCP that denies all S3 actions overrides an IAM policy that allows full S3 access, and the converse (an SCP allow with no IAM allow) still results in implicit deny. Second, a permissions boundary is the delegation tool: you let developers create roles for their workloads, but only if the role carries a boundary you defined, so the developer cannot hand out more than the boundary allows. The AWS Security Blog describes the effective permissions as the intersection of the boundary and the permissions policy.

blocks.title: Cross-account access needs two sides
blocks.body: For a resource in account A to be used by a principal in account B, the resource side must allow it (a resource policy such as a bucket policy, key policy or secret resource policy) and the principal side must also allow it (an identity policy in account B). The KMS documentation states this directly: the key policy sets the valid range, but users in the external account cannot use the key until IAM policies in their own account delegate the permissions. Secrets Manager behaves the same way, and the principal also needs access to the encryption key used for the secret.

Least privilege in practice means starting narrow and tightening with evidence. IAM Access Analyzer policy generation reads up to 90 days of AWS CloudTrail events for a user or role, using a service role you supply and a trail that is logging events for the account, and produces a fine-grained policy you review and attach. This is the documented answer when a requirement says 'reduce permissions of an over-privileged role without breaking the workload'. Other best practices from the IAM guide that map to exam wording: use roles with temporary credentials instead of long-lived access keys, scope policies to specific resources and conditions, and use permissions boundaries to delegate administration.

Workload identity is the other recurring theme. Applications on EC2, ECS, EKS and Lambda should obtain credentials from an attached role (instance profile, task role, execution/function role) rather than embedded access keys. In an ECS/Fargate design the task role gives the application container its AWS permissions, which is how you give two containers in the same cluster different permissions, while security groups (covered later) isolate them at the network level. The ECS-specific behaviors here come from the question reasoning rather than a page read in this build.

items: Use conditions to scope broad actions: for KMS, `kms:ViaService` limits a key to calls made through named services, for example EC2 and RDS in one Region; for S3 and API Gateway, `aws:SourceVpce` limits calls to a specific VPC endpoint.
Delegate with boundaries, restrict with SCPs: boundaries constrain individual roles that someone else creates; SCPs constrain whole accounts and OUs.
Deny-list SCPs (allow everything, deny specific actions) are the strategy used in the AWS SCP examples; allow-list SCPs require you to enumerate every permitted service.

Multi-tenant isolation in a shared data store is enforced by giving each tenant's requests credentials that are scoped to that tenant, so IAM, not application code, blocks cross-tenant reads. The exact DynamoDB condition keys used for this are not verified against AWS docs in this build.

blocks.body: Common mistakes: believing an SCP can grant permissions; forgetting that SCPs do not restrict users or roles in the Organizations management account (they affect only member accounts); using the root user or long-lived IAM user keys for automation; writing a cross-account bucket policy but forgetting the KMS key policy for SSE-KMS objects; and attaching a permissions boundary and expecting it to grant access.

When the stem says 'prevent any account in the organization from doing X, even administrators', the answer is an SCP deny. When it says 'allow developers to create roles but never exceed Y', the answer is a permissions boundary. When it says 'right-size permissions using actual usage', the answer is IAM Access Analyzer policy generation.

topics.title: Network flows: route tables, security groups and network ACLs

blocks.body: A VPC gives you two packet-filtering layers plus routing. Route tables decide where traffic goes (for example to an internet gateway, NAT gateway, peering connection or endpoint). Network ACLs (NACLs) filter at the subnet boundary. Security groups filter at the network interface (instance) level. You can secure instances with security groups alone; network ACLs are an additional layer of defense, according to the VPC infrastructure security guide.

rows: Rules evaluated in ascending number order until a match
Stateless: return traffic must be explicitly allowed
Each subnet has exactly one NACL at a time; default NACL used if none chosen
1 to 32766; leave gaps (10 or 100) to insert later

blocks.body: Because security groups only allow, you cannot use one to block a specific bad IP while allowing a wider range; that is a NACL job (a numbered deny rule with a lower number than the allow). Because NACLs are stateless, a rule allowing inbound HTTPS to the subnet does not allow the response; you need a matching outbound rule for the return traffic, and the reverse for outbound connections. NACLs evaluate traffic entering and leaving the subnet, not traffic between instances in the same subnet, and they cannot block DNS requests to the Route 53 Resolver.

blocks.title: Security group referencing is the least-privilege pattern
blocks.body: Instead of allowing a CIDR range, a security group rule can name another security group as the source. The database group allows the database port only from the application group, and the application group allows its port only from the load balancer group. New instances inherit access by joining the right group, and nothing else in the VPC can reach the database. The pattern is the standard answer when a stem asks for 'only the application tier can reach the database'. The VPC infrastructure security guide confirms that security group rules can reference other security groups, and the quota and behavior facts in this lesson come from AWS documentation.

rows: Inbound or outbound rules per security group
Per security group, enforced separately for inbound/outbound and for IPv4/IPv6

blocks.body: Design a three-tier flow like this: the internet reaches the Application Load Balancer (ALB) on port 443 only; the ALB group is the only source for the web tier; the web tier group is the only source for the data tier on the database port; the data tier has no route to an internet gateway. Add a NACL on the data subnets as a coarse second layer (for example, deny everything except the subnet CIDRs of the application tier) and remember to allow return traffic in both directions. When troubleshooting 'connection times out only for some clients', check whether a NACL deny or a missing return rule is responsible before touching security groups.

items: An instance that acts as a transparent proxy, NAT or inspection appliance must have the source/destination check disabled, otherwise it drops traffic that is neither to nor from itself (reasoning; the specific EC2 attribute page was not read in this build).
To inspect traffic copies without sitting in the path, VPC Traffic Mirroring is the purpose-built feature (not verified in this build).
Block a single hostile IP quickly: NACL deny rule with a low number. Block it at an application or CDN edge: AWS WAF IP set rule.

blocks.body: Stateful vs stateless is the most tested distinction. If a stem includes 'explicitly deny a specific IP address range' pick a NACL (or WAF at the edge). If it includes 'allow only the web tier to reach the database' pick security group referencing. If the symptom is that inbound is permitted but responses never arrive, suspect the stateless NACL.

links.label: Control subnet traffic with network ACLs

blocks.body: A VPC endpoint lets resources in a VPC reach an AWS service over the AWS network without an internet gateway or NAT device. There are two main types. Gateway endpoints exist only for Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB; they add routes to the route tables you select and carry no hourly or data-transfer charge. Interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) place elastic network interfaces with private IP addresses in your subnets, support many services, are controlled with security groups, and incur an hourly charge plus a data-processing charge.

rows: Many AWS services, your own services, partner services; also S3
Prefix-list route in the route table
DNS (private DNS name) resolving to ENI private IPs
Hourly per AZ plus per-GB data processing
Reach from on premises, peered VPC, Transit Gateway
Supported (for S3 this is the documented reason to choose an S3 interface endpoint)
Endpoint policy plus security groups on the ENIs

blocks.body: An endpoint policy is a resource-based policy attached to the endpoint that controls which principals can use the endpoint to reach the service; the default policy allows full access. For example, a gateway endpoint policy for DynamoDB can restrict use to read-only describe/list actions, or to one table ARN. Endpoint policies work together with identity policies; both must allow the call. To go the other direction (only allow the service to be reached through your endpoint) put a condition on the resource: an S3 bucket policy can deny all requests where `aws:SourceVpce` is not the expected endpoint ID. Be careful: such a deny also blocks console and administrator access from outside the VPC, so test before applying.

blocks.title: Why private subnets need endpoints
blocks.body: A workload in a private subnet with no NAT cannot reach public AWS service endpoints. For ECS/Fargate tasks on platform version 1.4.0 or later pulling images from Amazon ECR, the documentation requires both ECR interface endpoints (`com.amazonaws.<region>.ecr.api` and `com.amazonaws.<region>.ecr.dkr`) and the Amazon S3 gateway endpoint, because image layers are stored in S3. The `ecr.dkr` endpoint needs the private DNS name option enabled. For Systems Manager, managed instances without internet access need interface endpoints for `ssm`, `ssmmessages` and `ec2messages`; the alternative is outbound HTTPS (443) to those public endpoints.

Private APIs follow the same idea. An Amazon API Gateway private REST API is reachable only through an interface VPC endpoint for `execute-api`. Access is then authorized by a resource policy; the standard pattern from AWS documentation is a policy that allows `execute-api:Invoke` and denies requests whose `aws:sourceVpce` does not match your endpoint ID. In the AWS access-control comparison, resource policies and private endpoints are available for REST APIs but not for HTTP APIs, which matters when a question forces a choice between API types.

items: Exposing your own service privately to other accounts or VPCs: publish it as an endpoint service behind a Network Load Balancer (PrivateLink); consumers create interface endpoints. If the backend is an ALB, the pattern places an NLB (with the ALB as target) in front; both load balancers must be in the same VPC and account (from question reviewer notes; not verified against a page in this build).

Remote developers reaching a VPC-only service (for example an OpenSearch domain in a VPC): AWS Client VPN or Site-to-Site VPN into the VPC, not making the domain public. Client VPN supports Active Directory, mutual certificate and SAML authentication; MFA works with AWS Managed Microsoft AD or AD Connector. A server certificate in ACM is required for every Client VPN endpoint.

WorkSpaces access restricted to branch offices: IP access control groups list allowed public IP ranges (25 groups per directory, 100 per Region); if users come through NAT or VPN, use their static public addresses.
S3 from on premises over Direct Connect: a gateway endpoint does not extend to on premises; use an S3 interface endpoint (documented in the AWS Architecture Blog).

blocks.body: 'Without traversing the internet' plus 'S3 or DynamoDB from inside the same VPC' means gateway endpoint (free). 'Without traversing the internet' plus 'from on premises' or 'from another VPC/Region' means interface endpoint. If the stem shows a Fargate CannotPullContainerError in a private subnet, the fix is ECR endpoints plus the S3 gateway endpoint (or a NAT gateway if the stem allows internet egress). Do not confuse the endpoint policy (what the endpoint permits) with the bucket policy (what the bucket permits).
