topics.title: Encryption at rest: KMS keys and service integrations

blocks.body: AWS Key Management Service (KMS) creates and controls the keys that other services use for encryption. A KMS key (formerly called a customer master key, CMK; older exam wording still says CMK) never leaves KMS in plaintext. Services use envelope encryption: KMS protects a data key, and the data key encrypts the data. You choose between AWS managed keys (created per service in your account, such as aws/ebs; you cannot edit their policy and you cannot change their rotation), customer managed keys (you control policy, rotation, deletion and cross-account use), and AWS owned keys (managed by the service). Cross-account use requires a customer managed key, because you cannot modify the key policy of an AWS managed key.

rows: Always automatic, every year (changed from three years in May 2022); not configurable
Simple default with no key governance requirements
Optional automatic rotation for symmetric encryption keys; default period 365 days, configurable 90 to 2,560 days; on-demand rotation available
Control access per user/role, share cross-account, audit, scheduled rotation
You generate and import wrapped material
Automatic rotation is not supported; on-demand rotation can be used for symmetric keys with imported material
Regulation requires that you generate the key material, for example in your own HSM
Same key ID and material replicated to replicas
Rotation status is synchronized with the primary
Encrypt in one Region, decrypt in another without re-encryption or cross-Region calls

blocks.title: Imported key material (origin EXTERNAL)
blocks.body: To satisfy 'our on-premises HSM must generate the key material': create a KMS key with origin EXTERNAL (state PendingImport), download the wrapping public key and import token, encrypt (wrap) your key material with the wrapping key, then import it. The first material becomes usable immediately. You can set an expiration, after which KMS deletes the material and the key becomes unusable until you reimport the same material. You cannot import key material into a KMS key in a custom key store. AWS KMS cannot reach into your HSM to fetch material; you push it in.

Rotation details worth memorizing: previous key material is kept so existing ciphertext can still be decrypted; automatic rotation applies only to symmetric encryption KMS keys and cannot be enabled for asymmetric keys, HMAC keys, imported-material keys or custom-key-store keys; it does nothing while a key is disabled or pending deletion; the on-demand rotation API (`RotateKeyOnDemand`) is limited to 25 on-demand rotations per KMS key, a quota that cannot be increased; and the first two rotations add a monthly charge per key, after which the charge is capped.

Multi-Region keys solve client-side encryption across Regions. Because replicas share key ID and key material, ciphertext produced in us-east-1 can be decrypted in eu-west-1 with the replica key without a cross-Region call. A replica is otherwise independent: it has its own key policy, grants, aliases and tags; enabling or disabling one does not affect the others; and whether a key is single-Region or multi-Region cannot be changed after creation. This is the right answer when an application encrypts data before upload and S3 replication copies the objects to other Regions.

Key policies are the primary access control for KMS. The default key policy statement lets the account's IAM policies manage access; without that statement (or an explicit grant to the principal) an IAM policy alone is not enough. For AWS-service integrations the `kms:ViaService` condition restricts a key to requests that come through named services, and EBS/EC2 launches use grants (`kms:CreateGrant`) so the service can use the key on your behalf. For client-side encryption the calling role needs the KMS permissions for the operations it performs, typically `kms:GenerateDataKey` to obtain a data key for encrypting and `kms:Decrypt` to unwrap it.
The following bullets describe the main service integrations.

items: Amazon S3: since 5 January 2023 every new object is encrypted with SSE-S3 at no charge, so 'turn on default encryption' is already true. Choose SSE-KMS (or dual-layer DSSE-KMS) when you need control over keys, key rotation and access grants. With SSE-KMS as the default you can enable S3 Bucket Keys to reduce request traffic from S3 to KMS and lower cost. S3 does not validate the key ID you supply in PutBucketEncryption, so verify it. Existing objects are not re-encrypted by a setting change; copy them (for example with S3 Batch Operations) to change their encryption.

Amazon EBS: encryption by default is a Region-specific account setting; once on, you cannot disable it for individual volumes or snapshots in that Region. It affects only volumes and snapshot copies created afterward, not existing ones. The default key is aws/ebs or a symmetric customer managed key; volumes under aws/ebs cannot be shared across accounts. Copying a snapshot to a new KMS key produces a full (non-incremental) copy with extra storage cost. This is the least-effort answer to 'encrypt all new EBS volumes'.

Amazon RDS and Aurora: you can encrypt a DB instance only at creation. To encrypt an existing one, snapshot it, copy the snapshot with encryption enabled, and restore a new instance from the encrypted copy; you cannot create an encrypted read replica of an unencrypted instance or restore an unencrypted snapshot to an encrypted instance. Cross-Region encrypted snapshot copies need a KMS key in the destination Region.

Aurora Database Activity Streams: near-real-time audit stream of database activity delivered to Amazon Kinesis, always encrypted with a KMS key, started at the cluster level (instances added later are audited automatically; for an Aurora global database start one stream per cluster). Use it when database administrators must not be able to alter the audit trail.
Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString: encrypts the value (not the name or metadata) with KMS symmetric keys; standard parameters are limited to 4,096 bytes.

blocks.title: Immutability: S3 Object Lock
blocks.body: Object Lock gives write-once-read-many protection per object version. Compliance mode: no user, including the root user, can overwrite or delete a protected version, change the mode or shorten the retention period; the only way to remove it before expiry is to delete the AWS account. Governance mode: most users cannot overwrite or delete, but principals with `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention` who send the bypass header can. A legal hold has no expiry and is independent of retention. Retention and mode are set per object version or as a bucket default. For 'cannot be modified for at least one year, even by administrators, and immediately readable' use compliance mode with a one-year default retention on a versioned bucket. S3 Glacier Vault Lock is a separate feature for Glacier vaults; it is not verified in this build, so do not mix it with S3 Object Lock in an answer.

Preventing public exposure is a separate at-rest control. S3 Block Public Access has four independent settings: BlockPublicAcls (reject new public ACLs), IgnorePublicAcls (ignore any ACL that grants public access, including existing ones), BlockPublicPolicy (reject new public bucket policies) and RestrictPublicBuckets (ignore public and cross-account access granted through public policies). If objects became public through ACLs, IgnorePublicAcls neutralizes them even for ACLs already in place; if the exposure comes from a public bucket policy you also need RestrictPublicBuckets. Block Public Access can be set at account, bucket and access point level and overrides bucket policies and ACLs.

items: Enforce TLS and encryption in a bucket policy with explicit Deny statements: `aws:SecureTransport` false denies HTTP; a Deny on `s3:PutObject` without the required encryption header or KMS key denies unencrypted uploads (the exact header-based statement is not quoted from a page read in this build).
Compliance archive pattern: versioned bucket + Object Lock compliance + default retention + SSE-KMS; add cross-account or cross-Region copy for protection against compromised credentials (reasoning).
Sensitive data discovery: Amazon Macie (see the last service topic) finds PII, then re-encrypt or restrict the affected objects.

blocks.body: Decode the requirement words. 'Customer must control key material' = imported key material. 'Rotate keys automatically' = KMS automatic rotation on a customer managed symmetric key (not imported). 'Decrypt in another Region without re-encrypting' = multi-Region key. 'Encrypt an existing RDS instance' = snapshot, encrypted copy, restore. 'Encrypt new EBS volumes with least effort' = EBS encryption by default. 'Immutable even for root' = Object Lock compliance mode. 'Audit trail database admins cannot tamper with' = Database Activity Streams.

topics.title: Encryption in transit, TLS termination and certificates

blocks.body: Encryption in transit protects data moving between client and server (TLS, formerly SSL) and between services. Three decisions recur: where TLS terminates, which certificate service issues the certificate, and how you enforce that plaintext is refused.

rows: TLS terminated at the load balancer
ALB/NLB holds an ACM certificate and decrypts; backend traffic is a separate connection (HTTP or HTTPS)
Offload work, central certificate management; only if policy allows plaintext inside the VPC
Load balancer terminates client TLS and opens a new HTTPS connection to targets that hold their own certificates
Requirement says encrypted between client and the web server/instance; the instances must present certificates
NLB TCP listener forwards encrypted traffic to the target, which terminates TLS
True end-to-end encryption, client certificate handled by the target (reasoning; NLB behavior not read in this build)
Viewer-to-CloudFront HTTPS and CloudFront-to-origin HTTPS configured separately
Global delivery; both legs must be set to HTTPS to be encrypted end to end

blocks.body: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) issues and renews public certificates and integrates with Elastic Load Balancing, CloudFront and API Gateway. Regional rules matter: ACM certificates are Regional resources, so a certificate must be requested or imported in the same Region as the load balancer that uses it, and you cannot associate a certificate across Regions. For CloudFront viewer-to-edge HTTPS the certificate must be requested or imported in US East (N. Virginia); for the CloudFront-to-ALB leg, the origin load balancer's certificate can be in any Region. A company with applications in a single Region needs certificates in that Region only; adding a CloudFront layer adds a us-east-1 certificate.

blocks.title: Exportable ACM certificates changed an old exam rule
blocks.body: The classic rule 'ACM public certificates cannot be installed on EC2 instances because you cannot export the private key' is no longer universally true. ACM now offers exportable public certificates: you must choose export when requesting a new certificate (previously issued certificates cannot be exported, and the export setting cannot be changed after issuance), they are valid for 198 days, and there is a charge at issuance and again at renewal. Non-exportable ACM public certificates remain free and attach only to integrated services (ELB, CloudFront, API Gateway). When an exam item still assumes certificates cannot leave ACM, the better answer usually remains terminating TLS on a load balancer or using an imported/third-party certificate, but be aware of this change.

items: Client VPN requires a server certificate in ACM regardless of authentication type.

ALB user authentication (`authenticate-cognito` and `authenticate-oidc` actions) works only on HTTPS listeners; the load balancer sets a session cookie (default session timeout 7 days, configurable down to 1 second) and can deny, allow or redirect unauthenticated requests.

Enforce HTTPS at S3 with a bucket policy that denies requests where `aws:SecureTransport` is false. Config rule `s3-bucket-ssl-requests-only` expects exactly that explicit deny; a bucket policy that merely allows HTTPS may not comply.
IAM database authentication uses TLS; the SSL/TLS connection encrypts traffic to and from the database.

Prevent man-in-the-middle at the DNS layer: Route 53 DNSSEC signing protects against forged DNS answers (the Route 53 DNSSEC page was not retrieved in this build) combined with TLS on the load balancer.

blocks.body: In an end-to-end encryption requirement, work from the client outward. If a stem demands encryption 'between the client and the web server', a design that decrypts at a load balancer and forwards plaintext fails; the passing designs either re-encrypt to instances holding certificates or pass TLS through to them. If the stem demands HTTPS 'to the origin' in a CloudFront design, the origin protocol policy must be HTTPS-only and the origin must present a valid certificate; with S3 as the origin, a bucket policy denying non-TLS requests is the complement (these origin-protocol details are reasoning, not quoted from a page read in this build).

Look for the word 'client' and the word 'instance'. 'Client to load balancer' is satisfied by an ACM certificate on the listener. 'Client to web server' needs re-encryption or passthrough. Any CloudFront certificate question has a us-east-1 trap; any load balancer certificate question has a same-Region trap.

topics.title: Credential management and secure administrative access

blocks.body: The most common security finding on the exam is a credential that is stored where it should not be: a password in Lambda environment variables, an access key on an instance, an SSH private key in an S3 bucket. The fix hierarchy is: remove the credential entirely by using a role; if a secret is unavoidable, store it in a managed secret store and rotate it; if a human needs a shell, use a brokered session rather than a long-lived key.

rows: AWS API access for a workload
IAM role (instance profile, task role, function role)
Temporary credentials delivered by the platform; no keys to store or rotate
Database password that must rotate automatically
Rotation invokes a Lambda function (or managed rotation for secrets managed by another service); steps create_secret, set_secret, test_secret, finish_secret; one rotation schedule per secret
Database login without a stored password
IAM database authentication (RDS/Aurora MySQL and PostgreSQL)
Application requests a SigV4 authentication token valid 15 minutes; token is used only to authenticate and does not affect the established session; connection uses TLS
KMS-encrypted values; AWS docs recommend Secrets Manager for secrets needing automatic rotation, cross-account access or fine-grained audit
Interactive shell on EC2, no open ports
IAM-controlled; no inbound ports, bastion hosts or SSH keys; session activity logged to CloudTrail, S3 or CloudWatch Logs
API pushes a one-time public key to instance metadata for 60 seconds; needs `ec2-instance-connect:SendSSHPublicKey` permission
Per-device certificates and policies (not verified against docs in this build)

blocks.body: Secrets Manager rotation in detail. A rotation schedule invokes a Lambda function several times, each call carrying a Step parameter (create_secret, set_secret, test_secret, finish_secret), the secret ARN and a ClientRequestToken for idempotency. If any step fails, Secrets Manager retries the entire rotation process several times during open rotation windows. If you manually update the secret while rotation is configured, Secrets Manager treats that as a valid rotation when computing the next date. Schedules can use a cron-style expression (six fields, minutes must be 0), which lets you pin rotation to an off-peak window. In CloudFormation, `AWS::SecretsManager::RotationSchedule` configures the schedule and either a hosted rotation function (`HostedRotationLambda`) or an existing function ARN; for secrets defined in the same template as the database you attach the secret to the database with `AWS::SecretsManager::SecretTargetAttachment` and add a `DependsOn` so the rotation is configured after the connection details exist. Only one rotation schedule is allowed per secret.

Applications must read the secret at run time, not at deployment time, so that a rotation does not leave a stale value in an environment variable. Pass the secret's ARN or name to the function (a reference, not the value) and have the function call Secrets Manager using its execution role. Grant that role `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` for the single secret, plus `kms:Decrypt` on the customer managed key if one is used. For Fargate, ECS can inject a Secrets Manager value into the container as an environment variable at launch, so the credential is never written to disk in the image (ECS injection behavior is reasoning in this lesson, not quoted from a page read).

blocks.title: Cross-account and key considerations
blocks.body: To share a secret across accounts you need three things: a resource-based policy on the secret naming the external role, a statement in the key policy of the customer managed KMS key granting that role `kms:Decrypt` (plus `kms:GenerateDataKey` if it will write), and an identity policy in the external account. Because AWS managed keys cannot have their policies edited, a secret shared cross-account must use a customer managed key. A customer managed key is also the way to separate development and production access: developers may be allowed one key and secret but not the other.

items: Parameter Store vs Secrets Manager: choose Secrets Manager when the stem says rotate, replicate across Regions, share cross-account or audit access to a secret; choose Parameter Store when the stem is about configuration values and cost. The AWS Parameter Store page itself recommends Secrets Manager for credentials that need automatic rotation.

Rotating non-database secrets such as per-instance SSH key pairs: a custom Secrets Manager rotation Lambda that generates a new key pair and updates the instance, triggered on a schedule or on request with the rotate-secret call (reasoning; custom rotation is described in the Secrets Manager rotation documentation read here).

Remove SSH keys entirely: Session Manager gives IAM-based access and per-session logging; logging is configured in Session Manager preferences, not on by default. EC2 Instance Connect keeps SSH but replaces permanent keys with 60-second keys, and the key push call appears in CloudTrail (the SSH session itself is not logged by CloudTrail).
Detect credentials already committed to code with a scanning control and automate remediation; the exact AWS service for CodeCommit secret scanning is not verified in this build.

Active Directory integration for admin access: AWS Managed Microsoft AD for domain-joined Windows fleets, AD Connector to proxy to an on-premises or EC2-hosted directory, Client VPN for remote access with MFA when the directory supports it.

blocks.body: If the choices include 'store the password in an encrypted S3 file', 'Lambda environment variable', or 'hard-code in a config file', they are distractors. The winning option removes the secret (IAM role or IAM database authentication) or stores it in Secrets Manager with rotation. IAM database authentication only helps when the database engine supports it and the client can request tokens; if the requirement is 'rotate on a schedule with the same username and password flow', pick Secrets Manager. 'No SSH keys and audited sessions' = Session Manager.

topics.title: Attack mitigation for web applications and APIs

blocks.body: Large-scale web applications face distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) floods at layers 3 and 4 (network and transport), layer 7 (application) attacks such as HTTP floods and SQL injection, bots, and direct-to-origin bypass. The mitigation strategy is layered: absorb at the edge, filter at the application layer, restrict the origin, authenticate and throttle at the API, and keep everything else private.

rows: Caches, terminates viewer TLS, absorbs traffic at edge locations; can send a custom origin header and sign requests to S3 with origin access control

Web ACLs with managed and custom rules, rate-based rules, IP sets, geographic match, bot controls; attaches to CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway REST APIs, AppSync, Cognito user pools, App Runner and Verified Access

Standard: automatic, no additional charge, common network/transport-layer attacks. Advanced: paid, protects EC2 Elastic IPs, ELB, CloudFront, Route 53 hosted zones and Global Accelerator, adds automatic layer 7 mitigation, event visibility and Shield Response Team (SRT) support
Applies WAF and Shield Advanced settings across accounts in an organization
API Gateway authorizers, resource policies, usage plans
Authentication, authorization, per-client throttles and quotas

blocks.body: AWS WAF specifics. A web ACL has a scope: for CloudFront the scope is CLOUDFRONT and the API/CLI calls must target US East (N. Virginia); for regional resources (ALB, API Gateway REST API, AppSync, Cognito user pool, App Runner, Verified Access) the web ACL lives in the resource's Region. A web ACL cannot protect a standalone EC2 instance or an API on EC2 unless a supported front end such as an ALB sits in front. Rate-based rules count requests per aggregation key over a time window and can be combined with scope-down statements such as a geo match. Logging goes to CloudWatch Logs, Amazon S3 or Firehose (a Firehose delivery stream used for WAF logs must be named with the prefix aws-waf-logs-). WAF logs all inspected requests unless you apply a logging filter, so 'log only blocked requests' needs a filter. Geographic blocking for a web application behind an ALB is a WAF geo match rule, with logging enabled on the web ACL, rather than building the logic into security groups.

AWS Shield. Shield Standard is automatic. Shield Advanced is a subscription, and the security reference architecture advises protecting only the entry point of a data flow (for example the CloudFront distribution rather than both CloudFront and the ALB behind it) to avoid paying Shield data-transfer-out fees twice. Proactive engagement lets the SRT contact you during an event and relies on Route 53 health checks associated with the protected resources as an additional signal. Shield Advanced's automatic layer 7 mitigation generates AWS WAF rules for you. Pricing specifics for Shield Advanced are not verified in this build.

blocks.title: Lock the origin behind CloudFront
blocks.body: Putting CloudFront in front of an ALB does nothing if attackers can hit the ALB directly. The documented controls are used together: (1) configure CloudFront to add a secret custom header to origin requests (for example X-Origin-Verify) and add a WAF rule on the ALB that blocks requests whose header does not match; (2) restrict the ALB security group to the AWS managed prefix list `com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing` so only CloudFront addresses reach it at layers 3 and 4. AWS says to use both for the strongest protection. Rotating the secret header value can be automated with Secrets Manager, and the header is an origin-access control, not a substitute for application authentication. For S3 origins use origin access control (OAC), which supports all Regions, SSE-KMS and PUT/DELETE; the older origin access identity (OAI) is legacy. An S3 bucket configured as a static website endpoint is a custom origin, so OAC/OAI cannot be used for it.

API Gateway protection. Access-control methods are identity-based (IAM/SigV4, Lambda authorizers, Cognito user pool authorizers for REST APIs, JWT authorizers for HTTP APIs), resource-based (resource policies, REST APIs only), and network-based (private endpoints for REST APIs, mutual TLS for REST and HTTP APIs). Only one identity-based method can be associated with a particular endpoint. IAM authorization fits internal callers with AWS credentials and pairs with AWS X-Ray tracing for end-to-end latency analysis. A Cognito user pool authorizer fits end users and removes the need to run an identity server. Usage plans associate API keys with throttling (average rate and burst) and quota (requests per day, week or month) so each customer gets its own limits; API keys identify callers and meter use, so combine them with a real authorizer for authentication. Public partner APIs commonly add AWS WAF (IP allow list or rate limit) in front of a Regional REST API, since WAF supports REST API stages. A plan's quota should be treated as an approximate control rather than a hard guarantee (reviewer note; not verified against a page read in this build).

items: Non-HTTP or non-standard methods: WAF and CloudFront only apply to HTTP(S); for a UDP service use an NLB with a Network ACL and Shield Advanced on its Elastic IPs; for global anycast entry use AWS Global Accelerator. (Method support specifics for CloudFront/API Gateway are not verified in this build.)
ALB authentication offloads user login to Cognito user pools or any OIDC provider (federation details of user pools are not verified in this build); the application receives verified user claims.
Brute-force and bot mitigation: WAF rate-based rules and bot control at the edge; do not rely on instance-level fail2ban-style controls for a scaled-out fleet.
Replace bastions and open SSH with Session Manager so no management ports face the internet; place the database in private subnets with Multi-AZ for availability.
CORS problems with browsers calling an API are configuration, not security-service, issues: enable CORS on the API (details not verified in this build).

blocks.body: Match the attack to the service. Volumetric network flood = Shield (Advanced if the stem says SRT, cost protection, or protection for non-CloudFront resources). SQL injection, XSS, geo-blocking, IP allow list, rate limiting = WAF. Direct hits on the origin = custom header plus WAF plus CloudFront prefix list. Per-customer quota = usage plan. 'Authenticate users with no servers to manage' = Cognito authorizer. WAF cannot protect a bare EC2 instance with an Elastic IP; the fix is to put an ALB or CloudFront in front, or use Shield Advanced for DDoS only.

blocks.body: Preventive controls are not enough; the exam also expects you to add detective and corrective controls and to keep software current. The managed security services split by the question they answer.

rows: Foundational: CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs, Route 53 Resolver DNS query logs. Optional protection plans: S3, EKS, ECS/EC2 runtime, Malware Protection, RDS login events, Lambda network activity
Enabling it starts analysis automatically; you do not turn on the log sources; 30-day free trial per Region; does not block, it generates findings
AWS Security Hub CSPM (formerly Security Hub)

Delegated administrator (not the Organizations management account); central configuration policies from a home Region

EC2 instances, Lambda functions, ECR container images, code repositories

blocks.body: GuardDuty, Security Hub and Inspector are commonly connected through Amazon EventBridge to automate response (for example a Lambda function isolates an instance or revokes a key). Inspector finding events and container scan summaries are emitted to EventBridge, which lets a pipeline block an image or AMI from approval when findings exceed a threshold. For AMIs and golden images, the pattern is: build, scan with Inspector, approve through an automated rule, and rescan on a schedule or CVE publication (a composed pattern; no single page describes it).

blocks.title: Patch Manager and Quick Setup
blocks.body: Patch Manager (a Systems Manager capability) scans and installs OS patches using patch baselines. AWS-RunPatchBaseline is the command document: operation Scan reports missing patches and compliance; operation Install applies them and may reboot. The default patch baseline per OS decides approvals; for Windows the AWS default baseline includes critical updates and security updates rated critical or important. Custom baselines and Patch Group tags let you target different baselines at different fleets. An InstallOverrideList stored in S3 overrides which patches are installed (compliance is still reported against the baseline). Instances need to reach Systems Manager (VPC endpoints or internet) and the patch source buckets. For many accounts and Regions, Quick Setup patch policies let you define one policy with Organizations that applies across all accounts and Regions (or selected OUs), with separate schedules for scanning and installing, whereas maintenance windows, State Manager associations and Patch now target a single account-Region pair.

items: Patching isolated instances: no internet means VPC endpoints for ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages plus S3 access for patch operation buckets (gateway endpoint); a patch source in another account can be reached through peering or a shared source with cross-account permissions (from the question reviewer notes; not verified here).

Compliance with organizational standards: patch baselines define what 'compliant' means; Systems Manager Compliance shows which nodes are missing patches; Security Hub and Inspector report vulnerabilities against standards.
Immutable infrastructure alternative: rebuild AMIs/containers and redeploy rather than patching in place; Inspector scanning of ECR images fits this model.
Org-wide emergency patching: delegated administrator or Quick Setup patch policy in the management structure, targeting production or non-production OUs first, depending on the stem.

blocks.body: GuardDuty detects, WAF blocks, Shield absorbs, Inspector finds vulnerabilities, Macie finds sensitive data, Security Hub aggregates and measures compliance, Patch Manager remediates OS patch gaps. If the stem asks to 'automatically find AND remediate' you need an EventBridge or Lambda automation around the detective service. If it says 'across thousands of instances in multiple accounts', choose Quick Setup patch policies with Organizations over per-account maintenance windows.

blocks.body: Three worked scenarios show how requirements turn into controls. Each lists requirements, constraints, the chosen design, security, cost, and rejected alternatives.

blocks.title: Scenario 1 - Immutable financial statements with leaked-credential protection
blocks.body: Requirements: monthly statements stored 7 years, immutable, immediately available for the first 2 years, encrypted with keys the security team controls, no public access, and protection if an engineer's long-term access keys leak. Constraints: low operational overhead; existing account uses a single S3 bucket. Design: a new versioned bucket with Object Lock enabled and a default retention in compliance mode matching the legal period; SSE-KMS with a customer managed key (automatic rotation on) whose key policy names only the writer and reader roles; Block Public Access on at account level; a bucket policy that denies any request with `aws:SecureTransport` false; a gateway endpoint for access from the application VPC; and S3 lifecycle rules to move older statements to a cheaper storage class (storage-class details are not covered in this lesson). Security: compliance mode means even root or a leaked admin key cannot delete or shorten retention; the KMS key policy keeps decrypt rights separate from bucket rights. Cost: Object Lock itself is a configuration, SSE-KMS adds KMS request charges that S3 Bucket Keys reduce. Rejected: governance mode (a principal with the bypass permission could remove protection - fails the leaked-credential threat); relying on MFA delete alone; a Glacier-only design (statements must be immediately available, and Vault Lock is not an S3 bucket feature).

blocks.title: Scenario 2 - Serverless partner API with database
blocks.body: Requirements: external partners and web users call a REST API; each partner has a daily quota; a surge of requests from unknown sources must be blocked; Lambda reads an RDS MySQL database whose credentials must rotate and whose storage must be encrypted; the team wants no servers for identity. Design: API Gateway REST API with a Cognito user pool authorizer for end users and IAM or API keys plus usage plans for partners; AWS WAF web ACL on the stage with an IP allow list or rate-based rule; Lambda in private subnets using an execution role limited to one secret; Secrets Manager secret with a rotation schedule (30 days) and a customer managed KMS key; an encrypted copy of the existing database created from a snapshot and cut over, because an existing instance cannot be encrypted in place; interface endpoint for Secrets Manager so the function needs no NAT. Security: authenticated, throttled, filtered, secrets never in environment variables. Cost: interface endpoints bill hourly per AZ, which is usually cheaper than adding NAT gateways for one service; WAF bills per web ACL and rule (pricing not verified in this build). Rejected: API keys alone as authentication (they identify and meter, they do not authenticate); storing the password in an encrypted S3 file (no rotation); hosting a self-managed identity server (violates 'no servers').

blocks.title: Scenario 3 - Container web platform under attack
blocks.body: Requirements: public web application on ECS Fargate behind an ALB; tasks must run in private subnets; the company has seen DDoS and injection attacks; operators currently SSH to hosts; compliance requires monthly patch evidence across 40 accounts. Design: CloudFront in front with an ACM certificate in us-east-1; WAF web ACL on CloudFront with managed rules and a rate-based rule; Shield Advanced on the CloudFront distribution only (the entry point); ALB locked with a custom origin header checked by a WAF rule on the ALB plus its security group restricted to the CloudFront origin-facing managed prefix list; Fargate tasks pull images through ECR interface endpoints plus the S3 gateway endpoint; no SSH (Fargate has no host; for any EC2 hosts use Session Manager); GuardDuty and Security Hub enabled organization-wide through a delegated administrator; Inspector scanning ECR images; Quick Setup patch policy for any EC2 instances. Security: layered controls from edge to task. Cost: Shield Advanced is a subscription (cost details not verified) so protect the entry point only; gateway endpoint is free. Rejected: WAF on the ALB only (does not absorb volumetric load and leaves CloudFront bypass unaddressed); security-group-only filtering (cannot do layer 7 inspection); NAT gateway for ECR pulls when the requirement is no internet path.

links.label: Restrict access to Application Load Balancers

blocks.body: This topic gives console paths, CLI commands, policy JSON and a CloudFormation template for the controls in this lesson. Placeholders such as <account-id>, <region> and <secret> must be replaced. Commands are illustrative; no outputs are shown because none were executed in this build.

items: Encrypt an existing RDS instance: console RDS > Databases > select instance > Actions > Take snapshot; Snapshots > select > Actions > Copy snapshot > enable encryption and choose the KMS key; restore the encrypted snapshot to a new instance; repoint the application; delete the old instance after validation.
Turn on EBS encryption by default: EC2 console > Settings > Data protection and security > EBS encryption > Manage > Enable; keep aws/ebs or choose a customer managed key; repeat for every Region.
Create a private path to S3: VPC console > Endpoints > Create endpoint > AWS services > com.amazonaws.<region>.s3 type Gateway > select route tables > optionally edit the endpoint policy.

Lock down an S3 bucket: Permissions > Block public access (enable all four) and Bucket policy (TLS deny, optional aws:SourceVpce deny); Properties > Default encryption > SSE-KMS with the customer managed key and Bucket Key.
Add rotation: Secrets Manager > Store a new secret > Credentials for RDS database > choose DB > Automatic rotation > set schedule.

blocks.label: CLI - encryption controls
blocks.body:
# EBS encryption by default (per Region)
aws ec2 enable-ebs-encryption-by-default --region <region>
aws ec2 get-ebs-encryption-by-default --region <region>

# Encrypt an existing RDS instance via snapshot copy
aws rds create-db-snapshot --db-instance-identifier <db-id> --db-snapshot-identifier <snap-id>
aws rds copy-db-snapshot --source-db-snapshot-identifier <snap-id> \
  --target-db-snapshot-identifier <snap-id>-enc --kms-key-id <kms-key-id>
aws rds restore-db-instance-from-db-snapshot --db-instance-identifier <db-id>-enc \
  --db-snapshot-identifier <snap-id>-enc

# KMS key for imported material
aws kms create-key --origin EXTERNAL --description "HSM-generated material"
aws kms get-parameters-for-import --key-id <key-id> \
  --wrapping-algorithm RSAES_OAEP_SHA_256 --wrapping-key-spec RSA_2048
# wrap your key material with the returned public key, then:
aws kms import-key-material --key-id <key-id> \
  --encrypted-key-material fileb://<wrapped-material.bin> \
  --import-token fileb://<import-token.bin> --expiration-model KEY_MATERIAL_DOES_NOT_EXPIRE

# Automatic rotation (symmetric, KMS-generated material only)
aws kms enable-key-rotation --key-id <key-id> --rotation-period-in-days 180

# Object Lock bucket, compliance default retention
aws s3api create-bucket --bucket <bucket-name> --object-lock-enabled-for-bucket \
  --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint=<region>
aws s3api put-object-lock-configuration --bucket <bucket-name> --object-lock-configuration \
  '{"ObjectLockEnabled":"Enabled","Rule":{"DefaultRetention":{"Mode":"COMPLIANCE","Years":1}}}'

# Block Public Access
aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket <bucket-name> --public-access-block-configuration \
  BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true

CloudFormation
blocks.body:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: "2010-09-09"
Description: Secret with rotation, tier-to-tier security groups, S3 gateway endpoint
Parameters:
  VpcId: {Type: AWS::EC2::VPC::Id}
  RouteTableId: {Type: String}
  DbInstanceId: {Type: String}
Resources:
  DbSecret:
    Type: AWS::SecretsManager::Secret
    Properties:
      GenerateSecretString:
        SecretStringTemplate: '{"username":"admin"}'
        GenerateStringKey: password
        PasswordLength: 32
        ExcludeCharacters: '"@/\\'
  SecretAttachment:
    Type: AWS::SecretsManager::SecretTargetAttachment
    Properties:
      SecretId: !Ref DbSecret
      TargetId: !Ref DbInstanceId
      TargetType: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
  RotationSchedule:
    Type: AWS::SecretsManager::RotationSchedule
    DependsOn: SecretAttachment
    Properties:
      SecretId: !Ref DbSecret
      HostedRotationLambda:
        RotationType: MySQLSingleUser
      RotationRules:
        AutomaticallyAfterDays: 30
  AppSg:
    Type: AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup
    Properties:
      GroupDescription: Application tier
      VpcId: !Ref VpcId
  DbSg:
    Type: AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup
    Properties:
      GroupDescription: Database tier - only from AppSg
      VpcId: !Ref VpcId
      SecurityGroupIngress:
        - IpProtocol: tcp
          FromPort: 3306
          ToPort: 3306
          SourceSecurityGroupId: !Ref AppSg
  S3GatewayEndpoint:
    Type: AWS::EC2::VPCEndpoint
    Properties:
      VpcId: !Ref VpcId
      ServiceName: !Sub com.amazonaws.${AWS::Region}.s3
      VpcEndpointType: Gateway

blocks.title: Verification
blocks.body: Check effective settings rather than assuming: `get-ebs-encryption-by-default` per Region; RDS console shows Encryption enabled on the new instance; `aws kms describe-key` shows Origin, KeyState (PendingImport/Enabled) and rotation status via `get-key-rotation-status`; `aws s3api get-object-retention` on a test object; Systems Manager Compliance dashboard for patch status; WAF sampled requests and logs to confirm blocks; Secrets Manager shows last rotated date and the AWSCURRENT/AWSPENDING version stages.

items: Rotation fails: check the rotation Lambda can reach both Secrets Manager (endpoint or NAT) and the database (security group), that the Lambda execution role can call the Secrets Manager rotation APIs, and CloudTrail for the failing Step.

Fargate CannotPullContainerError in a private subnet: confirm ecr.api, ecr.dkr and S3 gateway endpoints exist in the task's VPC, private DNS is enabled on the interface endpoints, and the endpoint security group allows 443 from the task.
Session Manager instance not appearing: confirm SSM Agent runs, the instance profile allows Systems Manager, and endpoints for ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages (or outbound 443) are reachable.
S3 access denied after adding an aws:SourceVpce deny: administrators outside the VPC are also blocked; scope the deny or add an exception for an admin role.
SSE-KMS access denied cross-account: both the key policy and the caller's IAM policy must allow the KMS actions.
Connection works inbound but responses stall: inspect NACL return-traffic rules.

blocks.body: Security-requirement questions are won by reading in a fixed order. Step 1: find the primary requirement (the single outcome that must be true, such as encryption with customer-supplied key material, private connectivity, immutability, automatic rotation, DDoS protection). Step 2: list mandatory constraints (no internet path, no servers to manage, minimal changes to the existing design, lowest cost, quickest). Step 3: eliminate options that violate a documented fact (cannot encrypt in place, SCPs cannot grant, WAF cannot attach to a bare EC2 instance, gateway endpoints do not extend to on premises). Step 4: among the survivors pick by the qualifier.

rows: Managed services: Secrets Manager rotation, Cognito authorizer, EBS encryption by default, Quick Setup, Shield Standard
Self-managed identity servers, custom scripts, bastion hosts
Gateway endpoint over interface endpoint or NAT for S3/DynamoDB; Parameter Store for plain config; protect only the entry point with Shield Advanced
Edge or resource-policy controls (WAF, bucket policy, SCP, endpoint policy)
Even the root user / administrators cannot
Object Lock compliance mode, SCP deny, KMS key policy separation
Secrets Manager rotation, KMS automatic rotation (not imported keys)
CloudTrail, Session Manager logging, Database Activity Streams, Systems Manager Compliance

items: Service distinction rules: security group allows only and is stateful, NACL allows and denies and is stateless. Gateway endpoint is S3/DynamoDB and free, interface endpoint is PrivateLink and paid. Key policy is mandatory for KMS, IAM alone is not enough unless the key policy delegates. SCP limits but never grants. Permission boundary limits roles. WAF is layer 7, Shield is DDoS, GuardDuty detects, Inspector scans workloads, Macie classifies S3 data, Security Hub aggregates. Secrets Manager rotates, Parameter Store stores. Session Manager removes SSH, Instance Connect shortens SSH. Governance Object Lock can be bypassed, compliance cannot.
Trap: an answer that mentions the right service but wrong scope, such as ACM certificates for CloudFront in a Region other than us-east-1, or a WAF web ACL in the wrong Region.
Trap: 'enable encryption on the existing database' options. RDS needs snapshot copy; EBS default encryption affects new volumes only; S3 default encryption affects new objects only.
Trap: using IAM user access keys on instances or in Lambda variables because the option is the smallest change.
Trap: choosing two overlapping protections when the stem wants least cost; Shield Advanced on both CloudFront and the ALB behind it pays data-transfer fees twice.

blocks.title: Newer features and terminology
blocks.body: Exam items may use older names. A customer master key (CMK) is a KMS key; Amazon Elasticsearch Service is now Amazon OpenSearch Service; Security Hub is now called Security Hub CSPM in the documentation reviewed; Kinesis Data Firehose is now Amazon Data Firehose (the WAF destinations page calls it Firehose); S3 encrypts every new object by default with SSE-S3. Treat the underlying control, not the label, as the answer.

Emerging topics in the bank - AI agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (workload identity, gateways to internal tools, human approval workflows), Bedrock Guardrails for filtering and PII redaction, Amazon Connect call screening, and fan-out deletion of sensitive data across microservices - are not covered by documentation retrieved for this build, so their specifics are not verified. The reasoning rules still apply: give each workload its own identity with short-lived credentials, expose tools through a controlled gateway with authorization, filter inputs and outputs with a managed guardrail instead of custom code, put a human approval step in a workflow that can pause and resume, and distribute deletion events through a managed event bus rather than point-to-point calls.

When two options both seem secure, ask which one satisfies the requirement without extra effort the stem did not authorize. A correct-but-heavier option (adding a NAT gateway, building a custom Lambda, deploying a third-party appliance) loses to a native control that does the same thing. When all options look flawed, choose the one that fixes the stated failure and violates no explicit constraint.

items: Policy evaluation: implicit deny by default, explicit deny always wins, SCPs/RCPs/boundaries/session policies only limit, and cross-account access needs both sides to allow.
Least privilege tooling: roles over keys, permissions boundaries to delegate, SCPs to guardrail accounts, Access Analyzer policy generation (up to 90 days of CloudTrail) to right-size.

Network: security groups stateful/allow-only/instance-level; NACLs stateless/numbered/subnet-level; reference security groups between tiers; SG default quotas 2,500 per Region, 60 rules per group, 5 groups per interface (all adjustable).

Endpoints: gateway = S3 and DynamoDB, route-table based, free, VPC-local only; interface = PrivateLink, DNS based, paid, usable from on premises and peered networks; use endpoint policies and aws:SourceVpce conditions; Fargate in private subnets needs ECR api and dkr endpoints plus S3 gateway; Systems Manager needs ssm, ssmmessages, ec2messages.

KMS: AWS managed vs customer managed vs imported (EXTERNAL) vs multi-Region; automatic rotation only for symmetric KMS-generated material, default 365 days, configurable 90-2,560; on-demand rotation limited to 25 per key (not adjustable); key policy plus IAM; cross-account needs a customer managed key.

S3: SSE-S3 default since January 2023; SSE-KMS plus Bucket Keys; Block Public Access four settings; deny aws:SecureTransport false; Object Lock compliance (nobody can delete) vs governance (bypass permission) vs legal hold.
EBS: encryption by default per Region, new volumes only. RDS: encrypt only at creation, otherwise snapshot copy and restore.
TLS: ACM is Regional; CloudFront viewer certificates in us-east-1; exportable public certificates now exist (new requests only, charged); re-encrypt or pass through for client-to-instance encryption.

Credentials: roles first; Secrets Manager for rotation (Lambda four-step rotation, one schedule per secret, cross-account needs resource policy plus key policy); IAM DB auth tokens last 15 minutes; Session Manager removes inbound ports and SSH keys; Instance Connect pushes 60-second keys.

Attack mitigation: CloudFront + WAF + Shield, origin locked with secret header and CloudFront prefix list, OAC for S3 origins, API Gateway authorizers/resource policies/usage plans, WAF scope and Region rules, Shield Advanced on entry points only.

Detect and patch: GuardDuty (CloudTrail, flow logs, DNS), Security Hub CSPM (standards, delegated admin), Inspector (EC2, Lambda, ECR), Macie (S3 sensitive data), Patch Manager with AWS-RunPatchBaseline and Quick Setup patch policies for Organizations.

blocks.title: Common misconceptions
blocks.body: An SCP does not grant access. Security groups do not have deny rules. An IAM policy alone cannot unlock a KMS key unless the key policy delegates to IAM. Enabling default encryption does not encrypt existing data. Compliance-mode Object Lock cannot be shortened by root. A gateway endpoint does not work from on premises. API keys are not authentication. WAF cannot sit directly on an EC2 instance. Imported key material cannot use automatic rotation.

Takeaways: translate each requirement into the narrowest managed control that satisfies it; keep traffic on private paths when the stem says so; make keys, secrets and credentials short-lived or rotated; layer edge, application and origin defenses; and automate detection and patching across accounts. Several details in this lesson (shown as not verified) should be checked against the current AWS documentation before relying on them.

Task 2.4 of Domain 2 (Design for New Solutions) asks you to design a strategy that meets reliability requirements. Reliability here means a workload keeps performing its function when components, Availability Zones (AZs) or whole Regions fail, and recovers fast enough and with little enough data loss to satisfy the business. The exam turns this into trade-off questions: which combination of Multi-AZ, multi-Region, loose coupling, scaling and DNS routing meets a stated recovery objective at the lowest cost or operational effort.

blocks.title: Prerequisites
blocks.body: You should already know VPC basics (subnets, route tables, NAT gateways), EC2 and Elastic Load Balancing, IAM roles and resource policies, and the vocabulary RTO (recovery time objective: the maximum acceptable delay between interruption and restored service) and RPO (recovery point objective: the maximum acceptable amount of time since the last data recovery point, that is, the data-loss window).
Objectives. After this lesson you will be able to:

items: Choose between single-AZ, Multi-AZ, and multi-Region designs from stated RTO, RPO and budget, and name the AWS service feature that implements each.
Select the correct Route 53 routing policy and health check configuration (failover, latency, geolocation, weighted, multivalue answer) and predict what a client receives when an endpoint fails.
Decouple tiers with SQS, SNS, Lambda and Step Functions and choose queue type, dead-letter handling, and workflow type from the requirement (ordering, duplicates, duration).
Pick and tune Auto Scaling policies (target tracking, scheduled, predictive, queue-backlog) and explain health check, warm-up and AZ rebalancing behavior.

Design data-tier resilience: RDS Multi-AZ vs read replicas, Aurora replicas and Global Database, ElastiCache Multi-AZ, FSx Multi-AZ, DynamoDB global tables (MREC vs MRSC), S3 replication, RTC and Multi-Region Access Points.
Account for service quotas (scope, default, adjustable or hard) when a design depends on them.

blocks.body: Services and patterns covered: Regions and AZs; disaster-recovery strategies; Route 53 routing and health checks; Global Accelerator; CloudFront origin groups and custom error pages; Network and Application Load Balancers; NAT gateways; SQS standard and FIFO; SNS fanout; Lambda concurrency and event source mappings; Step Functions; EC2 Auto Scaling; RDS, Aurora, RDS Proxy; ElastiCache; FSx for Windows File Server; DynamoDB global tables; Kinesis Data Streams; S3 replication and Multi-Region Access Points.

blocks.title: Why it matters on the exam
blocks.body: Domain 2 (Design for New Solutions) is a heavily weighted domain of SAP-C02 and this task is one of its largest sources of questions: in the question bank mapped to this lesson, the items cluster around SQS/SNS/Lambda decoupling, multi-Region data and routing, and Auto Scaling, load-balancer and NAT behavior. The exact domain weighting percentage is not stated in the sources retrieved for this build; consult the current official exam guide.

Almost every question here is a constraint-matching exercise. Underline the recovery objective (RTO/RPO), the failure scope (instance, AZ, Region), and the qualifier (least operational overhead, most cost-effective, minimal changes) before reading options.

topics.title: Regions, Availability Zones and recovery strategies

blocks.body: An AWS Region is a separate geographic area; Availability Zones are isolated locations within each Region. The fault-isolation whitepaper describes an AZ as one or more discrete data centers with independent and redundant power, networking and connectivity, meaningfully distant from each other (up to 60 miles, about 100 km) to prevent correlated failures, yet close enough for synchronous replication with single-digit millisecond latency. AWS also separates service deployments to AZs in the same Region in time. This is why Multi-AZ designs can use synchronous replication (zero data loss within the Region), whereas cross-Region designs are almost always asynchronous (non-zero RPO) and are used for Regional events, compliance and latency.

rows: Auto Scaling replacement, load balancer health checks, managed failover
Spread across 2-3 AZs: ASG across AZs, Multi-AZ RDS, Aurora replicas, NLB/ALB in several AZs, one NAT gateway per AZ
Second Region with data replication (Aurora Global Database, DynamoDB global tables, S3 replication, cross-Region read replicas) and DNS or Global Accelerator routing
Asynchronous (strong consistency only in specific modes)

blocks.body: Disaster-recovery strategies. The Well-Architected reliability guidance (REL13-BP02) lists four multi-Region strategies in increasing cost and complexity and decreasing RTO and RPO: backup and restore (RPO in hours, RTO 24 hours or less), pilot light (RPO minutes, RTO tens of minutes; data replicated and always-on, compute created on demand), warm standby (RPO seconds, RTO minutes; a scaled-down but fully functional copy always running), and multi-site active/active. A strategy across multiple AZs in one Region protects against events such as fires, floods and power outages; a multi-Region strategy is needed only when the requirement is protection from a Region-wide event.

rows: RPO hours; RTO up to 24 h
Data stores and replication; no app servers
RPO minutes; RTO tens of minutes

blocks.title: Design principle
blocks.body: Design for failure: assume every component fails and remove single points of failure by default. Prefer managed features that fail over automatically (Multi-AZ RDS, Aurora, ElastiCache Multi-AZ, FSx Multi-AZ, SQS) over designs that need an operator or a script, and reduce dependency on control-plane operations (such as launching instances or editing DNS) during the failure itself; data-plane mechanisms such as health-check driven DNS or Global Accelerator health checks keep working.

Common mistakes: treating a read replica as a Multi-AZ standby; using multi-Region where Multi-AZ meets the stated objective (cost and complexity penalty); keeping all resources, including the NAT gateway or the database, in one AZ while the rest of the stack is Multi-AZ; forgetting that a cross-Region design still needs a routing layer to move clients.
If the stem says 'AZ failure' do not reach for multi-Region. If it says 'Region outage', 'disaster', or 'RTO of minutes across Regions', Multi-AZ alone is wrong.

topics.title: Route 53 routing policies and health checks

blocks.body: Route 53 is DNS: it changes which IP addresses or aliases a name resolves to, but it cannot interrupt connections already open and it is subject to resolver caching (TTL). Routing policies decide which record answers a query; health checks decide which records are eligible.

rows: Standard DNS; one record, or several values in one record
Use when one resource serves the name
Send a specified portion of traffic to each resource
Combine with health checks for weighted active-active
Route to the AWS Region with lowest latency; all resources must be in AWS Regions
Decision uses the recursive resolver IP or, if supported (EDNS0 client subnet), a truncated client IP, so a remote corporate resolver can produce an unexpected Region
Route by where DNS queries come from: continent, country or US state
Most specific location wins; create a default record or unmapped/unmatched locations get no answer
Route by location of users and resources
Listed in the console comparison; bias settings not covered in the sources retrieved
Route based on client IP ranges you know
Primary when healthy, secondary when unhealthy
Up to eight healthy records returned, chosen at random
Not a substitute for a load balancer; usable in private hosted zones

blocks.body: Health checks. Route 53 health checkers around the world send requests at a 30-second interval by default, or 10 seconds with the fast option. The failure threshold (consecutive observations) can be set from 1 to 10 with a default of 3. An endpoint is considered healthy if more than 18 percent of health checkers report it healthy. For HTTP/HTTPS checks the checker must connect over TCP within four seconds and then receive a 2xx or 3xx within two seconds; HTTPS checks do not validate certificates. For a string-matching check the string must appear in the first 5,120 bytes of the response body within a further two seconds. A rule of thumb from the AWS blog is failover time = TTL + (interval x threshold); with TTL 60, a 10-second interval and threshold 5 that is 110 seconds.

blocks.title: Alias records and Evaluate Target Health
blocks.body: For an alias record to a load balancer with Evaluate Target Health set to Yes, Route 53 treats the record as healthy only when the load balancer's target groups pass their thresholds, and treats it as unhealthy if all target groups behind it are empty. You do not create separate Route 53 health checks for the instances behind a load balancer. If you set Evaluate Target Health to No on an alias in a tree, Route 53 keeps choosing that branch even though its health checks fail, instead of backing out to a healthy Region.

items: Active-passive: failover policy, or multiple primary and secondary resources, or weighted records. Active-active: any non-failover policy with health checks attached.

Latency + failover: latency alias records per Region with Evaluate Target Health = Yes gives nearest-healthy-Region behavior; if the nearest Region is unhealthy, the next lowest-latency healthy record answers.

Geolocation + failover: AWS documents nesting a failover record under a geolocation record to fail over within a location; an unhealthy geolocation record otherwise falls to a larger associated geographic region and then to the default.
A CloudWatch-alarm-based health check type lets application-level signals (for example a 5XX error-rate alarm) drive DNS failover.

blocks.body: Common mistakes: no default geolocation record (users in unmapped locations receive 'no answer'); using multivalue answer to scale a fleet that really needs a load balancer; high TTLs that delay failback; fast health checks against an endpoint with small capacity (each check source adds requests); expecting DNS to move already-established connections.

Need the nearest Region AND automatic evasion of a failed Region: latency records with health evaluation. Need strict data-residency or language by country: geolocation. Need failover without waiting for DNS TTL expiry: look at Global Accelerator (next topic).

links.label: How Route 53 determines whether a health check is healthy

topics.title: Traffic entry resilience: Global Accelerator, CloudFront, load balancers and NAT

blocks.body: Where Route 53 steers by DNS, other services steer at the network or HTTP layer. Knowing which layer fails over, and how fast, is a recurring exam discriminator.

AWS Global Accelerator gives you static anycast IP addresses, announced from multiple edge locations, that front endpoints (ALBs, NLBs, EC2 instances, Elastic IP addresses) in one or more Regions. The addresses stay assigned to the accelerator for as long as it exists, so clients and allow-lists need no change when endpoints change. For standard accelerators it health-checks endpoints and sends traffic only to healthy ones (for ALB and NLB endpoints it reuses the load balancer's health checks). If an endpoint group has no healthy endpoint with weight above zero, it tries other endpoint groups (ignoring the traffic dial); after trying the three closest groups with none healthy it fails open. Because it does not rely on DNS TTL expiry, it adjusts routing more quickly than Route 53; return to normal routing after recovery is typically about 30 seconds, but established connections to a zero-weight Region are not moved until they reset.

CloudFront origin groups give per-request failover: a primary and a secondary origin (S3 buckets or custom origins) and the HTTP status codes that trigger failover. Failover is stateless (CloudFront does not track origin health, so each request tries the primary first and incurs timeout latency), and happens only when the viewer request method is GET, HEAD or OPTIONS. Timeout settings that influence failover include origin connection attempts (1-3), connection timeout (1-10 s) and, for custom origins, response timeout (1-60 s). Custom error responses can return a static page, ideally stored in S3, for chosen 4xx/5xx codes; the error caching minimum TTL is 10 seconds by default. You can choose origin failover or custom error response per status code.

Network Load Balancer (NLB) provides one static IP address per AZ (subnet), and for an internet-facing NLB each AZ has a static private and public address. Per-AZ static addresses are what make an NLB the usual answer to 'partners must allow-list fixed addresses'; for an internet-facing NLB you can also assign your own pre-allocated Elastic IP address to each AZ. Cross-zone load balancing on an NLB is off by default (and data transfer charges apply when on); with it off, each node sends only to targets in its own AZ, so you need enough capacity in every enabled AZ and an empty AZ is treated as unhealthy. DNS answers include only healthy zones, failing open if all are unhealthy. An NLB can have an Application Load Balancer as a target (target type alb), which combines static IPs with ALB Layer 7 routing; such a target group inherits the load balancer's cross-zone setting.

Application Load Balancer (ALB) sticky sessions bind a user to a target using a duration-based cookie (AWSALB, generated by the load balancer) or an application-based cookie; they are enabled per target group, require cookie-capable clients and at least one healthy instance in each AZ, and are not supported when cross-zone load balancing is disabled. Stickiness is session affinity, not durability: if the target fails the session state is lost unless it is held externally (for example in ElastiCache or DynamoDB). A stateless tier with an external session store is the more resilient design.

NAT gateways are zonal: each operates within one AZ and is redundant only within that AZ. Best practice is one NAT gateway per AZ with each private subnet's route table pointing to the gateway in its own AZ, so one AZ's failure does not affect resources in another and you avoid cross-AZ data transfer charges. Trusted Advisor flags traffic routed through a NAT gateway in a different AZ. If a requirement forces a single egress IP address, you accept a single-AZ dependency and must automate recovery; the standard AZ-independent design uses several gateways.

Health check detection, no DNS cache

blocks.body: 'Fixed IP addresses that partners can allow-list' plus HA across AZs: NLB with an Elastic IP per AZ (or Global Accelerator for multi-Region). 'Sticky sessions' alone never survives a target failure.

blocks.body: Loose coupling means a producer does not need the consumer to be up, fast, or even aware of it. A queue absorbs bursts and outages: messages persist until a consumer processes and deletes them, so a failed worker tier causes delay rather than data loss. SNS pushes one message to many subscribers; SNS plus SQS (fanout, also called topic-queue chaining) gives each subscriber its own durable buffer so one slow or failed subscriber does not affect the others.

rows: Nearly unlimited transactions per second per API action
Default up to 3,000 messages/s with batching or 300/s without; high throughput mode raises this (up to 70,000 messages/s without batching per the feature page; limits vary by Region)
Exactly-once processing; no duplicates introduced into the queue
MessageDeduplicationId or content-based (SHA-256 of body) within a 5-minute window
Parallel across message groups; messages in one group are processed one at a time

blocks.body: Key SQS settings (all per queue): visibility timeout default 30 seconds, range 0 to 43,200 seconds (12 hours): the period a received message is hidden from other consumers, which should exceed worst-case processing time; message retention default 4 days, 60 seconds to 14 days; long polling (ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds up to 20) reduces empty receives; maximum message size configurable up to 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes) per the SQS FAQ (some older documentation pages still cite 256 KiB). Changes to retention can take up to 15 minutes to apply.

blocks.title: Dead-letter queues
blocks.body: A redrive policy names the DLQ and maxReceiveCount, the number of receives before a message is moved. Set it high enough to allow retries (the Lambda troubleshooting guidance recommends at least 5 when Lambda is the consumer, because throttling also consumes receives). A DLQ must match its source queue type. A redrive allow policy controls which source queues may use the DLQ (all by default; up to 10 named source queues with byQueue). After fixing the consumer, you can redrive messages from the DLQ back to the source queue at a chosen velocity. Alarm on DLQ depth.

Consumers and scaling. Fleets of EC2 workers or containers poll the queue; a Lambda event source mapping polls for you. For FIFO, per-group ordering means throughput scales with the number of active message groups, so a single constant group ID serializes everything; the AWS guidance for high throughput is to increase the number of message groups. For long jobs (the exam favorite is media processing that takes up to an hour) put work in a queue, set the visibility timeout longer than the job (or extend it), and let an Auto Scaling group of workers drain the queue; do not hold the web tier open for the job.

SNS. Delivery uses a delivery policy with retries for server-side errors and, once exhausted, discards the message unless a dead-letter queue is attached to the subscription (the subscription DLQ must be in the same account and Region as the subscription). SNS supports cross-Region delivery to SQS queues and Lambda functions: run the subscribe command in the Region that hosts the topic, and grant the topic permission to send to the queue via the queue's resource policy (with an aws:SourceArn condition). For opt-in Regions the policy needs a regionalized SNS service principal. A multi-Region fanout is therefore one topic fanning out to queues in several Regions, not a subscription in the reverse direction.

Other durable buffers appear in answers. Kinesis Data Streams stores data synchronously across three AZs in the Region, with retention from 24 hours up to 365 days (shards are the unit of capacity: 1 MB/s writes and 2 MB/s reads per shard in the blog's description); it fits ordered, replayable, multi-consumer streaming and feeding a warehouse, whereas SQS fits work distribution with per-message deletion.

items: Common mistake: standard queue where duplicates or order break the business rule; or FIFO with a single message group when parallelism is needed.
Common mistake: visibility timeout shorter than processing time, so the message is processed twice.
Common mistake: maxReceiveCount of 1 sends transient failures straight to the DLQ.
Best practice: idempotent consumers even with FIFO (exactly-once applies to queue insertion within the dedup window, not to your side effects).
Pricing dimensions: not verified against AWS docs in this build; both services bill per request, and exam questions rarely hinge on exact rates.

blocks.body: 'Loosely coupled, highly available, most reliable' intake: put SQS between the front end and the processor. 'Each bid processed once and in order': FIFO. 'Move failed events to a separate queue for review': DLQ (SQS redrive or Lambda on-failure destination). 'Notify many systems of one event, each must not lose messages': SNS to SQS fanout.

topics.title: Lambda and Step Functions: concurrency, retries and orchestration

blocks.body: Lambda as a consumer. With an SQS event source mapping, Lambda polls the queue and invokes your function with batches. For standard queues it starts with five concurrent batches and, per the current page, can add up to 300 more concurrent invokes per minute up to 1,250 for the mapping. For FIFO it scales with the number of active message groups. BatchSize defaults to 10 (maximum 10,000 for standard, 10 for FIFO) and ReportBatchItemFailures lets a function report partial batch failures. Provisioned mode (dedicated pollers) is an alternative scaling configuration and is mutually exclusive with maximum concurrency.

blocks.title: Protecting a downstream dependency
blocks.body: Reserved concurrency caps the function, but the event source mapping keeps polling regardless: it can receive more messages than the function is allowed to process, producing throttles and burning receive counts toward the DLQ. AWS guidance is to cap concurrency with the SQS event source's maximum concurrency setting and to keep that value no higher than the function's reserved concurrency. Pair with a DLQ and a generous maxReceiveCount. For databases with limited connections, front them with RDS Proxy (see database topic) or cap concurrency.

Concurrency quotas. Per Region, per account, default account concurrency is 1,000 (adjustable via Service Quotas), and by default you can reserve up to 900 across functions because Lambda always keeps 100 unreserved for functions without reserved concurrency. Requests per second limits equal 10 times the concurrency quota. Provisioned concurrency is a separate feature from reserved concurrency (the Lambda page distinguishes them); its cold-start behavior was not verified in the pages retrieved for this build.

Asynchronous invocation (for example from S3 or SNS): Lambda queues the event, retries on function errors up to two times by default, and keeps events up to six hours when throttled or on service errors. Events that fail all attempts are discarded unless you configure a dead-letter queue (SQS or SNS) or an on-failure destination (SQS, SNS, Lambda, EventBridge, or S3 for failures only). Destinations carry richer invocation records than a DLQ and can be set for both success and failure. A DLQ needs the execution role to be allowed to write to the target.

Step Functions orchestrates multi-step workflows as state machines. Without error handling, any state error fails the whole execution; Retry (interval, max attempts, backoff rate) and Catch are available on Task, Parallel and Map states. Catchers do not cover top-level execution failures, so use parent/child workflows or EventBridge events for TIMED_OUT. The .sync job-run pattern and .waitForTaskToken callback let a workflow wait for long external work (a human approval, a Fargate or Batch job) without polling loops, which also reduces billed state transitions.

25,000 events per execution (hard); history viewable 90 days after close

Not supported (per the Step Functions documentation)

blocks.body: EC2 Auto Scaling keeps a fleet at a desired capacity between a minimum and a maximum, replaces unhealthy instances, and spreads instances across the AZs you enable. It is the primary mechanism for surviving instance and AZ failures in the compute tier and for matching capacity to demand.

rows: You pick a metric and target value; EC2 Auto Scaling creates and manages the CloudWatch alarms, like a thermostat
Default recommendation for demand that follows a metric such as average CPU or request count
Finer control; step is generally preferred over simple per the AWS blog
Scheduled actions set min, max and desired at a time, one-time or recurring (cron supported)
Known, one-time or fixed-calendar events (a ticket sale, a launch)
Analyses up to 14 days of history (min 24 hours) to forecast the next 48 hours, forecast updated every 6 hours; launches ahead of load; does not scale in
Regular daily or weekly cycles, slow-to-initialize apps; run with dynamic scaling

blocks.title: Scheduled vs predictive
blocks.body: Predictive scaling learns from regular patterns in historical data; a one-off event has no history to learn from, so schedule capacity explicitly (and still keep dynamic scaling for surprises). When you combine scheduled actions with scaling policies, set Min and Max sensibly, because capacity must remain within that range even after a policy activates.

Queue-driven scaling. Scaling on the raw message count ignores how many workers exist, so it can over-add instances while the queue drains. The documented approach is a backlog per instance metric: ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible divided by InService instances (metric math with GroupInServiceInstances), with the target value = acceptable latency divided by average processing time per message. In the documentation's example, 10 s acceptable latency and 0.1 s per message give a target of 100 messages per instance. Container services use the same idea: a service scaled only on CPU may react late or not at all if the bottleneck is something else (this is reasoning, not an AWS statement), so scale on a metric that reflects the bottleneck, and see the database topic for protecting the data tier from the scale-out.

Health and AZ behavior. The health check grace period is the time a new instance is kept in service before health failures can terminate it; default 300 seconds in the console and 0 when you create the group with the CLI or SDK. ELB health checks must be enabled on the group (health check type ELB) for it to replace instances that the load balancer deems unhealthy; the default is EC2 status checks. A stopped instance is replaced immediately even within the grace period. Too large a grace period weakens health checking. Instance warm-up controls when new instances count toward metrics, and default instance warm-up is recommended with predictive scaling's pre-launch.

AZ distribution. ASG balances capacity across enabled AZs. If an AZ fails, the group launches replacements in healthy AZs; when the AZ recovers it rebalances by launching in the emptier AZ then terminating elsewhere, launching before terminating so availability is not reduced, and may temporarily exceed max capacity (by default 10 percent or one instance, whichever is greater). Distribution strategies are balanced best effort (falls back to another healthy AZ on launch failure) and balanced only (keeps trying the same AZ, for quorum-style workloads). To tolerate a one-AZ loss at full load, provision enough capacity in the remaining AZs (simple arithmetic, not an AWS statement: with three AZs, total capacity of about 150 percent of requirement leaves 100 percent after losing one).

items: Multiple AZ subnets in the ASG plus a load balancer in the same AZs is the baseline Multi-AZ web tier.
Lifecycle hooks let you initialize instances before they enter service; with hooks the grace period can be 0.
Common mistake: a single-AZ ASG, or a max capacity equal to desired so AZ rebalancing or scale-out is blocked.
Common mistake: target tracking on CPU for an I/O- or queue-bound worker.

blocks.body: Fixed known event: scheduled. Daily repeating pattern: predictive (plus dynamic). Worker fleet draining a queue: target tracking on backlog per instance. Slow-booting app that suffers at the start of business hours: predictive with pre-launch or scheduled.
