topics.title: Relational, cache and file storage resilience

blocks.body: RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment: RDS provisions and maintains a synchronous standby replica in a different AZ and fails over automatically for planned maintenance, instance failure or AZ disruption. The DNS name of the DB instance stays the same, so the application reconnects without manual intervention. The standby cannot serve read traffic: to scale reads use read replicas or a Multi-AZ DB cluster. The RDS features page states a Multi-AZ SLA of up to 99.95 percent; Multi-AZ with two readable standbys (one primary, two readable standbys across three AZs) offers failovers typically under 35 seconds and additional read capacity. Aurora is described as up to 99.99 percent with failover to one of up to 15 Aurora replicas in any three AZs.

Read replicas use the engine's asynchronous replication. They scale reads and can be promoted to standalone instances for disaster recovery; cross-Region read replicas help with DR, with moving reads closer to users, and with Region migration. Monitor replica lag, because it bounds your RPO. To create an encrypted cross-Region replica the source must be encrypted. A cross-Region read replica is promoted manually, so it is a pilot-light/warm-standby pattern with a non-zero RPO. The per-source replica limit varies by engine: up to 15 for RDS for MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL, and up to 5 for RDS for Oracle and SQL Server (Db2 allows 3).

rows: Yes, to a replica by priority tier
Physical storage-level, typically under 1 s lag

blocks.body: Aurora. Replicas share the cluster's storage volume and are the failover targets; each replica has a priority tier (0-15), the lowest-numbered tier is promoted first, and equal tiers favor the replica the same size as the old primary. The cluster endpoint always points at the writer and the reader endpoint load-balances connections across replicas; during a failover, connections to the promoted replica drop and clients should reconnect. Place replicas in distinct AZs to survive an AZ failure. Aurora Global Database has a primary cluster in one Region and read-only secondary clusters in other Regions (up to 10 secondary clusters, each in a different Region; every secondary reduces by one the number of Aurora Replicas the primary cluster can have), using storage-level physical replication with typical lag under a second, which is why it meets low RPO and fast cross-Region recovery that cross-Region RDS read replicas cannot. All clusters must run the same supported major version.

Global Database recovery has two documented paths. Switchover is for planned operations (roles swap, replication reverses). For unplanned outages the current user guide describes managed failover (recommended for DR; the old primary is automatically re-added as a secondary when it returns) and manual failover (detach and promote, used when managed failover is not an option, for example incompatible engine versions); either can lose writes not yet replicated, and failovers are susceptible to split-brain, so fence the old primary. Older blog posts say a managed unplanned failover does not exist; that is outdated. For Aurora PostgreSQL the rds.global_db_rpo parameter makes the primary pause commits if all secondaries lag beyond the target RPO; in a two-Region global database keep its default in the secondary parameter group so a failover is not blocked. After a promotion or failover the writer endpoint changes, so use a DNS indirection (for example a Route 53 CNAME you control) or automation.

RDS Proxy pools and shares connections so thousands of Lambda invocations or containers do not exhaust database connections. During a failover the proxy keeps accepting connections at the same IP, redirects to the new writer, preserves idle client connections and queues requests; only in-flight transactions are cancelled. Clients using the proxy avoid DNS propagation and caching delays, and application topology-tracking logic becomes unnecessary. TLS-heavy connection churn is offloaded to the pooled connections.

ElastiCache for Valkey and Redis OSS: enable Multi-AZ, which places replicas in different AZs and enables automatic failover; on primary failure the replica with the least replication lag is promoted and writes resume within seconds, and a replacement replica is provisioned. Without Multi-AZ a failed primary with no replicas restarts empty, losing data unless restored from a snapshot. Cluster-mode-enabled replication groups require automatic failover. Global Datastore adds cross-Region replication with a read-only secondary cluster; failover to a secondary is not automatic and is manually initiated by promotion, typically completing in less than a minute. Use it for session state and caches that must survive a Regional event.

FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ file systems have an active and a standby file server in separate AZs with synchronous replication, automatic failover typically under 30 seconds (and failback similarly), with the file system DNS name unchanged so Windows clients fail over transparently; Linux clients do not automatically connect to the standby and resume after failback. It is the managed answer for shared, highly available SMB storage with Active Directory integration and ACLs behind a Windows web tier; Active Directory domain join specifics were not retrieved for this build.

items: Application tier statelessness: keep sessions in ElastiCache or DynamoDB so any instance (or Region) can serve a user; sticky sessions are a fallback.
Database single points of failure: a database on one EC2 instance in one AZ is a classic 'remove the SPOF' answer; migrate to RDS Multi-AZ or Aurora with replicas in two or more AZs.
Common mistake: assuming a Multi-AZ standby adds read capacity; assuming cross-Region read replicas give zero RPO or automatic failover.

blocks.body: Cross-Region DR with RTO of about a minute and RPO of about a second for MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible data: Aurora Global Database, not RDS cross-Region replicas or snapshot copies. Same-Region database HA: Multi-AZ. Lambda exhausting DB connections or failover disruption: RDS Proxy.

topics.title: Multi-Region data: DynamoDB global tables and S3 replication

blocks.body: DynamoDB global tables provide multi-active, multi-Region replication: a global table is a set of replica tables, one per Region, with the same name and primary key; a change to any item in any replica is replicated to all others. Applications read and write locally with single-digit-millisecond latency. Global tables are designed for 99.999 percent availability. Two consistency modes exist. Multi-Region eventual consistency (MREC, default): asynchronous, usually within one to two seconds, conflicts resolved by last writer wins using item timestamps, no SLA on replication latency (monitor the ReplicationLatency metric per Region pair), transactions are atomic only in the originating Region. Multi-Region strong consistency (MRSC): writes are synchronously replicated to at least one other Region before returning, strongly consistent reads on any replica return the latest item, zero RPO; it requires exactly three Regions (three replicas, or two replicas plus a witness that stores recent change data, cannot be read or written, and has no storage or write cost), higher write and strongly consistent read latency, does not support the transaction APIs, and a conflicting concurrent write fails with ReplicatedWriteConflictException which you retry. A table converted to MRSC must be empty.

Replication copies corruption too: an application bug or bad batch job that overwrites items is replicated to every Region. Pair global tables with point-in-time recovery (PITR) or backups to protect against logical corruption. All items are replicated to all participating Regions; use multiple global tables with different Region sets for different scopes. For read-after-write across Regions that must not be stale, use MRSC or route a user's writes and reads to one Region; MREC reads of replicated data are eventually consistent.

S3 replication copies new objects between buckets in the same Region (SRR) or different Regions (CRR) and across accounts. Requirements and behaviors confirmed in the docs: replication is configured on the source bucket; Batch Replication is the mechanism to replicate objects that existed before the rule (it requires an existing replication configuration and a manifest in the source Region); delete marker replication is optional per rule and is not supported for tag-based rules; you can replicate to more than one destination; lifecycle rules should be disabled while a Batch Replication job runs to keep buckets in parity. Versioning on both buckets is a standard prerequisite (listed in the question notes for this lesson; not restated in the pages retrieved).

S3 Replication Time Control (RTC) adds a service-level commitment: most objects replicate in seconds and 99.99 percent within 15 minutes; the SLA is on 99.9 percent of objects within 15 minutes in a billing month. Enabling RTC also enables replication metrics, and adds the events s3:Replication:OperationMissedThreshold, OperationReplicatedAfterThreshold and OperationNotTracked, which you route to SNS or EventBridge for the 'notify operations if any object exceeds 15 minutes' requirement. Only 15 minutes is accepted for the threshold values. RTC is enabled per replication rule, and a rule can be scoped by prefix (for example per radar station).

S3 Multi-Region Access Points present one global endpoint over buckets in several Regions and route requests over the AWS network (using Global Accelerator) to the closest bucket; if connectivity to a Region is lost, requests go to another. Failover controls let you mark Regions active or passive; shifting takes about two minutes. They do not replicate data; you configure CRR, and AWS recommends two-way (bidirectional) replication between buckets before failover so writes made in the failover Region replicate back. For 'application runs in two Regions and reads/writes the same logical bucket with least operational overhead': Multi-Region Access Point plus two-way replication.

Conditional writes provide optimistic concurrency in S3: If-None-Match makes a write succeed only if no object exists (first writer wins, others get 412 Precondition Failed); If-Match succeeds only if the object's ETag matches (412 on mismatch; 404/409 are possible with concurrent deletes or requests, and the client should re-read and retry). This lets many writers update the same JSON document without silent overwrites and without a locking service.

rows: Active-active, local reads/writes in several Regions, key-value data
Conflicts: last writer wins; also replicates corruption
Zero RPO across Regions for DynamoDB
15-minute replication objective with alerting for S3
Single endpoint, nearest healthy bucket, failover control
S3 Multi-Region Access Point + two-way CRR
Static assets resilient to a Region failure behind CloudFront
Two buckets with CRR + CloudFront origin group

blocks.title: Scenario 1: order intake that must not lose orders (single Region, Multi-AZ)
blocks.body: Requirements: an e-commerce web tier accepts orders; processing writes to DynamoDB; the CIO wants simple, highly available, loosely coupled, 'most reliable'. Existing environment: web servers call the processor directly, so a processor slowdown loses or rejects orders. Chosen architecture: web tier in an Auto Scaling group across three AZs behind an ALB; the web tier writes each order to an SQS standard queue (FIFO only if order sequence matters); a worker Auto Scaling group (or Lambda event source mapping) processes messages idempotently and writes to DynamoDB; a DLQ with maxReceiveCount of 5 captures poison messages with a CloudWatch alarm on DLQ depth; the worker group scales by target tracking on backlog per instance. Rationale: the queue persists orders while workers are down or scaling; DynamoDB and SQS are Regional managed services spanning AZs. Security: queue and DLQ with SSE, least-privilege roles for producers and consumers. Cost: pay per request; workers scale to the backlog. Rejected alternatives: synchronous calls to the processor (coupling, loss on failure); SNS alone (no buffering for a slow consumer); a self-managed broker on EC2 (operational burden, SPOF unless clustered); Kinesis (more capacity management than needed for per-message work distribution).

blocks.title: Scenario 2: global game or API with Region-failure tolerance
blocks.body: Requirements: players worldwide, lowest latency, survive loss of any Region, leaderboards and inventory available in all Regions, RPO of seconds. Chosen architecture: identical stacks (ALB + Auto Scaling or API Gateway + Lambda) in us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1; DynamoDB global table with replicas in all three Regions (MREC); Route 53 latency alias records to each ALB with Evaluate Target Health = Yes and a health endpoint that checks the local DynamoDB replica; static assets in S3 with CRR to a second bucket and a CloudFront origin group; consider Global Accelerator where DNS caching would prolong failover or static IPs are required. Rationale: active-active removes failover steps; latency routing with health evaluation sends users to the nearest healthy Region; MREC meets an RPO of seconds, with last-writer-wins conflicts acceptable for leaderboards if writes for an item are mostly homed to one Region. Security: Regional IAM roles, KMS keys per Region for replica encryption. Cost: highest of the options (three full stacks, replicated writes, cross-Region data transfer). Alternatives rejected: single Region with backup (RTO/RPO too large); Aurora cross-Region read replicas (single writer, manual promotion, not active-active); MRSC (adds write latency and needs exactly three Regions; use only if stale reads after failover are unacceptable); add PITR for protection against corrupt writes.

blocks.title: Scenario 3: relational workload, cross-Region disaster recovery with minute-level RTO
blocks.body: Requirements: web application in us-east-1 on ALB across three AZs with MySQL on a single EC2 instance; cross-Region DR with RTO of about a minute and RPO of about a second. Chosen architecture: migrate the database to Aurora MySQL with replicas in at least two AZs, add a secondary Region through Aurora Global Database, keep a pilot-light or warm-standby web tier (ASG at minimum capacity, AMIs/launch templates pre-staged) in the secondary Region, Route 53 failover records with health checks (or Global Accelerator) in front, and automation that performs managed failover and repoints the application (for example a Route 53 CNAME for the database writer). Rationale: storage-level replication gives typically sub-second lag; Aurora replicas give in-Region AZ failover; the warm web tier scales on demand. Alternatives rejected: RDS cross-Region read replica (asynchronous, manual promotion, no comparable RPO/RTO claim in the docs reviewed); snapshot copy and restore (RPO and RTO in hours); self-managed replication on EC2 (operational overhead). Cost: Aurora instances in two Regions plus replicated storage and inter-Region transfer; mitigate by keeping the secondary web tier small. Test with switchover, which is the planned, managed way to rehearse.

blocks.body: The snippets below use placeholders (<account-id>, <region>, names in angle brackets). They show the shape of each configuration; outputs are not shown because they depend on your account. The JSON policies were checked for syntactic validity; CLI flags for SQS, Route 53, Auto Scaling and S3 follow the documented API shapes seen in the pages retrieved, while the DynamoDB and Aurora global commands were written from API familiarity and are listed as not verified.

blocks.title: 1. Decoupling: SQS with a dead-letter queue (CLI)
blocks.body: Create the DLQ first, read its ARN, then attach a redrive policy to the source queue. The redrive attribute value is a JSON string.

blocks.label: CLI
blocks.body:
aws sqs create-queue --queue-name orders-dlq --attributes MessageRetentionPeriod=1209600
aws sqs get-queue-attributes --queue-url <dlq-url> --attribute-names QueueArn
aws sqs create-queue --queue-name orders-queue --attributes file://orders-queue-attrs.json

blocks.label: JSON (orders-queue-attrs.json)
CloudFormation (YAML)
blocks.body:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Description: Orders queue with dead-letter queue and DLQ alarm
Resources:
  OrdersDlq:
    Type: AWS::SQS::Queue
    Properties:
      MessageRetentionPeriod: 1209600
  OrdersQueue:
    Type: AWS::SQS::Queue
    Properties:
      VisibilityTimeout: 120
      RedrivePolicy:
        deadLetterTargetArn: !GetAtt OrdersDlq.Arn
        maxReceiveCount: 5
  DlqNotEmptyAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Properties:
      Namespace: AWS/SQS
      MetricName: ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible
      Dimensions:
        - Name: QueueName
          Value: !GetAtt OrdersDlq.QueueName
      Statistic: Maximum
      Period: 60
      EvaluationPeriods: 1
      Threshold: 0
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanThreshold
      TreatMissingData: notBreaching

blocks.title: 4. Auto Scaling on SQS backlog per instance
blocks.body: Target value = acceptable latency divided by average processing time per message (10 s / 0.1 s = 100 in the documentation's example). Save the specification as config.json.

CLI

aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy --auto-scaling-group-name <asg-name> --policy-name backlog-per-instance --policy-type TargetTrackingScaling --target-tracking-configuration file://config.json
aws autoscaling put-scheduled-update-group-action --auto-scaling-group-name <asg-name> --scheduled-action-name sale-event --start-time <YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ> --min-size <min> --max-size <max> --desired-capacity <desired>

blocks.title: 5. S3 CRR with Replication Time Control

items: Layer test: DNS-level steering (Route 53) is subject to TTL and cannot move established connections; Global Accelerator and CloudFront origin failover do not wait for TTL.
Synchronous vs asynchronous: Multi-AZ replication is synchronous; cross-Region is asynchronous except DynamoDB MRSC. If the stem demands zero data loss across Regions without MRSC, be suspicious.
Read scaling vs availability: read replicas and Aurora readers add reads; only Multi-AZ standby/promotion adds automatic failover for plain RDS.
Replication copies mistakes: logical corruption or accidental deletes need backups, PITR or versioning in addition to replication.
Single-AZ hidden SPOFs: NAT gateway, database on one instance, single-AZ file system, a queue consumer in one AZ.
Beware of questions with flawed wording (for example, a 'Multi-AZ DB cluster' for Aurora, garbled option text): choose the option that satisfies the stated constraints best.

blocks.body: Service-distinction rules to memorize: SQS buffers work for one logical consumer group, SNS broadcasts; Step Functions orchestrates stateful multi-step processes, Lambda is a step; ALB is Layer 7 with DNS name only, NLB is Layer 4 with static IPs; Route 53 failover is DNS, Global Accelerator is anycast network-level; Multi-AZ standby cannot be read, a read replica is not an automatic failover target; Aurora Global Database for cross-Region relational DR, DynamoDB global tables for cross-Region key-value active-active; S3 replication copies objects, a Multi-Region Access Point routes requests; reserved concurrency is not the SQS throttle, maximum concurrency on the event source is.

blocks.title: Key concepts
blocks.body: Reliability = remove single points of failure at the right scope (instance, AZ, Region), decouple with durable buffers, scale automatically, and replicate data in the mode that matches RPO. AZs allow synchronous replication; Regions mean asynchronous replication except DynamoDB MRSC.

items: Decision rules: AZ failure -> Multi-AZ; Region failure -> second Region with replication and a routing layer; spikes or slow consumers -> queue; ordering/duplicates -> FIFO; long waits and retries -> Step Functions Standard; known event -> scheduled scaling; cyclic load -> predictive scaling; queue workers -> backlog per instance.

Routing: Route 53 latency/failover/geolocation/weighted/multivalue with Evaluate Target Health; Global Accelerator for static IPs and fast, TTL-free failover; CloudFront origin group for GET/HEAD/OPTIONS failover; NLB for per-AZ static IPs.

Data: RDS Multi-AZ (sync standby, no reads), read replicas (async, reads/DR), Aurora replicas (failover targets, reader endpoint), Aurora Global Database (cross-Region, sub-second lag), RDS Proxy (connection pooling, quicker failover), ElastiCache Multi-AZ, FSx Multi-AZ, DynamoDB MREC vs MRSC, S3 CRR + RTC + Multi-Region Access Points.

blocks.title: Common misconceptions
blocks.body: Multi-AZ standby does not serve reads. Sticky sessions do not survive instance failure. Reserved concurrency does not stop an SQS event source from polling. DynamoDB global tables replicate corrupt writes. Predictive scaling cannot plan a one-off event and does not scale in. DNS failover is not instantaneous. A NAT gateway in one AZ is a cross-AZ SPOF. S3 RTC reduces replication time but is not synchronous. Multi-Region Access Points do not replicate data.

blocks.title: Takeaways
blocks.body: State the failure scope, objective and qualifier first. Choose managed automatic failover over manual steps. Decouple with SQS and SNS, orchestrate with Step Functions, scale with the right policy and metric, and replicate data in the consistency mode the business can tolerate. Verify quotas in the recovery Region before you need them.

blocks.title: Service quotas and limits (merged into this summary)
blocks.body: Quotas determine whether a design works at scale or during failover. The material below is what to know for this task; scope, default and adjustability are stated only where the documentation retrieved states them.

Quotas are a reliability concern because a scale-out, a failover into a second Region, or a burst can fail at a quota rather than at a hardware limit. Service Quotas is the console, API and CLI place to view default values, see whether a quota is adjustable, see applied values, track utilization and request increases; increases take time to review and some need manual approval. Some quotas are per account per Region (for example EC2 vCPU limits) and others are global per account, so a new or recovery Region starts at default quotas and needs proactive increases before a disaster, not during one.

blocks.body: When a stem says a function or fleet 'is throttled during the spike' the fix may be a quota or concurrency setting; when it says 'must run for 18 months', Step Functions Standard's one-year limit forces a continue-as-new design or a different service.

Task 2.5 asks you to design a solution that meets stated performance objectives: latency, throughput, IOPS, concurrency or time-to-complete. The professional-level skill is not memorizing numbers; it is mapping an access pattern (random small I/O, large sequential streams, bursty writes, read-heavy lookups, tightly coupled node-to-node traffic) to the service and configuration that removes the actual bottleneck, at the lowest operational overhead. Task 2.5 sits in Domain 2 (Design for New Solutions), one of the four scored exam domains; its exact percentage weight was not verified against AWS docs in this build.

items: Prerequisites: working knowledge of EC2, EBS, S3, VPC, IAM, CloudWatch, and the basics of DynamoDB and RDS.

Exam objectives (verbatim skills): designing large-scale application architectures for a variety of access patterns; designing an elastic architecture based on business objectives; applying design patterns to meet performance objectives with caching, buffering, and replicas; developing a process methodology for selecting purpose-built services for required tasks; designing a rightsizing strategy.
Knowledge areas: performance monitoring technologies, storage options on AWS, instance families and use cases, purpose-built databases.

blocks.body: By the end of this lesson:

You will be able to choose between AWS Lambda, AWS Fargate, AWS Batch and Amazon EC2 (with the right instance family and placement group) for a compute pattern.

You will be able to pick a purpose-built database and decide where a cache (Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX), Amazon ElastiCache, Amazon MemoryDB, Amazon CloudFront, or Amazon API Gateway caching) belongs.
You will be able to use Amazon SQS, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and Amazon Data Firehose as buffers so that bursts do not overwhelm a downstream store.
You will be able to define a rightsizing and elasticity process using Amazon CloudWatch metrics, AWS Compute Optimizer and scaling policies.

blocks.title: The method in one line
blocks.body: Identify the bottleneck (compute, storage I/O, network, database connections, a single hot key, or a slow origin), choose the AWS capability designed to remove that specific bottleneck, then prove it with metrics. Most wrong answers on this task fix a different bottleneck than the one the stem describes.

topics.title: Performance monitoring and the measure-first method

blocks.body: You cannot design for performance without measuring it. Amazon CloudWatch collects metrics (CPU, network, disk, and service-specific metrics such as EFS `BurstCreditBalance`, `PercentIOLimit` and `ThroughputUtilization`), alarms act on them, and Auto Scaling policies use them. AWS X-Ray provides distributed tracing and shows where latency is spent across microservices; per AWS docs, the X-Ray trace map correlates CloudWatch metrics, logs and traces for an end-to-end view that helps pinpoint bottlenecks and impacted users. CloudWatch Application Signals gives traces plus metrics (requests, availability, latency, errors, faults) with pre-built dashboards, whereas X-Ray alone gives traces; with Application Signals no extra instrumentation code is needed for Lambda, while X-Ray-only tracing needs the X-Ray SDK as a dependency.

For databases, the core metric is database load, measured in average active sessions (AAS): the number of sessions concurrently running queries, sliced by waits, SQL, hosts, users and databases. Comparing load to the Max vCPU line shows whether the instance is CPU-bound or waiting on I/O or locks. Service change to know: AWS states Performance Insights was replaced by CloudWatch Database Insights, with end of life on July 31, 2026, and that Performance Insights users were migrated; Database Insights Standard mode keeps flexible retention (1-24 months) at the Performance Insights price, and Advanced mode adds fleet monitoring and further diagnostics. If an older question says 'use Performance Insights', the intent is still 'use database-load analysis', now delivered by Database Insights.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Treating average CPU as the only signal. Memory, disk queue, network, connection counts and per-partition hot spots do not show up in CPU. Compute Optimizer can ingest external EC2 memory metrics from products such as Datadog and Dynatrace for better rightsizing.

Amazon EBS offers SSD volumes for IOPS-dominated transactional work and HDD volumes for throughput-dominated streaming work. Per the EBS volume-types page: gp3 supports 1 GiB-64 TiB, up to 80,000 IOPS and 2,000 MiB/s; gp2 up to 16,000 IOPS and 250 MiB/s; io2 Block Express up to 256,000 IOPS and 4,000 MiB/s with 99.999% durability and sub-millisecond latency (average under 500 microseconds for 16 KiB I/O); io1 up to 64,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s; st1 (Throughput Optimized HDD) 500 MiB/s and sc1 (Cold HDD) 250 MiB/s, neither usable as boot volumes. Multi-Attach is supported on io1/io2 only.

rows: Balanced SSD, IOPS and throughput set independently of size
Default for most workloads, boot volumes, medium databases
IOPS tied to size (3 IOPS/GiB, min 100, max 16,000)

blocks.body: gp2 sizing is a classic exam mechanic. Baseline performance scales at 3 IOPS per GiB, with a 100 IOPS minimum (at 33.33 GiB and below) and a 16,000 IOPS maximum (at 5,334 GiB and above); small volumes burst to 3,000 IOPS. A 1,000 GiB gp2 volume therefore has a 3,000 IOPS baseline and a 2,000 GiB volume 6,000. gp3 provides 3,000 IOPS baseline without paying for IOPS, and IOPS/throughput can be configured independently of capacity, so you stop over-provisioning storage to buy IOPS. AWS's migration guidance: any workload that used a gp2 volume up to 1,000 GiB can safely be configured with gp3 at its default baseline.

Instance store is physically attached, temporary block storage. Data survives a reboot but is lost if the instance stops, hibernates or terminates, or if the underlying disk fails. Use it for caches, buffers and scratch data, never for the only copy of anything. To fully use provisioned EBS IOPS you need EBS-optimized instances, and for io2 above 32,000 IOPS a Nitro-based instance (Nitro instances support up to 256,000 IOPS; other instance types can reach up to 32,000).

Amazon S3 performance is per prefix: at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per partitioned prefix, with no limit on the number of prefixes, so parallelizing across prefixes scales request rate (10 prefixes for reads gives 55,000 GET/s). Randomized key prefixes are no longer needed for performance. During sustained growth S3 may return temporary HTTP 503 SlowDown while it repartitions, so clients should retry with backoff. Byte-range GET requests let you read only the part of an object you need (for example a file header) and fetch ranges in parallel.

For analytics on S3, Amazon Athena cost and speed depend on how much data is scanned: convert to columnar formats (Apache Parquet or ORC), compress, and partition. Parquet default block size is 128 MB and ORC stripe 64 MB; for complex types (array, map, struct) Athena reads the entire row from Parquet, and AWS suggests ORC as a workaround.

items: Choose gp3 first; move to io2 Block Express only when sustained sub-millisecond latency or more than 80,000 IOPS / 2,000 MiB/s is required.
Throughput-heavy sequential scans: st1. Cheapest cold sequential: sc1.
Temporary high-speed scratch: instance store, accepting loss on stop/terminate.

blocks.body: If the stem says 'IOPS are insufficient but capacity is fine' on gp2, the cheapest fix is usually gp3 with higher provisioned IOPS, not a bigger gp2 volume. If it says 'more than 16,000 IOPS' or 'consistent sub-millisecond latency', think io2 Block Express.

topics.title: Shared file storage: EFS, FSx for Lustre and S3 access

blocks.body: Amazon EFS is a managed, elastic NFS file system for POSIX workloads shared by many clients. Two settings matter. Performance mode: General Purpose is the default, has the lowest per-operation latency and is the recommended mode for all file systems; Max I/O is described as a previous-generation mode for highly parallel workloads tolerating higher latency, and is not supported for One Zone file systems or Elastic throughput. Monitor `PercentIOLimit` for General Purpose IOPS limits. Throughput mode: Elastic (recommended for spiky or unpredictable workloads, or average-to-peak ratio of 5% or less; pay per GiB transferred, requires General Purpose), Provisioned (known requirements or average-to-peak above 5%; pay for provisioned MiB/s above the baseline that stored data gives), and Bursting (throughput scales with stored data and burst credits; watch `BurstCreditBalance`, and move off Bursting if above 80% of permitted throughput or out of credits).

Latency: EFS Standard gives about 1 ms reads and 2.7 ms writes; Infrequent Access and Archive classes have first-byte latencies of tens of milliseconds. Regional file systems are stored across multiple AZs; One Zone writes are about 1.6 ms. Throughput above a Region's maximum needs a quota increase handled case by case. A common pattern is EFS Standard with a lifecycle policy moving cold files to a cheaper class.

Amazon FSx for Lustre is a high-throughput parallel file system for HPC, ML training and media. Deployment types: scratch (temporary, data not replicated and lost if a file server fails; cheapest for short-term processing) and persistent (replicated within an AZ, servers replaced on failure; SSD or HDD). SCRATCH_2 adds in-transit encryption and higher burst throughput than SCRATCH_1; PERSISTENT_2 offers up to 1000 MB/s/TiB. A data repository association (DRA) links a file-system directory to an S3 bucket or prefix, with up to 8 DRAs per file system; metadata is imported so S3 objects appear as files and content is lazy-loaded on first access, and changes can be exported back to S3 automatically. DRAs and automatic export are not available on Scratch 1 or Lustre 2.10 file systems. Writes to the same file from both sides are not coordinated by FSx.

Other shared-data options. Mountpoint for Amazon S3 is a high-throughput open-source client that presents a bucket as a local file system on Linux for large read-heavy workloads (data lakes, ML training, ETL); it cannot modify existing files, delete directories, or use symbolic links and file locking, and AWS recommends FSx for Lustre linked to S3 when full POSIX is needed. EBS Multi-Attach lets io1/io2 volumes attach to up to 16 Nitro instances in the same AZ, but standard file systems (XFS, ext4, NTFS) are not built for concurrent access, so use a cluster-aware file system or NVMe reservations; for shared storage across AZs AWS points to managed services like EFS and FSx.

topics.title: Compute selection: instance families, placement groups and serverless

blocks.body: EC2 instance families: general purpose (balanced; burstable T family gives baseline CPU with bursts), compute optimized (batch, transcoding, HPC, game servers, ML inference), memory optimized (in-memory databases, large datasets), storage optimized (high sequential throughput and tens of thousands of low-latency random IOPS on local storage), accelerated computing (GPUs and other co-processors) and HPC-optimized. Rightsizing means matching the family to the limiting resource first, then size.

Placement groups control physical placement. Cluster: instances packed close in a single AZ (can span peered VPCs in the Region) for low latency, high per-flow throughput and high packet rate; best for tightly coupled HPC where most traffic is between group members; use one launch request and the same instance type to avoid insufficient-capacity errors; burstable T, Mac1 and M7i-flex types are excluded; choose enhanced-networking instance types for the lowest latency. Partition: instances spread over logical partitions with separate racks (Hadoop, Cassandra, Kafka). Spread: each instance on distinct racks for a small number of critical instances. Only cluster targets performance; partition and spread target fault isolation. Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) is an OS-bypass network device (used through Libfabric/MPI) for low-latency inter-node communication within a subnet; AWS recommends running EFA instances in a placement group in a single AZ, and EFA is not supported across AZs.

Serverless and container compute. Lambda: up to 15 minutes per invocation, memory 128-10,240 MB with CPU allocated proportionally (the equivalent of one vCPU at 1,769 MB, 6 vCPUs at 10,240 MB), deployable as zip or as a container image up to 10 GB (container-image functions do not support layers). Increasing memory is the first tuning step for slow functions, even if memory is not exhausted. New accounts have reduced concurrency and memory quotas that AWS raises automatically. AWS guidance for work exceeding Lambda limits: Step Functions when it can be split into steps under 15 minutes; Fargate when the process is monolithic, scheduled, longer than 15 minutes, or you want minimal refactoring; AWS Batch for batch jobs needing queues, dependencies and scheduling, with Fargate, Fargate Spot, EC2 On-Demand or EC2 Spot compute environments.

blocks.body: Edge and ML placement. SageMaker lets you host multiple model versions behind one endpoint using production variants; traffic splits by variant weights, and `TargetVariant` on a request overrides weights, enabling A/B tests and canary shifts (for example 5% to a new model) without downtime. Multi-model endpoints for multi-tenant hosting were not verified in this build. AWS IoT Greengrass runs cloud-trained ML inference locally on devices, reducing latency and working with limited or no connectivity; note Greengrass v1 is entering sunset per AWS availability notices, so v2 is the current runtime. AWS Outposts extends AWS infrastructure, APIs and services into your data center for low-latency, local-processing or data-residency needs; Local Zones place AWS compute near end-user metros for single-digit-millisecond latency without hardware to manage. Snowball Edge Compute Optimized and Storage Optimized moved to maintenance (closed to new customers from November 7, 2025), which matters when a question offers Snow devices as an edge-compute answer.

blocks.title: Network throughput gotcha
blocks.body: A cluster placement group raises per-flow throughput between members. Traffic to an instance outside the group is not accelerated, so the narrowest path (the outside instance or the Internet) limits throughput.

Purpose-built database selection starts with the access pattern, not the brand. Key-value/document at massive scale with single-digit-millisecond latency and schemaless items: DynamoDB. Relational with joins and transactions: Aurora or RDS. In-memory microsecond access: ElastiCache or MemoryDB. The exam rewards recognizing that a high-volume stream of small JSON sensor records with no joins is a DynamoDB (or Kinesis-fronted) problem, not a relational one.

DynamoDB capacity and hot keys. On-demand mode adapts to traffic and instantly accommodates up to double the previous peak; traffic that exceeds double the previous peak within 30 minutes can throttle (warm throughput can pre-warm for known events). Provisioned mode with auto scaling suits gradually changing traffic, retains up to 5 minutes of unused capacity as best-effort burst, and burst cannot fix a hot partition. Partition limits are 3,000 read units or 1,000 write units per second per partition; adaptive capacity (automatic, no extra cost) lets a hot partition borrow up to total table capacity, but poor partition-key cardinality still causes throttling that needs a data-model change. Time to Live (TTL) deletes expired items, typically within a few days of expiry, without consuming write throughput and at no extra cost; the attribute must be a Number in Unix epoch seconds, expired-but-undeleted items still appear in reads unless filtered, and deletions flow to Streams as service deletions. With global tables, the TTL delete does not consume WCU in the origin Region but the replicated delete does consume replicated write capacity in replica Regions. TTL is therefore the cheapest way to hold short-lived, high-volume small records.

DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a fully managed, API-compatible, read-through/write-through cache in front of DynamoDB returning cached responses in microseconds; it benefits eventually consistent, read-heavy workloads, requires no application rewrite beyond pointing at the DAX endpoint, and reduces read requests (and thus cost) on the table. A DAX cluster has exactly one primary node and 0 to 10 read replicas (up to 11 nodes); for production, AWS recommends at least three nodes in different Availability Zones.

Sessions, leaderboards, caching with rich structures

blocks.body: ElastiCache vs MemoryDB: Memcached is multithreaded and ideal as a simple scale-out object cache; Redis/Valkey adds data structures, replication and persistence, so ElastiCache manages it as a stateful entity with failover. ElastiCache for Valkey also offers a durability option backed by a Multi-AZ transactional log (synchronous writes lose no acknowledged writes; asynchronous mode can lose up to 10 seconds). MemoryDB stores its entire dataset in memory and uses a distributed transactional log across AZs, so you can use it as the single primary database instead of pairing a cache with a database; AWS cites failover typically under 20 seconds for unplanned outages and under 200 ms for planned. Engines can be upgraded but not downgraded in ElastiCache.

Relational scaling. Aurora supports up to 15 read replicas sharing the same storage as the primary (replica lag is usually well under 100 milliseconds), a reader endpoint that load-balances across replicas, replica auto scaling, and cross-Region read replicas (typically tens of milliseconds behind; up to 15 further replicas per cross-Region cluster) for local reads and DR. Pair latency-based DNS routing with a Regional replica to serve global readers locally while writes stay in the primary Region. RDS Proxy pools and multiplexes connections: it reuses a database connection after each transaction so thousands of application or Lambda connections share far fewer database connections, and it smooths failover. Pinning (session-state changes) forces a client to hold one database connection and reduces the benefit; many distinct database users also fragment the pool. Credentials come from Secrets Manager (one secret per DB user) or end-to-end IAM authentication.

blocks.title: Decision rules
blocks.body: Connection exhaustion (max_connections, Lambda fan-out) -> RDS Proxy. Read-heavy relational -> replicas or a cache. Read-heavy DynamoDB -> DAX. Needs durability with in-memory speed -> MemoryDB. Hot keys -> redesign the key, caching helps reads only. Short-lived records -> DynamoDB TTL.

Caching and edge services reduce latency by serving data nearer the user or avoiding the origin. Order of thought: cache static content at the edge (CloudFront), cache API responses (API Gateway stage cache), cache hot database reads (DAX/ElastiCache), and accelerate non-cacheable or non-HTTP traffic through the AWS backbone (Global Accelerator).

CloudFront with S3 or custom origins serves cacheable content (including large downloads) from edge locations. Origin groups provide failover: a primary and a secondary origin, with CloudFront switching on configured HTTP status codes (CDK default 500, 502, 503 and 504), connection failure or timeouts, only for GET, HEAD and OPTIONS requests, and still sending every new request to the primary first. Connection attempts (1-3), connection timeout (1-10 s) and custom-origin response timeout (1-60 s) control how fast failover happens. The two origins can be any combination of S3 buckets and custom origins. Lambda@Edge runs code on four events: viewer request (every request, before cache), origin request (cache miss, before the origin), origin response, viewer response. Use viewer request to alter the cache key or generate uncached responses; use origin request to select an origin dynamically (by header, cookie, country, A/B test), rewrite URLs to the origin (for example append index.html for S3 directory requests) or generate cacheable responses. CloudFront Functions can also update origins, but on viewer request (every request), which suits dynamic uncached traffic; Lambda@Edge origin request runs only on cache misses, which is cheaper for highly cacheable content and supports fetching data from DynamoDB or S3.

rows: Route A/B test users to different origins
Origin request (viewer request for CF Functions)

blocks.body: API Gateway caching: you provision a cache of a chosen size for a stage of a REST API, control cache keys and per-method TTL (CDK default 5 minutes), and can invalidate per stage. Caching is available for REST APIs; cache capacity affects the cache instance CPU, memory and network and should be load tested. CloudFront in front of an API Gateway endpoint can cache at the edge for geographically spread users. API Gateway HTTP APIs have direct service integrations, including SQS (see buffering).

AWS Global Accelerator gives two static anycast IPv4 addresses (four for dual-stack: two IPv4 and two IPv6) that bring client traffic onto the AWS global network at the nearest edge, then route to the optimal Regional endpoint (ALB, NLB, EC2 or Elastic IP) based on health, client location and policy. It handles TCP and UDP, so it fits UDP game traffic and custom TCP protocols that CloudFront (HTTP/S) cannot. Client IP preservation is supported for ALB, EC2 and NLB with security groups endpoints; it is not supported for NLBs without security groups or for Elastic IP endpoints. Without preservation, the source IP seen by the endpoint is Global Accelerator's edge address. Pricing is an hourly accelerator fee plus data transfer. Static IPs persist while the accelerator exists, even if disabled; deleting it loses them.

rows: Non-HTTP, fast regional failover, IP allow-listing, UDP gaming

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Putting CloudFront in front of UDP game servers or expecting Global Accelerator to cache. Cache = CloudFront; static IPs, UDP or custom TCP = Global Accelerator.

links.label: Origin updates: CloudFront Functions vs Lambda@Edge

blocks.body: Buffering turns a burst into a steady stream the downstream system can absorb, and decoupling lets producers and consumers scale independently. Choose the buffer by consumption model and ordering/replay needs.

Amazon SQS stores messages until a consumer deletes them or the retention period expires (default 4 days, configurable from 1 minute to 14 days). Lambda polls the queue; the event source mapping default batch size is 10 (up to 10,000 for standard queues, 10 for FIFO) with an optional batching window. Setting maximum concurrency on the event source mapping caps concurrent invocations per queue so a burst cannot exhaust account concurrency or overload a database; keep function reserved concurrency above that value to avoid throttling. This SQS-in-front-of-Lambda-in-front-of-database pattern is the standard way to protect RDS from write spikes. API Gateway HTTP APIs can integrate directly with SQS (SendMessage, ReceiveMessage, DeleteMessage, PurgeQueue) without a Lambda hop, a storage-first pattern.

Kinesis Data Streams is an ordered, replayable stream. Each shard supports 1 MB/s and 1,000 records/s writes and 2 MB/s reads; capacity is the sum of shards. On-demand mode manages shards automatically (default 4 shards on creation; a shard is split when its average ingest utilization reaches 50% for 1 minute, and splitting can take up to 15 minutes), while provisioned mode needs you to reshard. Enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer its own 2 MB/s per shard. Amazon Data Firehose buffers data and delivers it to destinations such as S3: buffer size 1-128 MB and interval 0-900 seconds, whichever condition is met first triggers delivery; larger buffers mean fewer S3 writes and larger files (better Athena performance) but higher latency; Parquet conversion or dynamic partitioning uses 64-128 MB; a zero buffer interval is possible for some application destinations but not for dynamic partitioning.

rows: Ordered log by shard; multiple consumers, replay
Per-shard limits (1 MB/s in, 2 MB/s out) or on-demand
Real-time ingest of device/click data, multiple readers
Load streams to S3 for query

blocks.body: Combined pattern for IoT or sensor bursts: devices -> IoT Core / Kinesis Data Streams -> Firehose (batch to S3 Parquet) and/or Lambda -> DynamoDB with on-demand capacity (or provisioned with auto scaling plus Kinesis batching to absorb bursts). Batching writes also reduces request counts.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Scaling the database to match the peak instead of buffering the peak. Buffering with SQS/Kinesis is usually cheaper and cannot be overwhelmed, at the cost of eventual (not immediate) processing.

Elasticity means capacity follows demand. EC2 Auto Scaling target tracking keeps a metric (for example average CPU 50% or request count per target) near a target by creating and managing the CloudWatch alarms for you, scaling out and in like a thermostat; set the instance warmup so new instances are not counted prematurely. Predictive scaling forecasts traffic (needs at least 24 hours of history) and sets minimum capacity ahead of demand, while target tracking handles the unpredicted deviations; scheduled scaling covers known events. Other layers scale on their own models: DynamoDB on-demand/auto scaling, Aurora replica auto scaling, Kinesis on-demand, EFS Elastic throughput, Lambda concurrency, ECS service auto scaling.

Rightsizing is a continuous process, not a one-time resize. AWS Compute Optimizer uses machine learning on historical utilization to recommend EC2 instances, EBS volumes and Lambda functions (and Auto Scaling groups). The default EC2 lookback is 14 days; optional lookbacks are 32 days or 93 days (the 93-day option needs the paid enhanced infrastructure metrics). Preferences let you tune CPU and memory headroom and thresholds (presets: maximum savings, balanced, maximum performance) and instance-family preferences. Process: (1) collect metrics including memory; (2) review Compute Optimizer findings (over-provisioned, under-provisioned, optimized); (3) test the recommended size; (4) apply, then re-measure; (5) move legacy resources forward (gp2 to gp3, older instance generations).

items: Scale on the bottleneck metric: queue depth or requests per target for workers, not only CPU.
Use warm capacity (predictive or scheduled scaling) when instances take long to become ready.
Over-provisioned and under-provisioned resources are both findings; performance rightsizing may increase size.
Fixed, steady demand favors committed pricing after rightsizing; spiky demand favors elasticity.

blocks.body: 'Minimize operational overhead' plus unpredictable load points to managed elastic options (Lambda, Fargate, DynamoDB on-demand, EFS Elastic). 'Known minimum and maximum load' lets you set Auto Scaling min/max boundaries. A monthly or quarterly pattern means the default 14-day Compute Optimizer window may be too short.

blocks.body: Scenario 1: Global multiplayer game, UDP. Requirements: players worldwide, UDP traffic, lowest latency, fast failover between Regions, game servers behind Network Load Balancers in two Regions. Constraint: no caching possible; operations team is small. Chosen architecture: Global Accelerator standard accelerator with a UDP listener and an endpoint group per Region pointing at the NLBs (client IP preservation if the NLBs have security groups and the game needs player IPs for allow/deny logic). Rationale: players enter the AWS backbone at the nearest edge and traffic is routed to the healthiest, closest Region; static anycast IPs mean clients never change addresses when Regions are added. Security: security groups on the NLBs, AWS Shield protections at the edge are not verified here. Cost: hourly accelerator fee plus data transfer. Rejected: CloudFront (HTTP/S only, no value for uncacheable UDP); Route 53 latency routing alone (DNS caching delays failover and gives no backbone optimization).

Scenario 2: HPC simulation, periodic, S3-resident data. Requirements: tightly coupled MPI jobs on hundreds of cores weekly, input of tens of TiB in S3, results must be kept, minimal cost when idle. Chosen architecture: compute- or HPC-optimized instances with EFA in a cluster placement group in one AZ, launched in a single request; an FSx for Lustre scratch file system linked to the S3 bucket with a data repository association (lazy-load inputs, export results), created per run and deleted afterwards; AWS Batch or ParallelCluster to orchestrate. Rationale: single-AZ cluster placement plus EFA minimizes inter-node latency; Lustre supplies parallel throughput; scratch is the cheapest tier for temporary data and S3 retains durability. Risk: scratch data is lost if a file server fails, so results are exported to S3. Rejected: EFS (higher latency, designed for general sharing), spread/partition groups (fault isolation, not latency), multi-AZ cluster (EFA not supported across AZs).

Scenario 3: Retail API with a bursty order database. Requirements: REST API serving mostly repeated product reads, order writes that spike during promotions, an Aurora MySQL back end suffering from connection exhaustion and CPU spikes, minimal code change. Chosen architecture: CloudFront plus API Gateway stage caching for product GETs; writes go to an SQS queue (API Gateway HTTP API direct integration or via Lambda) consumed by Lambda with maximum concurrency set to protect the database through RDS Proxy; Aurora read replicas behind the reader endpoint for reporting reads. Rationale: caching removes repeat reads, the queue converts spikes into a steady write rate, RDS Proxy pools connections for Lambda. Cost: replicas and cache add fixed cost but avoid scaling the writer for peaks. Rejected: scaling the writer to peak capacity (always-on cost), DAX (applies to DynamoDB, not Aurora), Memcached for orders (no durability).

The snippets below use placeholders; replace <account-id>, <region>, <vpc-id> and resource IDs. Verify each change with the checks listed. Command and parameter names are shown as commonly documented; confirm them in the CLI reference for your CLI version (the exact CLI syntax pages were not retrieved in this build).

items: EBS: change a gp2 volume to gp3 with explicit IOPS and throughput (online change, then monitor `VolumeQueueLength` and burst balance in CloudWatch).
EFS: create a General Purpose file system with Elastic throughput; verify `PercentIOLimit` and `ThroughputUtilization` in the console Monitoring tab.
EC2: create a cluster placement group and launch all instances of one type in a single request.
DynamoDB: enable TTL on an epoch-seconds Number attribute.
Lambda/SQS: create the event source mapping with a maximum concurrency cap.
Verify: check CloudWatch alarms, X-Ray trace map and Compute Optimizer after a full business cycle.

blocks.label: CLI
blocks.body:
# EBS gp2 -> gp3
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id <vol-id> --volume-type gp3 --iops 6000 --throughput 250

# EFS: General Purpose + Elastic throughput
aws efs create-file-system --performance-mode generalPurpose --throughput-mode elastic --encrypted --region <region>

# Cluster placement group, one launch request, one instance type
aws ec2 create-placement-group --group-name hpc-cluster --strategy cluster
aws ec2 run-instances --image-id <ami-id> --instance-type <efa-capable-type> --count 16 --placement GroupName=hpc-cluster --subnet-id <subnet-id>

# DynamoDB TTL (attribute holds epoch seconds as a Number)
aws dynamodb update-time-to-live --table-name Readings --time-to-live-specification Enabled=true,AttributeName=expireAt

# SQS -> Lambda with a concurrency cap
aws lambda create-event-source-mapping --function-name <fn> --event-source-arn arn:aws:sqs:<region>:<account-id>:orders --batch-size 10 --scaling-config MaximumConcurrency=10

Troubleshooting checklist: EFS slow -> check throughput mode, `BurstCreditBalance`, client mount options and per-client limits. S3 503 SlowDown -> spread keys over prefixes and retry with backoff. Lambda throttled behind SQS -> compare reserved concurrency with the mapping's maximum concurrency. RDS Proxy not reducing connections -> look for pinning and many distinct DB users. Placement group launch fails with insufficient capacity -> stop and start all instances in the group, or relaunch together using one instance type. FSx for Lustre files missing -> confirm the DRA import and metadata load. Global Accelerator source IP wrong -> check client IP preservation support for the endpoint type.

Step 1: find the primary requirement (lowest latency, highest throughput, absorb bursts, least operational overhead, minimal changes, lowest cost). Step 2: list mandatory constraints (protocol, UDP/TCP, POSIX, durability, Region count, existing engine). Step 3: eliminate options that fix a different bottleneck. Step 4: of the survivors, choose the more managed and more elastic, unless a constraint forbids it.

items: Ambiguity handling: if two answers both work, the exam wants the one that meets every stated constraint with fewer moving parts.
A cache helps reads only; a queue helps writes and bursts; replicas help reads; sharding/key redesign helps hot keys.
Distinguish performance (latency/throughput) from availability: placement 'spread' and origin groups are about failure, not speed.

blocks.body: Beware of options that sound faster but add a hop that cannot help the stated traffic (for example CloudFront for a non-cacheable UDP workload, or DAX for a relational database).

items: Measure first: CloudWatch metrics, X-Ray/Application Signals traces, and database-load analysis (Database Insights replaced Performance Insights, end of life July 31, 2026 per AWS).
EBS: gp3 default (3,000 IOPS baseline, independent IOPS/throughput, up to 80,000 IOPS), io2 Block Express for 256,000 IOPS / sub-ms; gp2 = 3 IOPS/GiB, 100-16,000.
S3: at least 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads per second per prefix; parallelize prefixes; Athena likes partitioned Parquet/ORC.
EFS: General Purpose always; Elastic for spiky, Provisioned for steady known, Bursting scales with size; Max I/O not with Elastic or One Zone.
FSx for Lustre: scratch (temporary) vs persistent; DRA links to S3 (max 8 per file system).
Compute: cluster placement group plus EFA in one AZ for tightly coupled HPC; Lambda 15 min and CPU scaling with memory; Fargate/Batch beyond that.

Databases: DynamoDB TTL (free deletes, within days), on-demand doubles previous peak instantly; DAX for DynamoDB reads; ElastiCache vs MemoryDB (durability); Aurora up to 15 replicas; RDS Proxy for connections.
Edge: CloudFront caches HTTP; Lambda@Edge origin request on cache misses; Global Accelerator for TCP/UDP, static IPs, client IP preservation (not with Elastic IP or NLB without security groups).
Buffers: SQS with Lambda max concurrency; Kinesis shard = 1 MB/s in, 2 MB/s out; Firehose 1-128 MB or 0-900 s buffer.
Elasticity: target tracking + predictive; Compute Optimizer 14/32/93-day lookback.

General Purpose is recommended; scale with Elastic/Provisioned throughput
Only cluster placement targets low latency

blocks.body: Takeaways: match access pattern to purpose-built service; buffer or cache before you scale up; prefer elastic managed modes when load is unpredictable; always verify the stated protocol, region, durability and POSIX constraints before choosing.

This lesson covers exam task 2.6: determine a cost optimization strategy to meet solution goals and objectives for NEW solutions (designing before you build). The exam rarely asks which service is cheapest in isolation. Instead, it asks you to meet a hard requirement (availability, latency, licensing, compliance, deadline) at the lowest cost, so you must know which cost levers are safe to pull for a given workload shape and which are traps.

Prerequisites: working knowledge of Amazon EC2, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling, Amazon S3, Amazon VPC networking (NAT gateways, VPC endpoints), AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), and AWS Organizations (consolidated billing, management account). The cost-strategy domain sits inside Domain 2 (Design for New Solutions), which carries the largest share of the SAP-C02 exam; cost shows up both as the main question and as a tie-breaker between otherwise valid designs.

Official skills for this task: identify opportunities to select and rightsize infrastructure for cost-effective resources; identify appropriate pricing models; perform data transfer modeling and select services to reduce data transfer costs; develop a strategy and implement controls for expenditure and usage awareness. Knowledge areas: cost and usage monitoring tools (AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Trusted Advisor, AWS Pricing Calculator), pricing models (Reserved Instances, Savings Plans), storage tiering, data transfer costs, and AWS managed service offerings.

items: You will be able to choose between On-Demand, Spot, Savings Plans, Reserved Instances, Capacity Reservations and Dedicated Hosts from a workload description (steady, spiky, interruptible, license-bound, capacity-critical).
You will be able to design a blended purchasing strategy (committed baseline + On-Demand + Spot) that still meets a deadline or SLA.
You will be able to select S3 storage classes and lifecycle rules from an access pattern, accounting for minimum storage durations, minimum object sizes and retrieval charges.
You will be able to model data transfer cost and reduce it with gateway/interface endpoints, per-AZ NAT gateways, CloudFront and Requester Pays.
You will be able to choose a managed or serverless service when it lowers total cost (including operations) and reject it when steady high utilization makes provisioned capacity cheaper.
You will be able to design spend controls and visibility: cost allocation tags, Budgets with actions, Cost Anomaly Detection, Compute Optimizer and Trusted Advisor.

blocks.title: Why it matters on the exam
blocks.body: Cost optimization is a Well-Architected pillar whose design principles are: implement cloud financial management, adopt a consumption model, measure overall efficiency, stop spending money on undifferentiated heavy lifting, and analyze and attribute expenditure. Exam questions are usually written so that exactly one option satisfies the non-negotiable requirement AND is cheapest; learn to find the non-negotiable requirement first.

rows: oversized instances, idle capacity, undifferentiated ops
access drops after N days, archive, compliance retention
NAT gateway bills, cross-AZ, global users, sharing data with partners

links.label: Choosing a purchasing option for Amazon EC2

blocks.body: You cannot optimize what you cannot attribute. The visibility and control toolset answers four different questions, and the exam tests that you pick the right tool for the question.

rows: What did we spend, and what should we commit to?

Used to view historical usage, get Savings Plans recommendations, purchase and manage Savings Plans. Savings Plans recommendations are calculated at hourly granularity from a 7, 30 or 60 day lookback and can be viewed for all accounts or per linked account.
Alert me, or act, when spend/usage crosses a threshold

Budgets can be set by time frame and filtered by dimensions such as service, linked account or tag; thresholds can be on actual or forecasted cost. Budget actions can apply an IAM policy, apply a service control policy (SCP), or target specific EC2/RDS instances, automatically or after manual approval.
Is something unusual happening that I did not budget for?
Monitors can be created on four dimensions: services, linked account, cost category, cost allocation tag. Each detection includes root cause analysis (account, service, usage type, Region).
Cost allocation tags and Cost Categories

User-created and AWS-generated tags can be activated for cost allocation in the Billing console (of the management account in an organization). Cost Categories group accounts and tags ('meta-tagging') for use in Cost Explorer, Budgets and the Cost and Usage Report.
What will this design cost BEFORE I build it?
Estimate tool for new designs; use it during design for storage-class and instance-purchase comparisons.
Which running resources are idle or underutilized?

Cost Optimization checks cover idle or low-utilization resources (for example idle load balancers, unassociated Elastic IPs, low-utilization EC2). The EC2 cost optimization check requires opting in to Cost Optimization Hub and AWS Compute Optimizer.
What size/family should this resource be?
Rightsizing recommendations; lookback period 14 days (default), 32 days, or 93 days (paid enhanced infrastructure metrics); presets trade savings against headroom.

blocks.body: Budget actions are the enforcement mechanism for 'implement controls'. Because an SCP can be applied by a budget action from the management account to another account, you can block provisioning in a development OU without deploying any new resources. Two traps are documented: (1) a budget action that stops an EC2 instance in an Auto Scaling group is ineffective because Auto Scaling restarts or replaces the instance, so combine it with an action that removes permissions on the role used to launch; (2) from the management account you can apply an SCP to another account but you cannot target EC2 or RDS instances in another account. Budgets needs an IAM role it can assume to execute actions.

blocks.title: Tagging mechanics
blocks.body: Tags only help cost allocation after you ACTIVATE them as cost allocation tags in Billing, and tags created on resources in member accounts can be used for cost allocation only from the management account. A cost allocation strategy should combine account structure (AWS Organizations), activated tags, and Cost Categories.

items: Use Pricing Calculator before the build, Cost Explorer after, Budgets to alert or act, Anomaly Detection to catch the unplanned, Trusted Advisor and Compute Optimizer to find waste.
Alerts are not controls: if the requirement says 'prevent' or 'automatically stop', the answer includes a budget action (IAM policy/SCP), not just an Amazon SNS notification.

Savings Plans purchased in any account of a consolidated billing family are shared by default; the management account can turn sharing off per account, and plans apply first to the purchasing account then to others with sharing on.

blocks.body: Keywords: 'chargeback/showback' -> activated cost allocation tags + Cost Categories; 'forecasted to exceed' -> Budgets on forecasted cost; 'unexpected spike with no fixed threshold known' -> Cost Anomaly Detection; 'estimate before deployment' -> Pricing Calculator; 'idle or underutilized running resources' -> Trusted Advisor / Compute Optimizer.

topics.title: EC2 purchasing options: On-Demand and Spot

blocks.body: Purchasing options decide how AWS calculates your bill for compute you use. They are independent of Capacity Reservations, which decide whether capacity is held for you. Keep these two dimensions separate; many incorrect exam options confuse a billing discount with a capacity guarantee.

On-Demand Instances are pay-as-you-go with no commitment and per-second billing (60 second minimum) for Linux, RHEL and Windows instances. They are the right answer for new applications with unknown usage, short irregular workloads that cannot be interrupted, and proofs of concept. The EC2 decision guide recommends starting with On-Demand and measuring with Compute Optimizer and Cost Explorer when usage is not yet known, then committing.

Spot Instances use spare EC2 capacity at up to a 90% discount versus On-Demand but can be reclaimed. Spot capacity is split into pools defined by instance type, Availability Zone and Region; the number of pools is AZs multiplied by instance types, so flexibility across types and AZs directly lowers interruption risk and speeds provisioning. When EC2 needs the capacity back it issues an interruption notice two minutes before reclaiming the instance, delivered both as an EventBridge event and in instance metadata. Savings Plans discounts do not apply to Spot usage.

rows: Batch, CI/CD, analytics, stateless and containerized fault-tolerant work
Single-instance stateful systems, hard-deadline work without a fallback

items: Allocation strategy: price-capacity-optimized picks pools with the lowest likelihood of interruption at the lowest price, with interruption rates comparable to capacity-optimized and typically lower total price. Lowest-price alone concentrates on few pools and is not optimized for capacity.

Design for interruption: handle the two-minute notice (drain connections, save state), respond to rebalance recommendations, break work into small tasks, and checkpoint to persistent storage so another instance can resume.
Burstable instances launched as unlimited that run immediately and briefly on Spot can incur surplus credit charges; launch burstable Spot in standard mode.

Spot blocks (defined-duration Spot) are no longer available to new customers (documented as unavailable to new customers from July 1, 2021). Answers that rely on a guaranteed-duration Spot purchase are outdated.

blocks.title: Risk-adjusted cost
blocks.body: The lowest nominal price is not always the lowest risk-adjusted cost. Spot can add engineering effort and outage cost if applied to the wrong workload. The exam signal for Spot is explicit interruption tolerance ('can withstand interruptions', 'stateless', 'results not time sensitive').

If a question states a deadline or SLA together with Spot, look for a hybrid: committed or On-Demand baseline that can meet the deadline alone, plus Spot to accelerate. A pure-Spot answer fails the SLA; a pure On-Demand answer fails 'most cost-effective'.

topics.title: Commitments: Savings Plans, Reserved Instances, Capacity Reservations, Dedicated Hosts

blocks.body: Commitment-based pricing trades flexibility for discount. The modern default is Savings Plans: you commit to an hourly spend (USD per hour) for one or three years and receive lower prices on matching usage. Payment options are All Upfront, Partial Upfront or No Upfront. The rates stay the same through the term. Right-size first: oversized instances waste money regardless of purchasing model.

rows: Any family, size, OS, tenancy and Region
One instance family in one Region; any size, OS, tenancy
Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, DocumentDB, Neptune, Keyspaces, Timestream, DMS, OpenSearch
Engine, family, size, AZ, Region; also serverless

items: Terms are 1 year (365 days) or 3 years (1,095 days). A plan cannot be modified after purchase; you can queue future purchases (up to 3 years ahead) and the decision guide notes plans cannot be cancelled, with a return window for plans of USD 100/hour or less that were purchased in the last 7 days and in the same calendar month.

Dedicated Instances are charged USD 2/hour in every Region where you run at least one; this fee is not discounted by Savings Plans. Both Compute and EC2 Instance plans apply to EC2 instances inside EMR, EKS and ECS clusters; EKS control-plane charges are not covered.

When several commitments are active AWS applies Reserved Instances first. Savings Plans then apply to the remaining usage, with EC2 Instance Savings Plans applied before Compute Savings Plans (which have broader applicability) and each plan applied to the usage with the highest savings percentage first.

Choose Compute Savings Plans when architecture is likely to change (new instance generations, Graviton migration, EC2 to Fargate or Lambda, Region moves); choose EC2 Instance Savings Plans for stable, known families in one Region.

blocks.body: Reserved Instances (RIs) are a billing discount applied to matching On-Demand usage. AWS now describes RIs as an older option generally recommended to be replaced by Savings Plans, and newer instance families might not support RI pricing; RIs remain relevant for services without a Savings Plan type (for example Redshift Reserved Nodes). Know the exam-era distinctions:

rows: Modify AZ, scope, networking type, size within same family
Exchange for another Convertible RI (different family, OS, tenancy) of equal or higher value
Workload likely to change; payer-account purchase

items: Regional RIs give a discount across all AZs in a Region but reserve no capacity. Zonal RIs reserve capacity in one AZ. Default limits quoted in the EC2 documentation: 20 Zonal RIs per AZ and 20 Regional RIs per Region, adjustable on request.
Unused RIs still incur charges; an RI does not launch anything, it only discounts matching usage.

blocks.body: On-Demand Capacity Reservations (ODCR) hold capacity in a specific AZ for any duration, with no term for immediate-use reservations. A reservation is billed at the equivalent On-Demand rate whether or not you use it and gives no discount by itself. Savings Plans and Regional RIs discount the reservation (used and unused capacity); Zonal RI discounts do not apply to Capacity Reservations. Future-dated reservations can start 5 to 120 days ahead and require a commitment duration (at least 14 days for C, G, I, M, R and T families; 12 weeks for U and X families). Share across accounts through AWS Resource Access Manager. Capacity Blocks for ML reserve GPU capacity for 1 to 14 days or in multiples of 7 days up to 182 days, are priced by supply and demand, and cannot be combined with Savings Plans or RI discounts. Use ODCR for mission-critical, disaster recovery, regulatory or event capacity, and layer a Savings Plan over it for cost.

Dedicated Hosts are physical servers dedicated to you, priced per host per hour regardless of how many instances run on it. They expose sockets and physical cores so you can use existing per-socket or per-core server-bound licenses (Windows Server, SQL Server, SUSE) and can lower license cost, for example licensing SQL Server at the physical core level rather than per vCPU. Host affinity set to Host makes an instance always restart on the same host after a stop; Default affinity restarts on any available host but tries the last host on a best-effort basis. AWS License Manager can track license rules including 90-day affinity, and AWS Config records host usage. Dedicated Instances isolate hardware per account but give no visibility or control of placement, so they do not satisfy physical-host license tracking. Dedicated Host pricing options include On-Demand, Dedicated Host Reservations and Savings Plans coverage.

rows: On-Demand Capacity Reservation (+ Savings Plan/Regional RI for discount)
Regional RI or Savings Plan alone (no capacity)
Per-core/per-socket BYOL, same host for N days
Expecting a Savings Plan discount on the block (not combinable)

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: Treating a Savings Plan or Regional RI as a capacity guarantee. Only a Zonal RI or a Capacity Reservation reserves capacity; Savings Plans give no capacity assurance.

'Project runs 3 years, 24x7 stateless baseline' -> commitment for the baseline (Savings Plan; Compute if flexibility matters, EC2 Instance if family is fixed) and On-Demand/Spot for peaks. 'License tied to a physical host for 90 days' -> Dedicated Host + affinity (+ License Manager). Both are commonly paired with distractors that offer Spot or Dedicated Instances.

links.label: Reserve compute capacity with On-Demand Capacity Reservations
Dedicated Host auto-placement and host affinity

topics.title: Blending purchase options for real workloads

blocks.body: A single purchasing option is rarely optimal. The AWS pattern is layering: commit the predictable baseline, serve variable demand with On-Demand, add Spot where interruption is tolerable, and add capacity reservations only for what cannot fail to launch.

rows: Savings Plans / RIs for the full baseline
Savings Plans for the trough; On-Demand Capacity Reservations or Capacity Blocks for predictable peaks
Spot, with checkpointing and flexibility across types and AZs
ODCR layered with a Savings Plan or Regional RI

blocks.body: Hybrid pattern for deadline-bound batch: define the completion deadline, provision a baseline of On-Demand or committed capacity that can meet the deadline by itself, then add Spot (for example equal to the baseline) to finish sooner and cheaper even if part of the Spot capacity is reclaimed. If an AZ fails you need the baseline to still meet the SLA; Spot margin is a bonus, not a guarantee, because Spot availability after an AZ failure is not assured.

EC2 Auto Scaling mixed instances groups express the blend directly: a base capacity filled with On-Demand Instances and a percentage above base that is On-Demand versus Spot. Spot is filled using an allocation strategy across multiple instance types and AZs; attribute-based instance type selection can supply many types without listing them. Existing commitments (Savings Plans, RIs) automatically discount matching On-Demand usage, so the group needs no special configuration for them.

items: AWS Batch: for Spot compute environments the AWS console help page recommends SPOT_CAPACITY_OPTIMIZED, while the CDK reference recommends SPOT_PRICE_CAPACITY_OPTIMIZED for most use cases (the default when Spot is enabled). Both avoid concentrating on one pool. BEST_FIT optimizes for cost but can stall the queue waiting for one instance type; BEST_FIT_PROGRESSIVE favors throughput for On-Demand.

Amazon EMR: instance fleets let you diversify instance types and set a Spot provisioning timeout with a SWITCH_TO_ON_DEMAND action when Spot is unavailable. The general design rule (Spot for stateless task nodes, On-Demand for core nodes holding HDFS data) is common EMR guidance, but it was not verified against a documentation page here. Answers that rely on Spot blocks (defined duration) are outdated.
Containers: Compute and EC2 Instance Savings Plans apply to EC2 instances in ECS, EKS and EMR clusters, and Compute Savings Plans also cover Fargate.

blocks.title: Order of preference for a fault-tolerant, deadline-free batch job
blocks.body: Spot with a diversified, capacity-aware allocation strategy beats On-Demand on cost. Add a small On-Demand/committed floor only when a deadline or SLA exists.

Decision rule: 'withstand interruptions' + 'not time sensitive' -> Spot (price-capacity-optimized or capacity-optimized), many instance types and AZs. 'Must finish by X' -> baseline that alone meets X + Spot accelerator. 'Same capacity must exist at failover' -> ODCR (single-AZ) in each AZ you fail over to.
