topics.title: Rightsizing and managed or serverless services

blocks.body: Rightsizing means matching resource type, size and count to measured need. It comes before any commitment, because a commitment on an oversized fleet locks in waste. Compute Optimizer analyzes utilization over a lookback period (14 days default; 32 days to capture monthly patterns; 93 days with the paid enhanced infrastructure metrics) and you can tune CPU/memory headroom and thresholds: the maximum-savings preset uses a P90 threshold with 0% headroom, balanced uses P95 with 30%, and maximum performance uses P99.5 with 30%. Preferences can be set at organization, account or Region level, and Compute Optimizer can restrict recommendations to instance types you allow.

items: Graviton: AWS documents up to 40% better price performance than comparable x86 instances for a wide range of workloads; a prescriptive-guidance example shows t4g.xlarge about 19% cheaper On-Demand than t3.xlarge. Moving requires software that runs on Arm, so it is a refactoring cost.

Burstable (T-family) instances suit workloads with low average CPU and occasional bursts: a t3.large has a 30% baseline per its documentation. T3 launches as unlimited by default; if average CPU over a rolling 24 hours exceeds the baseline you pay a flat extra rate per vCPU-hour, so sustained high CPU is cheaper on a fixed-performance family.

EBS gp3 costs about 20% less per GB than gp2, includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s at any size, and lets you provision IOPS (up to 80,000) and throughput (up to 2,000 MiB/s) independently of capacity for an extra fee. At equal performance gp3 is always cheaper, so migrating gp2 to gp3 is a standard no-regret saving.
Stop non-production resources outside working hours: the Well-Architected consumption-model example is a 75% saving (40 hours versus 168 hours per week).

rows: Per request and per GB-second; free tier of 1M requests and 400,000 GB-seconds per month (prescriptive guidance)
Steady, high, 24x7 volume where well-utilized containers on committed capacity can be cheaper
Per task runtime; covered by Compute Savings Plans
No instances to manage, scale to zero when idle
Very high steady utilization where packed EC2 + Savings Plans wins

Variable load, avoids provisioning for peak

Steady predictable traffic: provisioned (optionally with auto scaling and reserved capacity, up to 77% per the features page) is cheaper

blocks.body: DynamoDB Time to Live (TTL) is a cost control for ephemeral data: you store an expiry timestamp as a Number in Unix epoch seconds, and DynamoDB deletes expired items without consuming write throughput and at no extra cost. Deletion is best effort and typically occurs within a few days, so filter expired items out of reads if correctness matters before deletion. When no retention is required after an event ends (a contest, a session), serverless compute plus DynamoDB on-demand plus TTL removes servers, idle cost and delete workload.

Static front ends do not need compute. S3 website hosting serves HTTP only; for HTTPS and to keep Block Public Access enabled, put CloudFront in front using origin access control (OAC) with the S3 REST endpoint. Dynamic content can be served from the dynamic backend through a separate behavior or distribution origin while the static assets come from S3 and are cached at the edge. This pattern removes the web-server instances and the load balancer for the static tier.

blocks.title: Undifferentiated heavy lifting
blocks.body: The Well-Architected principle 'stop spending money on undifferentiated heavy lifting' means managed services reduce operational cost, not just the instance bill. On the exam, 'least operational overhead' plus 'cost-effective' favors managed/serverless unless the stem states steady high utilization or a capability the managed service lacks.

Rightsizing before commitment: if a stem says the instances are 'large' and utilization is low, the best first step is Compute Optimizer-guided downsizing or a burstable/Graviton family, not buying a larger Savings Plan. Do not recommend burstable instances for sustained high CPU.

blocks.body: S3 storage classes trade storage price against retrieval price, retrieval latency, minimum storage duration, minimum billable object size and AZ count. Get the access pattern first, then the class.

rows: No retrieval fee, no minimum duration

Small monthly per-object monitoring and automation charge; no retrieval charges, no lifecycle tiering charges, no minimum storage duration; objects under 128 KB are not auto-tiered and are charged at Frequent Access rates
Retrieval fee; 30 day minimum; charged as 128 KB if smaller; One Zone-IA keeps data in a single AZ
180 day minimum; about 40 KB extra metadata per object (32 KB at Deep Archive rate, 8 KB at Standard rate)

items: Intelligent-Tiering moves objects not accessed for 30 consecutive days to Infrequent Access (saves up to 40%) and after 90 days to Archive Instant Access (up to 68%); these tiers have millisecond latency. Optional asynchronous Archive Access (after a minimum of 90 days) and Deep Archive Access (minimum 180 days) tiers can be enabled and require RestoreObject before retrieval. Accessing an object returns it to Frequent Access. It is designed for 99.9% availability.

Lifecycle rules transition objects only down the storage-class waterfall, never back up. Objects stored for less than 30 days cannot be transitioned to Standard-IA or One Zone-IA, and by default objects under 128 KB (created after September 2024) are not transitioned unless you add an object-size filter. Lifecycle runs asynchronously, about daily.

Deleting, overwriting or transitioning an object before its minimum duration still bills the remainder (90 days for Glacier IR/FR, 180 days for Deep Archive), so lifecycle-to-Glacier of short-lived data wastes money.
Use S3 Storage Class Analysis to find the right transition day for Standard to Standard-IA.

blocks.body: Choosing between Intelligent-Tiering and lifecycle rules: use lifecycle rules when the pattern is predictable by age (for example 'accessed heavily for 6 months, then rarely, but must stay immediately available'), because they avoid the monitoring charge and give you deterministic Standard-IA or Glacier Instant Retrieval pricing. Use Intelligent-Tiering when the pattern is unknown or varies per object, and the objects are larger than 128 KB. For large video objects with an access decline and an 'immediately available' requirement, Intelligent-Tiering (or a lifecycle to a millisecond-latency class) satisfies availability, while Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive do not. Pair public content with CloudFront so repeated reads are served from cache.

Serverless analytics over S3: Amazon Athena charges per data scanned (the pricing example uses USD 5 per TB; check current pricing). Compression, columnar formats (Parquet, ORC) and partitioning reduce scanned bytes: the AWS example drops a 3 TB text-file query from USD 15 to USD 1.25 with 3:1 compression and single-column reads. AWS guidance recommends files above about 128 MB or splittable formats, and lifecycle policies on the Athena results bucket. Combined with a Glue Data Catalog and lifecycle transitions to archive classes for aged data, this replaces an always-on cluster.

blocks.title: Archive trap
blocks.body: Deep Archive is the cheapest to store but requires up to 12 hours default retrieval and a 180-day minimum. If analysts still query the data (Athena), it must stay in a class Athena can read directly, not in an archive tier.

Look for: 'immediately available' -> not Flexible Retrieval/Deep Archive/optional archive tiers; 'unknown access pattern' -> Intelligent-Tiering; 'compliance retention 7+ years, rare retrieval' -> Deep Archive via lifecycle; 'objects deleted after 10 days' -> do not use a minimum-duration class.

blocks.body: Data transfer is a design-time cost that is easy to miss in a Pricing Calculator estimate. Model it by listing every byte path: internet to AWS, AWS to internet, between AZs, between Regions, between VPCs, and between your VPC and AWS services. Then remove paths that are not needed.

rows: Data transfer within the same AZ is free
Co-locate chatty tiers, one NAT gateway per AZ with local routing
Cross-AZ traffic to a NAT gateway incurs charges
Create a NAT gateway in each AZ with resources and route locally (trade: extra hourly charge per NAT gateway)
Charged per hour available and per GB processed
Send S3/DynamoDB traffic through gateway endpoints; use interface endpoints for other AWS services
No hourly or data processing charge; works only from the VPC (not via peering, VPN, Direct Connect or transit gateway)
Hourly charge per endpoint per AZ plus per GB processed; reachable from on premises
Use when gateway endpoints cannot (on premises, cross-Region, other services)
Data transfer from AWS origins (S3, ELB, API Gateway) to CloudFront is free; you pay CloudFront data transfer out and requests; the origin's own data transfer out is replaced by CloudFront's
Cache static and cacheable content; a minimum-spend commitment discount exists
S3 Requester Pays makes the requester pay request and download costs; the owner still pays storage
Share large datasets with many cost-conscious consumers

items: CloudFront bills five areas: data transfer out, HTTP/HTTPS requests, invalidation requests (first 1,000 paths per month free, per the FAQ), real-time log requests and dedicated-IP custom SSL certificates. Pricing varies by geography and usage; a minimum-spend commitment (the CloudFront Security Savings Bundle) can save up to 30% over a one-year term.

S3 Requester Pays: requesters must send the x-amz-request-payer: requester header (or --request-payer requester in the CLI); without it S3 returns 403 Access Denied. The requester's IAM identity still needs permissions such as s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket. Requests paid by the requester mean the bucket owner is not charged for transfer to other accounts.

The documented interface-endpoint caveat: inter-AZ traffic to the endpoint ENIs is not charged by itself, but centralized hub-and-spoke endpoint designs add transit gateway or peering data processing and inter-AZ/inter-Region charges.
Inter-Region and internet egress rates were not verified against AWS price pages in this build; state them only as 'charged' and use the Pricing Calculator for numbers.

blocks.title: Data gravity
blocks.body: Compute tends to stay in the Region that holds the data because cross-Region egress and replication make moving data expensive. This is also why Compute Savings Plans (Region-portable) matter less for data-heavy workloads.

NAT gateway bill driven by S3/DynamoDB traffic -> gateway endpoint (free). Many external consumers of a petabyte-scale bucket with cost-sensitive consumers -> Requester Pays (not replicating copies to each, not making the owner pay egress). Global users reading large static files from EC2 or S3 -> CloudFront. Do not pick gateway endpoints for access from on premises.

blocks.body: Scenario 1: SLA-bound analytics migration. A company moves a scheduled analytics platform (hourly and daily jobs of 20 minutes to 2 hours plus ad hoc user queries) from a 12-server on-premises cluster to AWS. Jobs must meet completion windows even if one AZ fails. Existing environment: stateless job workers reading from S3. Constraint: minimize cost without missing SLAs (service level agreements). Chosen architecture: Auto Scaling groups across three AZs; a committed baseline (Compute Savings Plan on the On-Demand base capacity) sized so that the loss of one AZ still meets the deadline for scheduled jobs; Spot capacity layered over it with price-capacity-optimized allocation across many instance types; ad hoc queries on a separate Spot-heavy group with queueing. Rationale: baseline protects the SLA, Spot lowers cost and shortens runtimes, flexibility across pools lowers interruptions. Security: instance roles with S3 access through a gateway endpoint. Cost: Savings Plan discount on the baseline, up to 90% off on Spot, free S3 gateway endpoint. Alternatives rejected: all Spot (cannot guarantee deadlines or AZ-failure margin), all On-Demand (most expensive), Capacity Reservations in every AZ for the whole fleet (pays On-Demand rate for idle capacity; justified only for the SLA-critical floor).

Scenario 2: Server-bound license for 90 days. A vendor license must run on the same physical host for the duration of use (90 days), while instances are patched and restarted every 30 days. Constraint: temporary need, no long-term commitment desirable. Chosen architecture: allocate a Dedicated Host On-Demand, launch instances with host affinity set to Host, track the license rule in AWS License Manager and record in AWS Config; release the host after 90 days. Rationale: affinity returns restarted instances to the same host, and the host is billed per hour, not per instance. Security: no change to IAM beyond launch permissions. Cost: no Dedicated Host Reservation because the term is shorter than a reservation would require. Alternatives rejected: Dedicated Instances (no placement control or visibility, cannot prove same host), default tenancy with Default affinity (best-effort only), Spot (interruptible, may change host).

Scenario 3: Sharing a 2 PB research dataset. An institute updates a 2 PB S3 dataset and must give read access to a dozen partner organizations that are extremely cost-conscious. Chosen architecture: keep a single bucket, enable Requester Pays, grant partner accounts read via bucket policy, require partners to send x-amz-request-payer; use Intelligent-Tiering or lifecycle for older objects. Rationale: the owner pays storage once; each partner pays its own request and transfer costs; no duplicate copies. Security: cross-account bucket policy, the requester must be an authenticated principal in an AWS account that can be billed (anonymous access is disabled on Requester Pays buckets because the requester must be identifiable to be billed). Alternatives rejected: replicating to each partner (storage multiplied and replication transfer paid by the owner), owner-pays public bucket (owner pays all egress), shipping devices (slow for an updating dataset).

blocks.title: Cost versus requirement
blocks.body: In each scenario the cheapest tool is only chosen after the hard constraint (deadline, license host, who pays) is satisfied. Spot is not chosen where a guarantee is required; Dedicated Hosts are not chosen without a per-host license need.

blocks.body: Step 1: Find the primary requirement: is it cost, or cost subject to a hard requirement? Step 2: List mandatory constraints (SLA/deadline, license host, immediate availability, interruption tolerance, retention, who pays, minimal changes). Step 3: Eliminate any option that violates a mandatory constraint, even if cheap. Step 4: Among survivors choose the lowest total cost including operations and data transfer. Step 5: Check that the option actually exists today (for example, Spot blocks are no longer available to new customers).

items: Service-distinction rule: Savings Plan = billing discount, no capacity; Capacity Reservation = capacity, no discount; Zonal RI = both but inflexible.
Service-distinction rule: Dedicated Host (placement, sockets, cores, affinity) vs Dedicated Instance (isolation only).
Service-distinction rule: Budgets alerts and actions vs Cost Anomaly Detection (unplanned spikes) vs Trusted Advisor/Compute Optimizer (waste and sizing).
Service-distinction rule: Gateway endpoint (free, in-VPC S3/DynamoDB) vs interface endpoint (paid, reachable from on premises).
Service-distinction rule: Intelligent-Tiering (automatic, monitoring fee, no retrieval fee) vs lifecycle (rule-based, retrieval fees apply in IA/Glacier).
If two options both meet constraints, prefer the one with fewer moving parts and no custom code (least operational overhead).

blocks.title: Ambiguity handling
blocks.body: Some questions mix a correct concept with outdated mechanics (for example EMR Spot blocks, or older Savings Plans documentation that lists three plan types). Choose the option that best matches current AWS guidance and the stem's requirement; the documentation now lists four Savings Plan types and AWS recommends Savings Plans over RIs for most workloads.

Pitfalls: choosing Spot when the stem contains a hard deadline with no fallback; choosing Glacier classes for data that must be 'immediately available'; choosing EC2 Instance Savings Plan when the stem says the team will migrate instance families; choosing Dedicated Instances for host-bound licenses.

items: Key concepts: purchasing option (billing) is independent of capacity reservation (availability). Commit the baseline, flex the rest. Right-size before you commit. Choose managed/serverless when load is variable and ops cost matters.

Decision rules: steady -> Savings Plan; changing architecture -> Compute Savings Plan; fixed family/Region -> EC2 Instance Savings Plan; interruptible -> Spot; guaranteed capacity -> ODCR/Zonal RI; per-host license -> Dedicated Host with affinity.
Storage: access pattern first; mind minimum durations (30 days IA, 90 days Glacier IR/FR, 180 days Deep Archive), 128 KB sizes, retrieval fees; Intelligent-Tiering has no retrieval charge.
Data transfer: same-AZ free; per-AZ NAT; gateway endpoints free for S3/DynamoDB; CloudFront reduces origin egress; Requester Pays shifts transfer cost.
Controls: tags + Cost Categories, Budgets (forecast/actual, actions), Anomaly Detection, Compute Optimizer, Trusted Advisor, Pricing Calculator.

rows: Up to 120 days ahead, min 14 day commitment
30 days to IA, 90 days to Archive Instant; optional 90+/180+ archive tiers

items: Misconceptions: Savings Plans reserve capacity (no); Spot discounts stack with Savings Plans (no); Intelligent-Tiering charges retrieval fees (no); Convertible RIs can be sold on the Marketplace (no); gateway endpoints work from on premises (no); budget alerts stop spend (only actions do).

blocks.body: Operational excellence on the SAP-C02 exam is the ability to look at a running AWS environment and recommend how to see what it is doing, react when it misbehaves, change it safely, and rehearse its failure. Task 3.1 sits in Domain 3 (Continuous Improvement for Existing Solutions). The exam guide lists the knowledge areas as: alerting and automatic remediation strategies, disaster recovery planning, monitoring and logging solutions (for example, Amazon CloudWatch), CI/CD pipelines and deployment strategies (blue/green, all-at-once, rolling), and configuration management tools (for example, AWS Systems Manager). The skills are: determining the most appropriate logging and monitoring strategy, evaluating current deployment processes for improvement opportunities, prioritizing opportunities for automation within a solution stack, recommending the AWS solution that enables configuration management automation, and engineering failure-scenario activities that exercise recovery actions. Domain weights are not restated in the material available in this build, so treat Domain 3 as a substantial share of the exam and confirm the current percentage in the official exam guide.

blocks.title: Prerequisites
blocks.body: You should already know EC2, Auto Scaling groups, Application Load Balancers, IAM roles and instance profiles, Amazon S3, AWS CloudFormation basics, and the difference between a Region and an Availability Zone (AZ). Terms used below: a metric is a time-ordered set of data points; a managed node is any EC2 instance, on-premises server or VM that AWS Systems Manager can control; RTO (recovery time objective) is how long recovery may take and RPO (recovery point objective) is how much data loss is tolerable.
After this lesson you will be able to:

items: Choose between metric alarms, composite alarms, anomaly detection alarms, metric filters and Logs Insights for a given monitoring requirement, and state the limits that constrain each.
Design centralized, off-instance logging for fleets that scale in and out, including hybrid servers, using the CloudWatch agent and Systems Manager.

Select the right automation path for remediation (alarm actions, EventBridge, AWS Config remediation, Systems Manager Automation, Step Functions error handling) and explain the IAM role each one needs.
Recommend a configuration-management design with Systems Manager (Patch Manager, State Manager, Maintenance Windows, Session Manager) and diagnose why a node is not managed.
Compare deployment strategies (in-place rolling, blue/green, canary, linear, immutable instance refresh, Lambda alias shifting) and choose the one that meets a rollback, downtime or cost requirement.
Plan failure exercises with AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) and match a disaster recovery strategy to RTO/RPO targets.

blocks.body: Services and patterns covered: CloudWatch metrics, alarms, Logs, agent, cross-account observability and Container Insights; X-Ray and OpenTelemetry; ALB access logs with Athena; EventBridge and AWS Health; AWS Config remediation; Systems Manager Automation, Patch Manager, State Manager, Session Manager; AWS Budgets, Cost Anomaly Detection and Cost and Usage Reports; CodeDeploy; EC2 Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks and instance refresh; Lambda aliases; EC2 Image Builder; CloudFormation Git sync, import, drift detection and DeletionPolicy; AWS FIS and DR strategies.

blocks.title: Design principles to anchor every answer
blocks.body: The Well-Architected Operational Excellence pillar lists five design principles: perform operations as code; make frequent, small, reversible changes; refine operations procedures frequently; anticipate failure; and learn from all operational failures. When two answer options both work, the one that is more automated, more reversible and exercised by game days usually matches the exam's intent.

Most Domain 3 questions describe an environment that works but is manual, noisy, risky to change, or hard to troubleshoot. The correct answer is typically the managed, event-driven, least-operational-overhead option that keeps the existing workload running.

A CloudWatch alarm watches a metric (or the result of a metric math expression) over evaluation periods and changes state between OK, ALARM and INSUFFICIENT_DATA. Each state transition can run actions. This topic covers the alarm types you must distinguish on the exam.

rows: A metric or metric math result against a fixed threshold
The default choice when you know the right threshold.
A metric against a machine-learning band of expected values

Model uses up to two weeks of data, handles trends plus hourly, daily and weekly patterns, is specific to one metric and statistic, can exclude deployment windows from training, and incurs charges. Useful when you are unsure of thresholds or when the metric is seasonal.
The ALARM/OK states of other alarms through a rule expression using AND, OR, NOT

Cannot monitor metrics directly. Can send SNS notifications, invoke Lambda functions, and create Systems Manager OpsItems or incidents. Cannot start EC2 or Auto Scaling actions. Can nest other composite alarms.

blocks.body: Anomaly detection fits a requirement such as 'alert when usage deviates from normal without hand-tuning thresholds'. The band width is controlled by a threshold expressed in standard deviations (a higher value gives a thicker band of normal values). Because the model learns from history, a brand new metric has little to learn from, and you should exclude known events such as large deployments from training so they do not distort the band.

blocks.title: Composite alarms reduce alarm fatigue
blocks.body: Create the underlying metric alarms with no actions, then attach the notification to a composite alarm such as 'error rate high AND latency high AND healthy hosts low'. You are notified only when the combination holds. Because a composite alarm cannot start EC2 or Auto Scaling actions, keep a separate metric alarm for automatic instance recovery or scaling.

Alarm actions. A metric alarm can publish to an SNS topic, trigger an Auto Scaling policy, invoke Lambda (the SDK reference lists latest version, a specific version or an alias), and for EC2 instance alarms can stop, terminate, reboot or recover the instance. The reboot action works on all instance types and regardless of instance state, whereas recover applies only to a subset of instance types and when the instance is impaired (the recover action works only with the StatusCheckFailed_System metric and is supported only on some instance types, so check the current requirements before relying on it).

Usage and quota alarms. Services publish usage metrics in the AWS/Usage namespace that correspond to Service Quotas. For AWS Fargate the usage metric is ResourceCount with dimensions Service=Fargate, Type=Resource, Resource=vCPU and Class of Standard/OnDemand or Standard/Spot. From the Service Quotas console you can create a CloudWatch alarm at a chosen percentage of the applied quota. Note that Fargate quotas are now vCPU-based rather than task-count-based, so older phrasing such as 'maximum number of tasks' is outdated.

items: Common mistake: setting a static CPU threshold on a bursty or seasonal workload and being paged nightly; anomaly detection or a composite alarm is the better answer.
Common mistake: expecting a composite alarm to scale an Auto Scaling group or reboot an instance. It cannot.
Best practice: alarm on symptoms customers feel (error rate, latency, queue age) and use causes (CPU) for diagnosis.
Pricing dimension: alarms, custom metrics, anomaly detection models and metrics extracted from logs are billed; exact prices are not quoted here because they were not retrieved in this build.

topics.title: CloudWatch Logs and the unified agent

blocks.body: The CloudWatch agent collects logs and system-level metrics from EC2 instances and on-premises servers and sends them to CloudWatch Logs. Logs shipped off-instance survive instance termination, which is the central reason to use them with Auto Scaling groups: instances are disposable, so anything left on local disks is lost on scale-in or replacement.

blocks.title: Deploying and configuring the agent at scale
blocks.body: Systems Manager is the managed way to install and configure the agent. For EC2 and registered on-premises servers use Run Command with the AWS-ConfigureAWSPackage document (Action Install, Name AmazonCloudWatchAgent, Version blank for latest), then AmazonCloudWatch-ManageAgent with the configure action to start it from a configuration file stored in Parameter Store. For on-premises servers set Mode to onPremise. A State Manager association keeps the agent installed and configured on new instances that match a tag or Auto Scaling group, which fits the 'least operational overhead' phrasing better than editing user data on every launch template.

Hybrid servers must first be registered with Systems Manager (see the Systems Manager topic), and the agent needs AWS credentials. The AWS blog on hybrid monitoring points to temporary credentials obtained through SSM registration rather than long-lived access keys. The legacy CloudWatch Logs agent is superseded by the unified CloudWatch agent; the question notes mention the legacy agent is deprecated but this was not confirmed on a page read in this build.
Metric filters turn log events into CloudWatch metrics so you can alarm on them. Facts verified in the docs:

items: A log group can have at most 100 metric filters.
A filter can publish up to three dimensions. Dimensions are part of a metric's identity, so every distinct dimension value creates a new custom metric that is billed separately.
Do not use high-cardinality fields such as IP address or request ID as dimensions. CloudWatch Logs may disable a filter that generates 1,000 distinct dimension name/value pairs within an hour.
A default value (for example, 0) keeps the metric reporting during periods with logs but no matches, but you cannot set a default value when the filter uses dimensions.
Metric filters are not retroactive: only events ingested after creation produce data.
Regular expressions in filter patterns are allowed with quotas of two regex patterns per filter pattern and five per log group.

blocks.body: 'Count unique users per client' or 'per-IP' reports are poor metric-filter designs because of cardinality cost and because a metric filter cannot easily count distinct values. The question-note guidance is that CloudWatch Logs Insights queries over the logs fit analytical questions better, while metric filters fit alarms on counts and rates.

Subscription filters stream log events in near real time to Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon Data Firehose, Lambda (same account) or a cross-account logical destination (Kinesis Data Streams or Firehose). Each log group supports up to two subscription filters, and payloads arrive base64 encoded and gzip compressed. Use them to feed a SIEM, an S3 data lake via Firehose, or custom processing.

Best practice: set log retention explicitly; the default retention behaviour and pricing were not retrieved in this build, so verify before quoting costs.

Common mistake: copying logs to S3 on a timer (for example, every 15 minutes) from instances that can be terminated at any moment; use streaming from the agent or a termination lifecycle hook to flush.

topics.title: Observability across accounts, containers and requests

blocks.body: Metrics and logs answer 'what is happening'; traces and request logs answer 'why is this request slow or failing' and 'who called us'. This topic covers four building blocks the exam combines: CloudWatch cross-account observability, Container Insights, distributed tracing, and load balancer access logs.

blocks.title: CloudWatch cross-account observability
blocks.body: You designate one or more monitoring accounts and link source accounts. Shared telemetry can include CloudWatch metrics (all namespaces or a subset), CloudWatch Logs log groups (all or a subset), X-Ray traces, Application Signals services and SLOs, Application Insights applications and Internet Monitor monitors. A sink is the attachment point in the monitoring account (one sink per Region per account); an observability link is the resource in the source account that connects to the sink. It works within a single Region. Source accounts can be specified as account IDs, an AWS Organizations organization ID, or an organization path (OU paths must end with a slash). You can build alarms in the monitoring account that evaluate metrics from source accounts. Use Observability Access Manager (OAM) APIs or the CloudWatch console Settings page to configure it.

When a requirement says 'a central operations account must view metrics and logs from all workload accounts without copying data', this is the answer. It replaces older patterns such as cross-account IAM roles for each dashboard or log subscription plumbing for every account.

Container Insights collects CPU, memory, network and storage metrics for ECS at cluster, service and task level (and container instance level when the CloudWatch agent runs as a daemon), publishes them as custom metrics in the ECS/ContainerInsights namespace, and builds automatic dashboards. It is enabled per ECS cluster. Performance log events are queryable with Logs Insights. Fargate task usage against quota is a different signal: use the AWS/Usage vCPU metrics described earlier, and metric math if you need a percentage of quota.

Tracing. AWS X-Ray builds a service map and shows per-request traces made of segments and subsegments, so you can see which downstream call (API Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB, a database) adds latency or returns errors. For serverless 5xx or slow-response diagnosis, combine API Gateway and Lambda logs with X-Ray traces. Currency note verified in AWS material: the X-Ray SDKs and daemon entered maintenance mode on 25 February 2026 (security fixes only). The X-Ray service itself remains fully supported, and AWS recommends OpenTelemetry-based instrumentation (AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry) for new work. An answer option that uses X-Ray tracing is still functionally valid; a newer answer may mention OpenTelemetry.

ALB access logs record each request (client IP, request path, user agent, latencies, status codes, TLS details and more). They are disabled by default. Enabling them requires an S3 bucket in the same Region as the load balancer, with Amazon S3-managed keys (SSE-S3) as the only supported server-side encryption option, and a bucket policy that allows Elastic Load Balancing to write. The current policy uses the logdelivery.elasticloadbalancing.amazonaws.com service principal; Regions available before August 2022 also support a legacy policy that names a Region-specific Elastic Load Balancing account, and newer Regions support only the service principal. Query them with Amazon Athena; the logs are not stored in Hive-style partitions, so for large histories define partitions (partition projection or a Glue crawler with a custom classifier) to control query cost and speed. Because logging starts only when you enable it, a requirement for 90 days of history means you must enable it now and wait.

rows: Who accessed the app, from which IP and user agent?
ALB access logs in S3 + Athena
Which downstream call makes the request slow?
Per-account dashboards and manual role switching
Am I about to hit a Fargate quota?

items: Common mistake: forgetting the S3 bucket policy for ELB log delivery, so enabling access logs fails.
Common mistake: assuming cross-account observability works across Regions; the documentation scopes it to a Region (a separate cross-account cross-Region dashboard feature exists).
Best practice: use Organizations-based linking so new accounts join automatically.

blocks.title: AWS Health events
blocks.body: EventBridge rules for AWS Health receive account-specific events for your own account (public events can take up to an hour to start flowing after the rule is created; organization-wide events need organizational view with a delegated administrator). Delivery is durable and at least once. Targets include Lambda, Kinesis Data Streams, SQS, SNS and built-in targets. To push events to an HTTPS endpoint, route to an SNS topic that has an HTTPS subscription. Filter by event type category (issue for incident response, ACTION_REQUIRED actionability for planned lifecycle changes). The older names Personal Health Dashboard and Service Health Dashboard are legacy; current documentation uses AWS Health Dashboard.

AWS Config remediation. In the Config console, open a non-service-linked rule, choose Manage remediation, then choose automatic or manual and a Systems Manager Automation document (AWS provides managed ones, and you can author custom ones). You can pass the noncompliant resource ID into a runbook parameter, supply an AutomationAssumeRole, and set retries (for example, 5 retries in 300 seconds); repeated runs cost money because Automation is billed. Remediation is applied only to non-service-linked Config rules.

Systems Manager Automation runs runbooks (documents) that orchestrate steps across AWS APIs. Without an AssumeRole it runs with the caller's permissions; best practice is a dedicated Automation service role with only the permissions the runbook needs. For fleets you can specify targets (tags, resource groups) and rate controls such as max-concurrency and max-errors, so a remediation does not take down every instance at once. Incident Manager can start runbooks as part of a response plan using a runbook service role plus an Automation AssumeRole.

Step Functions error handling. By default an unhandled state error fails the whole execution. Retriers (interval, max attempts, backoff rate) and Catchers (route to a fallback state such as an SNS notification) are available on Task, Parallel and Map states, not on the top-level execution. For failures you cannot catch inside the workflow, listen for execution status events such as TIMED_OUT from Standard workflows on an EventBridge bus. Lambda Invoke integrations have one retrier configured by default in Workflow Studio. The question notes mention that a catch-all error name does not match every runtime error type; that nuance was not confirmed in the pages read here.
Spend signals are operational signals too. Learn the differences:

rows: Actual or forecasted cost/usage vs a threshold you set; RI or Savings Plans utilization and coverage

Cost, usage, RI utilization and coverage budget types; can also be daily or custom period; data refreshes up to three times a day (about 8 to 12 hours apart); alerts go to up to 10 email addresses and one SNS topic per alert; budget actions can apply for example an IAM policy that denies provisioning; usage budgets can track service limits.

Monitor dimensions: AWS services, linked accounts, cost categories, cost allocation tags. AWS managed monitors track up to the top 5,000 values independently and automatically include new ones; customer managed monitors aggregate selected values (up to 10 accounts or tag values; AWS services dimension is not supported as customer managed). Linked-account AWS managed monitors need the management account.

Delivered to S3; Athena integration uses a CloudFormation template that sets up a Glue crawler, database and a Lambda trigger so new report files add partitions automatically; if latest data is missing, check the S3 path and crawler status.

blocks.body: 'Identify the resources or accounts causing an unexpected spike' points to Cost Anomaly Detection (with root-cause output) rather than a Budget, because a Budget only compares to a threshold. 'Stop spending above a limit' points to Budgets with an action. 'Attribute cost to teams' points to cost allocation tags and CUR with Athena/QuickSight, and tags must be activated before they appear (activation behaviour not verified in this build).

items: Best practice: alert to SNS and let subscribers (chat, ticketing, Lambda) fan out.
Common mistake: writing a Lambda on a schedule to check conditions that an EventBridge rule or Config rule already detects.

Capacity example from the question set: a CloudWatch alarm on FSx for Windows free storage can invoke automation to expand capacity; the specific FSx automation was not verified in this build; a CloudWatch alarm is the standard trigger for a metric breach.

blocks.body: AWS Systems Manager (SSM) is the operations hub for fleets of EC2 instances, on-premises servers and VMs, collectively called managed nodes. The capabilities you must distinguish: Run Command (one-off or targeted commands), State Manager (keep a desired state by schedule), Patch Manager (patching), Maintenance Windows (schedule disruptive tasks), Automation (runbooks), Session Manager (shell without inbound ports), Fleet Manager, Parameter Store, Distributor, Explorer and Quick Setup.

blocks.title: What makes a node 'managed'
blocks.body: Three requirements: (1) SSM Agent installed and running on a supported OS (many AWS-provided AMIs include it); (2) an IAM instance profile for EC2, or an IAM service role for non-EC2 machines, that grants Systems Manager permissions, typically the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore managed policy (or AmazonSSMManagedEC2InstanceDefaultPolicy; Default Host Management Configuration can supply permissions without a per-instance profile on SSM Agent 3.2.582.0 or later); (3) network reachability from the agent to Systems Manager endpoints. In a VPC with no internet path you need interface endpoints for ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages. An SCP that explicitly denies the required actions will also break it. After registering, the service checks health about every five minutes. The ssm-cli get-diagnostics tool (agent 3.1.501.0 or later) and the AWSSupport-TroubleshootManagedInstance runbook diagnose why a node is missing.

Hybrid activation. For on-premises servers or VMs (including VMs imported or running in other clouds) create a hybrid activation, which returns an Activation Code and Activation ID; you pass them when installing or registering SSM Agent. Save them immediately: if lost you must create a new activation. An activation has an expiration window for registering new machines; expiry does not affect machines already registered, which stay managed until explicitly deregistered (Fleet Manager, deregister-managed-instance). Registered non-EC2 nodes appear in the console with an mi- prefixed ID (prefix not shown in the pages read here). If an imported VM is not showing up, check that the agent is installed and registered with the activation or has an appropriate role and connectivity, as the hybrid path differs from the EC2 instance-profile path.

Patch Manager. A patch baseline defines which patches are approved (auto-approval rules with a delay in days after release, plus approved and rejected lists). A Scan operation only reports missing patches; Scan and install applies them. Four methods run patch operations: a Quick Setup patch policy (recommended, uses Organizations to cover many accounts and Regions, and can scan and install on different schedules), a Quick Setup Host Management option (scan only with the default baseline), a Maintenance Window Run Command task using AWS-RunPatchBaseline, and a fourth, on-demand method (the page chunk read was truncated before it, so confirm its details in the Patch Manager documentation). Predefined baselines exist per OS and cannot be edited; create a custom baseline for a different approval delay. Most predefined baselines (for example, Windows Server and Amazon Linux) auto-approve patches seven days after release, whereas some, such as Debian, have no wait; a same-day-patching requirement on an operating system with a delay therefore needs a custom baseline with a zero-day delay.

items: Patch groups use the tag key Patch Group on the nodes (use PatchGroup, without a space, if tags in instance metadata are allowed). A node can be in only one patch group, and a patch group can be registered with only one patch baseline for each operating system type, so separate groups per environment and operating system keep baselines and schedules distinct (for example, appname-DEV-WIN and appname-DEV-RHEL). Patch policies do not use patch groups.
Typical staged rollout: patch the dev group first, then production, using separate maintenance windows with staggered cron schedules, and target windows by tag.

Compliance: Patch Manager reports patch compliance for all managed nodes, including on-premises nodes, from one place. For a single report spanning EC2 and on-premises servers that previously used different tools, register everything with Systems Manager and use Patch Manager compliance reporting (Explorer or exported data feeds dashboards).
For immutable fleets patch the golden AMI instead (see the deployment topic) so running instances never drift.

blocks.body: State Manager. An association defines the state you want, a target and a schedule. Static targets are reapplied on the schedule; dynamic targets such as an Auto Scaling group or resource group get the configuration applied as new nodes join. Examples: ensure anti-virus or the CloudWatch agent is installed and running, close certain ports, or enforce an agent configuration document. State Manager is also what Patch Manager uses for patch policies, and a failed or missing-patch association shows as non-compliant in the Compliance dashboard until fixed. Choose State Manager for continuous enforcement, Run Command for one-time actions, Maintenance Windows for scheduled disruptive tasks inside a defined window, and Automation for multi-step workflows.

Access without bastions. Session Manager gives browser or CLI shell access to managed nodes without opening inbound ports, managing bastion hosts or SSH keys, and session activity can be logged to CloudTrail, S3 or CloudWatch Logs. EC2 Instance Connect pushes a temporary SSH public key through the instance metadata service for 60 seconds; the IAM policy needs ec2-instance-connect:SendSSHPublicKey (scope it to instances by ARN or tags and set the ec2:osuser condition) and ec2:DescribeInstances for console use. It requires the instance to accept SSH from your network path. Both give per-user, CloudTrail-recorded access; Session Manager additionally needs no inbound port at all.

Security scanning dependency. Amazon Inspector agent-based EC2 scanning relies on SSM: it creates SSM associations and plugins to collect software inventory, and the instance must be an SSM managed node in the same account. ECR enhanced scanning is provided and billed through Inspector with continuous or scan-on-push filters, while basic scanning is provided and billed through ECR. For EKS worker nodes, managed node group AMIs normally include SSM Agent (not verified in the pages read here), so check the SSM role and agent first when Inspector shows no coverage.

blocks.body: A deployment strategy describes how a new version replaces the old one. The exam asks you to weigh downtime, blast radius, rollback speed, cost and operational effort. The strategies below map to specific AWS features.

Redeploy previous revision; user-visible impact in between
Update a few hosts at a time while others serve
CodeDeploy OneAtATime (default if unspecified) or HalfAtATime; ASG instance refresh
Redeploy previous version; capacity is reduced during the rollout
Build a full replacement (green), switch traffic, keep blue until safe
CodeDeploy blue/green with an ELB (Classic, ALB or NLB target groups) and optionally a copied Auto Scaling group; CloudFormation blue/green for ECS
Re-route traffic back to blue; no rebuild needed
Shift a slice of traffic first, then the rest (canary) or in equal steps (linear)

blocks.title: CodeDeploy details to remember
blocks.body: For EC2/on-premises the deployment configuration sets minimum healthy hosts; if none is specified the default is CodeDeployDefault.OneAtATime. HalfAtATime counts across multiple Auto Scaling groups together, so one group could be updated entirely. In blue/green deployments, the load balancer registers replacement instances and deregisters the originals (optionally terminating them). If you let CodeDeploy copy an Auto Scaling group it creates a new group named CodeDeploy_<deployment-group>_<deployment-id>. Blue/green with NLB on ECS supports only the all-at-once predefined configuration. Automatic rollback redeploys the last known good revision when a deployment fails or a monitoring threshold (CloudWatch alarm) is met, and you can be notified through SNS.

Why blue/green wins for fast rollback and zero downtime: you test green without touching blue, switch only traffic, and roll back by redirecting traffic rather than rebuilding. It also supports immutable infrastructure and avoids configuration drift. The cost is running two environments for the overlap, and you must handle stateful dependencies such as database schema changes separately.

EC2 Auto Scaling instance refresh replaces instances in a group after you change the launch template (new AMI or settings). The default strategy is Rolling; ReplaceRootVolume is an alternative that swaps only the root volume (requires a mixed instances policy with ImageId overrides, single-root-volume AMIs, and so on). Preferences include instance warmup, minimum and maximum healthy percentages, behaviour for Standby or scale-in-protected instances, auto rollback, checkpoints, CloudWatch alarms, bake time and SkipMatching (skip instances already on the desired template). Use it for immutable patching: bake a patched AMI, update the launch template (launch templates are the current mechanism; launch configurations are an older construct), start an instance refresh. This needs far less custom tooling than patching running instances.

Lifecycle hooks pause an instance in a wait state so you can act before it launches or terminates. A terminating hook (autoscaling:EC2_INSTANCE_TERMINATING) puts the instance in Terminating:Wait, letting you run a script (for example, through Systems Manager Run Command triggered by EventBridge) that flushes logs to S3 or drains work, then you call CompleteLifecycleAction. The heartbeat timeout ranges from 30 to 7,200 seconds, with a default of 3,600 (one hour); the DefaultResult applies on timeout or unexpected failure and defaults to ABANDON; hooks can notify an SNS topic or SQS queue. While an instance waits, scaling activity under simple scaling policies is paused. A scale-out hook (EC2_INSTANCE_LAUNCHING) lets you finish bootstrap before the instance takes traffic.

Lambda versions and aliases. A published version is a numbered snapshot; $LATEST is mutable. An alias is a stable pointer (and stable invocation ARN) to a version, so clients and event sources do not change when you deploy. A weighted alias routes a percentage of invocations to a second version (for example, 3 percent to version 2, 97 percent to version 1), which enables canary releases; rolling back is changing the alias weight or target, effective within seconds. Weighted routing is across all callers, not per user, and an alias can point to at most two versions in a weighted configuration. CodeDeploy automates the shifting and rollback on alarms for Lambda.

Golden images. EC2 Image Builder pipelines build, test and distribute AMIs (and container images) on a schedule or only when dependencies change (a new base image or a versioned build or test component). They can distribute to other Regions and accounts and notify through SNS so a downstream step can launch an instance refresh. This is the managed answer to 'reliably produce patched AMIs'. The question notes mention a CodeCommit availability change in 2024 to 2025; this was not verified here, so prefer reading the current CodeCommit status in AWS docs before relying on it in a design.

Evaluating the existing process. Signals that a process needs improvement: manual SSH deployments, long-lived snowflake servers, no automated rollback, no deployment health alarms, same environment for test and prod, patching by hand. Recommend: pipeline as code, small frequent changes, automated tests, alarm-gated rollouts, immutable images and traffic shifting. For AI agents deployed through CI/CD, the question set references AgentCore Evaluations as a quality gate; no AWS page for that was retrieved in this build, so treat the product details as unverified.

Keywords: 'rollback in seconds' or 'no downtime' suggests blue/green or alias shifting; 'minimal capacity loss' avoids in-place rolling with HalfAtATime on small fleets; 'least operational overhead for AMI changes' suggests launch template update plus instance refresh; 'stable ARN for clients' suggests a Lambda alias; 'flush logs before termination' suggests a terminating lifecycle hook.

topics.title: Infrastructure as code operations with CloudFormation

blocks.body: Operational excellence includes changing infrastructure through reviewed, repeatable code. CloudFormation features that appear in operations questions:

blocks.title: Git sync
blocks.body: Link a Git repository (GitHub, GitHub Enterprise, GitLab, GitLab self-managed or Bitbucket) through an AWS CodeConnections connection. CloudFormation monitors the template file and a stack deployment file (parameters and values). When a commit lands on the monitored branch CloudFormation updates the stack. With pull requests, a PR is created and you merge it to update the stack, so teammates review changes before deployment. Git sync gives you a status dashboard and commit history. The question notes mention PR comments summarizing the change set; the documentation says that comment feature must be enabled first, which was not confirmed in the pages read here.

DeletionPolicy. By default CloudFormation deletes a resource when the stack is deleted, or when you remove it from the template. Retain keeps the resource (valid for any resource type); Snapshot takes a snapshot first (only for resources that support snapshots such as EBS volumes, RDS instances and Redshift clusters); Delete is the default. Exception: the default is Snapshot for AWS::RDS::DBCluster and for AWS::RDS::DBInstance without a DBClusterIdentifier. The policy applies to removal from a template as well, but not to resources replaced during an update. If you intend to modify a resource outside CloudFormation, use Retain and delete the stack so the template and reality do not diverge.

Import and drift. You can bring existing resources under CloudFormation management: provide a template that includes the resources, a DeletionPolicy on each imported resource, and an identifier for each (for example, the table or bucket name). Imported resources must not already belong to another stack in the Region (watch global resources such as IAM roles). The newer automatic import works for named resources with a static custom name, a DeletionPolicy of Retain or RetainExceptOnCreate, via a change set created with the import-existing-resources option. After importing, run drift detection. DetectStackDrift checks resources that support drift detection and compares only properties explicitly defined in the template, so unmanaged changes to undeclared properties and resources that were never in the stack are not flagged. For finding resources outside any stack, use AWS Config or the resource inventory rather than drift detection.

Operational consequences. Recreating an IAM role with the same name creates a new role with a new unique ID, so existing trust and resource policies that reference the old principal ID break; importing or retaining the role avoids replacement (the unique-ID mechanics are general IAM knowledge, not verified from a page read in this build). A stack whose bucket still has objects can fail to delete, because CloudFormation requires all objects to be deleted before the bucket can be deleted; plan Retain, an empty-bucket step, or a custom resource.

items: Use change sets to preview updates, stack policies or termination protection to prevent accidental changes, and Git sync or a pipeline to enforce review.
Common mistake: editing a CloudFormation-managed resource in the console, which creates drift; fix by updating the template or reverting the resource.
Best practice: tag every resource through the stack so cost allocation and ownership follow automatically.

topics.title: Failure exercises and disaster recovery planning

blocks.body: The skill 'engineering failure scenario activities to support and exercise an understanding of recovery actions' means game days and chaos engineering: deliberately inject faults in a controlled way to prove that alarms fire, automation reacts, and people know the runbook.

blocks.title: AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS)
blocks.body: An experiment template has targets (specific resources or those matching tags/filters, with a selection mode such as a count), actions (what to do, how long, and when to start, for example stopping EC2 instances in an ECS cluster), and stop conditions (CloudWatch alarms that automatically stop the experiment when breached). FIS assumes an IAM role you provide to perform the actions. Start in pre-production, limit the blast radius with tags and counts, define stop conditions before the first run, and run experiments from a pipeline for continuous verification (the Architecture Blog shows CodePipeline integration).

A good exercise has a hypothesis ('if one AZ's instances are stopped, p99 latency stays under 500 ms and no pages fire incorrectly'), a measurable steady state in CloudWatch, a bounded fault, a stop condition, and a retrospective. The Well-Architected principles 'anticipate failure' and 'learn from all operational failures' call for regular game days, pre-mortems and shared lessons.
Disaster recovery strategies, in increasing cost and complexity and decreasing RTO and RPO (Well-Architected REL13-BP02):

headers: What runs in the recovery Region
rows: RPO hours, RTO 24 hours or less
Only backups; infrastructure is redeployed from infrastructure as code, data restored
RPO minutes, RTO tens of minutes
Data replication and core data stores always on; app servers and serverless compute created when needed
Scaled-down but fully functional copy always running
RPO near zero, RTO potentially zero

Full capacity serving traffic in more than one Region; data must be synchronized across Regions, and replication alone does not protect against data corruption unless point-in-time recovery is also in place

items: Multi-AZ designs protect against AZ-level events; multi-Region strategies protect against the unlikely loss of a whole Region.
Automated and continuous backups with point-in-time recovery can lower the backup-and-restore RPO to as low as five minutes in some cases.
Use infrastructure as code to reduce RTO when redeploying in the recovery Region.
Operational readiness: runbooks as SSM Automation documents, alarms with tested actions, and recovery drills that include the people.

blocks.body: If the stem gives an RTO of tens of minutes and a small steady cost, pilot light fits; if it asks for minutes and can afford a running scaled-down copy, warm standby; active/active when near-zero downtime is mandatory. Always check whether the requirement is for data loss (RPO) or downtime (RTO), as they drive different replication choices.

links.label: Chaos testing with FIS and CodePipeline

blocks.body: Scenario 1: Hybrid patching and one compliance report. Requirements: 300 EC2 instances and 120 on-premises Windows and Linux servers are patched by a mix of tools; management wants a single patch status report; maintenance must be staged dev then prod; minimal new tooling. Existing environment: a VPN to the VPC, no common agent. Chosen architecture: register the on-premises servers with a Systems Manager hybrid activation (IAM service role, SSM Agent installed with activation code and ID), give EC2 instances the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore instance profile, create custom patch baselines per OS and environment, tag nodes with Patch Group values, schedule staggered maintenance windows (or a Quick Setup patch policy through Organizations) that run AWS-RunPatchBaseline, and read compliance from Patch Manager and Explorer. Security: scoped Automation and maintenance window service roles, VPC interface endpoints for ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages if the VPC has no internet egress, Session Manager instead of bastions. Cost: Systems Manager capabilities used here are described without prices in the pages read; verify current pricing for on-premises managed nodes. Alternatives rejected: a third-party patch tool per environment (still fragmented reporting), custom scripts with cron (no baselines, no compliance), exporting patch data into a separate BI stack as a first step (extra moving parts before the data source is unified).

Scenario 2: Safe releases for a web tier behind an ALB. Requirements: no downtime, rollback within a minute, release small changes several times per day, keep cost reasonable. Existing: an Auto Scaling group behind an ALB, deployments by SSH and scripts. Chosen architecture: CodeDeploy blue/green with the ALB target group; CodeDeploy provisions a copy of the Auto Scaling group, deploys to it, registers it with the ALB, then deregisters and optionally terminates the old instances after a wait; CloudWatch alarms on ALB 5xx rate and p99 latency are attached to the deployment group for automatic rollback; the golden AMI is produced by an Image Builder pipeline for base patching; the Lambda-based API gets an alias with canary traffic shifting. Security: CodeDeploy service role and instance profile scoped to the artifact bucket. Cost: duplicate capacity only during the overlap. Alternatives rejected: all-at-once in place (outage risk), HalfAtATime in place (halved capacity during release and slower rollback), an ASG instance refresh alone (good for immutable AMI updates but rollback means another refresh), manual DNS cutovers (slow, error-prone).

Scenario 3: Centralized logs and alerts for a fleet that scales and spans on-premises. Requirements: logs from Auto Scaling instances must not be lost; security wants a searchable audit of all web requests with client IP and user agent; operations want alerts on application errors and on unusual spend. Chosen architecture: CloudWatch agent installed and configured through a State Manager association (config in Parameter Store) for both EC2 and on-premises nodes registered with SSM; metric filters on error patterns with alarms to SNS; ALB access logs delivered to S3 and queried with Athena; a terminating lifecycle hook triggers an SSM command to flush buffered files; a Cost Anomaly Detection monitor on AWS services plus a Budget with SNS alerts. Security: bucket policy permitting ELB log delivery, encryption and retention on log destinations, least-privilege roles. Alternatives rejected: cron copy to S3 every 15 minutes (loses data when instances terminate between runs), installing the agent in user data on each launch template (works, but State Manager is the more managed option and covers existing nodes), a self-hosted log stack (higher operational overhead).

blocks.body:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Parameters:
  TopicArn:
    Type: String
  AlbArnSuffix:
    Type: String
Resources:
  Http5xxAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Properties:
      AlarmName: alb-5xx-high
      Namespace: AWS/ApplicationELB
      MetricName: HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count
      Dimensions:
        - Name: LoadBalancer
          Value: !Ref AlbArnSuffix
      Statistic: Sum
      Period: 60
      EvaluationPeriods: 3
      Threshold: 20
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanThreshold
      TreatMissingData: notBreaching
  LatencyAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Properties:
      AlarmName: alb-latency-high
      Namespace: AWS/ApplicationELB
      MetricName: TargetResponseTime
      Dimensions:
        - Name: LoadBalancer
          Value: !Ref AlbArnSuffix
      Statistic: Average
      Period: 60
      EvaluationPeriods: 3
      Threshold: 1
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanThreshold
  ServiceDegraded:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::CompositeAlarm
    Properties:
      AlarmName: service-degraded
      AlarmRule: !Sub 'ALARM("${Http5xxAlarm}") AND ALARM("${LatencyAlarm}")'
      AlarmActions:
        - !Ref TopicArn
  DataBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain

blocks.body: Step 1: find the primary requirement (detect, remediate, deploy safely, patch, centralize, rehearse failure, control cost). Step 2: list mandatory constraints (no downtime, minimal changes, least operational overhead, existing on-premises servers, compliance reporting, RTO/RPO). Step 3: eliminate options that fail a hard constraint, such as rebuilding what could be reconfigured, using a service that cannot take the required action, or adding custom code where a managed feature exists. Step 4: among the remaining, choose the most managed, most automated and most reversible.

Service-distinction rule: metric filter makes alarm-able metrics from logs; Logs Insights is for interactive queries; subscription filters stream.
Service-distinction rule: State Manager enforces state continuously; Run Command is one-off; Maintenance Windows schedule disruptive tasks; Automation orchestrates multi-step runbooks.
Service-distinction rule: Budgets compare to a threshold you set; Cost Anomaly Detection learns normal spend; CUR is the raw data.
Service-distinction rule: Config detects and remediates configuration noncompliance via Automation; CloudFormation drift detection only compares template-declared properties of stack resources.
Service-distinction rule: CloudFormation DeletionPolicy controls what happens on deletion; import brings existing resources under management and needs DeletionPolicy.

Preventive versus detective: IAM conditions and SCPs prevent (for example, restricting which EC2 instance types may be launched), while alarms, Config and periodic reviews detect. The ec2:InstanceType condition key was not verified on a page read in this build, so confirm it before quoting it.

Beware outdated wording: CloudWatch Events is now EventBridge; Elasticsearch Service is OpenSearch Service; Fargate quotas are vCPU-based; launch configurations are the older Auto Scaling mechanism and launch templates are current.
When an option fixes the symptom manually (log in and restart) and another automates it through an event, pick the event-driven one unless a constraint says otherwise.

blocks.body: A frequent trap is an option that is technically valid but uses a more complex mechanism than the stem needs (for example, Lambda plus custom scripts where a Config remediation action or State Manager association exists). Another trap is picking CloudWatch alarms for something that needs an event (AWS Health notices, Config noncompliance).

items: Operational excellence = operations as code, small reversible changes, anticipate failure, learn from failures.

Alarms: static, anomaly detection (about two weeks of training, per metric and statistic), composite (states only, no EC2 or Auto Scaling actions). Metric filters: 100 per log group, 3 dimensions, no retroactivity, no default value with dimensions, high-cardinality dimensions get filters disabled at 1,000 pairs and cost money.
Subscription filters: 2 per log group, base64 and gzip payloads. Cross-account observability: monitoring and source accounts, one sink per Region, per-Region scope.

SSM managed node needs agent, role, connectivity. Hybrid activation: expiry blocks new registrations only. Patch group: one baseline per operating system type per group, one group per node. State Manager enforces, Run Command is one-off.

Deployments: CodeDeploy default OneAtATime; blue/green reroutes via the load balancer and rolls back by re-routing; weighted Lambda alias gives canary; instance refresh for immutable AMI rollout; lifecycle hook default 3600 seconds, range 30 to 7200, default result ABANDON.

CloudFormation: DeletionPolicy default Delete (Snapshot default for some RDS), Retain for anything, import needs DeletionPolicy, drift covers template-declared properties only, Git sync reviews via pull requests.
FIS: targets, actions, stop conditions (CloudWatch alarms). DR: backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby, active/active in rising cost and falling RTO/RPO.
Cost signals: Budgets (threshold), Cost Anomaly Detection (ML baseline, managed monitors up to 5,000 values), CUR + Athena (analysis).

Misconceptions: composite alarms can scale; metric filters are retroactive; an expired hybrid activation unregisters servers; drift detection finds unmanaged resources; blue/green needs no extra capacity; X-Ray service is retired (only the SDKs and daemon are in maintenance mode).

blocks.body: Takeaways: automate with managed building blocks, keep changes reversible, centralize telemetry off the instance, and prove recovery by practising it.

Task 3.2 of the SAP-C02 exam, 'Determine a strategy to improve security', sits in Domain 3 (Continuous Improvement for Existing Solutions). The premise is brownfield: a workload already runs, and an audit, an incident or a compliance change shows it is too permissive, too exposed, unpatched, unencrypted or not recoverable. You pick the smallest set of AWS controls that closes the gap with the least disruption and operational overhead. Check the current domain weighting in the official exam guide; it is not restated here because it was not retrieved in this build.

Prerequisites: working knowledge of IAM (identity policies, resource policies, roles, trust policies), AWS KMS basics (keys, key policies, envelope encryption), VPC networking, and the managed-service model of Amazon ECS, AWS Lambda, and Amazon RDS/Amazon Aurora. Terms used in this lesson: a 'detective control' finds problems after they exist; a 'preventive control' stops them; a 'responsive control' (remediation) fixes them. An 'immutable' backup cannot be altered or deleted by anyone until its retention ends.

items: You will be able to choose between AWS Secrets Manager and AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store for a given credential-handling requirement, and configure rotation and cross-account access.
You will be able to audit and reduce permissions using IAM Access Analyzer policy generation, and state exactly what a generated policy does and does not contain.
You will be able to design detection-and-remediation loops with AWS Config, Amazon EventBridge, AWS Systems Manager Automation, Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Security Hub and Amazon Inspector.

You will be able to select edge and network controls (AWS WAF rate-based rules, Count-mode rollout, Shield Advanced automatic mitigation, AWS Network Firewall domain lists) for a stated attack or exposure.
You will be able to design a patch process (Patch Manager patch policies) and a backup process (AWS Backup plans, cross-account copy, Vault Lock) that satisfy retention and immutability requirements.
You will be able to retrofit encryption on existing resources (EBS, Aurora/RDS, ElastiCache) and explain which changes require re-creating the resource.

blocks.title: Exam mindset
blocks.body: Questions in this task start with a working but weak environment. The correct answer is usually the managed, automated, least-change control: policy generated from real activity instead of hand-written, rotation instead of manual changes, Config auto-remediation instead of runbooks that people must remember, Session Manager instead of opening port 22.

links.label: AWS Config: setting up auto remediation
AWS Secrets Manager: what it is

blocks.body: Hard-coded credentials, long-lived access keys and shared database passwords are among the most common findings in a security review. The exam expects you to replace them with a managed secret store whose values are encrypted with AWS KMS, fetched at runtime through IAM, and rotated automatically.

blocks.title: Secrets Manager versus Parameter Store
blocks.body: AWS documentation recommends AWS Secrets Manager for secrets such as database credentials, API keys and tokens, because it provides automatic rotation and cross-Region replication. Parameter Store SecureString is positioned for configuration values that need encryption; the docs say it does not provide automatic rotation services for stored secrets, and recommend Secrets Manager when you need automatic rotation, cross-account access or fine-grained audit logging.

rows: Yes, scheduled; Lambda-based or managed rotation
Not provided; docs point to Secrets Manager
Resource-based policy on the secret plus KMS key policy (customer managed key required)
Docs recommend Secrets Manager for cross-account needs
AWS KMS; free with the aws/secretsmanager managed key, KMS charges apply for your own keys
AWS KMS; AWS managed key or customer managed key; only the value is encrypted, not name or metadata
Standard parameters cannot exceed 4096 bytes; advanced use envelope encryption
Per secret per month and per 10,000 API calls; no charge for secrets marked for deletion; Lambda charge for rotation functions except managed rotation
Parameter Store can reference a Secrets Manager secret through /aws/reference/secretsmanager/<secret-path>

blocks.body: How rotation works. Secrets Manager invokes a rotation Lambda function on the schedule you set. The same function is called repeatedly with a Step parameter: create_secret, set_secret, test_secret and finish_secret, plus a ClientRequestToken for idempotency. If any step fails, Secrets Manager retries the whole process several times during the open rotation windows. A manual update to the secret while rotation is on counts as a valid rotation when the next date is computed. For secrets owned by other services, 'managed rotation' avoids running your own Lambda function. The schedule can be a rate expression such as rate(10 days) or a cron expression with a rotation window (Duration).

Cross-account access needs two grants, which candidates often miss. The secret's resource-based policy must allow the other account's principal secretsmanager:GetSecretValue, and the KMS key that encrypts the secret must allow that principal kms:Decrypt (and kms:GenerateDataKey if it writes). The docs state that the AWS managed key aws/secretsmanager cannot be used for cross-account access, so the secret must be encrypted with a customer managed key that has a key policy granting the other account's principal access.

items: Quota facts seen: GetSecretValue is 10,000 requests per second per supported Region and is not adjustable; combined PutSecretValue/UpdateSecret and related write calls are 50 per second per Region, not adjustable. Cache secrets in the client rather than calling on every request.

Containers: an ECS task definition can reference a Secrets Manager secret or Parameter Store parameter, and the task execution role (not the task role) needs permission to fetch it, because the agent resolves it at launch.

Common mistakes: storing secrets in Lambda environment variables or user data; granting secretsmanager:* with Resource '*'; forgetting the KMS grant for cross-account; using a String parameter for sensitive data.
Best practice: one secret per credential, tags for ownership, CloudTrail for access audit (Secrets Manager events are logged as management events), alarm on unexpected GetSecretValue callers.

blocks.body: Keywords 'rotate automatically', 'no application changes' and 'database credentials' point to Secrets Manager with rotation. If the stem only needs encrypted configuration at low cost with no rotation, Parameter Store SecureString is acceptable. A secret shared with another account always implies a customer managed KMS key.

links.label: Access secrets from a different account

blocks.body: The principle of least privilege means each identity has only the permissions needed for its job. In an existing environment you rarely know what that is, so the tool of choice is to observe actual use and generate a policy from it. IAM Access Analyzer policy generation reads CloudTrail events for a user or role and produces a policy template containing the actions used.

items: Enable a CloudTrail trail that records the account's events (required before generation).
Choose the role, the time period (up to 90 days) and the trail, and an existing or new service role that lets Access Analyzer read the trail's S3 bucket and service-last-accessed data.
Review the generated template: for some services action-level detail is returned, for others only service-level; add actions, restrict resources, add conditions.
Save it as a customer managed policy and attach it in place of the broad policy, ideally first in a lower environment.

A CloudTrail trail logging events for the account; service role with cloudtrail:GetTrail, iam:GenerateServiceLastAccessedDetails/GetServiceLastAccessedDetails and s3:GetObject/ListBucket on the log bucket
Action-level activity for data events such as S3 object operations; iam:PassRole (not tracked by CloudTrail)
Policy generation reviews all events, including denied actions, so review before use

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.body: A generated policy is a starting point. Because data events and iam:PassRole are missing, an application that reads S3 objects or passes roles will break if you attach the output unreviewed. Add those statements manually, scoped to specific resources.

Container roles are a classic least-privilege trap. An Amazon ECS task has two distinct roles. The task execution role grants the ECS container agent (and Fargate agent) permission to act for the platform: pull images from Amazon ECR, send logs to CloudWatch Logs, and fetch Secrets Manager or Parameter Store values referenced in the task definition. Those credentials are not available to the containers. The task role provides credentials to your application code for calls such as S3 or DynamoDB; CloudTrail shows the taskArn in the session context for auditability. On EC2 launch type, a task role removes the need to widen the instance profile for every container. Note that containers are not a security boundary: on EC2, ECS Managed Instances, and ECS Anywhere there is no task isolation, so containers can potentially access credentials intended for other tasks. For strict isolation, use Fargate, where each task has its own isolation boundary.

Application gets access denied calling DynamoDB or S3
