items: Other least-privilege levers: permission boundaries, service control policies (guardrails that cap what any identity in an account can do), condition keys such as kms:ViaService and aws:SourceVpce, and removal of unused roles. Access Analyzer's external-access findings and unused-access analysis were not retrieved in this build.
Common mistake: using one shared role for hundreds of Lambda functions. Generate one policy per function role.

blocks.body: When a stem says 'hundreds of functions with broad permissions' and 'least effort', the answer is policy generation from CloudTrail per role, not manual analysis of code. If the generated policy must cover S3 object access, remember data events must also be logged separately and the generator will not reveal them.
Data retention, sensitivity and regulation drive which controls you add. Retrofitting encryption is often a rebuild, so know which resources can be changed in place.

headers: What you can do on an existing resource
rows: Cannot encrypt in place. Snapshot then create an encrypted volume, or copy the snapshot with encryption. Cannot change the KMS key of an existing encrypted volume either; copy via snapshot and choose a new key.
Regional account setting; applies to new volumes and snapshot copies only; no effect on existing volumes; cannot then be disabled per volume in that Region
Cannot change the key of an existing instance; snapshot, copy with the new KMS key, restore. For Aurora cluster snapshots, docs say an unencrypted cluster snapshot cannot be encrypted by copying it

For versions 7 and later, in-transit encryption can be turned on for existing clusters without rebuilding; AUTH tokens require in-transit encryption to be enabled (and, for Redis OSS, engine 4.0.10 or later)
S3 Block Public Access at account or organization level overrides public ACLs and policies; new buckets have it on by default

blocks.body: AWS KMS key rotation. KMS can rotate symmetric encryption keys automatically; the rotation period is configurable from 90 to 2,560 days (default 365 days when not specified) and the RotateKeyOnDemand API gives immediate rotation with a lifetime limit of 10 on-demand rotations per key. Rotation is not supported for asymmetric keys, HMAC keys, or keys in a CloudHSM-backed custom key store, and the condition key kms:RotationPeriodInDays can constrain what principals set. Automatic rotation keeps the same key ID and ARN, so applications and encrypted data need no change (key ID continuity is not stated in the retrieved pages; treat as general KMS behavior, not verified here). A 180-day policy therefore needs a customer managed key with a 180-day period. AWS managed keys rotate automatically every year (approximately 365 days); you cannot enable, disable, or change that schedule.

blocks.title: Aurora on the default key
blocks.body: If a cluster is encrypted with the default AWS managed key and policy demands a 180-day rotation with noncompliance alerts, you cannot change the key in place or shorten the managed key's schedule. Migrate: snapshot, copy the snapshot encrypting with a customer managed key that has a 180-day rotation period, restore, and add an AWS Config rule or equivalent to alert when the key setting is out of policy. The alerting rule name was not verified.

items: ElastiCache IAM authentication needs Valkey 7.2+ or Redis OSS 7.0+ and in-transit encryption; tokens last 15 minutes and connections are cut after 12 hours unless re-authenticated.
Snapshot copy with a different KMS key creates a complete (non-incremental) copy, which adds storage cost.
Default aws/ebs key volumes cannot be shared across accounts; use a customer managed key when sharing encrypted volumes or snapshots.
Cross-Region copy of an encrypted snapshot needs a KMS key valid in the destination Region (Region-specific or multi-Region key).

blocks.body: 'Encrypt existing X with minimal downtime' is almost always snapshot-copy-restore. 'Prevent new unencrypted X' is a regional default setting or an SCP/Config rule, not remediation of old data. Pay attention to engine version in ElastiCache questions; version 7+ changes what is possible in place.

Comprehensive traceability means you can answer who did what, to which resource, from where, and when, for both humans and services. The building blocks are AWS CloudTrail (API activity), AWS Config (resource configuration history), Amazon GuardDuty (threat detection findings), AWS Security Hub (aggregated findings; the docs now call the posture service 'Security Hub CSPM') and Amazon Security Lake (normalized security data lake).

rows: Secrets Manager events are logged as management events; first copy of management events is free
Data-plane calls such as S3 GetObject/PutObject/DeleteObject, Lambda Invoke
Off by default, must be added per resource type, incur extra cost, high volume (S3 docs recommend lifecycle rules on the log bucket)
What did the configuration look like and is it compliant
Configuration items and rules; aggregators collect data across accounts and Regions
Findings are delivered to EventBridge; suppression-rule findings are not sent
Findings and updates are sent to EventBridge as 'Security Hub Findings - Imported'; cross-Region aggregation available

blocks.body: Auditing deletes in S3 needs data events. The management-event trail will not show DeleteObject; you add S3 data events (Write events, optionally with a prefix) to a trail, deliver logs to S3 for retention (for example five years through the bucket's lifecycle and Object Lock/retention design), and route a matching EventBridge rule to Amazon SNS for email alerts. The retention and Object Lock details were not retrieved in this build.

SaaS plus workload analytics: AppFabric ingests audit logs from supported SaaS applications, normalizes them to OCSF and writes them into Security Lake as a custom source. Whether specific AWS-native sources such as EKS audit logs or VPC Flow Logs are native Security Lake sources was not verified here.

items: Config aggregator: an aggregator account collects configuration and compliance data from source accounts and Regions, or from an organization; with an organization aggregator no per-account authorization is needed. The aggregated dashboard has been described as no extra charge in a launch post (check current pricing).
Organization conformance packs let the management account deploy a common set of Config rules and remediation actions to member accounts and keep member accounts from modifying them.
Common mistake: assuming CloudTrail alone proves compliance. It is evidence of activity; Config evaluates state.

blocks.body: 'Who deleted/accessed objects' = CloudTrail data events. 'Which resources drifted' = Config. 'Is an instance talking to a known bad IP' = GuardDuty. 'Combine SaaS and AWS logs for analytics' = Security Lake with AppFabric.

links.label: Config conformance packs for an organization

blocks.body: The pattern for brownfield improvement is detect, decide, respond. Detection comes from AWS Config rules, GuardDuty, Inspector and Security Hub; decision logic lives in EventBridge rule patterns; response is an AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook, a Lambda function or an SNS notification.

blocks.title: AWS Config rules and remediation
blocks.body: A Config rule evaluates resources as COMPLIANT or NON_COMPLIANT. Rules have two evaluation modes: detective (resources already deployed) and proactive (evaluate resource properties before deployment). Proactive rules do not remediate or block deployment. You can associate a remediation action, which is a Systems Manager Automation document, with a rule and choose manual or automatic remediation. If the resource stays noncompliant you can set retries, for example 5 attempts in 300 seconds; retries cost Automation charges. Remediation can be managed only for non-service-linked rules.

items: Pass the noncompliant resource ID into the runbook through the Resource ID parameter; give Automation an AutomationAssumeRole with the least permissions to perform the fix.

Organizational rules: add remediation through an EventBridge rule on source aws.config, detail-type 'Config Rules Compliance Change', with Automation as target; deploy to member accounts with CloudFormation StackSets.

Preventive pairing: Config remediates after the fact. Preventive controls (S3 Block Public Access, EBS encryption by default, SCPs) stop the condition from arising. Choose both when a stem says 'detect and prevent'.

blocks.body: Amazon Inspector provides continual vulnerability scanning. Once activated it discovers EC2 instances, Lambda functions, ECR container images and code repositories, scans for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure, and rescans when a new CVE is published or the workload changes. EC2 scanning uses the SSM agent or EBS snapshots (agentless hybrid mode is the default when EC2 scanning is activated). Amazon ECR offers basic scanning (billed through ECR; on push or manual) and enhanced scanning (provided by Inspector and billed by Inspector; operating system and programming-language packages; continuous or on push, selected through repository filters). Inspector findings can be managed by Security Hub CSPM and EventBridge, which basic scanning does not support.

rows: Scan container images for OS and language package CVEs and rescan when new CVEs appear
ECR enhanced scanning with Inspector, continuous mode
Scan once at push and trigger a custom workflow
ECR scan on push plus EventBridge rule to Lambda/Step Functions (severity filtering is done in the workflow; the retrieved docs do not show severity counts in the event)
Prioritize by what is actually deployed
Inspector coverage and findings across ECR, EC2 and Lambda (deployment-aware prioritization is stated in the question set, not verified against the docs)

blocks.body: GuardDuty and Security Hub: GuardDuty findings flow to EventBridge as events; Security Hub also ingests them and re-emits as 'Security Hub Findings - Imported', so one EventBridge rule on Security Hub can cover many products. A published pattern remediates, for example, a CloudTrail-logging-disabled finding by invoking a Lambda function that restores the trail and notifies operators over SNS. Automation rules and custom actions in Security Hub help prioritize which findings are auto-processed.

items: Prioritizing automated responses: automate low-risk, high-confidence, reversible actions (re-enable logging, block public access, quarantine a security group); route high-impact actions (terminating instances, revoking production roles) to human approval.
Common mistake: auto-remediating without an exemption path or retry limit, causing remediation loops.

blocks.body: 'Automatically remediate noncompliant resources across accounts' = Config rule (or organization conformance pack) + Automation runbook. 'React to a finding' = EventBridge. 'Vulnerabilities in images/instances/functions' = Inspector. Do not pick a custom cron Lambda when a managed rule exists.

blocks.body: Security at every layer includes the edge (CloudFront/ALB with AWS WAF and Shield), the network (AWS Network Firewall) and the host. This topic covers the first two.

blocks.title: AWS WAF rate-based rules
blocks.body: A rate-based rule counts requests, groups them by aggregation keys (IP address, HTTP method, headers and others, or combinations) and applies an action to each aggregation instance that exceeds the limit. Valid limit range 10 to 2,000,000,000; evaluation windows of 60, 120, 300 or 600 seconds; the limit applies per aggregation instance, not to the rule as a whole. AWS WAF re-evaluates roughly every 10 seconds, so rates are approximate and a few extra requests pass before blocking. A rule change can take about 30 seconds to apply and changing a live rule's settings resets counts for up to a minute. Cost in web ACL capacity: base 2 WCUs plus 30 per custom aggregation key plus any scope-down statement. A scope-down statement narrows what is counted, for example only the login URI.

A login-flood scenario: aggregate by IP on requests to the login path with a limit tuned to legitimate per-user volume, action Block (or CAPTCHA/Challenge). If many source IPs participate, aggregate on another key such as a header or session cookie. Older documentation for AWS WAF Classic describes rate rules as a fixed five-minute period; WAFv2 supports the selectable windows above.

blocks.title: Count mode rollout
blocks.body: To avoid blocking legitimate traffic when introducing rules, set rules to Count, enable logging and sampled requests, associate the web ACL with the resource, review matches in CloudWatch metrics and logs, tune with scope-down statements or label-based exclusions, then promote rules to Block one at a time. Count mode leaves the application exposed to what the rule would have blocked during the test, a conscious trade-off. Sampled requests are stored for up to three hours, so use logging for longer analysis.

AWS Shield Advanced automatic application-layer DDoS mitigation creates, tests and applies AWS WAF rules for detected layer 7 attacks. It is available for Amazon CloudFront distributions and Application Load Balancers only, requires a protected resource with a WAFv2 web ACL associated, and places the rules in a Shield rule group inside that web ACL. You can run it in count-only mode first. Enabling or changing it is done through Shield Advanced APIs even if the web ACL was associated through the WAF console. Shield Advanced is a subscription product; its pricing was not retrieved here. A rate-based WAF rule is the cheaper first step for simple per-IP floods; Shield Advanced fits sudden, large, distributed layer 7 events where hand-written rules lag.

AWS Network Firewall filters VPC traffic with stateful rule groups. A domain list rule group supports allow and deny lists: for HTTP it inspects the Host header, for HTTPS the TLS Server Name Indication (SNI). An allowlist sends traffic only to named domains and drops the rest. With default action ordering, do not mix Reject or Alert domain groups with Allow domain groups, because the default drop added by the Allow group takes effect first. By default only traffic from the firewall's own VPC is inspected unless HOME_NET is extended. The target type AWS_ROUTE_53_RESOLVED_DOMAIN additionally ties matching to how the destination IP was resolved. VPC Flow Logs record IP-level metadata, not domain names (general knowledge; not verified in this build), so domain filtering is the Network Firewall job, and alert logs reveal which blocked destinations are attempted.

blocks.body: Reducing the attack surface of instances usually means removing inbound SSH/RDP, bastion hosts, and key files, and replacing them with identity-based, logged access. A repeatable patch process then keeps the operating system current.

blocks.title: Session Manager
blocks.body: Session Manager, a capability of AWS Systems Manager, provides interactive shell access to managed nodes without opening inbound ports, maintaining bastion hosts or managing SSH keys. Traffic is encrypted with TLS 1.2 or 1.3 by default and can additionally be encrypted with a customer managed KMS key. Sessions are controlled with IAM. Start and stop of sessions are captured in CloudTrail; full session activity (commands typed) can be logged to Amazon S3 or CloudWatch Logs if you enable that in Session Manager preferences, and the instance profile must be able to write to the destination. The Run As feature starts sessions under a chosen OS account instead of the default ssm-user.

items: Requirements: SSM Agent on the instance; an instance profile with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore (or the default-policy alternative); no SCP denying those permissions; and either outbound internet/NAT or interface VPC endpoints for ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages in private subnets.

Migration from SSH: attach the instance profile, confirm the node shows as managed, enable session logging, then remove port 22 from security groups. Hybrid and on-premises servers can be managed with Systems Manager too.
Common mistake: enabling Session Manager but forgetting logging preferences; CloudTrail alone does not record commands.

blocks.body: Patch Manager uses patch baselines: rules that auto-approve patches some days after release plus approved and rejected lists. An operation is either Scan (report missing patches) or Scan and install. Four methods run operations: a patch policy configured in Quick Setup (recommended, integrates with AWS Organizations, can cover multiple accounts and Regions or selected OUs), a Host Management option in Quick Setup (scan only), a maintenance window task, and a State Manager association or Patch now. The Quick Setup patch policy must be created from the organization's management account (not a delegated administrator). Defaults offered: daily scan at 01:00 UTC and weekly install at 02:00 UTC on Sunday; reboot-if-needed is optional and recommended but can affect availability. Maintenance windows, State Manager and Patch now are limited to one account-Region pair.

rows: No, scan only against default baseline

items: Immutable infrastructure alternative: rebuild AMIs and replace instances through Auto Scaling instead of patching in place (general design practice, not from the retrieved pages).
Use Inspector to find which instances are vulnerable and patch compliance reports to prove coverage.

blocks.body: 'Patch fleets in many accounts on a schedule with the least effort' = Quick Setup patch policy. 'Engineers need shell access, no SSH keys, auditable' = Session Manager with logging.

blocks.body: A backup design answers four questions: what is protected, how often and how long retained, where copies live, and who can delete them. AWS Backup centralizes this with backup plans (rules for schedule, window, lifecycle to cold storage and deletion, copy destinations) assigned to resources by tag or ID, stored in backup vaults.

items: Cross-account and cross-Region: backup rules can copy recovery points to another Region and to another account's vault. For cross-account copy the docs advise a customer managed KMS key on the source resource and vault, with permissions granted on the key and target vault.

Organization policies: a backup policy created in the Organizations management account standardises rules, lifecycle and resource assignment by tag across accounts and OUs; the vault must exist in every target account because AWS Backup does not check. Use SCPs to protect backup resources from modification.
Monitoring: AWS Backup Audit Manager has pre-built frameworks; backup events can be forwarded by EventBridge to a central bus and SNS.
Point-in-time recovery through continuous backups is optional for supported resources such as RDS and S3.

blocks.title: Vault Lock
blocks.body: AWS Backup Vault Lock has two modes. Governance mode lets users with sufficient IAM permissions manage or remove the lock. Compliance mode makes the vault immutable: once the grace time (cooling-off period, at least 72 hours) ends, the lock cannot be removed or altered by any user or by AWS, and recovery points cannot be deleted before retention ends; a vault can be deleted only if it holds no recovery points. During the grace period you can still change or remove the lock.

items: Encrypted snapshots copied with a new KMS key are full copies, not incremental, which raises cost.
Common mistake: treating replicas (Multi-AZ, read replicas) as backups. They replicate deletions and corruption; backups provide point-in-time recovery.
Exam link: data retention requirements decide lifecycle and lock mode; RTO/RPO decide frequency and copy strategy (RPO and RTO are covered in the resilience lessons).

blocks.body: 'Cannot be deleted by anyone including root until retention ends' maps to compliance-mode Vault Lock. 'Centrally enforce backups for every account' maps to AWS Backup organization policies.

blocks.title: Scenario 1: Overprivileged serverless estate
blocks.body: Requirements: an audit found hundreds of Lambda execution roles with full S3 and DynamoDB access; each function must get only what it uses; minimal engineering time. Constraints: a CloudTrail trail exists in each account; some functions read S3 objects. Chosen architecture: for each role run IAM Access Analyzer policy generation over a 90-day window, review, add the S3 and DynamoDB data-plane statements manually (data events and iam:PassRole are not captured), scope resources to named buckets/tables, test in staging, then swap the managed policies. Security: add a permission boundary or SCP to prevent re-granting wildcard S3/DynamoDB. Cost: policy generation has no extra charge beyond S3 request costs for reading the trail; logging data events adds CloudTrail cost. Alternatives rejected: hand-reading code (slow, error-prone for hundreds of functions); removing permissions and fixing failures in production (outage risk); using the service-last-accessed report alone (service-level only).

blocks.title: Scenario 2: Credentials, patching and SSH on a legacy fleet
blocks.body: Requirements: EC2 instances in private subnets, engineers use SSH keys, an application password sits in a config file, patches are applied by hand. Existing environment: VPC with NAT gateway, Site-to-Site VPN, multiple accounts in AWS Organizations. Chosen architecture: attach an instance profile with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore, enable Session Manager with S3 or CloudWatch Logs session logging and optional KMS encryption, then close port 22; move the application password to Secrets Manager with rotation and give the instance role secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for that one secret; create a Quick Setup patch policy from the management account with a daily scan and a weekly install in a maintenance period and reboot-if-needed. Security: IAM controls who can start sessions; CloudTrail records session start and stop; session logs hold the commands. Cost: Lambda charge for rotation, per-secret Secrets Manager fee, log storage; no bastion hosts to run. Alternatives rejected: bastion host (patching and key management burden remains); VPN-only SSH (still key sprawl, no command audit); storing the password in Parameter Store (no automatic rotation).

blocks.title: Scenario 3: Public web app under attack and unencrypted data stores
blocks.body: Requirements: an ALB-fronted application suffers weekly credential-stuffing spikes and sporadic layer 7 floods; an audit flags unencrypted EBS volumes on thousands of instances and an ElastiCache cluster without TLS or authentication; backups must be immutable for seven years (illustrative). Chosen architecture: WAF web ACL with a rate-based rule on the login path aggregated by IP, deployed first in Count mode with logging, then Block; if floods persist across many IPs, enable Shield Advanced automatic mitigation for the ALB. Turn on EBS encryption by default per Region to stop new unencrypted volumes; use a Config rule plus an Automation runbook (snapshot, encrypted copy, replace) for existing volumes; for ElastiCache on engine 7+ turn on in-transit encryption in place and add AUTH or IAM authentication, otherwise rebuild with encryption enabled. Backups: AWS Backup plan with cross-account copy and compliance-mode Vault Lock after a grace period. Cost: Shield Advanced is a subscription (price not verified); Count mode costs only logging; full snapshot copies add storage. Alternatives rejected: security groups for rate limiting (no rate awareness); NACLs (stateless, no request content); relying on replicas as backups.

blocks.body: This lesson covers SAP-C02 task 3.3, improving the performance of workloads that already run on AWS. Unlike the new-solution lesson, the starting point is a working system with a symptom: slow pages, throttling errors, exhausted database connections, cold starts, or a cache that stopped helping. Your job is to find the bottleneck with evidence, pick the lowest-effort fix that meets a measurable target, and avoid fixes that add cost or risk without addressing the real constraint.

Prerequisites: working knowledge of VPC networking, EC2 and Auto Scaling, S3, RDS/Aurora, DynamoDB, Lambda, API Gateway, CloudFront and CloudWatch. The lesson on new-solution performance objectives (2.5) introduces the same services from a design angle; here the emphasis is diagnosis and remediation.

The exam task statement lists these skills: translating business requirements to measurable metrics; testing potential remediation solutions and making recommendations; proposing opportunities to adopt new technologies and managed services; assessing solutions and applying rightsizing; and identifying and examining performance bottlenecks. Knowledge areas named are high-performing architectures (auto scaling, instance fleets, placement groups), global service offerings (Global Accelerator, CloudFront, edge computing), monitoring tool sets such as CloudWatch, and SLAs and KPIs.
Objectives. By the end you will be able to:

items: Convert a business statement such as 'checkout feels slow' into KPIs (for example p99 latency, error rate, cache hit ratio, DB load) and pick the AWS metric that exposes each.
Identify the bottleneck layer (edge, compute, cache, database, storage, network, downstream quota) from symptoms and metrics.
Choose between caching, read scaling, connection pooling, buffering, scaling policy changes, and storage or compute changes for a given symptom.
Select the correct global-delivery tool (CloudFront, Lambda@Edge/CloudFront Functions, Global Accelerator, S3 Transfer Acceleration, Route 53 latency routing) for a described traffic pattern.
Explain the limits that make a fix fail (burst-credit exhaustion, API Gateway account throttling, Lambda timeout, Kinesis shared read throughput, DynamoDB auto scaling lag).
Rightsize using utilization data and recognize when more memory-based or CPU-based capacity is the wrong answer.

blocks.body: Services and patterns covered: Amazon CloudWatch (including the agent), AWS X-Ray, CloudWatch Application Signals, Amazon RDS Performance Insights, AWS Compute Optimizer; EC2 Auto Scaling policies, warm pools, placement groups, enhanced networking, VPC endpoints; EBS volume types and Elastic Volumes; S3 request-rate guidance, Transfer Acceleration, Mountpoint, Bucket Keys; CloudFront cache keys, edge functions, Origin Shield, Global Accelerator, Route 53 latency routing; ElastiCache, DAX, API Gateway caching; RDS Proxy, Aurora reader and custom endpoints, Aurora global database, DynamoDB capacity modes, Redshift Concurrency Scaling; Lambda memory, provisioned concurrency, SnapStart, SQS buffering, Fargate offload; Kinesis enhanced fan-out, MSK, EMR scaling.

blocks.title: Why it matters on the exam
blocks.body: Domain 3 (Continuous Improvement for Existing Solutions) is one of the four SAP-C02 domains, and performance remediation questions are among its most scenario-heavy items. The exam weighting percentage for the domain was not retrieved from AWS documentation in this build and is not stated here. Expect long stems where several options are technically valid and only one addresses the stated bottleneck at the stated cost and effort.

topics.title: Measure first: KPIs, SLAs and finding the bottleneck

blocks.body: A service level agreement (SLA) is a commitment to a customer; a service level objective (SLO) is the internal target that protects it; a key performance indicator (KPI) is a measured number that shows progress. A business requirement like 'pages must feel instant for users worldwide' is not testable until it becomes, for example, 'p95 time to first byte under 300 ms in every continent and cache hit ratio above 90 percent'. Translate first, then pick the service that moves that specific number.
Symptom to layer mapping is the core diagnostic skill. Ask which resource is saturated or throttled, not which resource is biggest.

blocks.body: Tools. CloudWatch collects metrics, logs and alarms. EC2 sends CPU, network and disk-I/O metrics by default but does not provide operating-system memory or disk-usage metrics; install the unified CloudWatch agent to publish them as custom metrics. The same agent memory metric is what AWS Compute Optimizer reads to improve EC2 rightsizing recommendations (it must be published to the `CWAgent` namespace with the `InstanceId` dimension).

AWS X-Ray and CloudWatch Application Signals trace requests end to end. The X-Ray trace map shows nodes, latency, errors and connections so you can see which hop (for example Lambda to DynamoDB) is slow. Application Signals adds service-level views and health based on service level objectives and needs no extra instrumentation code once enabled, whereas X-Ray alone requires the X-Ray SDK as a function dependency. X-Ray is the right tool to find where time goes across services; it does not tell you why a database query is slow.

RDS and Aurora Performance Insights measures database load as average active sessions (AAS): sessions that have submitted work and are waiting for a response. It splits load into CPU and non-CPU (waits such as I/O or locks) and publishes DBLoad, DBLoadCPU, DBLoadNonCPU and DBLoadRelativeToNumVCPUs to CloudWatch so you can alarm on them. Enhanced Monitoring (operating-system level metrics from the DB host) and Performance Insights (what the database engine is doing) answer different questions; the exam pairs them with CloudWatch alarms for operational readiness.

AWS Compute Optimizer analyzes utilization history and flags EC2 instances, Auto Scaling groups, EBS volumes and Lambda functions as over- or under-provisioned. For Lambda it produces memory recommendations only for functions configured with 1,792 MB of memory or less that were invoked at least 50 times in the trailing 14 days. Rightsizing is a performance tool as well as a cost tool: an under-provisioned resource is a bottleneck, not a saving.

blocks.title: Method
blocks.body: 1) State the KPI and target. 2) Find the saturated or throttled resource with metrics. 3) Change one variable. 4) Re-measure against the same KPI. Test remediation in a non-production copy or with weighted/gradual rollout when the change affects caching or consistency.

If a stem gives a symptom plus a metric (BurstBalance, DBLoad, cache hit ratio, ReadProvisionedThroughputExceeded), the answer addresses exactly that resource. Options that scale something unrelated (bigger web tier for a database connection limit) are distractors.

links.label: Send memory and disk metrics to CloudWatch

blocks.body: Scaling policy choice. Target tracking holds a metric at a target (it scales out if any of several target-tracking policies calls for it and scales in only when all agree). Scheduled scaling changes minimum and maximum capacity at set times and suits predictable cyclical load. Predictive scaling forecasts from up to 14 days of metric history (needs at least 24 hours) and pre-launches capacity; in forecast-and-scale mode it never scales in, so you still need target tracking or step scaling to remove capacity. Combining scheduled and target tracking helps when demand jumps faster than reactive scaling can respond.

Slow instance start. If instances take minutes to become useful, scale-out lags demand. Pre-baked (golden) AMIs move installation and configuration out of boot time; EC2 Image Builder automates producing and distributing them. Warm pools keep pre-initialized instances ready to join the group faster. Instances in a warm pool have no health check grace period; health checking starts only after the lifecycle hook finishes.

Health check grace period. EC2 Auto Scaling does not mark an instance unhealthy from EC2 status checks or ELB health checks until the grace period expires. If the application takes longer to start than the grace period while ELB health checks are on, the group terminates and relaunches instances in a loop; the fix is a grace period longer than the real boot-and-warm-up time, not more capacity.

blocks.body: Network-bound tiers. Enhanced networking (SR-IOV) gives higher bandwidth, higher packets per second and lower latency at no extra charge; Nitro instances use the Elastic Network Adapter (ENA), which supports speeds of up to 100 Gbps on supported types according to the enhanced networking documentation (the EC2 FAQ cites higher speeds for newer types, so check the specific instance type). When the metric shows the network is the ceiling, move to an instance family or size with more network capacity and a current-generation type; adding more of the same small instances behind a load balancer also spreads flows. Benchmark candidate instance types rather than assuming.

Data-path cost and throughput. NAT gateway data processing is billed per GB. If most NAT traffic goes to S3 or DynamoDB in the same Region, a gateway VPC endpoint removes that traffic from the NAT gateway with no additional charge for the endpoint. Gateway endpoints do not work from on-premises networks (VPN or Direct Connect), from peered VPCs, or through a transit gateway; those cases need an interface endpoint, which is billed. Keep resources in the same Availability Zone as the NAT gateway they use because same-AZ transfer is free.

Kubernetes on Amazon EKS. Pod topology spread constraints (`topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone`, `maxSkew`, `whenUnsatisfiable`) tell the scheduler to distribute pods across Availability Zones and nodes. They are the right answer for uneven pod placement that concentrates load or failure domain; you can also use them to concentrate pods when network locality matters.

rows: Placement is within one Availability Zone

blocks.body: 'Instances keep being terminated right after launch while the ELB check is failing' points to health check grace period, not instance size. 'Pods all land in one zone' points to topology spread constraints.

EBS gp2 performance is tied to size: baseline is 3 IOPS per GiB (minimum 100, maximum 16,000 IOPS, reached at 5,334 GiB). Volumes under 1 TiB (below 3,000 baseline IOPS) can burst to 3,000 IOPS using I/O credits. A volume starts with 5.4 million credits, earns 3 credits per GiB per second while at or below baseline, and spends credits at (burst IOPS minus baseline IOPS). When credits run out, performance drops to baseline. A 100 GiB gp2 volume therefore has a baseline of 300 IOPS: a marketing campaign or batch run that sustains more than that will drain the bucket, and the database appears to slow down suddenly after weeks of normal behavior. The CloudWatch BurstBalance metric (a percentage) shows the remaining bucket and can be alarmed.

Remedies for gp2 credit exhaustion: change the volume to gp3 with Elastic Volumes (online), which lets you provision IOPS independently of size, or move to a Provisioned IOPS type. When you convert gp2 to gp3 without specifying IOPS or throughput, EBS provisions the higher of the source gp2 equivalent or the gp3 baseline (3,000 IOPS in the documented example). Making a gp2 volume larger raises baseline but ties IOPS to capacity you may not need.

Elastic Volumes lets you change size, type, IOPS and throughput of an in-use volume without detaching it. Constraints: wait for a modification to reach `completed` before starting another; at most four modifications in a rolling 24-hour period per volume (exceeding it returns an error saying when you can retry); modification is best-effort and can take minutes to hours (about six hours for a fully used 1 TiB volume); size increases take effect at the `optimizing` state, but you must still extend the file system. Predictable peaks such as month-end are a good fit: raise IOPS ahead of the window (finish before it starts), lower afterwards, and remember the cost while raised.

rows: Per volume; adjustability not stated on the page read

blocks.body: S3 request rates. S3 supports at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per partitioned prefix, with no limit on the number of prefixes. Scale by parallelizing across prefixes and connections. AWS states that randomizing key prefixes is not required to reach these rates, so 'add random prefixes' is an outdated answer. While S3 repartitions for a rising rate it may return HTTP 503 Slow Down; respond with retries, gradually increase request rates, and monitor 5xx counts with CloudWatch request metrics, S3 Storage Lens or server access logs.

Throughput techniques: issue many concurrent requests over separate connections; use byte-range GETs to fetch parts of large objects in parallel (aligned to the part size if the object was uploaded as multipart); use the SDK Transfer Manager, which automates scaling connections; keep compute and bucket in the same Region; keep SDKs current for built-in retry behavior.

S3 Transfer Acceleration routes traffic through the nearest CloudFront edge location and then over an optimized network path to the bucket. It helps clients far from the bucket's Region and works with presigned URLs for PUT and POST. It is enabled per bucket, uses the endpoint `bucket-name.s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com`, requires bucket names without dots, charges for data transfer in and for requests on the accelerated endpoint, can take up to 20 minutes to take effect, and does not support cross-Region CopyObject. Use the Speed Comparison tool before enabling. It addresses distance; multipart upload is complementary (parallel parts, retry of failed parts) but does not shorten the network path.

Mountpoint for Amazon S3 mounts a bucket as a local file system on Linux for read-heavy applications. It can list and read existing files and create new ones, but cannot modify existing files or delete directories, and does not support symbolic links, file locking, or POSIX ownership and permission metadata. It cannot read objects in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, S3 Glacier Deep Archive, or the S3 Intelligent-Tiering Archive Access and Deep Archive Access tiers. It lets instances read the current version of a shared object directly from S3 instead of copying a file at boot. For full POSIX semantics the documentation points to FSx for Lustre. Mountpoint's metadata-cache staleness window was not verified in this build; if reads must be exact to the second, validate.

SSE-KMS request cost. With SSE-KMS, object operations generate AWS KMS requests, which cost money and can be throttled. An S3 Bucket Key is a bucket-level key from which S3 derives data keys, cutting request traffic from S3 to KMS and reducing KMS request cost by up to 99 percent. The documentation describes enabling it for new objects, needs no client change, and says it is not supported for dual-layer DSSE-KMS. Switching encryption type to avoid KMS charges changes the security posture and is usually the wrong remedy.

blocks.title: Offload large static media
blocks.body: Serving large media from instance storage or a shared file system ties download throughput and cost to a few servers. Store objects in S3 and front them with CloudFront so the compute tier is no longer in the download path.

Weeks of normal operation, then slowness after a traffic spike, on a small General Purpose SSD volume, signals gp2 burst-credit exhaustion. Remote uploaders to a single regional bucket signal Transfer Acceleration. 503 Slow Down at high request rate is solved by spreading across prefixes plus retries and ramping, not by random prefixes.

topics.title: Global delivery: CloudFront, edge compute and Global Accelerator

blocks.body: CloudFront serves cached responses from edge locations. A cache hit happens when a request produces the same cache key as an earlier one and the object is cached and valid. The cache key is built from the values you include (headers, cookies, query strings). Including only the minimum necessary values raises the cache hit ratio; including values that do not change the origin response creates duplicate cached objects. A cache policy controls the cache key; an origin request policy forwards extra values to the origin without adding them to the cache key (it must be paired with a cache policy).

Normalizing the cache key. When query strings or headers vary only cosmetically, a function on the viewer request can rewrite the request before the cache lookup; the documentation says both a CloudFront Function and Lambda@Edge on a viewer request can modify the cache key. Origin-request functions run only after a cache miss, so they cannot raise the hit ratio of the lookup itself.

rows: Computationally intensive work, third-party libraries, calls to AWS services or the network
Origin request (runs only on cache misses)
Requests are dynamic and always reach the origin, or a viewer-request function already exists
Content is highly cacheable, or logic needs data from DynamoDB or S3

blocks.body: Authentication at the edge. A viewer-request function runs before the cache, for every request, so it can reject unauthenticated viewers without touching the origin; Lambda@Edge is the choice when validation needs external calls.

Origin Shield adds a centralized caching layer in the Region closest to the origin so requests from all edge and regional caches collapse to as few as one origin fetch. It improves cache hit ratio and protects fragile origins, and carries additional charges. For static assets S3 plus CloudFront is the standard offload.

API Gateway and CloudFront. Edge-optimized API endpoints use a CloudFront distribution that API Gateway manages and suit geographically dispersed clients. Regional endpoints have no managed distribution, enable HTTP/2 by default, give the lowest latency to callers in the same Region, and let you attach your own CloudFront distribution for caching control and AWS WAF placement.

AWS Global Accelerator provides static anycast IP addresses announced from multiple edge locations. Traffic enters the AWS global network at the nearest edge and is routed to an endpoint (ALB, NLB, EC2 instance, Elastic IP) based on user location, endpoint health, traffic dials and weights. Static IPs mean no DNS change when endpoints change. It suits non-cacheable and non-HTTP traffic and fast failover between Regions, whereas CloudFront suits cacheable HTTP content. It is not a cache and does not reduce origin load for cacheable content.

Route 53 latency-based routing answers with the Region of lowest measured latency to the DNS resolver, or to a truncated client subnet when the resolver supports EDNS client subnet. It is DNS only: a resolver far from the user can distort the decision, and it does not accelerate packets. An Aurora global database has one primary Region and up to five read-only secondary Regions, with replication typically under one second (asynchronous), which gives local reads; writes still go to the primary Region.

rows: Cache static or semi-static HTTP content near users
Static IPs, non-HTTP/non-cacheable traffic, fast regional failover
Direct users to the nearest Regional stack at DNS level
Local reads of a relational database in several Regions
Rewrite the request before the cache lookup
Block malicious traffic before it reaches the Region

blocks.body: Be explicit about cacheable versus non-cacheable traffic. CloudFront in front of a Regional API helps cacheable responses and connection setup, but non-cacheable POSTs still reach the origin. A WAF in each Region is costlier and later in the path than one at CloudFront for a globally distributed site; this placement rationale is reasoning rather than a retrieved statement.

links.label: Choose between CloudFront Functions and Lambda@Edge

topics.title: Caching and offload layers: ElastiCache, DAX, API Gateway

blocks.body: A cache trades freshness for speed and removes repeated reads from the slow tier. Choose the layer matching the data and the consumer: CloudFront (HTTP content at the edge), API Gateway caching (API responses), DAX (DynamoDB item and query results), ElastiCache (arbitrary application data, sessions, computed results).

ElastiCache strategies. Lazy loading caches only requested data and tolerates node failure, but has a miss penalty (three trips) and can serve stale data; write-through updates the cache on each write; TTLs bound staleness. Engine choice: Memcached is multithreaded, simple, scales out by adding nodes and suits object caching. Valkey and Redis OSS support richer data structures such as sorted sets (leaderboards, ranked lists), replication with Multi-AZ failover and persistence options. A ranking requirement points to sorted sets, therefore Valkey/Redis OSS. Session data that must survive node loss also points to a replicated engine; moving sessions off a relational database removes write and read load from it.

DAX is a write-through cache for DynamoDB with an item cache and a query cache, accessed through the DAX client and a cluster endpoint that load balances across nodes. A cluster has one primary node plus up to 10 read replicas (11 nodes in total). A cache miss is read from DynamoDB with an eventually consistent read and stored. Strongly consistent reads are not cached, so such workloads get no benefit. The default TTL is five minutes. Use multiple nodes for availability because patching a single node causes misses (AWS recommends at least three nodes in different Availability Zones for production). Write-around (writing straight to DynamoDB) cuts write latency for bulk loads but leaves cached items stale until evicted; the item cache and query cache are independent, and cached query results are not refreshed when items change.

API Gateway caching for REST APIs is provisioned per stage with a size in GB; cache settings control the cache key and TTL per method, and management APIs invalidate the cache. Capacity affects the cache instance's CPU, memory and bandwidth, so load-test the size. Cache hits reduce backend traffic and help you stay under throttling limits.

API Gateway throttling uses a token bucket. The documented account-level quota is 10,000 requests per second per Region with a maximum bucket (burst) capacity of 5,000 requests; exceeding it returns 429 Too Many Requests. The account-level quota can be raised on request. Caching, usage plans with API keys and client retry are the other levers. Usage plans apply throttle and quota per API key, which suits rate-limiting consumers; whether they enforce strict cost caps is disputed (see discrepancies).

rows: Paid per stage; REST APIs only
Microsecond hits for eventually consistent reads; API-compatible client
Strongly consistent reads bypass; stale with write-around

blocks.body: Put the cache in front of the actual bottleneck and match the access pattern: DynamoDB read hot spots go to DAX; relational reads and sessions go to ElastiCache; repeated identical GET API calls go to API Gateway stage caching; static media goes to CloudFront.

links.label: Comparing Valkey, Memcached and Redis OSS

topics.title: Database scaling: connections, replicas, capacity modes

blocks.body: RDS Proxy sits between application and database and keeps a pool of established connections. By default it can reuse a connection after each transaction (multiplexing), so thousands of short client sessions share far fewer database connections. When a session changes state the proxy cannot safely share (for example certain SET statements), it pins the client to one database connection until the session ends, which reduces reuse; if nearly all connections pin, change the application. Each proxy serves a single Aurora DB cluster and tracks the current writer automatically. Lambda functions and autoscaling fleets are the classic cause of connection storms because every new execution environment or instance opens its own connections; point them at the proxy endpoint instead of the cluster endpoint.

Proxy endpoints. You can create additional read/write and read-only proxy endpoints for Aurora. The documentation notes applications reconnect faster to proxy endpoints than to the Aurora reader endpoint when readers become unavailable. A read-only proxy endpoint is therefore the way to give Lambda pooled access to Aurora Replicas.

Aurora reader scaling. The cluster reader endpoint load balances connections across Aurora Replicas using DNS, at connection level not query level. If clients cache DNS (including JVMs with indefinite TTL) or keep pooled connections, one replica can receive most traffic; new replicas may get traffic late. Aurora Replicas share the cluster storage volume so replica lag within a Region is typically in the tens of milliseconds. Custom endpoints group chosen instances (for example larger instances for analytics) and give finer control than the single reader endpoint. Offloading read-only queries to replicas via the reader endpoint is the standard fix for read-heavy contention on the writer.

DynamoDB capacity. Provisioned mode throttles with ProvisionedThroughputExceeded when consumption exceeds provisioned RCUs/WCUs, with only about five minutes of banked burst. Application Auto Scaling for DynamoDB scales up after two consecutive minutes above the target utilization and scales down after 15 consecutive data points below it (the AWS Database Blog describes this as 20 percentage points under the target), and the UpdateTable call itself takes minutes, so it lags sudden spikes and is bounded by the maximum you configure. Scheduled scaling raises capacity ahead of a known daily or seasonal peak; on-demand capacity mode responds better to unpredictable spikes. Throttling can occur even with auto scaling enabled. Pair throttling fixes with the right diagnosis: X-Ray points at the slow hop, CloudWatch throttle metrics confirm capacity.

Redshift Concurrency Scaling adds query-processing clusters automatically when queries queue. Enable it per workload-management queue (mode auto). `max_concurrency_scaling_clusters` defaults to 1. Each cluster earns up to one hour of free concurrency-scaling credit per day; usage beyond credits is billed per second. Use usage limits to alert or disable. It is the answer for bursty, read-heavy concurrency without permanently resizing the cluster.

rows: Max connections reached after Lambda scale-out
Bigger instance raises limit but not churn; replicas do not pool
Writer CPU high from read-only queries
Caching helps only for repeated identical reads
Repeated identical key lookups on DynamoDB
Raising RCUs costs more for the same reads
Bursty BI queries queue on Redshift
Resizing pays for peak all day

blocks.body: Connection-count problems are solved by pooling (RDS Proxy), not by larger instances or more replicas. Read-contention problems are solved by replicas or caches. Capacity throttling on DynamoDB is solved by capacity configuration or a cache, depending on whether reads repeat.

blocks.body: Lambda memory is the main performance lever: CPU is allocated in proportion to memory (128 to 10,240 MB; 1,769 MB equals roughly one vCPU). More memory can shorten duration for CPU-, network- or memory-bound functions, sometimes lowering cost; past the CPU-bound point extra memory only costs more. Use the open-source Lambda Power Tuning tool (Step Functions based) or Compute Optimizer recommendations to find the inflection point.

Cold starts. Initialization time (loading code, starting the runtime, running init code) is the largest contributor to cold-start latency. Provisioned concurrency keeps environments initialized; it applies to a published version or alias (not $LATEST), is billed for the allocation plus usage, can be scheduled or scaled with Application Auto Scaling, and a function with N provisioned concurrency handles up to 10N requests per second before spilling over (watch ProvisionedConcurrencySpilloverInvocations). SnapStart snapshots the initialized execution environment when you publish a version and resumes new environments from it; it supports Java 11 and later, Python 3.12 and later and .NET 8 and later per the page retrieved, works only on published versions and aliases, and does not support provisioned concurrency, EFS or ephemeral storage above 512 MB. SnapStart works best at scale; the docs say provisioned concurrency is the choice for strict cold-start requirements.

Long-running work. Lambda has a 15-minute maximum timeout for synchronous invocations. For work that cannot be split, containerize on Fargate; for work splittable into steps under 15 minutes each, Step Functions with Lambda; AWS Batch for job-style processing. Lambda Managed Instances allow up to 90 minutes for asynchronous and most event-source invocations, but that does not change the 15-minute synchronous limit. Raising memory does not extend the timeout.

Buffering and concurrency. Putting an SQS queue in front of Lambda absorbs bursts; a dead-letter queue captures messages that keep failing. Use the SQS event source's maximum concurrency setting to protect downstream systems (for example a third-party API or a database) instead of reserved concurrency; keep maximum concurrency at or below the function's reserved concurrency. The default account concurrency quota is 1,000 per Region; by default an SQS event source mapping can scale to invoke up to 1,250 concurrent instances, and provisioned mode scales higher (up to 100,000). FIFO queues cap concurrency at the number of message group IDs.

API Gateway limits seen with Lambda: account-level throttle (10,000 rps, 5,000 burst per Region), per-stage and per-key throttles from usage plans, and the integration timeout. 429 means throttled by API Gateway; 5xx from the backend means the integration failed. Diagnose which with CloudWatch metrics (Count, 4XXError, 5XXError, Latency, IntegrationLatency) before changing anything. These metric names are standard API Gateway metrics and were not separately re-verified.

Kinesis Data Streams. In the shared throughput model all consumers share 2 MB/s per shard and 5 read transactions per second; extra consumers cause ReadProvisionedThroughputExceeded. Enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer a dedicated 2 MB/s per shard over HTTP/2 push, with up to 20 EFO consumers per stream (50 with On-demand Advantage).

Amazon MSK. Express brokers always replicate across three Availability Zones. Rack-aware replication uses the broker.rack setting at AZ level so each replica of a partition sits in a separate AZ with RF 3. Consumers can fetch from the closest replica (Kafka 2.4 or later, two configuration settings) to reduce cross-AZ traffic cost and latency. Moving a Standard cluster to Express requires a new cluster (this migration detail was not verified in the pages read).

Amazon EMR. Managed scaling adjusts instances or units automatically from workload metrics (instance groups or fleets) in recent EMR versions (5.30.0, 6.1.0 and later except 6.0.0). Automatic scaling with a custom CloudWatch-metric policy is available only with instance groups, not fleets; configure both scale-out and scale-in rules or you must reset manually.

rows: Cold start on infrequent Java API
SnapStart (cheaper), provisioned concurrency for strict latency
Increase memory; verify with power tuning
Many consumers slow on one stream
Managed scaling, or custom policy on instance groups

blocks.body: Provisioned concurrency solves cold starts, not throttling by a downstream; SQS maximum concurrency solves downstream protection, not cold starts. Provisioned concurrency costs money while idle, so for sporadic traffic with relaxed latency SnapStart or no change may be preferred.

Scenario 1: Month-end slowdown on a self-managed database. A finance application on EC2 uses MySQL on a 500 GiB gp2 volume. For three days each month IOPS demand exceeds baseline and latency climbs. Requirements: no re-architecture, no downtime, pay for extra IOPS only when needed. Existing environment: current-generation instances, one volume. Chosen design: convert to gp3 with Elastic Volumes and provision higher IOPS and throughput before the window, then lower afterwards; alarm on BurstBalance until conversion. Rationale: gp3 decouples IOPS from size; the change is online. Security: unchanged. Cost: pay for provisioned IOPS only during the peak, remembering the four-modifications-per-24-hours limit. Alternatives rejected: enlarging the gp2 volume (pays for unused capacity), moving to a larger instance (volume is the limit), re-platforming to Aurora (not required and not minimal change).

Scenario 2: Global web application with slow, cache-poor delivery. A site behind an ALB has a falling CloudFront hit ratio because URLs carry tracking query strings and differently ordered parameters. Users on three continents complain; the origin CPU is rising. Constraints: minimal application change. Chosen design: a cache policy that includes only the query strings that affect output, with an origin request policy if the origin needs the rest; a viewer-request CloudFront Function to normalize parameter order and case; enable Origin Shield in the Region closest to the origin; move large images to S3 with CloudFront. Rationale: raising the hit ratio cuts origin load and latency together. Security: WAF stays attached to CloudFront. Cost: Origin Shield and function invocations are billed; fewer origin fetches typically offset them. Alternatives rejected: Global Accelerator (does not cache), scaling the origin (treats the symptom), Lambda@Edge origin-request (runs after the cache lookup, so cannot fix the key).

Scenario 3: Lambda and Aurora under a promotion. A serverless API on Lambda reads from an Aurora MySQL cluster. During promotions Lambda scales out, the database hits max connections, and the writer CPU is high from read-only queries. The first request after quiet periods is also slow (Java). Chosen design: RDS Proxy with a read-write endpoint for writes and a read-only endpoint for queries; add Aurora Replicas; enable SnapStart on a published version; cache hot product lookups in ElastiCache if reads repeat. Rationale: pooling removes the connection storm; replicas offload reads; SnapStart reduces init latency (it has its own pricing section in the Lambda docs; check it). Security and cost: how the proxy authenticates and how it is priced were not covered by the pages read for this lesson; confirm before proposing it. Alternatives rejected: larger DB instance (connections still churn), provisioned concurrency for sporadic traffic (idle cost), moving the workload to Fargate (not needed).

Troubleshooting checklist. Volume modification rejected: you exceeded four modifications in 24 hours or the previous one has not completed. Accelerated endpoint fails: bucket name contains dots or acceleration not yet active (up to 20 minutes). Provisioned concurrency still shows cold starts: invoking $LATEST or an unaliased version, or concurrency above the allocation (check spillover metric); also remember each unit handles up to 10 requests per second. CloudFront hit ratio unchanged: a header, cookie or query string still in the cache key, or TTL zero from the origin. RDS Proxy not reducing connections: heavy pinning from session-state changes. Aurora replicas uneven: client DNS caching.

Step 1: find the primary requirement (lower latency, higher throughput, absorb bursts, reduce database load) and the bottleneck it implies. Step 2: list mandatory constraints (no code change, minimal operational overhead, cost-effectiveness, existing engine, Region, consistency). Step 3: eliminate options that do not touch the bottleneck, that violate a constraint, or that depend on outdated assumptions. Step 4: among survivors pick the most managed, least-change option.

Read-heavy relational contention: replicas or ElastiCache; connection exhaustion: RDS Proxy.
Long distance uploads: Transfer Acceleration; long distance downloads of cacheable content: CloudFront.
Lambda cold start: SnapStart or provisioned concurrency; Lambda runtime over 15 minutes: Fargate, Step Functions or Batch.
Shared-stream read limit: enhanced fan-out.
Wrong-way distractors: bigger instance for a connection limit, Global Accelerator for cacheable content, random S3 prefixes, origin-request edge function to fix a cache key.

blocks.body: Legacy forwarded-headers or whitelist settings in CloudFront have been superseded by cache policies and origin request policies; random S3 key prefixes are not needed; Elasticsearch Service is now OpenSearch Service (this rename is from question-bank notes, not a page retrieved here). Select the answer consistent with current guidance when the stem allows.

When two options both work, compare effort and side effects: one that needs no code and no new infrastructure beats one that adds a service. Beware options that solve a different valid problem (e.g. cost reduction when latency is asked).
