blocks.body: This lesson covers SAP-C02 task 3.4, determining a strategy to improve the reliability of solutions that already exist. The skill is diagnostic: you are handed a running architecture with a symptom (outages, throttling, slow failover, lost messages) or a requirement (survive an Availability Zone failure, absorb growth) and must pick the smallest set of changes that remove the weakness. Reliability, in the Well-Architected sense, is the ability of a workload to perform its intended function correctly and consistently when expected to, across its whole lifecycle. The AWS design principles for it are: automatically recover from failure, test recovery procedures, scale horizontally to increase aggregate availability, stop guessing capacity, and manage change in automation.

Prerequisites: working knowledge of Amazon VPC subnets and Availability Zones (an AZ is one or more discrete data centers with independent power and networking inside a Region), Amazon EC2, Elastic Load Balancing (ELB), Amazon RDS and Amazon Aurora, Amazon SQS, AWS Lambda, and Amazon CloudWatch alarms. Earlier lessons on resilient architectures (recovery time objective (RTO), recovery point objective (RPO), and disaster recovery (DR) strategies) and on new-solution reliability (task 2.4) are assumed; this lesson applies those ideas to remediating what is already deployed.

items: You will be able to inspect an existing architecture and list its single points of failure (single instance, single AZ, single NAT gateway, single-AZ file system or database, synchronous chains).
You will be able to configure Auto Scaling groups for self-healing: correct health check type, grace period, multi-AZ spread, scale-in protection and lifecycle hooks.
You will be able to choose between Multi-AZ, read replicas, Aurora replicas, RDS Proxy and cache replication to meet a failover or read-scaling requirement.
You will be able to decouple components with SQS, SNS, Lambda event source mappings and Step Functions, and size visibility timeouts, redrive policies and concurrency so that failures are contained.
You will be able to design DNS and edge failover (Route 53 failover with health evaluation, CloudFront origin groups) and explain what each mechanism can and cannot detect.
You will be able to find and monitor service quotas that become reliability limits as usage grows, and choose remediations that avoid throttling.

blocks.title: Verbatim exam objectives (task 3.4)
blocks.body: Title: Determine a strategy to improve reliability. Knowledge of: AWS Global Infrastructure; data replication methods; scaling methodologies (for example, load balancing, auto scaling); high availability and resiliency; disaster recovery methods and tools; service quotas and limits. Skills in: understanding application growth and usage trends; evaluating existing architecture to determine areas that are not sufficiently reliable; remediating single points of failure; enabling data replication, self-healing, and elastic features and services.

rows: EC2 Auto Scaling, health checks, lifecycle hooks, warm pools, scale-in protection, instance refresh, Spot diversification, EC2 auto recovery
Instances replaced too early/late; long jobs killed; Spot interruptions
ALB/NLB health checks, cross-zone, Route 53 failover, CloudFront origin groups, PrivateLink
Which layer detects the failure; why 502/504
RDS/Aurora Multi-AZ and replicas, RDS Proxy, ElastiCache, DynamoDB, Redshift snapshots, FSx
Reduce failover time; remove single-AZ database/file system
SQS + DLQ, SNS fanout, Lambda event source mapping, Step Functions
Protect a database or third party from bursts; do not lose messages
Service Quotas, CloudWatch usage metrics, Lambda concurrency, Fargate vCPU quotas
Alarm before exhaustion; isolate noisy neighbors

blocks.body: Task 3.4 sits in the Continuous Improvement for Existing Solutions domain. The exact percentage weight of that domain was not verified against AWS documentation in this build; confirm it in the current official exam guide. Expect scenario questions where several options technically work and the winner is the one that removes the single point of failure with the least change and least operational overhead.

Before remediating, you must find what is weak. Two inputs drive the assessment: the architecture itself (where can one failure take the workload down?) and the trend data (where will growth push a component past a limit?).

blocks.title: Single point of failure (SPOF)
blocks.body: Any component whose failure stops the workload because there is no redundant peer or automatic replacement. Common SPOFs in existing estates: one EC2 instance serving a tier, all instances in one AZ, one NAT gateway serving several AZs, a Single-AZ database or file system, a self-managed database on one EC2 instance, a single queue consumer, a synchronous call to a slow third party.

AWS Trusted Advisor has a fault tolerance category whose checks read like a SPOF checklist. The documented check names include: ALB Multi-AZ; EC2 Auto Scaling not deployed in multiple AZs or not meeting the minimum number of AZs; EC2 Auto Scaling without ELB health check enabled; Auto Scaling group with Capacity Rebalancing enabled; EC2 Availability Zone balance; Amazon RDS DB instances not using Multi-AZ deployment; RDS DB clusters with all instances (or all readers) in the same AZ; RDS backups and continuous backup; ElastiCache Multi-AZ clusters; EFS no mount target redundancy; Amazon CloudFront origin failover; DynamoDB point-in-time recovery; EBS snapshots; and Auto Scaling available IPs in subnets. Treat that list as a mental audit template.

rows: Is there more than one instance, in more than one AZ, and is a failed one replaced automatically?
Auto Scaling group across 2+ AZ subnets with ELB health checks
Does the load balancer or DNS stop sending traffic to a dead target or AZ?
ALB/NLB health checks; Route 53 failover with Evaluate Target Health; CloudFront origin group
Is there a synchronous standby or replica in another AZ, and are backups enabled?
RDS/Aurora Multi-AZ, Aurora replicas in distinct AZs, ElastiCache Multi-AZ, FSx Multi-AZ
Does each AZ have its own NAT gateway and route table?
Does a slow or failing dependency block callers? Are failed messages isolated?
SQS buffer, DLQ, Step Functions retries, Lambda concurrency limits
Which quotas will growth exhaust and is there an alarm?
Service Quotas usage alarms, quota increase requests

blocks.body: Understanding growth and usage trends means looking at the metrics that map to limits: concurrent Lambda executions, Fargate vCPU usage, DynamoDB consumed versus provisioned capacity, RDS connections, load balancer capacity, queue depth and age of the oldest message. Services that integrate their usage metrics with Service Quotas publish them in CloudWatch; the documented list includes Amazon EC2, Elastic Load Balancing, AWS Fargate, Amazon DynamoDB, AWS KMS, CloudWatch and CloudWatch Logs, Amazon Data Firehose, and AWS Fault Injection Service. You can graph usage against the quota with the `SERVICE_QUOTA(m1)` metric-math function and alarm at a percentage of it (the documentation's worked example alarms above 80 percent).

Finally, test. A fix you have not exercised is an assumption. AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) runs fault experiments with stop conditions: a stop condition is a CloudWatch alarm on a steady-state metric (latency, error rate, retries) that halts the experiment if the application becomes unacceptable, and a stopped experiment cannot be resumed. Some failures cannot be simulated end to end; for example, the EC2 system status check failure that drives automatic recovery cannot be artificially produced by customers, so you can only verify that the alarm action fires (with `set-alarm-state`).

items: Config drift: if the DR or secondary copy of an environment is built by hand, it drifts. CloudFormation drift detection identifies stack resources whose configuration was changed outside CloudFormation, so you can bring them back in line with the template; defining both Regions from the same template is the preventive control.
Common mistake: fixing capacity (bigger instance) when the problem is redundancy. Scaling up one instance does not remove the SPOF.
Common mistake: assuming a managed service is automatically multi-AZ. Several (RDS instances, FSx for Windows, ElastiCache, Redshift) need an explicit Multi-AZ or replica configuration.

blocks.body: When a question describes 'an application that is down whenever X fails', find X and ask what is redundant with it. The correct option usually adds automatic replacement or an automatic standby, not a manual runbook.

links.label: Visualize service quotas and set alarms

topics.title: Self-healing compute with EC2 Auto Scaling

blocks.body: An EC2 Auto Scaling group (ASG) keeps a fleet at a desired capacity between a minimum and maximum, spreads instances over the Availability Zones of the subnets you give it, and replaces instances that it judges unhealthy. It is the primary self-healing construct for EC2-based tiers.

blocks.title: Health checks: who decides an instance is unhealthy
blocks.body: By default the ASG relies on the EC2 status checks (instance not running, or impaired). Elastic Load Balancing health checks are ignored by default. After you set the health check type to ELB, when the load balancer reports a registered instance Unhealthy, the ASG marks it Unhealthy on its next periodic check and replaces it. You can also report health from your own system with the SetInstanceHealth API. If connection draining (deregistration delay) is enabled, Auto Scaling waits for in-flight requests or the timeout before terminating.

rows: EC2 (default) vs ELB (adds load balancer results)
ELB must be turned on explicitly; the load balancer must be attached and InService
Minimum time a new instance stays in service before being replaced for unhealthy results
Console default 300 seconds; 0 seconds when created with the CLI or an SDK; 0 turns it off
Applies to new instances, instances returned from standby and attached instances
If the instance is no longer in the EC2 running state it is replaced immediately, grace period or not
Instance waits in a wait state until completion or timeout
One hour heartbeat timeout; global maximum is 48 hours or 100 times the heartbeat timeout, whichever is smaller
Group balances capacity evenly across enabled AZs and rebalances launch-before-terminate
Can exceed the maximum temporarily by 10 percent or one instance, whichever is greater, during rebalancing

blocks.body: Multi-AZ behavior. If you give the group subnets in several AZs, Auto Scaling balances evenly. If an AZ becomes unavailable it launches replacements in the healthy AZs; when the zone recovers it rebalances by launching in the emptier zone before terminating elsewhere. Rebalancing can be triggered by detaching or placing instances in standby, changing the AZ list, or an AZ recovering from insufficient capacity. Being at or near the maximum capacity can impede rebalancing, which is why the temporary overshoot exists. An instance maintenance policy can bound how far capacity moves while this happens.

Protecting work that must not be interrupted. Instance scale-in protection stops the ASG from choosing a protected instance when scaling in, which suits long-running queue workers. It has important limits: it does not protect against health check replacement, Spot interruptions, a Capacity Block reservation ending, or manual termination through terminate-instance-in-auto-scaling-group or EC2 APIs. If every instance is protected when a scale-in event occurs, desired capacity is decremented but nothing is terminated until protection is removed. Unhealthy instances bypass both custom termination policies and scale-in protection; only suspending the HealthCheck, ReplaceUnhealthy or Terminate process prevents replacement of an unhealthy instance. Lifecycle hooks and instance lifecycle policies apply to both healthy and unhealthy instances.

items: Troubleshooting an unhealthy instance you want to keep for analysis: suspend both Terminate and HealthCheck. If you suspend only Terminate, the instance is still marked Unhealthy when you stop or reboot it, and Auto Scaling replaces it as soon as Terminate is resumed. Alternatively use a Terminating lifecycle hook (Terminating:Wait) or Standby.

If a group does not scale or replace as expected, check: already at min/max, suspended processes (Launch, Terminate, AlarmNotification, ReplaceUnhealthy, HealthCheck), scale-in protection, simple-scaling cooldown, and disabled scale-in portion of a target tracking policy.
Termination lifecycle hooks are best effort by default: if the hook times out or is abandoned, Auto Scaling terminates immediately.

blocks.body: Launch latency and warm pools. A warm pool holds pre-initialized instances (stopped, running, or hibernated) beside the group so scale-out is faster for applications with long boot times. Pool instances are stopped or hibernated without waiting for user data to finish, so use an EC2_INSTANCE_LAUNCHING lifecycle hook to hold an instance until its bootstrap completes. Instances in the pool pause at Warmed:Pending:Wait for launching hooks and again at Pending:Wait when they enter the group; if the pool is exhausted the group can launch directly. A pre-baked AMI cuts boot work further. Instances launched from a warm pool inherit the group's scale-in protection setting.

Changing the fleet safely. Instance refresh replaces instances to roll out a new AMI or launch template. The default rolling strategy terminates and launches in batches while maintaining desired capacity and availability; a replace-root-volume strategy updates the root volume without terminating the instance but requires a mixed instances policy with ImageId overrides. Scaling policies: target tracking keeps a metric near a target; for queue workers use a backlog-per-instance metric (ApproximateNumberOfMessages divided by InService instances) with a target equal to acceptable latency divided by average processing time per message, rather than raw queue length, which ignores fleet size.

items: Single bastion or admin host: an ASG with minimum, maximum and desired of 1 across subnets in two AZs gives automatic replacement after instance or AZ failure with no standby cost. State that is not in the AMI must be rebuilt by bootstrap or lifecycle hooks.
Many small instances versus few large ones: more, smaller instances spread across AZs reduce the share of capacity lost per failure and give the group finer-grained scaling.

blocks.body: Keywords: 'instances are terminated while still processing' points to scale-in protection (or a termination lifecycle hook). 'Instance passes EC2 checks but the app is broken' points to ELB health checks on the ASG. 'New instances are killed before they finish booting' points to grace period or a launch lifecycle hook. 'Keep a failed instance for forensics' points to suspending Terminate and HealthCheck, or Standby.

links.label: Health checks for Auto Scaling instances

topics.title: Load balancer health checks and traffic failover

blocks.body: A health check is only as good as what it measures. A shallow health check tests the local instance (processes running, file system, software behaving). A deep health check also exercises off-box dependencies such as a database, DNS or a downstream API. The choice, and whether the Auto Scaling group consumes the result, changes the failure behavior.

rows: Shallow check on ELB and added to ASG
Local failures are detected by both; transient dependency failures do not terminate instances
Deep check on ELB, not added to ASG
Load balancer routes around impaired instances or AZ gray failures quickly; ASG still uses only EC2 status checks so a persistently broken instance may never be replaced
Needs an extra mechanism (for example a heartbeat table plus a watcher calling SetInstanceHealth, with velocity control)
Deep check on ELB and added to ASG
A transient dependency failure can make every target fail simultaneously; the load balancer fails open but the ASG starts replacing the whole fleet
Do not do this; it can cause mass termination

blocks.title: Fail open
blocks.body: If all targets of a target group are unhealthy, the load balancer routes to all of them anyway rather than none. With ALB, target group health thresholds let you define a minimum healthy count or percentage; below the DNS-failover threshold the unhealthy zone's IP addresses are removed from DNS, and below the routing-failover threshold the load balancer routes to any target in the group. The DNS failover threshold must be greater than or equal to the routing failover threshold.

items: ALB health check defaults (instance or IP targets): protocol HTTP, path /, timeout 5 seconds, interval 30 seconds, healthy threshold 5, unhealthy threshold 2, success code 200. Ranges: interval 5 to 300 seconds, timeout 2 to 120 seconds, thresholds 2 to 10. A newly registered target must pass one health check to be considered healthy, but a target that has been marked unhealthy returns to service only after it passes the healthy threshold number of consecutive checks, so recovery time is roughly interval times healthy threshold.

Each load balancer node health-checks independently. The target shows healthy in the console if at least one node reports it healthy, whereas the UnhealthyHostCount metric with the Maximum statistic reflects any node reporting unhealthy.

Cross-zone load balancing: always on for ALB at the load balancer level (you can change it per target group); off by default for NLB and Gateway Load Balancer, and enabling it on an NLB incurs inter-AZ data transfer charges. With it off, each node sends traffic only to targets in its own zone, so an AZ with no healthy target loses its DNS IP address.
An empty target group on an ALB may not report an error, whereas an empty NLB target group is reported unhealthy.

blocks.body: Avoid health check design that couples availability to a dependency you can survive without. If the database is down and the web tier can serve cached or degraded pages, a deep check that fails every instance converts a partial outage into a total one. Prefer graceful degradation and retries with backoff for dependency failures, shallow checks for replacement decisions, and zonal shift or deep checks for isolating a single AZ with a gray failure.

A scenario that says 'a database problem causes the ASG to terminate healthy web servers' is warning about deep ELB health checks attached to the ASG. The remedy is shallow checks for instance replacement, or deep checks on the load balancer only.

blocks.title: Route 53 failover
blocks.body: In active-passive failover, Route 53 returns the primary record while it is healthy and the secondary when it is not. If both are unhealthy it returns the primary record. For AWS resources that support alias records, do not create a separate health check: set Evaluate Target Health to Yes on the alias record. For resources you cannot alias (for example an IP address or an on-premises server) associate a Route 53 health check. A health check can monitor an endpoint (TCP, HTTP, HTTPS), other health checks, a CloudWatch alarm, or a Route 53 Application Recovery Controller routing control. When the primary recovers, Route 53 fails back automatically; use weighted routing or health check changes to control failback.

items: Health check mechanics: requests come from multiple AWS Regions; the default interval is 30 seconds, with an optional fast interval of 10 seconds (it triples the request load on your endpoint and costs extra); the failure threshold is 1 to 10 consecutive observations, default 3. The request interval cannot be changed after the health check is created. An endpoint is healthy when enough checkers report healthy (the AWS blog states at least 18 percent of checkers, by default 3 of 16).

Failover time is approximately DNS TTL + (interval x threshold). The AWS example: TTL 60 seconds, 10-second interval, threshold 5 gives 110 seconds. Lower thresholds fail over faster but can trigger on short overloads.

Automatic failover through health checks runs in the Route 53 data plane; relying on control-plane API calls to force failover adds a dependency. Health-check-driven failover therefore suits recovery that must not depend on operator action.

Combining routing policies (for example latency records each with health evaluation, under failover) builds a tree; Evaluate Target Health is checked by default in traffic policy rules for alias targets.

blocks.title: CloudFront origin failover
blocks.body: Create an origin group with a primary and secondary origin (S3 buckets or custom origins) and specify the status codes that trigger failover. CloudFront fails over only when the viewer request method is GET, HEAD or OPTIONS, and also when the connection to the primary fails or times out. It is stateless: every request tries the primary first, so failover is immediate per request but adds latency while the primary times out. Tunable settings: connection attempts 1 to 3, connection timeout 1 to 10 seconds, response timeout 1 to 60 seconds (custom origins only). For quick failover (for example live segments) use fewer attempts and shorter timeouts. A hybrid design with Route 53 failover in front of CloudFront origins adds health-state awareness.

items: CloudFront returns 504 when the origin returns 504, does not respond before the request expires, a firewall or security group blocks CloudFront, or the origin is not reachable from the internet. It returns 502 when an intermediary such as an ALB cannot connect to its origin; troubleshoot the ALB's own 502 causes.

ALB 504 causes include connection to the target not established within 10 seconds, no response before the idle timeout, a network ACL blocking ephemeral ports 1024-65535 from targets back to the load balancer nodes, and an SSL handshake timeout of 10 seconds. Keep CloudFront origin keep-alive lower than the ALB idle timeout.

blocks.title: PrivateLink to an NLB-fronted service
blocks.body: An endpoint service is available only in the Availability Zones enabled on its Network Load Balancer. For resilience, enable at least two AZs, run targets in each, and register them. Cross-zone load balancing on the NLB is an alternative when you cannot have targets in every zone, but consumers then lose the service from both zones if the zone hosting it fails, and data transfer charges apply. Troubleshooting checklist from AWS: endpoint connection state (accepted), AZ mapping and independence, NLB listener port and response, NLB security group (must allow client IPs unless PrivateLink inbound rule evaluation is turned off), zonal DNS name, and security group and network ACL rules.

Route 53 failover answers 'which Region or endpoint should clients be sent to', based on health. CloudFront origin groups answer 'retry this request against another origin' per request. ALB health checks answer 'which target in this group'. Auto Scaling health checks answer 'should this instance be replaced'. Match the mechanism to the layer in the question.

items: Weighted target groups on an ALB listener rule (weights 0 to 999) shift a percentage of traffic between target groups, which suits canary and blue/green releases. Target group stickiness (default 1 hour, 1 second to 7 days) keeps a client on the same target group; it is distinct from sticky sessions, which pin a client to a target within a group. AWS states that weighted target groups are not a best practice for failover, because the ALB keeps distributing by weight even if every target in a group fails health checks. Use Route 53 or health-aware mechanisms for failover.

links.label: Improve website availability with CloudFront (origin failover)
Share your services through AWS PrivateLink

topics.title: Capacity resilience: Spot, placement groups and EC2 recovery

blocks.body: Even a correctly spread ASG fails if it cannot obtain capacity. Capacity pools are per instance type per AZ, so resilience comes from diversifying across both.

blocks.title: Spot diversification
blocks.body: A Spot Instance pool is one instance type in one AZ. Interruptions and shortages are per pool, so a group that requests one type in one AZ is fragile. Give the ASG a mixed instances policy with many instance types (or attribute-based instance type selection, which describes vCPU and memory requirements and lets Auto Scaling pick every matching current-generation type) and subnets in all AZs. Auto Scaling first balances capacity across AZs, then applies the Spot allocation strategy within each AZ.

rows: Diversifies over low-priced pools that are also optimized for capacity availability
Documented as the balanced choice in the AWS compute blog
Chooses pools optimized only for available capacity (capacity-optimized-prioritized honors your type order best-effort)
By default uses the two lowest-priced pools, not optimized for capacity; the SDK default if unspecified

items: Capacity Rebalancing: when enabled, Auto Scaling proactively replaces Spot Instances that receive an EC2 rebalance recommendation (an elevated-risk signal), launching a replacement before terminating the old instance. Without it, Auto Scaling replaces Spot capacity only after the interruption and failed health check. EC2 always sends the rebalance recommendation and the two-minute interruption notice, but a lifecycle hook cannot stop a Spot reclaim. During replacement the group may briefly exceed its maximum and you pay for both instances.

Mix On-Demand and Spot with OnDemandBaseCapacity and OnDemandPercentageAboveBaseCapacity to keep a guaranteed floor. Changing allocation strategy on a running group does not change existing instances; it applies to future launches.
Instance scale-in protection does not protect against Spot interruptions.

blocks.body: Placement groups influence where instances sit. A cluster placement group packs instances close for low latency in one AZ; if capacity is insufficient at launch an InsufficientInstanceCapacity error is returned. Documented mitigations for capacity errors: retry after a few minutes, request fewer instances, omit the AZ or choose a subnet in another AZ, and use a different instance type (you can resize after launch). If the error persists, move the instance to another AZ; an account-level restriction is then possible and needs AWS Support. A partition placement group splits instances across partitions on separate racks (maximum seven partitions per AZ) to contain correlated hardware failures for replicated systems such as HDFS, HBase and Cassandra, and shows which instance is in which partition; if there is not enough distinct hardware the request fails and you retry later. A spread placement group puts each instance on distinct hardware (up to seven running instances per AZ per group, per the Karpenter-documented description of the strategy). Do not choose a cluster placement group for resilience; it trades availability for latency.

Single-instance recovery. For an instance that cannot be clustered, EC2 can recover it when the system status check fails (underlying host problem). Create a CloudWatch alarm on StatusCheckFailed_System (value 1) with the recover action. The recovered instance keeps its instance ID, private IP, Elastic IP addresses and EBS attachments, and is restarted on new hardware, so the application must start automatically at boot. Recovery works for system status check failures, not instance status check failures (guest OS problems need a reboot or different action), cannot recover a terminated instance, and is not available for every instance type or configuration. Simplified automatic recovery is built into EC2 with no customer alarm; its outcome shows as AWS Health events.

Choose the right tool by failure type. Host hardware impaired, single instance, must keep ID and IP: CloudWatch recover action. Instance replaceable and stateless: Auto Scaling group. Spot interruptions: diversify types and AZs, enable Capacity Rebalancing. InsufficientInstanceCapacity in a cluster placement group: relax the placement or instance type, or launch together.

topics.title: Data tier reliability: databases, caches and warehouses

blocks.body: The data tier is usually the hardest SPOF to remove because state must be replicated, not just restarted. Match the mechanism to the requirement: automatic failover with no data loss, read scaling, cross-Region recovery, or connection stability.

rows: Synchronous to a standby in another AZ; standby cannot serve reads
Automatic, name record unchanged; AWS states 60 to 120 seconds depending on activity
High availability and durability in a Region
One writer and two readable standbys across three AZs, engine-native replication
Automatic; standbys also serve reads via reader endpoint
HA plus read capacity and low commit latency (documented for MySQL and PostgreSQL)
Asynchronous; can be same AZ, cross-AZ or cross-Region
Read scaling; cross-Region replicas for DR
Shared cluster volume; typical lag tens of milliseconds
Aurora promotes a replica by priority tier 0 to 15; with none it creates a new instance (longer)
HA and read scaling; place replicas in different AZs
Storage-level asynchronous replication, typically under a second, up to five secondary Regions
ElastiCache Valkey or Redis OSS Multi-AZ
Asynchronous primary to replicas (up to five per primary)
Automatic promotion of the lowest-lag replica; DNS endpoint preserved
Cache HA; Memcached has no replication or failover

blocks.body: Multi-AZ versus read replicas is a classic trap. Multi-AZ is for availability and durability: synchronous, automatic, not for reads (in the single-standby model). Read replicas are for read scaling and Region-level DR: asynchronous, manually promoted. A Single-AZ RDS instance that fails may need point-in-time recovery, which AWS says can take several hours and loses data after the latest restorable time. In Multi-AZ deployments, backups and snapshots for MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle and PostgreSQL are taken from the standby, and OS maintenance and scaling operations are applied to the standby first, followed by a failover, which also shortens maintenance impact. Converting Single-AZ to Multi-AZ is a modify operation on the instance.

blocks.title: Aurora failover and endpoints
blocks.body: Within a cluster, replicas share the writer's storage volume, so promotion needs no data copy. Applications should connect through the cluster (writer) endpoint, which AWS repoints on failover, and the reader endpoint to load-balance reads across replicas; a connection to a replica that is promoted is dropped and must reconnect. Put replicas in distinct AZs, and set failover priority (tiers 0 to 15) so the replica you prefer is promoted first; replicas with equal priority are chosen by size or arbitrarily. Trusted Advisor flags clusters with a single instance or with all instances or all readers in one AZ.

blocks.title: RDS Proxy
blocks.body: A managed connection pooler between the application and the database. Benefits documented by AWS: connection pooling and multiplexing (fewer database connections, less memory and CPU spent on connection handling), and faster, smoother failover. During a failover the proxy keeps accepting connections at the same IP address and routes them to the new primary; clients are not exposed to DNS propagation, local DNS caching (including applications that cache the endpoint beyond its TTL), or connection timeouts. Idle connections stay alive; only connections in the middle of a transaction or statement are canceled; while the writer is unavailable the proxy queues requests. For Lambda, the proxy lets many concurrent invocations share a pool instead of exhausting database connections, and AWS recommends it for functions that open and close many short connections. Lambda must be in the same VPC as the database to reach the proxy.

items: Credential and IAM handling: RDS Proxy uses a Secrets Manager secret and an IAM role that the console can create; IAM authentication can be used from Lambda instead of embedding credentials.

Redshift: automated snapshots and recovery points are free and allow cluster or table restore to an earlier point; cross-Region snapshot copy (automatic, with retention you configure; KMS-encrypted clusters need extra configuration) allows rebuilding in another Region; Multi-AZ deployment runs the warehouse in more than one AZ; cluster relocation moves an RA3 cluster to another AZ in one step. Restoring from a snapshot rebuilds the cluster, so it fits recovery objectives that tolerate a rebuild rather than near-instant failover.

DynamoDB: provisioned mode throttles with ProvisionedThroughputExceededException when consumption exceeds provisioned capacity. It banks up to 5 minutes of unused capacity as burst, best effort and not to be planned on; hot partitions can throttle regardless (per-partition limits of 3,000 RCU or 1,000 WCU). Auto scaling reacts with a lag and is bounded by your configured maximum. On-demand mode accommodates up to double the previous peak instantly; spikes beyond that can still throttle. Prefer on-demand for unpredictable load, spread keys, and buffer writes through a queue when bursts exceed what the table can absorb.
Point-in-time recovery and backups: Trusted Advisor checks DynamoDB PITR, RDS backups and continuous backup, and whether EBS, RDS and DynamoDB are in AWS Backup plans.

blocks.body: 'Reduce database failover time' points to RDS Proxy (and Aurora with replicas), not just Multi-AZ, because the proxy removes DNS and connection re-establishment delay. 'Lambda exhausts database connections' points to RDS Proxy, or to an SQS buffer with limited concurrency in front of the database. 'Automatic failover and zero data loss in-Region' points to Multi-AZ; 'DR in another Region' points to cross-Region replica or Aurora Global Database.

topics.title: Decoupling: SQS, SNS, Lambda and Step Functions

blocks.body: Tight coupling turns the slowest or flakiest dependency into the availability ceiling of the whole system. A queue between producer and consumer absorbs bursts, lets consumers fail and retry independently, and gives you a place to isolate bad messages. This is the standard remediation for throttling, connection storms and lost work.

blocks.title: SQS visibility timeout and retries
blocks.body: When a consumer receives a message it stays in the queue but is hidden for the visibility timeout (default 30 seconds, range 0 seconds to 12 hours). If the consumer does not delete it in time, it reappears and is delivered again: standard queues are at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent. The number of in-flight messages is limited (approximately 120,000 for most standard queues and 120,000 for FIFO) while stored messages are unlimited; delete messages after processing to avoid OverLimit errors.

blocks.title: Dead-letter queues
blocks.body: A redrive policy on the source queue names the DLQ and maxReceiveCount, the number of times a message may be received before SQS moves it to the DLQ. Set it high enough to allow retries: AWS recommends at least 5 for Lambda consumers, because throttled or erroring invocations also consume receives. A FIFO source needs a FIFO DLQ and a standard source a standard DLQ. A redrive allow policy controls which source queues may use the DLQ (default all; byQueue allows up to 10). Retention expiry is based on the original enqueue timestamp, which is not reset when the message moves, so set the DLQ retention longer than the source queue's (default 4 days, range 60 seconds to 14 days). Alarm on DLQ depth and, after fixing the consumer, redrive messages back to the source queue from the console.

items: Lambda with SQS: Lambda polls the queue and invokes the function with a batch; success deletes the batch. By default an error returns the whole batch to the queue after the visibility timeout; enable partial batch responses (ReportBatchItemFailures) so only failed messages return. Set the queue visibility timeout to at least six times the function timeout (the Knowledge Center adds the batch window to that sum), and the function timeout must not exceed the visibility timeout. Duplicate invocations are possible, so make handlers idempotent.

Lambda concurrency: the account default is 1,000 concurrent executions per Region (adjustable via Service Quotas). Reserved concurrency carves capacity out of that pool for a function, guarantees it, and also caps it; because event sources such as SQS poll, a cap smooths traffic into a downstream database, with excess events waiting durably. AWS always keeps 100 units unreserved, so with a 1,000 limit you can reserve at most 900. Synchronous callers above a function's cap get throttling errors; provisioned concurrency is a separate feature from the reserved cap (its cold-start behavior was not verified against AWS docs in this build).

Lambda asynchronous invocation: default two retries, events held up to six hours; configure MaximumRetryAttempts (0 to 2) and MaximumEventAgeInSeconds (60 to 21,600), and attach a DLQ or on-failure destination, otherwise exhausted events are discarded.

SNS to SQS fanout: publish once to an SNS topic and have a queue per subscriber. The queue acts as a persistent buffer, so a subscriber outage of hours or days loses no messages, and each consumer scales independently. This is the answer when one event must trigger several independent actions and downstream capacity differs.

blocks.body: Step Functions replaces chains of Lambda functions calling each other. A chain couples timeouts, hides failures and makes retry logic per function. A state machine puts orchestration outside the code: Task states support Retry (ErrorEquals, IntervalSeconds, MaxAttempts, BackoffRate, optional jitter) and Catch to route to fallback states. This gives workflow-level error handling with exponential backoff across multiple services, and Lambda service exceptions such as Lambda.ServiceException and Lambda.TooManyRequestsException should be handled explicitly.

Queue-based scaling: scale consumers on backlog per instance, not raw queue depth, and size the target as acceptable latency divided by per-message processing time. Buffering also protects fixed-capacity targets: a DynamoDB table with provisioned writes, a relational database with a connection ceiling, or a third-party API with a rate limit. The consumer concurrency (reserved concurrency, batch size, ASG size) becomes the knob that sets the downstream request rate.

When the requirement is 'do not lose requests when the backend is slow, throttled or down', the answer is a durable queue (SQS) between tiers plus a DLQ, not a bigger backend. When the stem says 'minimal code changes', prefer enabling a feature (DLQ, partial batch response, RDS Proxy) over rewriting. Beware answers that use SNS alone as the buffer: SNS pushes and does not queue for slow consumers unless you subscribe an SQS queue.

items: Stream sources (Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams) behave differently from SQS: a poison record can block a shard. Configure the event source mapping with MaximumRetryAttempts, MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds, BisectBatchOnFunctionError (splits a failed batch to isolate the bad record; splitting does not consume the retry quota) and an on-failure destination (SQS or SNS) that receives batch metadata. With default settings a bad record can block the affected shard for up to one week (per AWS), and records are discarded if all handling fails.

links.label: SQS event source mapping for Lambda

topics.title: Removing single points of failure in storage, network and platform

blocks.body: Several SPOFs are not compute or database. They are easy to miss because the service looks managed.

blocks.title: FSx for Windows File Server
blocks.body: Single-AZ file systems have one Windows file server and storage in one AZ. FSx replaces failed components automatically, but AWS documents roughly 30 minutes of downtime during failure recovery and during the maintenance window, and in rare cases the file system is unrecoverable and must be restored from backup. Multi-AZ file systems run a Windows Server Failover Clustering pair of servers in a preferred and a standby AZ, with synchronous replication within and between AZs and automatic failover. The deployment type cannot be changed on an existing file system (Security Hub control FSx.5 states this, and AWS Backup states it cannot be changed during restore). The documented migration path is to create a new Multi-AZ file system and copy data and share configuration, for example with AWS DataSync plus Systems Manager automation, then cut clients over.

blocks.title: NAT gateways
blocks.body: A NAT gateway lives in one AZ. If it fails, or its AZ fails, instances routing through it lose internet egress. Create one NAT gateway per AZ and point each AZ's private route table at the gateway in the same AZ; this also avoids cross-AZ data charges. A single NAT instance is a SPOF you manage yourself; replace it with managed NAT gateways. Trusted Advisor has an AZ-independence check for NAT gateways.

blocks.title: Elastic Beanstalk
blocks.body: A single-instance environment still uses an Auto Scaling group, but min, max and desired are fixed at 1, so there is no redundancy or scaling. Convert to a load-balanced, scalable environment (load balancer plus Auto Scaling group spanning AZs). Default scaling triggers use outbound network traffic (scale out above 6 MB, in below 2 MB of outbound traffic per instance over five minutes), so change the trigger to a metric that reflects your load such as CPU utilization, latency or request count. Edit scaling via the environment configuration, not in the EC2 console, or Beanstalk may overwrite it. Spot instances with Capacity Rebalancing can be enabled in Beanstalk environments.

items: EFS and others: Trusted Advisor flags EFS file systems without mount target redundancy and without a backup plan. Use mount targets in each AZ used.

Self-managed databases or middleware on one EC2 instance: move to the managed Multi-AZ equivalent (RDS Multi-AZ, Aurora, ElastiCache Multi-AZ). Where a managed service is not possible, ASG min=max=1 across AZs plus replicated storage gives automatic replacement but with downtime.
Stateful web tiers: externalize session state to ElastiCache or DynamoDB so any instance can be replaced; this is a precondition for horizontal scaling and for cross-AZ failover with no user impact.
Subnet sizing: Trusted Advisor checks available IPs in subnets used by Auto Scaling; an ASG cannot launch replacements in a subnet without free IPs.

blocks.body: For 'a managed service in a single AZ' look for the option that changes the deployment mode or topology (Multi-AZ, replicas, mount targets per AZ) rather than the one that adds monitoring. When the service cannot convert in place (FSx for Windows deployment type), expect a create-new-and-migrate answer.

items: FSx for Windows storage type: you can update HDD to SSD at any time (update-file-system --storage-type SSD) but cannot switch from SSD back to HDD; throughput capacity can also be modified after creation. This is an in-place performance change, unlike the deployment type (Single-AZ to Multi-AZ), which is fixed at creation. Whether both changes can be requested in one call was not verified; do them as separate administrative actions and monitor progress with describe-file-systems.

links.label: FSx for Windows: Single-AZ vs Multi-AZ

blocks.body: Quotas turn growth into outages: a limit that was never approached at launch becomes the failure mode when usage doubles. Reliability engineering for limits has three parts: know the value and scope, alarm before exhaustion, and design so one workload cannot consume the shared pool.

rows: 1,000 default; 900 reservable because 100 stay unreserved; requests-per-second limit is 10x concurrency; new accounts can have lower values
Guarantees and caps that function; synchronous overflow is throttled
About 120,000 for most standard queues and for FIFO; standard returns OverLimit
Increase via Support request for standard
Auto Scaling health check grace period
Maximum 7 partitions per AZ; instance count limited by account limits
Quotas are expressed as concurrent vCPUs (earlier count-based quotas were migrated); the current default values were not verified in this build
30 seconds default or 10 seconds fast; cannot be changed after creation
3,000 RCU and 1,000 WCU per second; on-demand adapts to double previous peak instantly

items: Monitoring: services that publish usage metrics to CloudWatch (EC2, Elastic Load Balancing, Fargate, DynamoDB, KMS, among others) can be graphed against the quota with SERVICE_QUOTA(m1) and alarmed at a percentage such as 80 percent. In the Service Quotas console you can create the alarm directly from the quota. Fargate publishes ResourceCount in the AWS/Usage namespace with Service=Fargate, Resource=vCPU and Class=Standard/OnDemand or Standard/Spot.

Requesting increases: Service Quotas is the route; AWS advises requesting well ahead of need (the Knowledge Center suggests at least two weeks for Lambda concurrency). Some limits are Region-specific so a multi-Region DR plan needs matching quotas in the recovery Region; unchecked quota parity is a common DR failure.

Isolation: one function exhausting the account's concurrency starves others. Use reserved concurrency to protect critical functions and to cap noisy ones; split workloads across accounts when quotas are account-scoped.
Growth sizing: required Lambda concurrency is approximately average duration in seconds multiplied by requests per second (60 seconds x 20 requests per second = 1,200, per the AWS example).

blocks.body: If a stem says the workload failed 'when traffic grew' and the symptom is throttling or launch errors, the remedy is a quota increase plus an alarm, together with architecture that smooths load (queue, reserved concurrency). A quota increase alone is rarely the whole answer; an alarm alone never fixes it.

blocks.title: Scenario 1: Single-AZ web application that goes down every maintenance window
blocks.body: Requirements: survive the loss of an instance or an AZ without manual action; keep the existing PostgreSQL-compatible engine and application code; minimize operational overhead. Existing environment: one EC2 instance running the web tier and a Single-AZ RDS instance, session data stored in local memory, one NAT gateway, DNS pointing at the instance's Elastic IP. Constraints: no application rewrite, budget for a modest increase in run cost.

items: Chosen architecture: place an ALB in public subnets across at least two AZs; move the web tier into an Auto Scaling group with subnets in those AZs, ELB health check type, a grace period matched to boot time, and target tracking on CPU or request count per target; externalize session state to ElastiCache Multi-AZ; modify the RDS instance to Multi-AZ (or migrate to Aurora with a replica in a second AZ if read scaling is also wanted) and connect through RDS Proxy to shorten failover; create one NAT gateway per AZ with per-AZ route tables; point DNS at the ALB with an alias record.

Rationale: each change removes one SPOF with a managed, automatic mechanism. Multi-AZ gives a synchronous standby with automatic failover (AWS cites 60 to 120 seconds), and RDS Proxy reduces client-visible delay by keeping connections and avoiding DNS propagation issues. Shallow health checks on the ASG avoid the mass-termination risk of deep checks.

Security: security groups chain ALB to web to database; the proxy uses a Secrets Manager secret and IAM role; ElastiCache and RDS stay in private subnets; encryption settings are set at creation and must be planned.
Cost: roughly doubles database instance cost for the standby, adds ALB and extra NAT gateway hourly charges, and ElastiCache replica cost. Scaling-in at night offsets compute.

Alternatives rejected: a larger instance (still a SPOF); a read replica (asynchronous, manual promotion, not automatic HA); a second-Region warm standby with Route 53 failover (addresses Region loss, higher cost and complexity than the stated AZ-level requirement); CloudWatch auto-recovery on the single instance (handles host failure only, not AZ loss, and leaves downtime).

blocks.title: Scenario 2: Order-ingest Lambda overwhelms the database and loses orders during sales
blocks.body: Requirements: no order loss when the database or a third-party payment API is slow; protect the database from connection storms; keep API latency low. Existing environment: API Gateway invokes a Lambda function that writes to a provisioned-capacity DynamoDB table or an RDS instance and then calls a partner API synchronously. During promotions the function is throttled, the database hits its connection or write limit, and customers see errors. Constraints: minimal change to the order-handling code.

items: Chosen architecture: the API publishes the order to an SQS queue (or SNS topic fanning out to per-consumer queues if inventory, billing and notifications each react). A Lambda consumer reads from the queue with partial batch responses enabled, reserved concurrency set to the rate the database sustains, queue visibility timeout at least six times the function timeout, and a DLQ with maxReceiveCount of at least 5 and retention longer than the source queue. For RDS, connect through RDS Proxy; for DynamoDB use on-demand capacity or provisioned with auto scaling plus the queue smoothing writes. Multi-step flows with the partner API move into a Step Functions state machine with Retry (exponential backoff) and Catch to a compensation state. Alarms: DLQ depth, ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage, and a Service Quotas usage alarm for Lambda concurrency.

Rationale: the queue is durable, so spikes become backlog instead of errors; the concurrency cap converts a burst into a steady downstream rate; the DLQ isolates poison messages without blocking the queue; Step Functions replaces hidden retry logic.

Security and cost: queue encryption and least-privilege consumer role; costs are per request for SQS and per state transition for Step Functions, usually less than over-provisioning the database for peak.

Alternatives rejected: increasing database size or provisioned capacity (pays for peak all day, still synchronous); raising Lambda concurrency (makes the connection storm worse); invoking the partner API from the API tier with client retries (retries amplify load); SNS without queues (a slow subscriber gets no durable buffer).

blocks.title: Scenario 3: Spot-based queue workers that lose long jobs and a fleet that stalls at its quota
blocks.body: Requirements: process uploaded files within an agreed latency, tolerate Spot reclaims, never kill a worker mid-job when the fleet scales in, and be warned before a quota is hit. Existing environment: an ASG of one Spot instance type in two AZs polling an SQS queue, scaling on CPU, with two placement groups of identical instance types. Symptoms: capacity shortages, jobs repeating after interruptions, long jobs terminated during scale-in, and launches failing after growth.

items: Chosen architecture: convert to a mixed instances policy using attribute-based instance type selection (or a broad list of types) with the price-capacity-optimized or capacity-optimized strategy across subnets in all AZs; enable Capacity Rebalancing; keep a small On-Demand base. Scale with target tracking on backlog per instance (queue length divided by InService instances, target = acceptable latency / seconds per message). Protect a worker with instance scale-in protection (set by the worker while it holds a job) and handle Spot interruption with idempotent processing and a visibility timeout longer than the longest job, with a DLQ. Add a Service Quotas CloudWatch alarm at 80 percent for the relevant EC2 or Fargate usage metric.

Rationale: diversification addresses the true cause (a single capacity pool per AZ), not more placement groups. Scale-in protection does not stop Spot reclaim, so job idempotency and the queue's redelivery are the safety net.
Cost: Spot discount retained, On-Demand base is the reliability premium; Capacity Rebalancing briefly runs duplicate instances.

Alternatives rejected: more cluster placement groups (does not add capacity pools and can worsen insufficient-capacity errors); scaling on CPU (does not reflect queue work); termination protection or scale-in protection alone (ignored by Spot interruption); all On-Demand (reliable but defeats the cost goal).

links.label: Scaling policy based on Amazon SQS

blocks.body: Console, CLI and template steps for the most common remediations. Replace placeholders such as <account-id>, <region>, <asg-name> and <db-instance-id>. Commands change production resources: apply to a test environment first, and expect brief performance impact or a failover when modifying databases.

items: Auto Scaling health: open the Auto Scaling group, Details, Health checks, Edit; turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks and set the grace period to cover your boot and warm-up time. Confirm in Activity history that replacements occur after you stop the application on a test instance.

RDS Multi-AZ: select the DB instance, Modify, set Multi-AZ deployment, choose when to apply (immediately or maintenance window), then confirm the Multi-AZ standby shows in the console. Test with a reboot with failover in a non-production copy and watch RDS events.

RDS Proxy: create a proxy in the same VPC, select the database and a Secrets Manager secret, create or choose the IAM role, then change the application (or Lambda configuration) to use the proxy endpoint; Lambda must be attached to the VPC.
NAT: create a NAT gateway in a public subnet of each AZ, then edit each private route table so 0.0.0.0/0 targets the same-AZ gateway.

SQS and DLQ: create the DLQ first (longer retention), then set the source queue's dead-letter queue and maximum receives; add a CloudWatch alarm on the DLQ's visible messages; set the Lambda event source mapping to report batch item failures.
Quotas: Service Quotas console, choose the service and quota, Create alarm under CloudWatch alarms, pick a threshold percentage such as 80, and attach an SNS topic.

Route 53 change batch: failover alias records with Evaluate Target Health (aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --hosted-zone-id <zone-id> --change-batch file://failover.json)
CloudFormation: ASG with ELB health checks, SQS queue with DLQ, and DLQ alarm
blocks.body:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Parameters:
  Subnets:
    Type: List<AWS::EC2::Subnet::Id>
  TargetGroupArn:
    Type: String
  LaunchTemplateId:
    Type: String
Resources:
  OrdersDLQ:
    Type: AWS::SQS::Queue
    Properties:
      MessageRetentionPeriod: 1209600
  OrdersQueue:
    Type: AWS::SQS::Queue
    Properties:
      VisibilityTimeout: 180
      MessageRetentionPeriod: 345600
      RedrivePolicy:
        deadLetterTargetArn: !GetAtt OrdersDLQ.Arn
        maxReceiveCount: 5
  DlqDepthAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Properties:
      Namespace: AWS/SQS
      MetricName: ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible
      Dimensions:
        - Name: QueueName
          Value: !GetAtt OrdersDLQ.QueueName
      Statistic: Maximum
      Period: 60
      EvaluationPeriods: 1
      Threshold: 1
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold
      TreatMissingData: notBreaching
  WebAsg:
    Type: AWS::AutoScaling::AutoScalingGroup
    Properties:
      MinSize: '2'
      MaxSize: '6'
      HealthCheckType: ELB
      HealthCheckGracePeriod: 300
      VPCZoneIdentifier: !Ref Subnets
      TargetGroupARNs:
        - !Ref TargetGroupArn
      LaunchTemplate:
        LaunchTemplateId: !Ref LaunchTemplateId
        Version: '1'

items: Verify: ASG Activity history and instance health states; target group health in the console or with describe-target-health; RDS events for failover; DLQ visible-message alarm state; Route 53 health check status; CloudWatch usage metric against SERVICE_QUOTA. Do not fabricate expected outputs: record your own results in the change record.

Troubleshoot: new instances keep being replaced (grace period too short, health check path or security group blocks the load balancer, or the app needs a launch hook); group will not scale in (all instances protected, minimum reached, or suspended Terminate); messages reach the DLQ though valid (maxReceiveCount below 5, visibility timeout shorter than six times function timeout, throttled consumer); Aurora clients slow after failover (DNS cache; use RDS Proxy or the cluster endpoint with retry logic); CloudFront 502 or 504 (see load balancer and origin causes above).

links.label: Test and verify EC2 automatic recovery

items: Identify the primary requirement: availability (automatic failover), durability (no data loss), scalability, recovery in another Region, or limit avoidance.
List the mandatory constraints: minimal code change, least operational overhead, lowest cost, existing engine or protocol, RPO/RTO, data residency, no downtime window.
Locate the failing component or SPOF in the described architecture; ignore options that add capacity to the wrong place.

Eliminate distractors: manual steps, scale-up instead of redundancy, options that fix a different layer, and services that do not meet a stated constraint (for example Memcached for failover, read replicas for automatic HA).
Of the remaining options choose the managed, automatic, native feature with the least change.

rows: Managed Multi-AZ, Auto Scaling, RDS Proxy, SQS; avoid custom scripts and self-managed failover
Enable a feature (Multi-AZ, DLQ, RDS Proxy, ELB health checks) instead of rewriting
Spot with diversification, on-demand DynamoDB for spiky load, queue buffering instead of over-provisioning, snapshot restore when RTO allows
Multi-AZ synchronous replication; Aurora replicas share storage
Aurora Global Database or cross-Region replica; Route 53 failover
Automatically recover a single instance, same IP/ID
Instance scale-in protection or termination lifecycle hook; also idempotency for Spot
Quota increase plus alarm, reserved concurrency, queue buffer, on-demand capacity
RDS Proxy; avoid DNS caching dependence

items: Multi-AZ is not a read replica; read replicas are not automatic HA. Aurora Replicas are failover targets and readers at once.
ELB health checks on the ASG replace instances; EC2 checks alone do not detect a hung application.
Deep health checks on an ASG can terminate the whole fleet during a dependency outage.
Route 53 failover uses health evaluation for alias targets; weighted ALB target groups are not failover.
CloudFront origin groups retry per request (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS only); Route 53 changes DNS answers after health checks fail and TTL expires.
SQS decouples; SNS fans out; Step Functions orchestrates and retries; Lambda reserved concurrency throttles; RDS Proxy pools connections.
One NAT gateway per AZ; Single-AZ FSx for Windows cannot be converted in place; Memcached has no replication or failover.
Scale-in protection does not stop health replacement, Spot interruption or manual termination.
Partition placement groups contain hardware failures; cluster placement groups trade availability for latency; diversify instance types for capacity.

blocks.body: Two answers can look right when one fixes the symptom (bigger instance, higher timeout, manual runbook) and the other removes the cause (redundancy, automatic replacement, buffering, quota alarm). Pick the cause. When two remove the cause, pick the one with fewer moving parts and less custom code. Some questions in this area are intentionally under-specified; when ambiguity remains, choose the option that is documented AWS best practice for the named service.

items: Remove SPOFs layer by layer: instances (ASG across AZs), entry point (ALB health checks, Route 53 or CloudFront failover), data (Multi-AZ, replicas, ElastiCache Multi-AZ), egress (NAT per AZ), file storage (FSx Multi-AZ), integration (queues, DLQs, orchestration).

Self-healing needs the right detector: ELB health checks on the ASG for application failures, a grace period long enough for boot, lifecycle hooks for initialization and graceful shutdown, shallow checks for replacement decisions.

blocks.body: This lesson covers exam task 3.5, identifying cost optimization opportunities in an existing solution. 'Existing' matters: the scenarios give you a running workload plus a bill or a utilization symptom, and you decide what to change with the least disruption. Domain 3 (Continuous Improvement for Existing Solutions) is listed at 25% of scored questions for SAP-C02 in the AWS comparison page; task 3.5 is one of its tasks, and cost-driven choices also appear inside questions from other domains.

Prerequisites: EC2 instance families, Auto Scaling groups and load balancers; S3 storage classes and lifecycle rules; VPC subnets, route tables, NAT gateways and VPC endpoints; AWS Organizations with consolidated billing; basic IAM policy reading.
Objectives. After this lesson you will be able to:

items: Choose among On-Demand, Savings Plans, Reserved Instances and Spot for a described usage pattern, and explain what each commits you to.
Find over-provisioned, idle and unused resources using AWS Compute Optimizer, AWS Trusted Advisor and Cost Optimization Hub, and know each tool's data window and prerequisites.
Locate avoidable network and data transfer charges (NAT gateway processing, cross-AZ traffic, interface versus gateway endpoints, CloudFront price classes) and fix them.
Select storage and database cost levers: S3 lifecycle and Intelligent-Tiering, gp3 volumes, DynamoDB capacity mode, Aurora serverless auto-pause.
Design cost visibility and control: cost allocation tags, Cost Explorer, Data Exports (CUR 2.0), AWS Budgets with actions, CloudWatch billing alarms and Cost Anomaly Detection.

blocks.body: Services and patterns covered: Savings Plans, Reserved Instances, Spot Instances and Auto Scaling mixes, scheduled and target-tracking scaling, Instance Scheduler, Compute Optimizer, Trusted Advisor, Cost Optimization Hub, S3 storage-class and lifecycle tuning, EBS gp2 to gp3, DynamoDB and Aurora serverless cost modes, NAT gateways, VPC endpoints, CloudFront price classes, tags, Cost Explorer, Data Exports, Budgets, billing alarms, Cost Anomaly Detection.

blocks.title: The method in one line
blocks.body: Measure first, then remove waste (idle, oversized, unattached), then change architecture (serverless, managed, Graviton, endpoints), and only then commit spend (Savings Plans/RIs) to what remains. Committing before rightsizing locks in waste for one to three years.

Note the time frame: SAP-C02 is the exam in use until November 16, 2026, and the AWS comparison page says SAP-C03 begins November 17, 2026. The study material here follows the SAP-C02 task statements.

topics.title: Commitment pricing: Savings Plans and Reserved Instances

blocks.body: Both models trade a time commitment (one or three years) for a lower rate than On-Demand. They are billing constructs: they do not change how an instance runs, and they apply automatically to matching usage.

Savings Plans commit you to an amount of compute spend per hour (for example a dollar amount per hour), not to specific instances. The Savings Plans documentation says AWS offers four types: Compute, Database, EC2 Instance and SageMaker AI. You can pay for Savings Plans with All Upfront, Partial Upfront or No Upfront payment, and the rate stays the same for the term.

rows: Hourly spend on EC2, Fargate and Lambda
Any instance family, size, OS, tenancy and Region; can move EC2 to Fargate or Lambda
Hourly spend on one instance family in one Region
Size, OS and tenancy within the family
Engine, instance family, size, AZ, Region; also serverless usage
Up to 35% (Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, DocumentDB, Timestream, Neptune, Keyspaces, DMS, OpenSearch Service)
A specific instance configuration for 1 or 3 years
Modify AZ, scope, networking type and size within the family; can be sold on the RI Marketplace
A configuration that you may exchange
Exchange for another Convertible RI (different family, OS, tenancy) of equal or higher value; cannot be sold on the Marketplace

blocks.body: How Savings Plans are applied. Savings Plans apply after Reserved Instances. EC2 Instance Savings Plans are applied before Compute Savings Plans because Compute plans have broader applicability. Within that order, each plan is applied to the usage with the highest savings percentage first, until usage or the commitment runs out; the remainder bills at On-Demand rates. The benefit is computed every hour and unused commitment is not carried to the next hour. In a consolidated billing family, plans apply first to the owner account and then to others when sharing is on.

Reserved Instance scope. A regional RI does not reserve capacity but gives Availability Zone flexibility and, for Amazon Linux/Unix default-tenancy RIs, instance size flexibility within the family. A zonal RI reserves capacity in one AZ and gives no AZ or size flexibility. Only zonal RIs (or On-Demand Capacity Reservations) provide capacity assurance; Savings Plans never do. AWS notes you can still buy Capacity Reservations and pay lower prices on them with Savings Plans.

Choosing. The AWS guidance in the Knowledge Center article is: use Savings Plans where you need to change instance types or use several compute services; use RIs for stable, predictable workloads that need AZ-specific capacity or a specific configuration; mixing is a stated best practice. Convertible RIs are recommended when purchased in a payer account, when workloads are likely to change, or when you want to hedge against price drops.

Sizing a purchase. Use the Savings Plans Recommendations page in Cost Explorer. It computes, from your selected lookback period, the commitment that yields the largest estimated monthly savings given term and payment option. Compute and EC2 Instance recommendations are generated independently from the same usage, so choose one set at a time. After a purchase or expiry, recommendations take up to 24 hours to reflect it. The recommended commitment is expressed as the Savings Plans rate, not the On-Demand spend.

items: Right-size first. A plan sized to oversized instances commits you to the waste.
Commit to the steady floor of usage (the lowest hourly level that persists), not the peak. Hourly accounting means any hour with less usage than commitment wastes the difference.

Prefer Compute Savings Plans when the roadmap includes Fargate, Lambda or Graviton moves; prefer EC2 Instance Savings Plans or Standard RIs when the family and Region are certain and the extra discount matters.

Use Database Savings Plans or service-specific reserved nodes/capacity for databases; the Database Savings Plan page lists the covered services. Whether a particular service (for example MemoryDB) is covered was not confirmed in the pages read.

rows: Buying a zonal RI for flexibility
Zonal RIs give no AZ or size flexibility; regional RIs do.
Expecting a Savings Plan to guarantee capacity
Savings Plans do not provide capacity reservations.
Unused hourly commitment is lost; it does not roll over.
Buying a Compute Savings Plan and an EC2 Instance Savings Plan from the same recommendation
The two recommendation sets are independent and overlap on the same usage.

blocks.body: Keywords: 'workload may move between instance families, Regions, or to Fargate/Lambda' points to Compute Savings Plans; 'must reserve capacity in an AZ' points to a zonal RI or Capacity Reservation; 'steady baseline plus unpredictable spikes' points to a commitment for the baseline and On-Demand or Spot for the rest. 'Previous-generation' instance names in older questions do not change the pattern.

links.label: How Savings Plans apply to usage

topics.title: Spot, scaling, rightsizing and removing idle compute

blocks.body: After you know the baseline, reduce what you pay for the variable part and stop paying for compute that does no work.

Spot Instances use spare EC2 capacity at up to a 90% discount compared with On-Demand (AWS Spot pages). They suit stateless, fault-tolerant or flexible work such as big data, containers, CI/CD, HPC and test environments. The cost of the discount is interruption. A Spot Instance interruption notice arrives two minutes before interruption as an EventBridge event and in instance metadata. A rebalance recommendation signals elevated interruption risk, can arrive earlier than the two-minute notice (but not always; it can arrive together with it), and is emitted on a best-effort basis. By default Spot Instances are terminated on interruption; for time-flexible workloads you can configure stop or hibernate.

items: Design for interruption: checkpoint to S3, EFS or FSx; break work into short tasks (tasks finishing within two minutes are unaffected); drain load balancer connections on the notice.

Diversify: in Auto Scaling groups use a mixed instances policy with many instance types and all AZs. The price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy diversifies across low-priced pools optimized for capacity availability; the lowest-price strategy by default allocates across the two lowest-priced pools, which are not optimized for capacity.
Keep a floor: set an On-Demand base capacity so the minimum resources stay available when Spot capacity is unavailable; a commitment (Savings Plan or RI) can cover that floor.
Use services that handle Spot for you: EKS managed node groups replace nodes on rebalance recommendations or interruption notices; the Spot whitepaper also names other services.

blocks.label: Auto Scaling mixed instances policy (illustrative, from the documented shape)

blocks.body: Scaling policies. Target tracking keeps a metric near a target (for example 50% average CPU): it scales out when above and in when below, so you do not hold idle capacity. Scheduled scaling changes the desired capacity (and min/max) at set times for predictable load, for example up on Wednesday morning and down on Friday evening. The two can be combined: after a scheduled action runs, the scaling policy keeps adjusting within the min and max the scheduled action set. Rule of thumb: predictable pattern means scheduled actions; unpredictable means target tracking; usually both.

Rightsizing. Use measured utilization, not guesses, and check which metrics a tool actually sees: Compute Optimizer can ingest external EC2 memory utilization metrics from observability products such as Datadog and Dynatrace to generate more accurate rightsizing recommendations, and enhanced infrastructure metrics extends the history it analyzes (next topic). Whether CloudWatch agent memory metrics alone are sufficient was not verified in this build. A memory-bound fleet that is CPU-idle is a signal to change instance family (memory-optimized, smaller vCPU count), not just size. Switching to Graviton-based instances is documented as up to 40% better price-performance than comparable x86 instances for a wide variety of workloads (Graviton getting-started guide); it requires arm64-compatible software, which Compute Optimizer's Graviton view helps assess with a migration-effort column.

Turning off what is not needed. Non-production environments rarely need to run nights and weekends. AWS Instance Scheduler on AWS starts and stops EC2 and RDS instances by tag: an instance tagged Schedule with a schedule name (for example one that runs 9 to 5 on weekdays) follows that schedule. The AWS blog about RDS notes a Lambda plus EventBridge approach with tags such as StartWeekDay and StopWeekDay. Trusted Advisor has an 'Amazon EC2 Instances Stopped' check, which is a prompt to review instances left stopped and the volumes attached to them. For Aurora, auto-pause and stop/start options exist (storage topic).

Replacing idle compute with event-driven or managed services. A fleet that polls an S3 bucket or queue on a timer is paying for idle time. S3 event notifications, SQS or EventBridge triggering Lambda, or Fargate tasks launched on a schedule, bill for work done. Check duration, memory and ephemeral storage limits before choosing Lambda; those limits were not re-verified in this build.

rows: Queue workers, batch, CI, stateless containers on On-Demand
Spot with checkpointing; mixed instances group with On-Demand base
Change instance family after checking Compute Optimizer
Instance Scheduler or scheduled stop/start; consider Aurora auto-pause
Event-driven Lambda or Fargate on schedule

blocks.body: A trap: Spot for a stateful, single-instance, latency-critical component. Another: choosing 'reserve everything' for a spiky workload. For 'steady baseline plus bursts' the best pattern is commitment for the baseline, scaling for the burst, Spot where the work tolerates interruption. If the question stresses 'minimal operational overhead' prefer managed Spot handling (EKS managed node groups, Auto Scaling mixed groups) over custom scripts.

links.label: Scheduled scaling for EC2 Auto Scaling

topics.title: Finding waste: Compute Optimizer, Trusted Advisor and Cost Optimization Hub

blocks.body: Three AWS tools produce recommendations, and the exam expects you to match the symptom to the tool.

AWS Compute Optimizer analyzes configuration and utilization metrics and reports whether resources are optimal, over-provisioned or under-provisioned, with projected utilization for each alternative. Supported resources include EC2 instances, EC2 Auto Scaling groups, EBS volumes, Lambda functions (memory size), ECS services on Fargate, commercial software licenses (SQL Server on EC2) and Aurora/RDS databases. It also produces idle-resource recommendations for resources such as EC2, Auto Scaling groups, EBS, ECS on Fargate, RDS/Aurora, NAT Gateway, DynamoDB provisioned tables, ElastiCache, MemoryDB, DocumentDB, WorkSpaces and SageMaker endpoints; recommendations are refreshed daily.

rows: Extends analysis to up to 93 days (three months); activate at organization, account or resource level; applies to EC2, Auto Scaling groups and RDS
14, 32 or 93 days (93 requires enhanced infrastructure metrics); preference changes show within 24 hours
Idle checks for EBS and NAT Gateway
Attachment status analyzed over a 32-day lookback
14 days default (32 selectable); WorkSpaces use 63 days of connection activity
Max savings, Balanced, Default, Max performance, or custom CPU and memory headroom
'CPU architecture preference' set to Graviton (aws-arm64) compares price with the current instance; also shows migration effort

blocks.body: When the workload has a monthly or quarterly peak, a 14-day window can understate the true peak and recommend a size that is too small. The remedy documented by AWS is enhanced infrastructure metrics (paid) for the longer window. Compute Optimizer must be opted in before it produces recommendations (the documentation refers to 'after you opt in'); organization-wide opt-in mechanics for Compute Optimizer itself were not verified in this build.

AWS Trusted Advisor inspects the environment and reports across categories including cost optimization. Cost checks relevant to this task include low-utilization EC2 instances, idle load balancers, unassociated Elastic IP addresses, underutilized EBS volumes, idle RDS DB instances, stopped EC2 instances and S3 or ECR resources without lifecycle policies. Trusted Advisor also gives Savings Plans and Reserved Instance recommendations. Support-plan dependence matters: the Trusted Advisor documentation says checks are available with Business Support+, Enterprise Support or Unified Operations plans, and that with Basic Support the console gives the Service limits category and selected security and fault tolerance checks. The same pages announce that Developer Support and Business Support are being discontinued on January 1, 2027, so verify the current plan matrix before relying on a cost check in a design.

Cost Optimization Hub consolidates and prioritizes recommendations from multiple AWS services (for example rightsizing from Compute Optimizer and Savings Plans from Billing and Cost Management) across accounts and Regions, estimates savings using your own discounts, and deduplicates overlapping savings (an idle recommendation and a rightsizing recommendation on the same resource count only the larger saving). In an organization, you opt in from the management account (for the management account only, or for it and all member accounts) or through a delegated administrator. Its recommendations can also be exported through Data Exports.

rows: Per-resource sizing with utilization projections, Graviton view, Lambda memory, EBS and Fargate sizing
Broad checklist of idle or unused items (idle ELB, unassociated EIP) and service limits
