items: Treat 'low utilization' as a question, not an instruction: AWS notes that low-use instances may be test or batch resources, in which case resizing or auto-shutdown is better than termination.
Act on idle and unattached resources first (cheapest, lowest risk), then rightsizing, then commitments.
Do not delete before checking tags and owners; this is where cost allocation tags pay off.

blocks.body: If a question says analysis must cover memory or a long cycle (month-end, quarterly), the answer involves memory metrics reaching Compute Optimizer and/or enhanced infrastructure metrics, not 'wait and observe in CloudWatch'. If it says 'identify unused resources across all accounts with the least effort', think Trusted Advisor organizational view or Cost Optimization Hub rather than custom scripts.
Storage and databases are billed on capacity, requests and sometimes retrieval, so the main levers are the right class, the right capacity mode and lifecycle rules that stop old data accumulating.

Amazon S3. Pick the class from the access pattern. For unknown or changing patterns use S3 Intelligent-Tiering: objects not accessed for 30 consecutive days move to the Infrequent Access tier (documented as 40% savings) and after 90 days to Archive Instant Access (68%); opt-in Archive and Deep Archive Access tiers exist; there are no retrieval charges; there is a small per-object monitoring and automation charge. Objects smaller than 128 KB are not eligible for auto-tiering, are billed at Frequent Access rates and carry no monitoring charge. Since the 2021 change, S3 Intelligent-Tiering has no minimum storage duration.

rows: 30 days (objects cannot be transitioned there before 30 days)
Lifecycle does not transition objects smaller than 128 KB from Standard or Standard-IA unless you add an object-size filter
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval and Glacier Flexible Retrieval
Early delete or transition incurs prorated charge for the remaining days
180 days; default retrieval 12 hours per CDK reference text
40 KB metadata per object (32 KB at Deep Archive rate, 8 KB at Standard rate)
Monitoring charge for objects of 128 KB or more

items: Lifecycle rules move objects only down the storage-class waterfall, never back up. Transitions and expirations are asynchronous, but billing changes apply as soon as the rule is satisfied (except transitions to Intelligent-Tiering).

Add a rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads. Parts of uploads that are never completed are billed until removed; S3 Storage Lens flags buckets with incomplete multipart uploads older than 7 days and buckets lacking such rules.
Expire noncurrent versions in versioned buckets; Storage Lens also flags buckets accumulating noncurrent versions.

Many small objects: consolidate before storing (batching, larger Firehose buffers) because per-object overheads, minimum sizes and request charges favor fewer, larger objects; this reasoning was not tied to a single AWS page in this build.
Use S3 Storage Lens cost-optimization metrics and S3 Storage Class Analysis (a paid, per-object feature) to find cold buckets and decide transitions.

blocks.body: Analytics. Replacing a persistent cluster that serves intermittent SQL with Athena over S3 shifts cost from always-on nodes to per-query scanning, so reduce scanned data: partition by time prefix, store in a columnar compressed format such as Parquet, and prune with partition predicates. The 'Parquet' and partition advice is general practice and was not verified against a specific page here. For VPC flow logs, Cost and Usage data and similar log analytics the same approach applies.

Amazon EBS. gp3 is listed at $0.08 per GiB-month versus $0.10 for gp2 (US East example), about 20% lower, with 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s included and separate pricing above those. AWS states gp3 is always cheaper than gp2 at the same performance levels. Do not blindly migrate volumes that rely on gp2 burst or high baselines without checking required IOPS. Compute Optimizer and Trusted Advisor flag unattached and underutilized volumes, and an unattached volume should be snapshotted and deleted rather than left billing.

Amazon DynamoDB. On-demand mode is pay per request and, per the Serverless Applications Lens text, is the default and recommended option for most workloads; it suits unpredictable traffic and scales to zero when not used. Provisioned mode bills for provisioned capacity whether consumed or not, so it is more cost-effective when utilization is decent and predictable; add auto scaling for gradual change and reserved capacity for steady baselines (provisioned mode and the Standard table class only; a one-year term saves up to 54% and a three-year term, offered in select Regions, up to 77%). You can switch from provisioned to on-demand up to four times in a rolling 24 hours. The table class (Standard versus Standard-IA) changes storage versus request pricing, so IA suits tables with large, rarely read data. Database Savings Plans now also list DynamoDB. A DAX or ElastiCache layer cuts read cost only if reads are repetitive; whether a cache is worthwhile depends on read pattern, which the question stem must state.

Aurora serverless. The Aurora documentation now calls this Aurora serverless (the capacity model formerly written as Serverless v2). Capacity is measured in ACUs and scales with load. In recent Aurora MySQL and PostgreSQL versions the minimum can be 0 ACUs, enabling automatic pause after an idle period (between 300 seconds and 86,400 seconds; default 300 seconds); setting minimum capacity to 0.5 or more disables auto-pause. For older versions the lowest minimum is 0.5 ACU. The whole cluster can also be stopped and started for dev/test, in all Aurora serverless versions. Database Savings Plans cover serverless usage. Aurora Serverless v1 behavior was not researched; treat the question's version wording carefully.

rows: Constant high load where provisioned plus a commitment is cheaper
Mostly tiny objects, or data known to be cold on day one

blocks.body: Look for 'unpredictable access' (Intelligent-Tiering), 'rarely accessed, retrieval within hours' (Glacier Flexible or Deep Archive with retrieval time stated), 'incomplete uploads' (abort rule), and RTO/retrieval-time limits that can rule out Deep Archive. 'Idle most of the day' databases point to Aurora serverless or scheduled stop/start.

links.label: S3 Intelligent-Tiering update (small and short-lived objects)

blocks.body: Data transfer is often the least visible line item. Learn where charges arise and which architectural change removes them.

NAT gateways. You pay for each hour the gateway is provisioned (partial hours billed as full hours) and for each gigabyte processed, regardless of the traffic's source or destination, plus standard data transfer charges. The VPC pricing page example for US East (Ohio) lists $0.045 per hour and $0.045 per GB processed; prices change, so treat these as an example only. AWS cost guidance for NAT gateways: keep resources in the same Availability Zone as the NAT gateway they use (same-AZ transfer is free) or create a NAT gateway per AZ, and replace NAT traffic to AWS services with VPC endpoints.

Gateway endpoints exist for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB. They add a route-table target, need no internet gateway or NAT device, and have no additional charge (no hourly or data processing charge). Limits: they do not allow access from on-premises networks, from peered VPCs in other Regions, or through a transit gateway. For those cases use an interface endpoint, which costs extra.

Interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) create elastic network interfaces in your subnets. They are billed per hour for each AZ in which the endpoint is provisioned and per GB processed (first-PB tier example: $0.01 per GB). They reach over 140 services and support on-premises connectivity over Direct Connect or VPN. The Knowledge Center advice: S3 or DynamoDB traffic in the same Region goes through a gateway endpoint; S3 or DynamoDB traffic to a different Region uses an interface endpoint; other AWS services that support interface endpoints (ECR, SQS, CloudWatch and similar) can use them so the traffic no longer pays NAT processing, though you pay the endpoint's own charges. Break-even depends on volume: at low volumes, the endpoint's hourly cost per AZ can exceed the NAT savings, so verify this against the pricing pages.

rows: NAT gateway to S3 or DynamoDB
Gateway endpoint to S3 or DynamoDB
Interface endpoint to S3 or DynamoDB or other service

blocks.body: Between Availability Zones in the same Region, data transfer is charged on both the sending and receiving side (the CUR usage type is Region-DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes; some services have in-Region traffic at no cost, so check each service). The EKS cost guidance quotes $0.01/GB each way. Same-AZ traffic over private IPs is free. Keep high-volume chatty tiers AZ-local where resilience allows (AZ affinity, topology-aware routing, RDS read replicas in the caller's AZ), but never trade away the multi-AZ design the availability requirement needs. RDS Multi-AZ synchronous replication does not itself incur additional data transfer charges according to the AWS architecture blog, though consumers outside the primary's AZ do.

Other levers. Amazon CloudFront price classes let you exclude more expensive edge locations to reduce delivery prices, at the cost of possibly higher latency for viewers outside the chosen locations; CloudFront may still occasionally serve from an excluded location and charges the rate of the cheapest location in the class. Exact transfer-out rates per class must be taken from the CloudFront pricing page, which was not read in this build. Transit Gateway adds hourly attachment charges and per-GB data processing; VPC peering within an AZ is free and cross-AZ peering traffic is charged.

items: To find the source of NAT traffic use the documented approach of identifying traffic sources and CloudWatch NAT gateway metrics before changing anything.

One NAT gateway per AZ is both a resilience best practice (a NAT gateway lives in one AZ) and a data transfer cost control; the hourly cost of extra gateways is offset by avoided cross-AZ transfer when traffic is large, but the net depends on volume.
Trusted Advisor can check NAT gateway AZ independence.

blocks.body: If most NAT traffic is to S3 in the same Region, answer gateway endpoint (free). If clients are on premises or in another Region, a gateway endpoint will not work; use an interface endpoint. When a question says 'reduce cost without reducing availability', cross-AZ avoidance means affinity and per-AZ NAT, not single-AZ deployment.

topics.title: Cost allocation: tags, Cost Explorer and Data Exports

blocks.body: You cannot optimize what you cannot attribute. This cluster covers how spend is tagged, explored and exported at fine granularity.

Cost allocation tags. A three-step process: attach tags to resources, activate the tag keys in the Billing and Cost Management console under Cost allocation tags, then filter or group by them. After applying user-defined tags it can take up to 24 hours for tag keys to appear on the Cost allocation tags page and up to another 24 hours to activate. Activating a key affects all values for that key. AWS-generated tags such as createdBy are activated by the management account owner and then are activated for all member accounts, and are visible only in the Billing and Cost Management console and reports. With AWS Organizations, activation is done in the payer (management) account.

Enforcing tags. AWS Organizations tag policies define allowed tag keys, capitalization and values (for example CostCenter limited to listed values) and can optionally prevent noncompliant operations for chosen resource types; without enforcement they only report noncompliance. Tag policies evaluate only tags defined in the policy; they do not by themselves force a resource to be tagged at all. Requiring a tag at launch needs a different control (for example a service control policy condition or provisioning guardrails); that mechanism was not researched in this build.

Cost Explorer. By default it provides the current month plus up to 13 months at daily and monthly granularity (another page says up to 14 months). Management-account opt-ins add multi-year data (up to 38 months, monthly), hourly granularity for all services for the past 14 days, EC2 instance resource-level hourly data and resource-level daily data for selected services, for the last 14 days. Changes can take up to 48 hours to appear and you cannot change the preferences again for 48 hours. Hourly data is useful for sizing Savings Plans or RI purchases because commitments are hourly. Cost Explorer also hosts Savings Plans and RI recommendations, utilization and coverage reports.

AWS Data Exports and CUR 2.0. The Cost and Usage Report is the most detailed source of cost data. AWS Data Exports creates recurring exports to Amazon S3 (usable with Athena, Redshift or QuickSight) of several tables: CUR 2.0 (the recommended table), Cost Optimization Hub recommendations, FOCUS 1.2 and 1.0 with AWS columns, and carbon emissions, plus a cost and usage dashboard and the legacy CUR. CUR 2.0 has a fixed schema, nested key-value columns (such as resource_tags, cost_category, product, discount) and extra account-name columns. You can select columns and filter rows with basic SQL from the CLI or SDK. Delivery can take up to 24 hours to start and then refreshes at least daily. The page lists a limit of 5 exports for the CUR 2.0 table (per table; the page does not state whether the quota is adjustable). Resource IDs and hourly granularity are options that matter for investigation: the Cloud Intelligence Dashboards FAQ configuration uses Include Resource IDs, Hourly, Parquet, Athena integration.

items: Investigating at line-item level: query CUR 2.0 in Athena, group by line_item_usage_type and product to find the usage type driving growth (for example the Region-DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes usage type identifies inter-AZ transfer; read the exact NAT and other usage-type strings from your own data).
Use resource-level data in Cost Explorer for the last 14 days when you need to find which instance, function or bucket caused a spike and CUR is not yet set up.
Cost categories and tags let you group spend by business unit; unallocated spend is a symptom of poor tag coverage.

rows: Which resource ID or usage type explains a spike, at hourly granularity?
CUR 2.0 data export in S3 queried with Athena
Activated cost allocation tags or cost categories
Organizations tag policies with enforcement for supported resource types

blocks.body: Common distractor: 'tag the resources' as the full answer. A tag is not visible in billing until the key is activated. Another: choosing CloudWatch metrics to attribute cost; metrics do not carry price. For 'granular, queryable, retained cost data', the answer is Data Exports (CUR 2.0) to S3 with Athena.

links.label: Exploring more data for advanced cost analysis

topics.title: Cost alerting: Budgets, billing alarms and anomaly detection

blocks.body: Three alerting tools answer different questions. Choose by what you need to detect and whether the response must be automatic.

AWS Budgets tracks cost, usage, Savings Plans or RI utilization and coverage against a threshold, with alerts on actual or forecasted values. Budget types are cost, usage, RI utilization and RI coverage, and Savings Plans utilization/coverage/cost budgets can also be set (templates or custom). Budgets can track blended, unblended, net unblended, amortized and net amortized costs, include or exclude discounts, refunds, support fees and taxes, use fixed, variable or custom periods, and notify by email or Amazon SNS. Budget information is updated up to three times a day, typically 8 to 12 hours apart, so Budgets is not a real-time control.

Budget actions run on your behalf when a threshold is crossed, automatically or after approval. Available actions: apply an IAM policy, apply a service control policy (SCP), or target specific EC2 or RDS instances in the account. From the management account you can apply an SCP to another account, but you cannot target EC2 or RDS instances in another account. Budgets needs an IAM role it can assume (trust principal budgets.amazonaws.com) with permissions for the actions you configure. Action notifications require a recipient. An example is a variable-target monthly budget with an 80% threshold that attaches a deny policy blocking further provisioning.

CloudWatch billing alarms use the EstimatedCharges metric in the AWS/Billing namespace. You must enable billing alerts (in the management/payer account when using consolidated billing) and create the alarm in US East (N. Virginia), because billing metric data is stored there and represents worldwide charges. The metric is in USD. The documented console example uses statistic Maximum, a 6-hour period, a static threshold and 1 out of 1 datapoints. The alarm can notify through SNS. A Knowledge Center article shows metric math to turn the cumulative metric into a daily estimate. Dimension ServiceName narrows to one service.

AWS Cost Anomaly Detection uses monitors to detect unusual spend and alert subscriptions to notify. Monitor dimensions: AWS services, linked accounts, cost categories and cost allocation tags. AWS managed monitors track up to the top 5,000 values of a dimension independently and add new values automatically; customer managed monitors evaluate chosen values in aggregate (up to 10 member accounts or tag values). Alert frequency can be individual (immediate, delivered through SNS), daily summary or weekly summary (email, up to 10 recipients). Thresholds can be an absolute dollar amount, a percentage, or both combined. A launch blog describes a default daily summary for anomalies that exceed 40% and $100 of expected spend. Anomalies below the threshold remain visible in the console and API.

rows: Alert at 80% of a monthly cost target, including forecast
Automatically deny new provisioning or stop instances at a threshold
AWS Budgets action (IAM policy, SCP, EC2/RDS target)
Know when Savings Plans/RI utilization drops below 80%
Simple cumulative-spend alarm wired into existing CloudWatch/SNS pipelines
Detect an unexpected spike with no fixed threshold, per service/account/tag

blocks.body: Designing alarms from expected usage. Base thresholds on the baseline you measured: set a cost budget a little above forecast with alerts at several percentages (for example 80%, 100% and a forecasted 100%), a usage budget for quota-sensitive services, utilization budgets on commitments, and anomaly monitors on the dimensions your tags define (per team, per account). Review thresholds as usage grows.

'Automatically prevent further spend' is Budgets actions, not an alarm or anomaly subscription (those notify). 'Unexpected spike with no known threshold' is Cost Anomaly Detection. 'Billing alarm' questions usually hide the Region (us-east-1) or the prerequisite (billing alerts enabled).

links.label: Managing your costs with AWS Budgets
Getting started with Cost Anomaly Detection

blocks.body: Scenario 1: baseline plus nightly peak. A retailer runs an order-processing tier in an Auto Scaling group on On-Demand instances. Utilization history shows a steady floor of about 20 instances all day, peaks to 60 for four hours at night, and an SQS-fed image-resizing tier that tolerates restarts. Compute Optimizer marks the order tier over-provisioned on CPU but memory-bound. Requirements: lower cost, no availability loss, minimal code change.

items: Chosen architecture: first move the order tier to the recommended memory-optimized family or size after reviewing Compute Optimizer projected utilization (with enhanced infrastructure metrics if the peak is monthly). Then buy a Compute Savings Plan sized to the new steady floor (from the Cost Explorer recommendation after the change). Add scheduled scaling for the nightly rise and a target-tracking policy for variance. Move the resizing workers to a mixed instances group with a small On-Demand base and Spot for the rest using price-capacity-optimized and many instance types, with idempotent SQS processing.
Rationale: rightsizing precedes commitment, the commitment covers only the persistent floor, predictable peaks use scheduled capacity, and interruptible queue work uses Spot.
Security: no new data paths; the launch template's IAM role is unchanged. Cost: savings come from three separate mechanisms that can be measured separately in Cost Explorer.

Alternatives rejected: three-year zonal Standard RIs for all 60 instances (locks in peak capacity for most of the day and gives up flexibility); Spot for the order tier (stateful order handling cannot tolerate two-minute interruption without redesign); a larger commitment sized on the first recommendation before rightsizing (commits to waste).

blocks.body: Scenario 2: private subnets and a large NAT bill. A fleet in private subnets across three AZs writes about 100 MB per second of logs per instance to S3 and pulls container images from ECR. The only NAT gateway sits in one AZ. The bill shows high NAT gateway data processing and inter-AZ data transfer. An EMR cluster reads the logs later. Requirements: reduce network cost, keep multi-AZ resilience, keep traffic off the public internet.

items: Chosen architecture: add an S3 gateway endpoint and a DynamoDB gateway endpoint (if used) to the private route tables, so S3 traffic bypasses the NAT gateway at no charge; add interface endpoints for ECR (and the services whose volume justifies the per-AZ hourly cost); deploy one NAT gateway per AZ with each AZ's route table pointing to its local gateway for the residual internet traffic; apply an S3 lifecycle rule to move old logs to a colder class and expire them, plus an abort-incomplete-multipart rule.
Rationale: gateway endpoints remove both hourly and per-GB charges for S3; per-AZ NAT removes cross-AZ NAT transfer and removes a single-AZ failure point.
Security: endpoint policies and bucket policies can restrict access to the endpoint; no internet gateway route is required for S3.
Cost trade-off: each extra NAT gateway and interface endpoint adds hourly charges, justified only if avoided transfer and processing exceed them; measure with Cost Explorer or CUR before and after.

Alternatives rejected: a bigger or second NAT gateway in the same AZ (does not remove processing charges); an S3 interface endpoint for in-VPC EC2 (costs hourly plus per GB when a free gateway endpoint works); moving instances to a single AZ (violates resilience).

blocks.body: Scenario 3: an unexplained bill increase across an organization. A company with 40 accounts in AWS Organizations sees spend rise 30% with no owner identified. Teams use inconsistent tag keys. Finance wants monthly chargeback and engineering wants alerts before surprises.

items: Chosen architecture: define tag policies (CostCenter, Project, Environment) at the organization root with allowed values and enforcement for key resource types; activate those keys in the management account; enable Cost Explorer hourly and resource-level data where investigation is needed; create a CUR 2.0 data export with resource IDs to S3 and query with Athena; create an AWS managed Cost Anomaly Detection monitor for services, one additional AWS managed monitor for linked accounts (the quota is one additional AWS managed monitor beyond the services monitor per management account), and a customer managed monitor for the tag values, with SNS-backed individual alerts for large anomalies and a daily summary otherwise; set per-account cost budgets with 80% actual and 100% forecasted alerts and a budget action (deny policy) for sandbox accounts; opt in to Cost Optimization Hub in the management account for prioritized savings.
Rationale: attribution first, then alerts tuned to each owner, then automation where the blast radius is acceptable (sandbox).
Security: the Budgets execution role needs the narrow permissions documented for the chosen actions; export bucket policy grants only the billing service.
Alternatives rejected: relying on resource names; a single organization-wide threshold (misses small-account anomalies); applying SCP budget actions to production accounts without an approval step.

blocks.body: All identifiers are placeholders. Command and field names for Budgets, Cost Explorer, Compute Optimizer and S3 lifecycle are composed from the API field names seen in AWS documentation; confirm exact flags with the CLI help before use.

1. Billing alarm (console path from documentation): in the management/payer account, enable Receive billing alerts under Billing preferences, switch to US East (N. Virginia), create an alarm on Billing > Total Estimated Charge (EstimatedCharges) with statistic Maximum, period 6 hours, static threshold, 1 of 1 datapoints, and an SNS action.

blocks.body: Cost optimization of an existing solution is a sequence: gain visibility, remove waste, reduce unit cost, and commit last.

items: Key concepts: Savings Plans commit to hourly spend, RIs to configurations; Spot trades interruption for up to 90% savings; Compute Optimizer, Trusted Advisor and Cost Optimization Hub find savings; gateway endpoints are free; NAT gateways charge per hour and per GB; tags must be activated; Budgets can act, alarms and anomaly detection notify.

Decision rules: rightsize before committing; commit to the floor; Compute Savings Plan for flexibility, EC2 Instance Savings Plan or Standard RI for the larger discount with fixed family; schedule predictable load, track unpredictable load; use Spot only where interruption is safe; use lifecycle plus abort-multipart plus noncurrent expiry on S3; gp3 over gp2 when performance allows.

blocks.body: Task 4.1 of the SAP-C02 exam (Domain 4, Accelerate Workload Migration and Modernization) asks you to select which existing workloads and processes are worth migrating, and in what order. Before anything is moved you must know what exists (discovery), how it behaves (utilization and dependencies), what it costs today versus on AWS (total cost of ownership, TCO), and what to do with each application (the 7 Rs). The exam tests whether you can pick the right data-collection tool for a described estate and the right planning decision for a described business goal.

Prerequisites: working knowledge of Amazon EC2 and Amazon EBS sizing, Amazon VPC connectivity to on premises, AWS IAM users and managed policies, Amazon S3 and Amazon Athena basics, and the high-level meaning of rehost versus replatform. The follow-on lesson (migration approach) covers the tools that actually move data; this lesson stops at the decision of what, why and when.
You will be able to:

items: Choose between the Application Discovery Service Agentless Collector, the Discovery Agent, and file-based import for a described estate (VMware, physical, Hyper-V, mixed), based on the data each can and cannot collect.
Explain how dependency data is collected, visualized (Migration Hub network diagram) and queried (Athena data exploration), and why collection should run for weeks.
Use Migration Evaluator (and, where relevant, AWS Transform assessments) to build a directional TCO business case from agentless collection or existing inventory exports.
Assign each application one of the 7 Rs using discovery evidence such as utilization, connections and licensing, and justify the choice.
Prioritize applications and build migration waves, including how to pick a low-risk first workload.

Recognise service-availability changes (Migration Hub, Application Discovery Service and Strategy Recommendations are closed to new customers; AWS Transform is the pointed-to successor) and how they affect answer choices.

blocks.body: Services and patterns covered: AWS Application Discovery Service (ADS) with its Agentless Collector and Discovery Agent; ADS file import; ADS data exploration in Amazon Athena; AWS Migration Hub (home Region, application grouping, network diagram, status tracking); Migration Hub Strategy Recommendations; AWS Migration Evaluator; AWS Transform assessments and its discovery tool; Migration Readiness Assessment (MRA); portfolio assessment stages; the 7 Rs; wave planning.

blocks.title: Why it matters on the exam
blocks.body: Domain 4 carries 20% of the scored SAP-C02 content in the published exam guide (weighting recalled from the exam guide; not verified against an AWS documentation page). Task 4.1 questions are usually short scenarios with four near-identical tool combinations; the winning answer is determined by one or two data requirements (running processes, network dependencies, physical servers, no agent allowed, CMDB export only, cheapest). Learn the capability matrix, not marketing descriptions.

Many question stems use older names such as 'Agentless Discovery Connector' or 'AWS Server Migration Service'. The Discovery Connector reached end of support on November 17, 2025 and was replaced by the Agentless Collector; treat the old name as the current Agentless Collector when reasoning about capabilities.

blocks.body: A portfolio assessment is the process of gathering application, infrastructure and business-context data to discover, analyze and plan the move of an entire IT estate. AWS Prescriptive Guidance describes it as progressive: you do not need all data up front, and assessment continues for the whole program rather than being a one-off task. The assessment stages map to the AWS phases of migration (assess, mobilize, migrate and modernize).

Detailed assessment and target design for applications that can move soon to build experience and the landing zone

blocks.body: The timeline is described by AWS as indicative; the stages remain valid outside AWS's own framework. In the first stage the goal is a directional business case using benchmarks; later stages replace assumptions with facts such as actual utilization, dependency data, compliance requirements, key dates (data center exit, license renewals) and team readiness.

blocks.title: Migration Readiness Assessment (MRA)
blocks.body: The MRA is the readiness part of the assess phase. It is based on the AWS Cloud Adoption Framework and answers three questions: where is the organization in its cloud journey, what are its strengths and weaknesses, and what action plan closes the gaps. It is a process (typically a workshop led by AWS or a partner), not a discovery tool: it does not inventory servers. One AWS whitepaper describes eight evaluated dimensions while the Prescriptive Guidance describes the six CAF perspectives (business, people, governance, platform, security, operations); do not rely on a count for the exam.

The Migration Acceleration Program (MAP) wraps this in three phases: assess (MRA, rapid discovery, high-level TCO), mobilize (landing zone, operating model, detailed plan and business case), and migrate and modernize (migration factory working a prioritized backlog).

items: Assessment feeds other workstreams: landing-zone design needs portfolio data, security needs compliance requirements, and the migration factory needs dependency-based waves.
Wave sizes are bounded by the capacity of the migration workstream and the complexity, dependencies and business constraints (budget, deadlines, resource availability).

Discovery tooling is useful across the whole project lifecycle; the Prescriptive Guidance suggests budgeting for at least six months if funds are limited, because lacking tooling typically increases manual effort.

blocks.body: When a question asks what to do FIRST in a migration program, think assess-phase outputs: readiness assessment, rapid discovery and directional business case. Detailed target design and replication tooling come later.

AWS Application Discovery Service collects usage and configuration data about on-premises servers and databases. All discovered data is stored in your AWS Migration Hub home Region, which you must set before any discovery, and ADS agents, collectors and imports work only in that home Region. Note the availability change described at the end of this topic.
ADS offers three collection methods. In addition, third-party discovery tools from AWS Partner Network (APN) partners can write to ADS through its public API:

items: Agentless Collector: an OVA virtual machine deployed in VMware vCenter. It is modular: a VMware module, a database and analytics module (integrated with AWS DMS for target recommendations), and a network-traffic module for Windows or Linux servers.

Discovery Agent: software installed on each Windows or Linux server (physical, VM or EC2). It needs root privileges, registers with the home Region and polls about every 15 seconds, uploading every 15 minutes over TLS.
File-based import: CSV (Migration Hub import template) or RVTools export uploaded to S3 and imported; a single snapshot, no continuous collection.

rows: Database inventory (Oracle, SQL Server, MySQL, PostgreSQL)

blocks.title: The decision rule
blocks.body: Need running processes, per-process dependency detail, time-series export or Athena analysis, or the estate has physical servers: Discovery Agent. Fast, low-touch inventory and sizing of a VMware estate with no agent installs: Agentless Collector. Existing data in a CMDB or RVTools: import. Combine them: the docs state you can run both on VMware VMs simultaneously, installing agents only where deeper detail is needed.

A nuance: the comparison table lists TCP network connections for the Agentless Collector, but an older overview sentence in the ADS API reference says the collector does not collect network dependency data, and the network diagram prerequisite still names the Discovery Agent. The collector's network-traffic module was added later. Exam questions written against the older material expect: agentless = no processes and no dependency detail; agent = processes and network connections.

Discovery Agent specifics: the host needs an IAM user whose access keys are supplied at install time with the AWSApplicationDiscoveryAgentAccess managed policy (grants arsenal:RegisterOnPremisesAgent and mgh:GetHomeRegion); outbound TCP 443 to the regional arsenal endpoint (no inbound ports); S3 access in the home Region for auto-upgrade; Linux hosts need at least Intel i686 (P6) architecture; agents auto-upgrade by default. Supported OS lists include Amazon Linux, Ubuntu, RHEL, CentOS, SUSE and Windows Server 2003 R2 SP2 through 2022.

rows: No (only imported servers is documented as adjustable)

blocks.body: Common mistakes: installing 1,000 agents when you only need sizing (the 1,000 active-agent quota and operational effort argue for agentless plus selective agents); expecting the Agentless Collector to see inside a VM; forgetting the home Region; assuming import gives dependency data; using the legacy Discovery Connector, which stopped being supported on November 17, 2025 (historic data remains available).

blocks.title: Availability change
blocks.body: The ADS user guide states that ADS is no longer open to new customers and points to AWS Transform for similar capabilities; existing customers continue as normal. The exam (and the mapped question bank) was written before this, so answers still use ADS, but your design advice today should mention AWS Transform's discovery tool for new accounts.

blocks.body: Dependencies decide what must move together. Servers that talk frequently, share databases or have latency-sensitive calls should migrate in the same wave (a move group) so users do not see cross-site latency or broken connections. ADS provides two analysis routes for connection data: visual (the Migration Hub network diagram) and analytical (data exploration in Athena).

Network diagram. Migration Hub's network diagram visualizes a server's connections so you can group servers into applications. Its documented prerequisites: the Discovery Agent must run on all servers you want mapped; AWS recommends collecting server and network connection data for two to six weeks to capture month-end or year-end patterns; the IAM policy may need the `discovery:GetNetworkConnectionGraph` action. Documented limits: data ingestion stops after 180 days, and the diagram can show up to 1,500 server nodes.

Data exploration in Athena. Turning on Continuous Export (console or CLI) streams Discovery Agent data through Amazon Data Firehose into an S3 bucket and Glue-cataloged tables that Athena can query; the account then uses the service-linked role `AWSServiceRoleForApplicationDiscoveryServiceContinuousExport`, and an IAM role named `AWSApplicationDiscoveryServiceFirehose`, which you create with the `AWSDiscoveryContinuousExportFirehosePolicy` policy attached, lets Firehose write to S3. This route is for agent data (the comparison table shows export to Athena as Discovery Agent only). Athena and S3 usage is billed to your account even though Migration Hub itself is free.

items: Typical queries: frequency of communication between server pairs, process-level inbound and outbound connections, listening ports, per-server performance.
Place servers that talk frequently with large data exchange in the same move group.
Shared servers that serve multiple applications create many-to-many mapping; use tags and Athena rather than a single application grouping.

topics.title: Migration Evaluator and TCO business cases

blocks.body: Total cost of ownership (TCO) compares the all-in cost of running workloads on premises (hardware, licenses, facilities, staff over the asset's useful life) with running them on AWS. Migration Evaluator (formerly TSO Logic) is a complimentary service that builds a data-driven, directional business case: it analyzes server configuration, utilization, annual operating cost and bring-your-own-license eligibility, statistically models utilization, matches each workload to EC2 and EBS placements, and outputs a comparison of current state against several future-state configurations.

Inputs. Migration Evaluator accepts (a) its own agentless collector, a Windows Server VM deployed in your network using VMware vSphere, WMI (Hyper-V and Windows), SNMP and T-SQL, with read-only access and no agents on servers; (b) exports from third-party inventory or monitoring tools or a CMDB, with benchmarks applied where utilization is missing; or (c) data already collected by ADS, which can be exported to a business case so the same collector serves dependency mapping and the business case. An AWS blog notes a default collection period of 7 days for assessments.

blocks.title: Quick Insights versus Business Case
blocks.body: Quick Insights shows projected EC2, EBS and operating-system license costs on a one-year, no-upfront basis. The fuller Business Case (requested through your solution architect) adds cost models, SQL Server license analysis and match exports, and can model all public Regions except mainland China.

AWS Transform assessments. AWS Transform generates a TCO business case from a server inventory in minutes and supports refinement by natural-language chat; its discovery tool (self-contained, no cloud connectivity needed) finds servers, databases and network dependencies, and ingestion formats include RVTools, Migration Evaluator and other exports. The Migration Evaluator FAQ itself now points to AWS Transform assessment as AWS's agentic approach. Treat it as the forward-looking equivalent when an option names it.

AWS Pricing Calculator estimates the cost of a specific architecture on AWS; it is not a discovery tool and does not read your on-premises estate. For a CMDB export and a cost-effective business case, the answer pattern is to upload the export to Migration Evaluator rather than deploy new collection.

topics.title: Migration Hub, Strategy Recommendations and availability changes

blocks.body: AWS Migration Hub is the single console that aggregates discovery data and migration status. In your home Region you view discovered servers, obtain EC2 recommendations, visualize network connections, group servers into applications, and track the status of each application's migration. Migration tools such as Application Migration Service, AWS DMS and partner tools send status updates to Migration Hub, but only after you connect (authorize) the tool; without that, Migration Hub does not track the migration.

items: Home Region: choose before any write action; stores discovery and migration-tracking data for migrations into any target Region, giving one view across many Regions.

Applications: logical groups of servers (and other resources); the unit of status tracking. Servers shared by several applications are handled with tags. Quota: 400 servers per application, 1,000 applications per account.
Updates: tool-sent progress events; there can be a delay of up to five minutes before the first update appears.
You can migrate with or without discovery first; if no discovery was done, Migration Hub adds servers to the list automatically when updates arrive.
Hub data can be exported for use in Application Migration Service, carrying application and wave groupings and recommended instance types.

blocks.body: Migration Hub Strategy Recommendations analyzes server inventory, runtime environments and (for Microsoft IIS and Java Tomcat/JBoss applications) application binaries, optionally source code and databases, against your business goals. It recommends an R strategy for each application (rehost, replatform, refactor) with tools, and reports anti-patterns (incompatibilities) such as unsupported components. Registration of servers with ADS is a prerequisite. Its agentless collector deploys as a VM in vCenter (or an AMI for EC2). The on-premises variant is described as being in KTLO (keep the lights on) mode: existing customers can continue to use it.

blocks.body: The Migration Hub documentation (including Strategy Recommendations pages) states: 'AWS Migration Hub is no longer open to new customers as of November 7, 2025' and refers to AWS Transform for similar capabilities. ADS carries the same kind of notice. Exam questions that predate the change still treat the services as the correct answer; do not reject an option solely because of availability unless the stem mentions a new account or a current-state design.

topics.title: Prioritisation, the 7 Rs and wave planning

blocks.body: The 7 Rs are the migration strategies AWS Prescriptive Guidance defines: retire, retain, rehost, relocate, repurchase, replatform, refactor or re-architect. Common strategies for large migrations are rehost, replatform, relocate and retire. Refactoring is not recommended for large migrations because modernizing during migration is the most complex and costly route; the recommendation is to rehost, relocate or replatform first and modernize afterwards.

blocks.body: Using discovery data in the decision: utilization numbers identify retire candidates; connection data identifies retain/hybrid dependencies; database inventory (engine and schema complexity from the Agentless Collector database module, with DMS target recommendations) separates homogeneous from heterogeneous database paths and license-reduction opportunities; Strategy Recommendations adds anti-pattern detection.

Prioritization and waves. AWS guidance builds a migration candidate queue from explicit prioritization criteria that reflect business priority, application owner input, infrastructure and complexity, so owners can see why applications are ordered as they are. Wave plans start with less complex applications, apply lessons from earlier waves, and move to increasingly complex ones. Best practices: prioritize noncritical, simple applications in the first two waves; distribute criticality and complexity evenly; keep waves small (the portfolio analysis guidance cites a typical length of 4-8 weeks, while the wave planning guide recommends 6-10 weeks and states there is no predefined duration); keep enough candidates in the queue to replace applications that slip; account for landing-zone, security and skills readiness; and honour key dates such as a data center contract expiry.

Build the inventory and enrich with owner, criticality and function.
Collect utilization and dependency data for weeks.
Assign an R to each application and note blockers.
Group applications by dependency into move groups.
Sequence waves: simple, low-criticality first; hardest later; reserve backlog.
Per wave: detailed assessment, readiness, infrastructure build and test, data transfer, cutover, closure and lessons learned.

blocks.title: Picking a first workload
blocks.body: A good first workload builds skills and minimises business risk while being achievable fast: low criticality, few dependencies, a simple strategy (typically rehost or relocate), a well understood owner, and not tied to an unresolved compliance or specialised hardware question. A mission-critical, tightly coupled system is a poor first move even if it has the biggest savings.

When the stem has a hard deadline (for example data center contract expiry in under six months) and a wish to build skills with minimal risk, choose a low-complexity workload rehosted first, not a full refactor and not the most critical system. When the stem says 'reduce licensing and operational overhead' for databases, think replatform to managed or open-source engines, with DMS/SCT covering heterogeneous cases.

Scenario 1: Acquired company, undocumented data center. A company acquires a business whose data center has about 1,500 servers: roughly 1,100 VMware VMs and 400 physical Linux and Windows machines, with stale documentation, Oracle and PostgreSQL databases, and a board that wants a business case within six weeks. Constraint: the acquired IT staff will allow a read-only appliance in vCenter but are wary of installing software on 400 physical hosts. Chosen architecture: deploy the ADS Agentless Collector in vCenter for the VMware estate (profile, utilization and database inventory), set a Migration Hub home Region, import the physical servers from the acquired company's CMDB export using the import template, and send the combined inventory to Migration Evaluator for a directional business case (complimentary). After the board approves, install Discovery Agents on the application tiers that matter (physical servers and any VMs whose processes or dependencies are unclear) and collect 2-6 weeks of connections for the network diagram and Athena. Security: agent IAM user limited to AWSApplicationDiscoveryAgentAccess, outbound 443 only. Cost: collectors and Migration Hub are free to use; pay for S3 and Athena. Rejected: agents on all 1,500 hosts up front (effort, 1,000 active-agent quota), a manual spreadsheet (no utilization), Pricing Calculator alone (no discovery).

Scenario 2: Choosing the first wave. A retailer must exit a leased data center in 8 months, has no AWS migration experience, and wants to avoid customer-facing outages. Discovery shows: a point-of-sale back end (high criticality, 40 dependencies), an internal reporting tool (low criticality, three servers, one database), a dormant promotion site (3% average CPU, no inbound connections for 120 days), and a mainframe batch job. Decision: retire the dormant site, retain the mainframe job until a separate assessment, and use the reporting tool as the first rehosted workload to exercise landing zone, replication and cutover runbooks. Wave 2 adds similarly simple internal applications; the point-of-sale system is scheduled in a later wave after its dependencies are grouped and tested. Rationale: first wave builds skills, minimises risk and fits the deadline; AWS guidance supports noncritical simple applications in the first two waves and retire based on utilization and connection history. Alternatives rejected: starting with POS (risk), refactoring the reporting tool (slower, not needed for the deadline).

Scenario 3: Cost-justify without new tooling. A manufacturer has a CMDB export with server specs and 30-day average utilization for 600 Windows and Linux servers on Hyper-V, and wants a credible savings figure including existing SQL Server licenses within two weeks, with no agents allowed on production. Choice: upload the CMDB export to Migration Evaluator and request a Business Case modelling BYOL; if utilization is incomplete, the service applies benchmarks and can additionally use its read-only collector. Cost: complimentary. Security: collector uses read-only WMI/SNMP access; data encrypted in transit and at rest. Rejected: Agentless Collector (VMware only, wrong hypervisor), Discovery Agent (agents prohibited), Strategy Recommendations (wrong question), AWS Pricing Calculator (needs a target architecture, does not discover). Residual risk: dependency data is absent, so the business case is directional and wave grouping waits for another source.

Task 4.2 asks you to pick the optimal migration approach for an existing workload. Discovery feeds the strategy decision. AWS Application Discovery Service identifies servers, VMs and network dependencies in on-premises data centers. It has three collection methods: the Agentless Collector (an OVA virtual machine installed in VMware vCenter that gathers server profile, utilization, database metadata and network traffic data without touching each host), the Application Discovery Agent installed on individual hosts (richer data: running processes, performance, resource use and network dependencies), and AWS Partner Network (APN) solutions that write to the service API. The API reference states that only agent-based discovery collects network dependency information, whereas the Agentless Collector page lists a network-traffic module; for the exam, treat agent-based discovery as the safe answer for network dependency mapping, and verify the current collector capability before designing for it. The collector's database and analytics module integrates with AWS DMS to produce target recommendations.

topics.title: Server rehost: AWS Transform MGN and VM Import/Export

blocks.body: AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) is the primary rehost tool. The current documentation brands it AWS Transform MGN; this lesson uses MGN for both names. You install the AWS Replication Agent on each source server (Linux or Windows; physical, virtual or another cloud). The agent continuously replicates block-level data to lightweight replication servers (EC2 instances) in a staging area subnet that MGN creates and manages from your replication settings template. When you launch a test or cutover instance, MGN converts the replicated disks so the server boots and runs natively on EC2, and you then decommission the source.

items: Initialize the service and create the replication settings template (staging subnet, instance type, EBS encryption, security groups).

Launch cutover instances at the planned time. MGN first deletes any prior test instance and launches an instance reflecting the latest replicated state; replication continues afterwards into the staging area, not into the cutover instance.
Finalize the cutover, then decommission the source and optionally modernize.

VM Import/Export is the simpler alternative when you have a VM image rather than a running server. It imports image files to create EC2 instances or AMIs (and exports back). Supported formats: OVA, stream-optimized VMDK created by the OVF export process, fixed and dynamic VHD/VHDX, and raw. Windows and Linux are supported. VMs produced by physical-to-virtual (P2V) conversion are not supported. You upload the image to S3 and use a service role. It is a point-in-time copy: there is no continuous replication, so the source keeps changing until you cut over, and any gap means downtime or manual re-sync.

topics.title: Database migration: AWS DMS, DMS Schema Conversion and AWS SCT

blocks.body: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) moves data between databases. A replication instance (or a serverless replication) runs tasks that read from a source endpoint and write to a target endpoint. A task has one of three migration types: full-load (one-time copy), cdc (ongoing changes only) and full-load-and-cdc (initial copy, then continuous replication). Full load plus CDC is the standard pattern for near-zero downtime: the source stays live, DMS applies changes until the databases converge, and you cut the application over in a short window.

rows: Reads the source transaction log with engine-specific APIs. Oracle: LogMiner or binary reader, requires supplemental logging. MySQL: requires row-level binary logging. SQL Server: MS-Replication or MS-CDC.
Not real-time. Latency varies with source workload, network, replication instance resources and target ingest; there is no latency SLA.
Specify a native start point (for example a MySQL binlog file and position) or a time, so CDC begins where a prior bulk load or snapshot ended.
Views migrate only with full-load-only tasks; CDC tasks migrate tables only.
Remove triggers on the target during CDC (MySQL guidance).

Full LOB mode migrates everything but piece by piece and can be slow. Limited LOB mode needs a maximum size (up to 102,400 KB) and truncates larger LOBs with a warning. Inline LOB mode (full-load only) sends small LOBs with the row.
Either the source or the target must be on an AWS service (for example, RDS or EC2); on-premises to on-premises migration is not supported.

Replication instance always lives in a VPC. Its security group needs egress to the endpoints' DB ports (default egress is all). Endpoint security groups must allow ingress from the instance. Cross-VPC needs peering or Transit Gateway; on-premises sources need VPN or Direct Connect routing.
Evaluates a task configuration for unsupported data types and missing prerequisites before it runs; AWS calls it a best practice.

Capacity measured in DMS capacity units (DCU), 2 GB RAM each, valid values 1 to 384 (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 192, 256, 384); scales between a minimum and maximum DCU. Increase the minimum DCU if scaling cannot keep up with spikes; for steady predictable load a standard replication instance is more stable.

For like-for-like engines (for example MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB to RDS, Aurora or DocumentDB) DMS runs serverless and uses native tools (for example pg_dump and pg_restore) and logical replication for CDC.

blocks.body: Schema conversion is separate from data movement. When the engine changes (heterogeneous migration, such as Oracle to PostgreSQL), the schema, stored procedures and code must be converted first. Two tools do this. The AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) is a downloadable application that supports more sources and targets and produces an assessment report listing what converts automatically and what needs manual work; it can also scan application SQL. DMS Schema Conversion is the in-console alternative. Its sources include Oracle, SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Db2 and SAP ASE, and AWS SCT supports more sources and targets. Supported conversion paths depend on the source (for example, Oracle or SQL Server to Aurora PostgreSQL, RDS for PostgreSQL, Aurora MySQL or RDS for MySQL, and Oracle to Amazon Redshift), so check the current path table before relying on a specific pair. The typical heterogeneous flow is: assess with SCT or DMS Schema Conversion, convert and apply the schema to the target, run DMS full-load-and-cdc, validate, cut over.

For very large data warehouses, SCT data extraction agents (installed on Linux, running in parallel) extract, optimize and upload data to Amazon Redshift, and for large datasets the extracted files can be shipped on Snowball. Because Snowball Edge is closed to new customers, a current design would use DataSync, Direct Connect or Data Transfer Terminal for the bulk copy and keep DMS for CDC.

blocks.body: Choosing DMS alone for an engine change (it does not convert code), expecting CDC to be real-time, forgetting to enable log settings on the source, truncating LOBs unknowingly with default limited LOB settings, and sizing the replication instance too small for many parallel tables.

'Same engine, one-time, can tolerate downtime' may be native dump and restore or a snapshot. 'Cannot use public internet' adds Direct Connect or VPN plus TLS on endpoints. topics.title: Online data transfer: DataSync, Transfer Acceleration and Transfer Family

blocks.body: AWS DataSync is a managed online transfer service for file and object data. A location describes a source or destination, a task joins two locations with options, and a task execution is one run. For on-premises sources you deploy an agent (a VM on VMware ESXi, Linux KVM, Nutanix AHV or Hyper-V, or an EC2 instance for in-VPC or other-cloud storage). Between AWS storage services in the same account no agent is needed. Data between locations is encrypted with mutual TLS 1.3; reads and writes use the storage system's own protocol security.

rows: Re-running a task copies only files added or changed since the last run
cron or rate expressions; minimum interval 1 hour (cannot be faster)
Always checks during transfer; optional end-of-transfer verification of transferred data or the entire dataset (checksum and metadata comparison)

Enhanced mode: virtually unlimited objects per execution, prepares, transfers and verifies in parallel and verifies each object as transferred. Basic mode: 50 million items per execution between self-managed and AWS storage, 25 million between AWS storage services, sequential phases
Include and exclude filters, or a manifest listing exactly what to copy

VPC (PrivateLink) service endpoint keeps agent-to-service traffic in your VPC, reachable over Direct Connect or VPN; agent needs TCP 1024-1064 (control) and 443 (data plane) to the endpoint; each task uses four IP addresses for execution endpoints
Per-GB fee for data transferred; Enhanced mode tasks also pay a per-task-execution fee; inter-Region copies are billed as data transfer out from the source Region
Tasks per account per Region: 100, adjustable. DataSync does not support Kerberos with NFS file servers

blocks.title: DataSync versus a gateway
blocks.body: DataSync is a bulk and scheduled mover. After the copy the application keeps using its own storage. Storage Gateway is a long-lived front end that applications mount. If the question says 'migrate and then retire the NFS/SMB server', think DataSync; 'applications keep writing through a local cache to S3', think S3 File Gateway.

S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads and downloads between a distant client and an S3 bucket by entering the AWS network at the nearest CloudFront edge location and using an optimized path to the bucket. Requirements: virtual-hosted-style requests, a DNS-compliant bucket name without periods, acceleration enabled on the bucket (it can take up to 20 minutes to take effect), and use of the bucket-name.s3-accelerate.amazonaws.com endpoint. It carries additional data transfer charges, you are charged only when it can potentially improve performance, it does not support cross-Region CopyObject, and AWS networking guidance says benefits are minimal for data under about 1 GB. It helps most for large objects over long distances on a fast internet connection. It is a client-side acceleration feature, not a managed migration workflow with scheduling, filtering or verification.

AWS Transfer Family provides managed SFTP, FTPS, FTP and AS2 endpoints in front of S3 or EFS, so partners keep their existing clients while the data lands in AWS. Authentication can be service managed, Microsoft Active Directory, or a custom identity provider through API Gateway and Lambda. Endpoint type determines network behavior:

rows: Elastic IPs (AWS-owned or your own BYOIP), unchanging
Internet and VPC-connected networks; security groups and NACLs
Within the VPC and over Direct Connect or VPN

blocks.body: Many exam options pair 'S3 Transfer Acceleration' with a recurring on-premises file sync; reject it, because it has no agent, schedule or verification. Choose Transfer Acceleration for geographically dispersed users uploading to one bucket. Choose Transfer Family when the requirement is to keep an SFTP/FTPS interface with fixed IPs that partners allow-list.

topics.title: Hybrid file access and physical transfer: Storage Gateway, Snow family, Data Transfer Terminal

blocks.body: AWS Storage Gateway connects on-premises applications to cloud storage through a local appliance (a VM on VMware, Hyper-V, Linux KVM or Nutanix, a hardware appliance, or an EC2 instance). Gateway types:

rows: S3 objects, with local cache (up to 64 TB of recently used data per AWS blog)
Database dumps and backups, archive with lifecycle tiering, data-lake ingest, apps that cannot call S3
Cached volumes (data in S3, hot subset local) or stored volumes (all data local, async snapshots as EBS snapshots)
Block storage and backup; stored volumes can be recovered to EC2

No longer available to new customers

blocks.body: S3 File Gateway nuance: objects written through the gateway become native S3 objects. If other writers (the S3 console, CLI or another gateway) change the bucket, the gateway's view is stale until the RefreshCache operation lists the bucket and runs HEAD on each object. RefreshCache time grows with object count, and a file share supports two concurrent refreshes; splitting prefixes across multiple shares reduces it. Not needed if only the gateway writes.

Physical transfer. AWS Snowball Edge is no longer available to new customers (effective November 7, 2025); existing customers are unaffected. AWS will no longer offer any Snow Family devices for new customers to order. AWS directs new customers to DataSync for online transfers, AWS Data Transfer Terminal for secure physical transfers and AWS Partner solutions, with Outposts for edge compute. Data Transfer Terminal is a physical location where you bring your own storage devices and upload at high throughput to endpoints such as S3 or EFS; the connection does not provide default encryption, so you must encrypt the data yourself.

Judging online versus offline is arithmetic on bandwidth. For example (own arithmetic, not from AWS docs): 100 TB over a fully utilised 1 Gbps link is about 8 x 10^14 bits divided by 10^9 bits per second, roughly 9.3 days, and real throughput is lower. Also check whether the link is shared with production traffic. If the network can finish within the project deadline, AWS states its customers strongly prefer online migration.

DataSync (agent), over Direct Connect or VPN with a VPC endpoint if private
Apps need SMB/NFS access to S3 with caching

The exam logic is 'bandwidth cannot meet the deadline, so ship data physically, then use CDC or DataSync for the delta'. Keep that logic and substitute current services only if the answers allow.

topics.title: Network path and DNS cutover: Direct Connect, Site-to-Site VPN, Route 53

blocks.body: Replication and cutover depend on the network. Direct Connect (DX) is a private dedicated link; Site-to-Site VPN is encrypted IPsec over the internet. They are often combined, with VPN as quick start or backup.

rows: Can often be provisioned faster, hours to days if a partner already has a port
Several weeks to months if new; days if your equipment is already in the DX location
Separate devices in more than one location; designed for 99.99 percent SLA when requirements are met
Connections in multiple locations; 99.9 percent SLA
Separate devices in one location; no SLA
Standard tunnel up to 1.25 Gbps and 140,000 packets per second (not adjustable); large-bandwidth tunnel up to 5 Gbps; each connection has two tunnels
On a transit gateway, ECMP across multiple tunnels requires dynamic (BGP) routing, not static

blocks.body: Route 53 supports DNS-based cutover. Weighted records shift a percentage of traffic from the old endpoint to the new one, so you can move 10 percent, observe, and continue. DNS caching controls how fast clients move: lower the TTL ahead of the change (AWS suggests 60 to 300 seconds for production endpoints; records tied to health checks should use 60 seconds or less), and remember that long-lived connections and some resolvers ignore TTL. All weighted records of the same name and type share one TTL value. For weighted alias records to ELB, the load balancer's own 60 second TTL applies. A quick all-at-once switch is simplest but exposes every user if the new environment fails under load.

blocks.title: Plan the TTL before cutover day
blocks.body: Lowering TTL on cutover day does nothing for clients that cached the old record for the previous TTL. Reduce it days earlier, then raise it again after the migration is stable.

If the stem says the migration must start this week and no DX exists, the answer is VPN (or an existing partner hosted DX), not a new dedicated DX. If 'consistent throughput' and 'weeks of lead time' are given, DX is correct. If a single VPN is saturated, aggregate with ECMP on a transit gateway or use larger tunnels.

topics.title: Securing migration tools and choosing a governance model

blocks.body: Security applies at four layers: network path, encryption, permissions and identity. Network: use private connectivity (DX or VPN) and PrivateLink where available; MGN replication encrypts data with TLS 1.2 end to end; DataSync uses mutual TLS 1.3 between locations; DMS endpoints can use SSL/TLS. Encryption at rest: choose a KMS key in the MGN replication settings (a customer managed key is needed if you must share the resulting snapshots or AMIs with other accounts, and its key policy must allow those accounts); DMS uses KMS for intermediate storage. Permissions: each tool uses service roles (MGN replication servers get an instance profile with a managed policy; DMS requires fixed-name roles; VM Import/Export needs a service role). Scope trust policies with aws:SourceAccount or aws:SourceArn.

rows: Need a real AD in AWS: trusts, Group Policy, schema extensions, RDS and FSx for Windows integration, many users
Standard Edition up to 30,000 objects, Enterprise Edition up to 500,000; can be shared across accounts; AWS suggests it for more than 5,000 users or when trusts with on-premises are needed
Only need to let on-premises AD users sign in to AWS apps and join EC2 to the existing domain
Proxy only; no directory data cached or replicated; uses your AD policies; cannot be shared across accounts; Small and Large sizes
Low-scale basic AD compatibility (up to 5,000 users, Samba 4)
No longer open to new customers; AWS recommends Managed AD or AD Connector instead. Small supports up to 500 users and Large up to 5,000. IAM Identity Center does not support Simple AD

blocks.body: IAM Identity Center is the workforce single sign-on layer. It can use its own store, an external SAML 2.0 identity provider with SCIM provisioning, or Active Directory through Directory Service (AWS Managed Microsoft AD, a trust to a self-managed domain, or AD Connector). It syncs users, groups and memberships, not passwords. For migrations it removes per-account IAM users for the migration team.

Governance for the landing zone. AWS Control Tower sets up a multi-account landing zone using Organizations, Service Catalog and IAM Identity Center. It uses SCPs for preventive controls and AWS Config for detective controls, creates log archive and audit accounts, provisions accounts through Account Factory, and can enroll existing accounts into an OU without changing their VPC configuration. Customizations for AWS Control Tower (CfCT) add templates and SCPs. SCPs in AWS Organizations set the maximum available permissions for IAM users and roles in member accounts; they never grant permissions, they do not affect the management account or service-linked roles, and they need all features enabled. Attach them to OUs rather than individual accounts where possible.

blocks.title: Migration governance pattern
blocks.body: Land migrated workloads in dedicated accounts under OUs with SCPs that restrict Regions and services, centralize CloudTrail and Config in the log archive and audit accounts, and use IAM Identity Center permission sets for the migration team. Share the Managed AD directory with workload accounts instead of building one per account.

'Without replicating directory data to AWS' or 'use the existing AD policies' points to AD Connector. 'Trust relationships, RDS Windows authentication, more than 5,000 users' points to AWS Managed Microsoft AD. 'Prevent any account in the OU from using unapproved Regions' is an SCP, not an IAM policy. 'Set up a secure multi-account environment quickly with guardrails' is Control Tower.

blocks.body: Scenario 1: rehost a 300-server data center exit in 6 months. Requirements: no application changes, cutover per application with under 1 hour of downtime, mixed physical and VMware Windows and Linux servers, existing 1 Gbps Direct Connect. Constraints: security forbids public data paths; the migration team uses corporate AD. Existing environment: on-premises AD, no AWS landing zone. Architecture: build a Control Tower landing zone first; create a workload account per application group under an OU with SCPs limiting Regions; deploy MGN with a dedicated staging subnet per account, reached over the Direct Connect private VIF (TCP 1500 to the staging subnet and 443 to the MGN endpoint); customer managed KMS key for EBS; IAM Identity Center connected to AD for the team. Waves of servers are tested at least two weeks before cutover and cut over with post-launch actions installing the SSM agent. Security: TLS 1.2 end to end, no public IPs on replication servers. Cost: MGN is free for 90 days of replication per server, so wave scheduling avoids paying hourly fees; staging EC2 and EBS are the main cost. Alternatives rejected: VM Import/Export (point-in-time, no physical support, long outage), refactor (violates no changes and does not scale), agentless vCenter replication (not available for new deployments).

Scenario 2: Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL with a 15-minute outage limit. Requirements: 4 TB OLTP database, PL/SQL packages, application SQL embedded in code, AWS target in another account, link by VPN. Chosen architecture: run SCT or DMS Schema Conversion to assess and convert schema and code, with the assessment report guiding manual rework; create DMS replication instance in the target account VPC with TLS endpoints; run a premigration assessment; full-load-and-cdc task with Oracle supplemental logging enabled; validate data; lower application DNS TTL days ahead; at cutover stop writes, wait for CDC to drain, repoint using Route 53 weighted shift. Rationale: engine change needs schema conversion plus continuous replication. Security: TLS on endpoints, KMS key, dms-vpc-role with SourceAccount condition, source credentials in Secrets Manager. Cost: replication instance sized for full-load parallelism and reduced afterwards; serverless is an option if load is spiky. Rejected: native dump and restore (outage proportional to size and engine mismatch), DMS without schema conversion (does not convert code), Snowball seed (optional only if the VPN cannot move 4 TB in time; Snowball Edge not available to new customers).

Scenario 3: 80 TB of NFS file data plus an SFTP partner feed. Requirements: copy 80 TB from NAS to S3 and EFS over an existing 10 Gbps Direct Connect, then keep changes synced until cutover; partners push files via SFTP and allow-list the endpoint IP. Architecture: DataSync agent VMs (more than one if throughput requires) with a VPC endpoint over DX; Enhanced or Basic mode chosen by object count (Basic is limited to 50 million items per execution on self-managed to AWS, so split by directory with filters if needed); an initial full pass, then scheduled incremental runs at no faster than hourly, then a final run after the freeze; verification enabled. Transfer Family on a VPC internet-facing endpoint with Elastic IPs (BYOIP if partners already trust those addresses) writes to S3. Rationale: DataSync gives scheduling, incremental copy, and integrity verification; Transfer Family preserves the SFTP contract. Cost: per-GB DataSync fee; Transfer Family hourly endpoint fee (not verified in this build). Rejected: S3 File Gateway (permanent front end not needed), Transfer Acceleration (distance not the bottleneck and no scheduling), Snowball (not available to new customers and bandwidth is sufficient).
