blocks.title: Misconceptions
blocks.body: DMS does not convert stored procedures. Transfer Acceleration is not a migration service. SCPs do not grant permissions. Increasing Direct Connect redundancy needs separate devices and locations, not just more ports. CDC has no latency SLA.

Task 4.3 ("Determine a new architecture for existing workloads") sits in the Migration and Modernization domain. You are given a workload that already exists, usually on premises or on self-managed servers, and you must pick the target AWS compute, container, storage and database services. The exam rarely asks for feature trivia. It asks you to match stated constraints (minimal changes, least operational overhead, high availability, a protocol such as iSCSI or MongoDB compatibility) to the one service whose design fits.

items: Prerequisites: VPC basics (subnets, route tables, security groups), the 7 Rs of migration (rehost, replatform, refactor and so on), IAM roles, and Multi-AZ versus Multi-Region concepts.

Services covered: Amazon EC2, AWS Elastic Beanstalk, AWS Lambda; Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS, AWS Fargate, Amazon ECR, Amazon ECS Anywhere; Amazon EBS, Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx, Amazon S3, AWS Storage Gateway (Volume Gateway); Amazon RDS, Amazon Aurora, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon DocumentDB, Amazon ElastiCache, Amazon OpenSearch Service; plus the supporting edge, load-balancing, and event-driven services that appear in target designs (Amazon CloudFront, Elastic Load Balancing (ELB), Amazon S3 event notifications, AWS Transfer Family, AWS Step Functions, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and Amazon Data Firehose, AWS IoT Core, Amazon API Gateway, Amazon SES).

blocks.body: Objectives. By the end of this lesson:

items: You will be able to select a compute platform (EC2, Elastic Beanstalk, Lambda) from stated constraints such as runtime length, operational effort and code change tolerance.
You will be able to choose between ECS, EKS, Fargate, App Runner (closed to new customers), and ECS Anywhere for a containerized or hybrid workload.
You will be able to match a storage requirement (block, shared file, SMB/Windows, object, iSCSI from on premises) to EBS, EFS, FSx, S3 or Storage Gateway.
You will be able to choose a target database (RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, DocumentDB, OpenSearch, ElastiCache) and its high-availability configuration.
You will be able to externalize state so a stateful web tier can scale horizontally behind a load balancer.
You will be able to eliminate distractors by identifying the primary requirement and mandatory constraints in a migration scenario.

blocks.title: Why it matters on the exam
blocks.body: This lesson maps to the task statement's four skills: selecting the compute platform, the container hosting platform, the storage service and the database platform. It is a 'recognize the right service' task, so many mapped questions also draw on application-integration and serverless reasoning that is developed further in the Modernization lesson (task 4.4). The exam guide domain weighting is not reproduced here because it is not part of the AWS service documentation this lesson draws on; check the official exam guide.

topics.title: Compute platform: EC2, Elastic Beanstalk and Lambda

blocks.body: Amazon EC2 gives you virtual servers you manage: operating system, patching, scaling policy and application install. It is the lowest-friction target for a rehost or a replatform where the application expects a server. Elastic Beanstalk is a platform-as-a-service layer: you upload application code and Beanstalk provisions and manages the underlying EC2 resources. AWS Lambda runs code per event with no servers to manage.

Elastic Beanstalk environment tiers. The documentation defines a web server tier (an application on EC2 serving HTTP requests), a worker tier (a backend on EC2 that pulls tasks from an Amazon SQS queue) and a cluster tier (containers on Amazon EKS). A worker tier is the Beanstalk answer for background tasks such as report generation or sending email: messages from the SQS queue are delivered by HTTP POST to a configurable local URL, and Beanstalk creates the queue if you do not supply one. Both single-instance and load-balanced, auto-scaled worker environments are possible.

rows: EC2 (with Auto Scaling and a load balancer)
OS, patching, runtime, scaling policy, AMIs
Rehost/replatform of server-based apps; custom OS or software; licensed software tied to instances
Highest operational overhead of the three; you design Multi-AZ yourself
Application code and configuration; Beanstalk handles provisioning of the underlying resources
Lift-and-shift of conventional web apps (for example .NET or Java) with minimal re-architecture and little infrastructure effort
It still runs on EC2 underneath; not event-driven; less control than raw EC2
Event-driven or short-lived work, spiky or unpredictable load
Execution time limits and a 3-second default timeout (see below); stateless; may need refactoring

blocks.body: Lambda limits to remember. The function timeout defaults to 3 seconds and can be raised in 1-second increments to a maximum of 900 seconds (15 minutes). The documentation notes a higher 5,400-second (90-minute) ceiling for functions that use Lambda Managed Instances, but only for asynchronous invocations and event source mapping invocations (excluding Amazon MQ and Amazon DocumentDB), so do not assume it applies to an ordinary function. Ephemeral storage in /tmp defaults to 512 MB and can be configured between 512 MB and 10,240 MB in 1-MB increments. The pages reviewed for this lesson do not state whether these quotas can be raised beyond those figures, so check the Lambda quotas documentation before assuming they can.

items: Choose Lambda when the work is event driven, finishes inside the timeout and can be stateless.
If a stem describes a process that runs longer than 15 minutes per item, a standard Lambda function is eliminated; look for a container task (ECS on Fargate) or an EC2-based option instead.
Choose Elastic Beanstalk when the requirement is 'move a standard web app with least infrastructure management and minimal code change'.
Choose plain EC2 when the application needs OS-level control, specific instance types, or software that cannot be containerized or deployed through a platform.

blocks.body: Phrases such as 'minimal changes to the application' push toward rehost on EC2 or Elastic Beanstalk. 'Least operational overhead' pushes toward Beanstalk, Fargate or Lambda. Always check the runtime length before picking Lambda.

topics.title: Container hosting: ECS, EKS, Fargate, ECR and hybrid options

blocks.body: AWS separates container decisions into layers: capacity (where containers run), orchestration (how they are scheduled), and vertical solutions (opinionated services for teams with little container or infrastructure experience). The decision guide lists AWS Fargate, Amazon EC2 and AWS Outposts as capacity; Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS and Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS as orchestration; AWS App Runner, Lambda, Lightsail and AWS Batch as vertical solutions; Amazon ECR as the supporting registry; and Amazon ECS Anywhere, Amazon EKS Anywhere and Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes for on-premises flexibility.

rows: Fully managed container orchestrator with no control plane, add-ons or nodes for you to manage
You want the simplest AWS-native orchestration; an easy lift for apps that run on VMs
Two launch types: EC2 (container instances run the ECS agent) and Fargate
Serverless compute for containers; no servers or clusters to manage
Least operational overhead for containers; per-task isolation; no node patching
Priced per second (one-minute minimum) for vCPU and memory; works with ECS and EKS
Kubernetes is the required interface, existing Kubernetes skills or manifests, or platform-team standards
Optimized for teams with central platform teams who keep clusters up to date with Kubernetes versions
Run containerized web apps and APIs from an image or source repository, with load balancing and TLS built in
Fastest path to a running HTTPS endpoint
Closed to new customers (from April 30, 2026); AWS recommends Amazon ECS Express Mode instead
Register on-premises servers or VMs as external instances in an ECS cluster
Containers must keep running on premises while using the ECS control plane
One activation key can register 1 to 1,000 machines; you install the open-source ECS agent with the key and Region

blocks.body: ECS launch types. With the EC2 launch type you own the container instances, which means patching, capacity and AMIs. With Fargate you define the task and AWS supplies the compute. For a team replatforming a three-tier web app into containers that wants a managed database and little undifferentiated effort, ECS on Fargate in front of an Application Load Balancer, with the database on RDS Multi-AZ or Aurora, is the usual answer.

EKS managed node groups and custom AMIs. EKS managed node groups can use an EC2 launch template, and the launch template may specify a custom AMI. Documented considerations: do not set instanceTypes, diskSize or remoteAccess in the node group configuration when using a launch template (set them in the template); the instance role and subnets can only be set on the node group; EC2 Spot market options in a launch template are not supported for managed node groups; updating to a new launch template version recycles all nodes. With a custom AMI, EKS does not merge user data, so you must supply the bootstrap commands for nodes to join the cluster. A node group also cannot be switched from the EKS-optimized AMI to a custom AMI in place; you create a new node group. Choose this path when a security or compliance baseline requires a hardened corporate AMI but you still want node groups managed by EKS.

Amazon ECR is the private registry for images. Lifecycle policies are rules that expire or archive unused images by age or count; images expire within 24 hours after they meet the criteria, and policies only act in the Region where they were created, so with replication enabled you create a lifecycle policy in each destination Region and account.

items: Event-driven, long-running processing (for example 25 minutes per file): Lambda's standard 15-minute maximum rules it out; trigger an ECS task on Fargate from the S3 event (via EventBridge) instead.
Hybrid: ECS Anywhere keeps workloads on premises under an ECS control plane; the mapped scenarios on hybrid container capacity point here rather than to rebuilding on EKS.
Common mistake: choosing EKS because 'containers' appear in the stem. EKS is justified by Kubernetes, not by containers in general.

blocks.body: ECS for simplicity, EKS only when Kubernetes is named or implied, Fargate for 'no servers to manage', ECS Anywhere for 'on-premises servers must remain'. Treat App Runner options with caution because the service is closed to new customers.

topics.title: Storage services: EBS, EFS, FSx, S3 and Storage Gateway

blocks.body: Pick storage by access model first, then by performance and cost. EBS is block storage attached to an EC2 instance, with the lowest latency for a single instance. EFS is a shared NFS file system accessible concurrently by thousands of clients (EC2, containers, Lambda, on-premises). S3 is object storage reached through an API. FSx offers four managed file systems. Storage Gateway lets on-premises applications use cloud storage through familiar protocols.

rows: Single-instance block device, databases, boot volumes
A volume attaches to an instance in the same Availability Zone. Types: gp3, gp2, io1, io2, st1, sc1, magnetic. SSD for transactional workloads, HDD for throughput-intensive.
Shared POSIX file system for many Linux clients

Regional file systems are stored redundantly across multiple AZs, with one mount target per AZ. One Zone file systems have a single mount target in one AZ and data may become unavailable if that AZ fails.
Windows SMB, NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS or HPC Lustre
Four file systems: Windows File Server, Lustre, NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS. Choose by existing familiarity and feature match.
Objects, static content, data lakes, uploads
Object storage reached via API; storage classes for access and cost; S3 plus CloudFront for read-heavy delivery.
On-premises iSCSI block volumes backed by AWS

iSCSI target; cached mode keeps primary data in S3 with a local cache of hot data; stored mode keeps all data locally with async backup. Snapshots are stored as EBS snapshots; AWS Backup can protect both modes.
File-based access to S3 for SMB-dependent apps
Gives file access to S3 without a full application rewrite (migration guidance for file servers).

blocks.body: Volume Gateway in depth. Applications attach volumes over iSCSI from on-premises or EC2 servers. In cached mode the primary data lives in S3 while frequently accessed data is kept in a local cache, so the data center footprint shrinks as data grows. In stored mode the complete dataset stays local with asynchronous backup. In both modes you take point-in-time snapshots, which are incremental (only changed blocks), compressed and stored as EBS snapshots; you can drive them with the native snapshot scheduler or with AWS Backup, which supports both cached and stored volumes. The iSCSI requirement is the discriminator: if a stem says legacy applications need block storage mounted via iSCSI and the company wants to cut local storage while keeping snapshots, think cached Volume Gateway plus AWS Backup, not S3 File Gateway or EFS.

EBS versus EFS. EBS delivers the lowest latency to one instance and is scoped to an Availability Zone; if the new design must share one file tree across instances in several AZs, EBS is the wrong answer and EFS (Regional) is the fit. If a stem asks for a durable, highly available, low-latency store for reports or documents, with no mention of a file system, S3 (often with CloudFront) is typically the managed answer. The specific latency and recovery figures in some stems were ambiguous in the source questions and should be read carefully.

items: Do not use One Zone EFS when the requirement is Multi-AZ resilience.
Do not use EBS for data that must be mounted by many instances at once across AZs.
S3 is not a POSIX file system; applications that require file locking and directory semantics need EFS or FSx.
Quotas for volume size, IOPS, and throughput are outside the scope of this lesson; check the AWS documentation for current limits.

topics.title: Relational and in-memory databases: RDS, Aurora and ElastiCache

blocks.body: For a relational workload (MySQL, PostgreSQL and so on) the first decision is self-managed on EC2 versus managed. Self-managed databases on EC2 give full OS and engine control but you own patching, backups, replication and failover. RDS and Aurora remove most of that. The exam usually expects a managed service unless the stem names a requirement RDS cannot meet (for example OS access or an unsupported engine feature).

RDS Multi-AZ. A Multi-AZ DB instance deployment has one synchronous standby in a different AZ; it provides failover support but does not serve read traffic. A Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment has two standby instances that provide failover and can also serve reads. With Multi-AZ the DNS name of the DB instance stays the same, so applications reconnect without manual intervention. The AWS Database Blog states that RPO for an instance failover is zero because replication is synchronous, failover usually takes 1 to 2 minutes, and in-flight queries are terminated during failover. Backups and snapshots are taken from the standby. To scale reads in a Multi-AZ instance deployment, add read replicas; Multi-AZ itself does not scale reads.

Aurora. Aurora separates compute from a purpose-built storage layer that keeps six copies of data across three Availability Zones. The cluster volume grows automatically (in 10 GiB increments, according to the AWS Database Blog), and space is released when data is deleted. Storage maximum: the cluster volume limit depends on engine version. It is 256 TiB for Aurora PostgreSQL 17.5 and higher, 16.9 and higher, and 15.13 and higher, and for Aurora MySQL version 3.10 and higher; it is 128 TiB for all earlier Aurora PostgreSQL versions, Aurora MySQL 3 versions lower than 3.10, and Aurora MySQL version 2 (2.09 and higher). Check the current limit for your engine version. Aurora I/O charges are independent of storage, and the I/O-Optimized configuration can save up to 40% when I/O spend exceeds 25% of Aurora database spend, according to the blog. Aurora Serverless v2 (renamed Aurora serverless in 2026 per a note on AWS blogs) measures capacity in ACUs, each about 2 GiB of memory with matching CPU and networking; the minimum is 0.5 ACU (0 ACU on Aurora versions that support automatic pause) and the maximum is 256 ACU for recent Aurora versions (128 ACU for older versions), with per-second billing for capacity used according to the blog.

Aurora Global Database write forwarding. A secondary-Region cluster is read-only by default. With write forwarding enabled, SQL write statements issued on the secondary cluster are forwarded to the primary cluster, which applies them and propagates the changes back to all secondary Regions; Aurora handles the cross-Region networking, and the consistency mode you configure determines whether the application gets read-after-write consistency. The writes still execute in the primary Region, so write latency from the secondary Region still includes the cross-Region round trip. Write forwarding saves you from building your own routing layer and lets the application keep one endpoint configuration across a Regional failover.

ElastiCache for Valkey or Redis OSS. A replication group has one primary and 1 to 5 read replicas, replicated asynchronously. Enable Multi-AZ so replicas sit in different AZs and automatic failover promotes the replica with the least replication lag; ElastiCache then provisions a replacement replica in the failed primary's AZ. Without Multi-AZ, if no replicas exist the new primary starts empty and data is lost unless restored from a snapshot. Because replication is asynchronous, a failover can lose recent writes, and AWS guidance is to keep crucial data (for example transactional or purchase data) in a durable database such as DynamoDB or RDS. Use ElastiCache for sessions, caching, leaderboards and recommendation lookups, not as the system of record.

topics.title: NoSQL, document, search and analytics targets: DynamoDB, DocumentDB, OpenSearch and Athena

blocks.body: Match the data model to the engine. Key-value or document access with predictable single-digit-millisecond latency and no servers: DynamoDB. A MongoDB-compatible application that should change as little as possible: Amazon DocumentDB. Full-text search, log analytics and dashboards: OpenSearch Service. Ad hoc SQL over data already in S3: Athena.

DynamoDB capacity modes. On-demand mode is pay-per-request, needs no capacity planning, and is described as the default and recommended option for most workloads. Provisioned mode bills for the read and write capacity you provision (with optional auto scaling), suits steady and predictable traffic, and rejects requests that exceed the allocation. You can switch from provisioned to on-demand up to four times in a rolling 24-hour window, and from on-demand to provisioned at any time. Watch for stems that apply the phrase 'on-demand capacity mode' to a different service such as DocumentDB: that is a wording trap.

Private access to DynamoDB. A gateway VPC endpoint lets resources in a VPC reach DynamoDB without an internet gateway or NAT device and at no additional charge; you add it as a route-table target. It does not allow access from on-premises networks, from peered VPCs in other Regions, or through a transit gateway; for those cases use an interface endpoint, which has an additional cost. In a migration where the application moves into a VPC and only needs DynamoDB, the gateway endpoint is the no-cost in-VPC choice.

Amazon DocumentDB. Instances are spread across the AZs in the cluster's subnet group (at least two AZs are required). The first instance is the primary; others are read-only replicas, and up to 15 replicas per cluster are documented. If the primary fails, a replica is promoted, with a brief interruption in which requests to the primary fail; promotion is much faster than re-creating the primary, which is what happens if there are no replicas. Replicas used as failover targets should have the same instance class as the primary and live in different AZs. Replicas share the same underlying storage, so a promotion loses no data. So 'multi-AZ high availability' for DocumentDB means adding replicas in other AZs.

Amazon OpenSearch Service. For production, use dedicated master nodes: AWS recommends Multi-AZ with Standby, which adds three dedicated master nodes, and in any case three, never an even number. One dedicated master is prohibited; two cannot form a quorum; four is no better than three and can cause issues across AZs; five works but means four idle nodes. Even if you choose two AZs for the domain, dedicated masters are distributed across three AZs so the loss of a zone keeps quorum (2 of 3). A typical ingestion path: producers send to Amazon Data Firehose, which can transform records with Lambda and deliver to OpenSearch Service (also to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch Serverless, Splunk, HTTP endpoints and others), and analysts explore data in OpenSearch Dashboards.

Athena. Athena is serverless SQL on data in S3, integrated with the AWS Glue Data Catalog for table metadata and with Quick (QuickSight) for visualization. You pay for the volume of data scanned, and columnar formats such as Parquet and ORC give faster queries at lower cost. When several teams hold large databases and need ad hoc queries without managing infrastructure, the pattern is to land the data in S3, catalog it with Glue, and query with Athena.

DocumentDB with replicas in multiple AZs
DynamoDB needs a data-model and API rewrite
A relational engine needs capacity planning and connection management

Athena queries S3; it is not a search cluster
Ad hoc SQL on S3, no cluster
Private DynamoDB access from inside the VPC at no cost

topics.title: Edge delivery, load balancing and the stateless web tier

blocks.body: Most target architectures for web workloads share a pattern: users reach CloudFront, which caches and fronts the origin; an Application Load Balancer spreads requests across instances or containers; the web tier is stateless; data lives in a managed database and cache.

CloudFront as an offload layer. CloudFront serves cacheable objects from edge locations, so requests it can answer from cache never reach your origin. Regional edge caches act as a mid-tier, and Origin Shield adds another caching layer between the regional edge caches and the origin, consolidating requests to reduce origin load further. The origin can be S3 or a custom origin (an EC2 instance, a load balancer, or another reachable HTTP server). For a popular site in an on-premises data center expecting a traffic surge and unable to add capacity quickly, putting CloudFront in front of the existing origin is the fast way to decrease origin load.

rows: Viewer request, viewer response, origin request, origin response
Up to millions of requests per second
Up to 10,000 requests per second per Region
Header manipulation, redirects/rewrites, cache-key normalization, token validation (submillisecond)
Work taking several milliseconds or more, adjustable CPU/memory, third-party libraries or SDK calls, network or file system access, access to the request body

blocks.body: Header manipulation example: to remove a response header for certain client types, a CloudFront Function on the viewer response event can inspect the request's User-Agent and delete the header, with no change to the origin. Domain redirects are also listed as a CloudFront Functions use case; Lambda@Edge is the choice when logic needs more than lightweight processing. You can associate up to four edge functions per cache behavior, one per event type.

Load balancers. ALB works at layer 7 (HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC) and targets IPs, instances and Lambda functions. NLB works at layer 4 (TCP, UDP, TLS), targets IPs, instances and ALBs, preserves the client source IP by default, has a static IP per AZ (Elastic IPs can be assigned) and suits long-lived TCP connections. Gateway Load Balancer inserts network appliances. A typical web tier needs an ALB; choose NLB for non-HTTP protocols or a fixed-IP requirement.

Stateful web tiers. If the application keeps sessions in instance memory you have two options. Sticky sessions (session affinity) on an ALB bind a user's session to one target using duration-based (lb_cookie) or application-based (app_cookie) cookies, enabled per target group; the client must support cookies. This leaves the application unchanged but ties users to individual targets. The cloud-native fix is to externalize session data into ElastiCache or DynamoDB so every instance is interchangeable, which is the better answer when the requirement is scalability and high reliability. The data tier scales separately: for a MySQL back end, Aurora with replicas and storage that grows automatically is the usual target.

items: If the stem allows application changes, prefer externalized state; if it forbids them, use stickiness.
CloudFront in front of an on-premises origin helps offload; it does not by itself make the origin highly available.
Place the web tier in an Auto Scaling group across multiple AZs behind the load balancer (standard practice; Auto Scaling quotas are outside the scope of this lesson).

blocks.body: 'Reduce load on the origin quickly' with no capacity available points to CloudFront. 'Per-request header edits at huge scale' points to CloudFront Functions. 'Needs the request body or an SDK call' points to Lambda@Edge. A stem mentioning RTMP distributions reflects a retired feature: CloudFront deprecated RTMP distributions effective December 31, 2020.

blocks.body: SES SMTP in a replatformed application. A migrated application that already speaks SMTP can point at the SES SMTP endpoint with minimal code change. Authentication needs SES SMTP credentials (created in the SES console, or converted from IAM credentials); connecting with ordinary AWS credentials fails. Permissions on an instance role do not replace the SMTP credentials. The SES SMTP endpoint requires TLS. It supports STARTTLS on ports 25, 587, and 2587, and TLS Wrapper (SMTPS) on ports 465 and 2465. Amazon EC2 throttles port 25 by default, so use another port or request removal of the restriction.

IoT enrichment pattern. Devices publish MQTT messages to IoT Core. A rule's SQL selects and enriches the payload (for example adding a field derived from the topic), a Firehose action delivers to a delivery stream, and Firehose lands data in S3, where Athena can query it. If the sensors cannot speak MQTT, some integration is needed first; do not assume IoT Core fits without it.

Kinesis Data Streams versus Firehose: Streams is for custom consumers (for example, Lambda reading the stream); Firehose is a managed delivery service to storage and analytics targets with no consumer code. Retention, shard, and replay specifics are outside the scope of this lesson. A stem naming 'Kinesis Data Analytics' refers to a service now named Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink (renamed in August 2023).

items: Replace polling with events: S3 events or EventBridge beat a script scanning a file system.
Prefer direct service integrations (API Gateway to DynamoDB, IoT rule to Firehose) over glue Lambda functions when no custom logic is needed; this reduces operational overhead.
IAM, not the token, is what authorises a callback: grant SendTaskSuccess/SendTaskFailure only to the principals that should complete the task.

blocks.body: Scenario 1: On-premises retail site with a stateful web tier and MySQL. Requirements: handle a seasonal traffic surge, survive an AZ failure, keep application changes small. Existing environment: a pair of web servers keeping sessions in memory, one MySQL server. Chosen architecture: web tier in an Auto Scaling group across two or more AZs behind an ALB; sessions moved to an ElastiCache replication group with Multi-AZ (or, if code changes are forbidden, ALB stickiness as a stopgap); MySQL replatformed to Aurora MySQL with a reader in a second AZ; CloudFront in front for static and cacheable content. Rationale: removes single points of failure, scales the tier horizontally, and Aurora storage grows automatically. Security: security groups chaining ALB to web to database, encryption in transit. Cost: Aurora and ElastiCache cost more than a single server but remove DBA and failover tooling. Alternatives rejected: a single large EC2 instance (no AZ resilience), RDS Multi-AZ instance deployment alone (acceptable for HA but the standby serves no reads, so read scaling needs extra replicas), stickiness only (sessions lost when a target fails).

Scenario 2: MongoDB-based listings application, move with least change. Requirements: keep the MongoDB API, multi-AZ high availability, managed service. Chosen architecture: Amazon DocumentDB cluster with a primary and at least one replica in a different AZ from the primary, application on ECS Fargate behind an ALB. Rationale: DocumentDB is the MongoDB-compatible managed option; replicas in other AZs are the failover targets and share storage with the primary. Security: DocumentDB in private subnets, security group allowing only the application. Cost: replicas cost instance hours but avoid a failover that re-creates the primary. Alternatives rejected: DynamoDB (different API and data model, so application rewrite), self-managed MongoDB on EC2 (operational overhead), a single-instance DocumentDB cluster (primary is re-created on failure, which is slower than promoting a replica).

Scenario 3: Hybrid data center with legacy block-storage applications. Requirements: shrink on-premises storage growth, applications need iSCSI volumes, centralized backup and compliance reporting, no application change. Chosen architecture: Storage Gateway Volume Gateway in cached mode (primary data in S3, hot data cached locally), snapshots managed by AWS Backup, stored as EBS snapshots. Rationale: iSCSI presented to existing servers with little change, backups centralized. Cost: S3 storage rather than local arrays; the local appliance needs a cache. Alternatives rejected: S3 File Gateway (file protocol, not block), EFS (NFS, would need a protocol change), stored mode (keeps the entire dataset local so it does not cut local storage). Also note: if the same company has on-premises containers that must stay on premises, ECS Anywhere keeps them in an ECS cluster rather than forcing an EKS rebuild.

blocks.body:
Resources:
  WebServer:
    Type: AWS::EC2::Instance
    Metadata:
      AWS::CloudFormation::Init:
        config:
          packages:
            yum:
              httpd: []
          services:

                ensureRunning: true

Troubleshooting checks. Gateway endpoint not working: confirm the route table of the subnet has the endpoint route, the endpoint policy allows the action, and remember it does not work from on premises. EKS nodes with a custom AMI not joining: check the launch template user data includes the bootstrap command and the security groups allow communication with the cluster endpoint. Transfer workflow decrypt failing: the file must be encrypted to a named recipient (anonymous PGP encryption can fail) and the key secret name must match what the workflow expects. SES SMTP authentication failing: check you are using SES SMTP credentials and not AWS access keys. Lambda timing out: check the function timeout against the 900-second maximum before redesigning.

cfn-init reads the AWS::CloudFormation::Init metadata to install packages, write files and start services, and is typically called from user data. It is the declarative alternative to a long shell script in user data. The template properties and the policy action names above are written from standard syntax and were not each verified against AWS documentation (see unverified).

Method. First, find the primary requirement: what outcome does the scenario demand (availability, lowest change, lowest operational overhead, lowest cost, protocol compatibility)? Second, list the mandatory constraints: existing protocol (iSCSI, SMB, MongoDB API, SMTP), runtime length, Region or AZ scope, on-premises presence. Third, eliminate options that violate a mandatory constraint. Fourth, among the survivors choose by the tiebreak keywords.

blocks.body: Service distinction rules to apply.

items: Multi-AZ RDS instance deployment: failover only. Read replica or Multi-AZ DB cluster or Aurora reader: reads.
EBS: one instance, one AZ, block. EFS: many clients, NFS, Regional is multi-AZ. FSx: choose by protocol or file system (Windows, ONTAP, OpenZFS, Lustre). S3: objects.
Volume Gateway: iSCSI block with EBS snapshots. File gateway: file protocols to S3.
CloudFront Functions: lightweight header, URL and cache-key logic at the viewer events. Lambda@Edge: heavier logic, origin events, request body.
ALB: HTTP-aware layer 7. NLB: TCP/UDP, static IP, source IP preservation.
Stateful tier: externalize sessions (ElastiCache or DynamoDB) when allowed; ALB stickiness when the app cannot change.
DocumentDB is MongoDB-compatible; DynamoDB is not.
Gateway endpoints: free, VPC-only, S3 and DynamoDB. Interface endpoints: cost money, work from on premises over private connectivity.

blocks.body: Reading imperfect questions. Some exam items contain typos, older service names or ambiguous wording ('Amazon Recognition', 'SOS queue', Kinesis Data Analytics, Amazon ES). Decode them to the intended service and then reason from the constraints. If two options are defensible, re-read for the stated constraint that breaks the tie, such as a missing configuration step or an explicit protocol.

Do not stop at the first workable answer. The exam rewards the option that satisfies every constraint with the fewest moving parts. If two answers both work, the one that avoids managing servers, avoids rewrites when 'minimal changes' is stated, and uses a direct service integration usually wins.

items: Compute: EC2 for control and rehost, Beanstalk for managed web app platform (web, worker, cluster tiers), Lambda for short event-driven code (timeout default 3 s, max 900 s; /tmp 512 to 10,240 MB).

Containers: ECS for simple orchestration, Fargate for serverless capacity, EKS only when Kubernetes matters, ECS Anywhere for on-premises servers, ECR for images, App Runner is closed to new customers.
Storage: EBS single-AZ block; EFS shared NFS (Regional multi-AZ, One Zone single-AZ); FSx for Windows, ONTAP, OpenZFS, Lustre; S3 object; Volume Gateway iSCSI with EBS snapshots (cached vs stored).

Databases: RDS Multi-AZ (synchronous standby, zero RPO instance failover, 1 to 2 minute failover), Aurora (six copies across three AZs, auto-growing storage, write forwarding in Global Database), DynamoDB (on-demand default), DocumentDB (MongoDB-compatible, replicas in multiple AZs), OpenSearch (three dedicated masters), ElastiCache (Multi-AZ replication group, asynchronous).
Edge and web tier: CloudFront offloads origins; Functions vs Lambda@Edge; ALB vs NLB; externalize state.

blocks.body: Misconceptions: Multi-AZ RDS does not scale reads; a gateway endpoint does not work from on premises; DynamoDB is not a drop-in for MongoDB; Lambda is not for jobs over 15 minutes; EKS is not automatically better than ECS; ElastiCache replication is asynchronous so it is not a system of record; Aurora Global Database write forwarding still executes writes in the primary Region.

Limits to remember (scope as stated in docs): Lambda timeout per function, default 3 s, configurable to 900 s; Lambda ephemeral storage per function 512 to 10,240 MB; ECS Anywhere activation key registers 1 to 1,000 machines; ElastiCache replication group 1 to 5 replicas; DocumentDB up to 15 replicas per cluster; DynamoDB mode switch to on-demand 4 times in 24 hours; Lambda@Edge 10,000 requests per second per Region; OpenSearch dedicated masters 3 recommended; ECR lifecycle expiry within 24 hours. The pages reviewed for this lesson do not state whether each limit can be adjusted.

Takeaways: identify the protocol or API the workload depends on, then the availability scope, then the operational-overhead preference. Pick the managed service that preserves the dependency, and eliminate anything that breaks a mandatory constraint.

Task 4.4 (Domain 4, Accelerate workload migration and modernization) asks you to determine opportunities for modernization and enhancements. Modernization means changing how an existing workload is built or run so that it uses managed, elastic, loosely coupled AWS building blocks instead of servers you patch and scale yourself. The exam rarely asks you to recall a feature in isolation; it gives you a legacy system and asks which target design best meets stated constraints (least operational overhead, lowest cost, minimal code change, near-real-time, and so on).

Prerequisites: working knowledge of EC2, VPC, IAM roles, S3 and a relational database; the migration-strategy vocabulary from the migration-approach lesson (rehost, replatform, refactor); and the new-architecture ideas about stateless tiers and caching. Terms used here: a queue buffers messages until a consumer pulls them; a topic fans a message out to many subscribers; an event bus routes events by rule; an orchestrator (state machine) sequences steps with retries; idempotent means repeating an operation has the same effect as doing it once.

items: You will be able to identify tightly coupled components (in-memory queues, cron jobs on one host, shared file shares, direct synchronous calls) and choose SQS, SNS, EventBridge or Step Functions to decouple them.
You will be able to decide when a workload fits Lambda and when it should run on ECS, EKS or Fargate, using documented limits (15-minute timeout, 10,240 MB memory, 6 MB synchronous payload).
You will be able to select the container service and capacity layer (ECS vs EKS; Fargate vs EC2) that matches skills, portability and operational-overhead requirements.
You will be able to match a data access pattern to a purpose-built database (DynamoDB, Aurora serverless, ElastiCache) and explain the capacity-mode and scaling trade-offs.
You will be able to choose between Standard and Express Step Functions workflows and between SQS, SNS and EventBridge from their delivery, ordering, persistence and filtering properties.
You will be able to flag stale or retired services in an exam scenario (App2Container, App Runner, Pinpoint, Aurora Serverless v1) and name the current direction.

blocks.title: Services and patterns covered
blocks.body: Lambda, API Gateway and Lambda function URLs; ECS, EKS, Fargate, Elastic Beanstalk, App Runner status; S3, EFS and Transfer Family; DynamoDB (+Streams), Aurora serverless, the RDS Data API, ElastiCache; SQS, SNS, EventBridge (buses, Pipes), Step Functions; IoT Core, Amazon MQ, SES and other managed replacements for self-run components.

Domain 4 carries 20 percent of the SAP-C02 scoring (not re-verified against AWS docs in this build; confirm in the current exam guide). Modernization questions are among the most numerous in the bank: expect a legacy description plus a phrase such as 'least operational overhead' or 'minimal code changes' that decides between a refactor-to-serverless answer and a lift-and-shift-to-managed answer.

links.label: Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS, or Amazon EventBridge?
Choosing workflow type in Step Functions

blocks.body: Modernization is a spectrum. At one end you keep the application code and move it to a managed runtime (replatform): a Tomcat app to Elastic Beanstalk, a self-managed Kubernetes cluster to Amazon EKS, a self-run RabbitMQ broker to Amazon MQ. At the other end you rewrite pieces to use cloud-native services (refactor): an in-memory queue becomes SQS, a cron job becomes an S3 event plus Lambda, a monolith becomes functions behind an API. The stem tells you where on the spectrum you are allowed to land through phrases such as 'does not want to rewrite the application' or 'no source code access' (stay near replatform) versus 'improve availability, durability and scalability' (decouple and refactor).

Decoupling means components communicate through an intermediary rather than a direct call, so that each side can fail, scale, deploy and be throttled independently. AWS Prescriptive Guidance describes messaging as a way for services to communicate synchronously or asynchronously and says the choice should follow your integration needs. Signs of coupling to look for: work held in process memory (lost if the instance fails); a single host running both producer and consumer; a fixed-size consumer fleet that cannot absorb spikes; a cron job that polls for work; shared mutable state on a file share; one component calling another and waiting.

blocks.title: Decoupling is not free
blocks.body: Asynchronous designs add eventual consistency, duplicate delivery (at-least-once) and the need for idempotent consumers and dead-letter handling. If a stem requires a synchronous response that depends on the result, a queue in the middle is usually the wrong answer; if it requires durability and spike absorption, it is usually right.

items: Common mistake: choosing a bigger instance or more instances to fix a coupling problem; that raises cost without removing the single point of failure.
Common mistake: adding a queue but keeping a single consumer instance; the queue is durable but the consumer remains a bottleneck and a failure point.
Best practice: put a durable buffer (SQS) between a bursty producer and a slower consumer, and scale consumers on queue depth.

topics.title: Serverless compute: Lambda and API front ends

blocks.body: AWS Lambda runs your code in response to invocations without you managing servers. Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to configured memory; at 1,769 MB a function has the equivalent of one vCPU. It is designed for short-lived compute tasks that do not retain or rely on state between invocations. Persistent state belongs in DynamoDB, S3, EFS or a database.

blocks.body: Lambda scales by creating execution environments. A cold start happens when Lambda must initialize a new environment. Provisioned concurrency keeps a set number of environments pre-initialized for predictable latency and incurs additional charges; reserved concurrency only caps and guarantees a function's share and does not pre-initialize anything. For supported Java managed runtimes, SnapStart has no extra cost (other supported runtimes incur snapshot caching and restoration charges), and it cannot be combined with provisioned concurrency on the same function version (the docs text mentions Java 11 and 17; check current runtime support).

blocks.title: When Lambda fits
blocks.body: Event-driven or request-driven work that finishes in under 15 minutes, is stateless, tolerates cold starts or can use provisioned concurrency, and has variable or low traffic (you pay for use, not idle). Typical modernization targets: S3-triggered processing, queue consumers, API back ends, scheduled jobs, stream processors.

blocks.title: When Lambda does not fit
blocks.body: Processes that need more than 15 minutes (the 5,400-second Managed Instances extension applies only to asynchronous and most event-source invocations), long-lived connections or in-memory state, specialized OS-level dependencies that exceed the 10 GB image limit, or steady very-high-throughput workloads where per-request pricing exceeds the cost of always-on containers. Split long jobs into Step Functions steps or move to Fargate/ECS.

Calling Lambda over HTTP. Lambda function URLs give a function a built-in HTTPS endpoint with optional CORS and dual-stack support and are designed for simplicity; AWS says they lack advanced features. API Gateway adds API versioning, stage management, API keys for usage plans, OpenAPI documentation, WebSocket APIs, private APIs within a VPC, AWS WAF integration, canary deployments and integrations with other services. Within API Gateway, REST APIs support more features (API keys, per-client throttling, request validation, WAF integration, private endpoints) while HTTP APIs are designed with minimal features at a lower price; HTTP APIs support OIDC and OAuth 2.0 authorization and built-in CORS.

topics.title: Containers: ECS, EKS, Fargate and migration paths

blocks.body: Containers package an application with its dependencies so it runs the same everywhere. AWS describes three layers: capacity (EC2 instances, AWS Fargate, AWS Outposts) where containers run; orchestration (Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS, Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS) that schedules and scales them; and vertical solutions (App Runner, Lightsail, AWS Batch, Lambda container images) that bundle more of the stack. Amazon ECR stores images.

Managed Kubernetes control plane; upstream Kubernetes API and tooling
Team has no Kubernetes investment; want least operational overhead; AWS-only

blocks.title: Capacity layer: Fargate vs EC2
blocks.body: With Fargate you specify resources per task or pod and AWS removes server provisioning and patching; with EC2 you get control (GPU or network-optimized instances, custom AMIs) but you own patching, instance selection, networking and instance security. ECS supports mixed clusters of both. Fargate provides 20 GiB of ephemeral storage by default per task or pod (ECS tasks can be configured up to 200 GiB), and you pay only for additional storage you configure. Compute Savings Plans apply to both EC2 and Fargate, and Fargate Spot offers no-commitment discounts for interruption-tolerant work (the pricing page cites up to about 70 percent and up to about 52 percent for a 3-year Savings Plan; discount levels vary and are not guaranteed).

Persistent storage for containers. Fargate tasks (platform version 1.4.0 and later) support Amazon EFS volumes for persistent shared storage, Amazon EBS volumes, and bind mounts for ephemeral storage. To mount EFS, allow inbound NFS (port 2049) on the file system security group from the task security group and the matching outbound rule on the task. This is the standard answer when a containerized app needs a shared NFS-style file system without managing servers. EFS spans multiple Availability Zones for shared access; EBS volumes are single-AZ block storage and are not a shared file system (the EBS Multi-Attach constraints were not verified in this build).

EKS specifics. EKS provides a highly available Kubernetes control plane. AWS now states that EKS Auto Mode is the recommended approach moving forward over EKS with Fargate: Auto Mode is fully Kubernetes conformant (supports primitives and tools such as Istio that Fargate cannot) and supports all EC2 purchase options including GPU and Spot. Fargate for EKS remains available. For on-premises needs, the container decision guide lists ECS Anywhere, EKS Anywhere and EKS Hybrid Nodes, plus Outposts as a capacity layer; a stem demanding that both control plane and data plane run on premises with AWS-managed tooling is testing which of these fits (details of EKS local clusters on Outposts were not verified in this build).

Other targets. Elastic Beanstalk deploys and manages the environment (capacity, load balancing, scaling) for an uploaded application; AWS documents Java (Tomcat) with a WAR/JAR, PHP, and Windows/.NET paths. For IIS applications, the EB CLI command `eb migrate` discovers IIS sites and applications, preserves configuration and deploys them; the older Windows Web Application Migration Assistant (WWAMA) PowerShell tool does a similar job for ASP.NET sites with little or no change. AWS App Runner deploys from source or an image with minimal setup but is no longer open to new customers (AWS recommends Amazon ECS Express Mode); treat it as a legacy answer.

blocks.title: Retired or closed tooling you may see in older questions
blocks.body: AWS App2Container, Porting Assistant for .NET, Toolkit for .NET Refactoring and Microservice Extractor for .NET are no longer open to new customers (sign-up deadline was 7 November 2025); AWS points to AWS Transform for .NET modernization. The architecture an old question chooses (containerize .NET onto ECS) may still be the best of the listed options, but do not present these tools as current guidance.

topics.title: Purpose-built databases: DynamoDB, Aurora serverless and ElastiCache

blocks.body: A purpose-built database is chosen for its access pattern rather than defaulting to one relational engine. Modernization questions typically replace an over-provisioned relational database, a self-run cache, or a store of unstructured catalog data with a service whose scaling model matches the workload.

Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL key-value and document database with single-digit-millisecond performance at any scale. It has two capacity modes. On-demand has pay-per-request pricing, needs no capacity planning, and instantly accommodates up to double the table's previous peak traffic; throttling can occur if traffic exceeds double the previous peak within 30 minutes. The Well-Architected serverless lens calls on-demand the default and recommended option for most workloads. Provisioned mode bills for provisioned capacity regardless of use, suits steady predictable workloads (optionally with auto scaling and reserved capacity), and rejects requests beyond capacity. You can switch from provisioned to on-demand up to four times in a rolling 24 hours; on-demand to provisioned any time. A hot partition throttles at about 3,000 RCU or 1,000 WCU per partition per second regardless of table capacity, so partition key cardinality matters.

rows: Only if traffic exceeds 2x previous peak abruptly or hot partition
If demand exceeds provisioned capacity or burst

blocks.body: DynamoDB Streams records a time-ordered, deduplicated sequence of item-level changes for 24 hours; older data can be trimmed at any time. The native Lambda integration polls the stream and invokes your function synchronously; Lambda reads from DynamoDB Streams are available at no additional cost, and docs warn that subscribing more than two Lambda functions to the same stream shard (more than one for global tables) can cause read throttling. If the function errors, Lambda retries the batch until it succeeds or the data expires (configurable retry, batch splitting and on-failure destinations exist). Use Streams for change-driven workflows, audit trails, replication and near-real-time analytics; because retention is only 24 hours, archive records to S3 or another sink if you need longer history.

Amazon Aurora serverless (Aurora Serverless v2, renamed 'Aurora serverless' in April 2026 per the AWS Database Blog banner) scales a MySQL- or PostgreSQL-compatible cluster in fine-grained Aurora capacity units (ACUs; each is about 2 GiB of memory with proportional CPU and networking). You set a capacity range per cluster. Documented bounds: minimum as low as 0.5 ACU, or 0 ACU where auto-pause is supported, and maximum capped at 256 ACU for recent Aurora versions (128 on older). Setting minimum to 0 enables automatic pause after a configurable idle period (300 to 86,400 seconds; default 300); a minimum of 0.5 or greater disables auto-pause. Features can raise the minimum, for example Performance Insights requires at least 2 ACU, and a paused instance does not collect Performance Insights or Enhanced Monitoring data. You pay per second for capacity used while active. Aurora Serverless v1 is superseded by v2; the AWS blog documents upgrading v1 to v2 (including a MySQL 5.7 to 8.0 upgrade first) using blue/green deployments for minimal downtime, and the exact v1 retirement date was not verified in this build.

RDS Data API gives HTTP-based, connectionless SQL access to Aurora clusters (the AWS blog describes enabling it with `aws rds enable-http-endpoint` on Serverless v2 or provisioned clusters). Callers authenticate with IAM and pass database credentials via a secret in AWS Secrets Manager (name or ARN of the secret). This suits Lambda and other serverless callers that would otherwise exhaust database connections, but it is not a drop-in replacement for JDBC/ODBC drivers: applications must call the Data API.

Amazon ElastiCache provides managed in-memory caches (Valkey, Redis OSS, Memcached). Documented strategies: lazy loading (cache-aside) populates the cache on a miss, tolerates empty nodes but can serve stale data; write-through updates the cache on every write so data stays fresh but can fail with empty nodes and fill the cache with data never read. Adding a TTL to each write combines the advantages. ElastiCache for Valkey is described as serving frequently requested items at sub-millisecond latency to ease load on relational or NoSQL databases. Use it for read-heavy hot data, session state and leaderboards; it is not a system of record.

topics.title: Storage and file transfer: S3, EFS and Transfer Family

blocks.body: Modernization often replaces file servers and ad hoc file handling with managed storage. Amazon S3 is object storage used for data lakes, media, static assets and event sources; Amazon EFS is a managed shared NFS file system for containers and instances; AWS Transfer Family provides managed SFTP, FTPS, FTP and AS2 endpoints in front of S3 or EFS so you can retire self-run transfer servers.

Static front ends. A single-page application built from static files can be served from S3 with Amazon CloudFront in front. An S3 bucket configured as a website endpoint does not support HTTPS connections; the CloudFront documentation states you cannot configure CloudFront to use HTTPS to an S3 website-endpoint origin. CloudFront with a custom or ACM certificate provides HTTPS and integrates with AWS WAF. The dynamic API behind the SPA becomes API Gateway plus Lambda (or containers), and the relational data moves to Aurora (automatic storage growth for an unpredictable data volume is a property of Aurora not separately verified in this build).

Large objects and metadata. A common modernization pattern stores large binary content (video, images, documents) in S3 and keeps searchable metadata in DynamoDB or a relational table, rather than putting blobs in a database. S3 event notifications can then trigger Lambda or a queue for processing such as enrichment or transcoding (S3-to-EventBridge notifications must be enabled on the bucket; the exact setting was not verified in this build).

Transfer Family endpoint types. A Public endpoint supports SFTP, cannot take a static IP (AWS-provided addresses can change) and cannot use source-IP allow lists. A VPC endpoint with internet-facing access supports SFTP, FTPS and AS2 in the matrix; you can attach Elastic IP addresses (AWS-owned or BYOIP) that do not change, and you control source IP access with security groups and network ACLs. A VPC endpoint with internal access supports SFTP, FTP, FTPS and AS2 and is reachable only inside the VPC and connected networks such as Direct Connect or VPN. The old VPC_ENDPOINT type is deprecated and cannot be created by new accounts. FTP in particular is limited to internal access; for internet-facing FTP-like requirements you may need to front or restrict it differently (details not verified beyond the matrix).

blocks.title: Data sharing as a product
blocks.body: AWS Data Exchange for Amazon Redshift lets a provider license Redshift data (schemas, tables, views, user-defined functions) as AWS Data Exchange datashares. Subscribers automatically become consumers with read-only access, and AWS manages billing, invoicing and entitlement. It replaces the pattern of unloading data to S3 files and distributing them manually.

If the legacy design is 'EC2 SFTP server plus cron job moving files to S3', the modernization is Transfer Family writing straight to S3 plus an S3 event trigger. If clients depend on a fixed IP, the endpoint must be the VPC type with an Elastic IP.

topics.title: Integration services I: SQS and SNS

blocks.body: Amazon SQS is a fully managed queue. Consumers pull (poll) messages; messages persist until processed or expired. Amazon SNS is a push-based pub/sub service: a publisher sends to a topic and SNS delivers to each subscriber; SNS does not persist messages for later retrieval. Combining them as topic-queue chaining (fanout) is a core pattern: SNS replicates the message to several SQS queues, and each queue buffers independently so a slow or failed subscriber does not lose messages for hours or days.

blocks.body: Visibility timeout and dead-letter queues. When a consumer receives a message it becomes invisible for the visibility timeout; if the consumer does not delete it, it reappears and is retried. A dead-letter queue (DLQ) collects messages that exceed a maximum receive count so failed items are retained for analysis instead of blocking or being lost; a redrive allow policy controls which source queues may use a DLQ. Set the DLQ retention longer than the source queue's, and alarm on DLQ depth. Retaining failed orders in a DLQ while keeping operating cost low is a classic exam requirement.

Lambda with SQS. Lambda polls the queue through an event source mapping. BatchSize default is 10; maximum 10,000 for standard queues (with a batching window) and 10 for FIFO. Without partial-batch handling, an error makes every message in the batch visible again, including successes, causing duplicates. Enabling `ReportBatchItemFailures` in FunctionResponseTypes lets the function return only the failed message IDs in batchItemFailures. With FIFO queues the function should stop after the first failure and return all failed and unprocessed messages to preserve order. Scaling can be capped using maximum concurrency on the mapping (ScalingConfig).

SNS specifics. Subscribers include HTTP/S, email, SMS, mobile push, Lambda and SQS. Subscription filter policies route a subset of messages to each subscriber (attribute-based by default; payload-based when the subscription's FilterPolicyScope is MessageBody). SNS offers at-least-once delivery for HTTP/S and exactly-once for Lambda and SQS subscribers, per the decision guide. SNS FIFO topics preserve ordering and deduplication but can deliver only to SQS (standard or FIFO); they cannot deliver to email, SMS, mobile push or HTTP(S) endpoints, and to reach Lambda you subscribe a queue and trigger from it. SNS delivery includes built-in retry logic and dead-letter queue support for subscriptions, per the decision guide. A 2020 AWS Compute Blog comparison table says EventBridge had no dead-letter queue support at that time; that is outdated: EventBridge now supports a dead-letter queue per rule target for events that cannot be delivered after retries.

blocks.title: Why SQS in front of consumers
blocks.body: A queue acts as a buffering load balancer: a surge is absorbed, consumers scale out on queue depth (for example ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible per task), and a crashed consumer's messages reappear. Scaling on queue backlog is the standard way to autoscale containers (EKS or ECS) or Lambda concurrency for variable message rates.

Need ordering and no duplicates: SQS FIFO (or SNS FIFO + SQS FIFO). Need one event to many independent consumers with filtering and buffering: SNS topic to SQS queues. Need to retain failed orders cheaply: SQS plus DLQ. Idempotent consumers are required even with standard queues, because delivery is at-least-once. Watch for answers that put the queue after the consumer or that use in-memory buffers.

items: Common mistake: choosing SNS alone when subscribers can be offline; SNS does not persist, so pair with SQS.
Common mistake: choosing FIFO for throughput-sensitive workloads that do not need ordering.
Common mistake: visibility timeout shorter than processing time, causing duplicate processing.

topics.title: Integration services II: EventBridge and Step Functions

blocks.body: Amazon EventBridge is a serverless event bus: producers (AWS services, your applications, SaaS partners) put events on a bus; rules match events by pattern and route them to targets. Per the decision guide it provides content-based filtering and complex pattern matching, at-least-once delivery, no ordering guarantee, and does not persist events. By default EventBridge retries delivery for up to 24 hours and up to 185 times with exponential backoff and jitter. It integrates with Lambda, Step Functions, SQS, SNS and Kinesis among others, plus API destinations for HTTP endpoints.

Cross-account event sharing. On the receiver account, edit the event bus resource-based policy to allow specified accounts, an organization, or all accounts to put events. On the sender account, create a rule whose target is the receiver's event bus; when the target is an event bus, use an IAM role that allows `events:PutEvents` on the destination bus. Events sent cross-account are charged to the sending account as custom events; the receiving account is not charged for them. This is the usual answer for a central event broker with microservices in many accounts.

EventBridge Pipes connects a single source to a single target with optional filtering and enrichment. Sources documented in the knowledge-center article: DynamoDB stream, Kinesis stream, Amazon MQ, MSK, self-managed Kafka, and SQS. Filtering is by event patterns and you pay only for events that match the filter; enrichment can use API destinations, API Gateway, Lambda or Step Functions. Use Pipes instead of glue Lambda functions when you only need to filter, enrich and forward.

rows: Until consumed or expired (up to 14 days)
HTTP/S, email, SMS, push, Lambda, SQS

blocks.body: AWS Step Functions orchestrates workflows defined in Amazon States Language. Standard workflows run up to one year, execute exactly once per state (unless Retry is configured), keep an execution history queryable for up to 90 days, and are billed per state transition; they suit long-running, auditable, non-idempotent actions such as payments or starting an EMR cluster. Express workflows run up to five minutes, use an at-least-once model (async) or at-most-once (sync), support a start rate over 100,000 per second, send history to CloudWatch Logs, and are billed by executions, duration and memory; they suit high-volume idempotent event processing. The workflow type is immutable after creation. Express supports only Request Response integrations; Standard additionally supports Run a Job (.sync) and Wait for Callback (.waitForTaskToken) where the service allows (ECS/Fargate, EKS, Batch, Athena, CodeBuild, API Gateway callbacks, etc.). Over two hundred services are reachable through AWS SDK integrations.

blocks.title: Orchestration vs choreography
blocks.body: Use Step Functions when you need ordering, branching, parallelism, retries and a visible execution (orchestration). Use EventBridge/SNS when services react independently to events (choreography). A workflow that launches a Fargate task and waits for completion, then calls the next step, is Standard with the ECS `.sync` integration. Avoid polling loops that burn state transitions; use callbacks or .sync.

'Exactly once', 'payment', 'wait for human approval up to days' = Standard. 'Hundreds of thousands per second, short, idempotent' = Express. 'Route events from a central account to team accounts by content' = EventBridge with bus policy. 'Transform a queue message by calling an API before invoking a workflow without writing code' = EventBridge Pipes.

items: Common mistake: using EventBridge when ordering is required.
Common mistake: choosing Express for a job that lasts 20 minutes.
Best practice: make consumers idempotent for at-least-once services; configure a DLQ on each rule target to capture events that exhaust their retries.

Do not eliminate an option solely because it uses an old service name; ask whether the architecture is right. Do eliminate options that rely on a mechanism that does not exist (for example resource policies on Redshift tables that grant public access), or that mix services in impossible ways (DMS migrates data, not server images).

blocks.body: Scenario 1: Order intake that loses requests. Requirements: improve availability, durability and scalability of a legacy Java app that runs on one high-memory EC2 instance, accepts HTTP requests, queues them in memory and returns 200; a second process drains the queue. Constraints: clients must still get a fast acknowledgement; no lost orders; failed orders must be kept for inspection; minimize operating cost. Chosen architecture: API Gateway (HTTP API or REST API with a direct SQS integration) writes to an SQS standard queue; consumers run in an Auto Scaling group, ECS on Fargate or Lambda with an SQS event source mapping and ReportBatchItemFailures; a DLQ with redrive policy catches poison messages; consumers are idempotent. Security: IAM role for API Gateway limited to sqs:SendMessage on one queue, queue policy, SSE on the queue, consumer role limited to receive/delete. Cost: pay per request and per message; no idle large instance. Rejected: a bigger EC2 instance or a replica pair (still in-memory, still coupled); SNS alone (no persistence); FIFO (only if ordering is required, and it lowers default throughput to 300 or 3,000 messages/s).

Scenario 2: Self-managed Kubernetes and SFTP ingestion to a managed platform. A retailer runs microservices on a self-managed Kubernetes cluster whose deployment manifests are in Git, a PostgreSQL database, and an EC2 SFTP server with a cron job that moves partner files into S3. Constraints: minimal re-engineering, reduce operations, keep partner whitelisting of a fixed IP. Chosen: Amazon EKS (managed control plane; Auto Mode or managed node groups) and apply the same manifests with changes for storage classes, load balancers and IAM; database to a managed PostgreSQL-compatible service (RDS or Aurora); Transfer Family SFTP on a VPC internet-facing endpoint with an Elastic IP writing straight to S3, replacing the cron mover with an S3 event to Lambda or a queue. Security: partner SSH public keys imported; per-partner IAM roles scoped to a prefix; security groups restrict partner source IPs. Alternatives rejected: ECS (requires rewriting manifests into task definitions, contradicting minimal re-engineering); a public Transfer Family endpoint (cannot attach a static IP or allow-list by source IP); Lambda for the microservices (rewrite, and may exceed limits).

Scenario 3: Spiky seasonal workload with a stable core. A ticketing company sees bursts every seven days. The stateless web tier sits behind a load balancer on a fixed EC2 fleet; an Oracle database stores unstructured catalog data; an API layer runs on EC2. Goal: handle bursts, cut cost and database license spend. Chosen: web tier in an Auto Scaling group using a mixed instance policy (On-Demand base with Spot for burst, with scheduled or target-tracking scaling), catalog moved to DynamoDB on-demand (key-based access to unstructured items, no capacity planning, up to 2x previous peak instantly), caching of hot catalog reads with ElastiCache, and the API layer on API Gateway with Lambda or containers on Fargate. Cost: pay per request for DynamoDB and Lambda, Spot for interruptible capacity; no Oracle licensing for the catalog. Rejected: provisioned DynamoDB at peak capacity (pays for idle capacity most of the week); Aurora serverless if the catalog truly needs joins or relational integrity (then it would be the better answer); keeping Oracle and only adding read replicas (does not remove licensing or the over-provisioning).

blocks.title: Pattern to notice
blocks.body: In all three scenarios the right answer removed a single point of failure or an always-on resource (in-memory queue, cron host, over-provisioned database) while respecting the constraint that limited how far to refactor.

items: Decouple intake: create the DLQ first, then the source queue with a redrive policy (maxReceiveCount) and a visibility timeout longer than the consumer's processing time.
Create the consumer (Lambda or container) with a role allowing sqs:ReceiveMessage, sqs:DeleteMessage and sqs:GetQueueAttributes on the queue only.
Add the event source mapping with ReportBatchItemFailures; set maximum concurrency to protect downstream databases.
Front the queue with API Gateway (service integration with a role allowing sqs:SendMessage) or have producers call the SQS API.
Alarm on ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage on the main queue and on DLQ depth; test by sending a poison message and confirming it lands in the DLQ.

blocks.label: CloudFormation
blocks.body:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Description: Orders queue with dead-letter queue and Lambda consumer (sketch)
Resources:
  OrdersDLQ:
    Type: AWS::SQS::Queue
    Properties:
      MessageRetentionPeriod: 1209600
  OrdersQueue:
    Type: AWS::SQS::Queue
    Properties:
      VisibilityTimeout: 180
      RedrivePolicy:
        deadLetterTargetArn: !GetAtt OrdersDLQ.Arn
        maxReceiveCount: 5
  OrdersMapping:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::EventSourceMapping
    Properties:
      EventSourceArn: !GetAtt OrdersQueue.Arn
      FunctionName: <consumer-function-name>
      BatchSize: 10
      FunctionResponseTypes:
        - ReportBatchItemFailures
      ScalingConfig:
        MaximumConcurrency: 50

Troubleshooting: messages processed twice -> consumer not idempotent or visibility timeout too short, or batch failure without ReportBatchItemFailures.
Troubleshooting: EventBridge cross-account events not arriving -> receiver bus policy missing the sender account, or the sender rule has no role with PutEvents permission to the receiver bus.
Troubleshooting: SNS-to-SQS delivers nothing -> queue policy lacks sns.amazonaws.com SendMessage with the topic ARN condition.
Troubleshooting: Fargate task cannot mount EFS -> security groups do not allow TCP 2049 in both directions, or platform version is older than 1.4.0.
Troubleshooting: Aurora does not pause -> minimum capacity is 0.5 or greater, or the auto-pause feature is not supported on the engine version.
Verification: aws sqs get-queue-attributes (attributes ApproximateNumberOfMessages, RedrivePolicy); aws events list-rules; aws stepfunctions describe-execution.

items: Identify the primary requirement: availability, cost, speed of migration, operational overhead, latency, or compliance.
List mandatory constraints: no code changes, no source access, Kubernetes manifests, fixed IP, ordering, exactly-once, 10-minute downtime, data residency.
Discard options that violate a hard constraint (for example a 20-minute job on Lambda, HTTPS from an S3 website endpoint, a public Transfer Family endpoint with static IP).
Among the remaining options, prefer the most managed one that satisfies the constraints, unless the stem demands control (OS patches, GPU) or portability (Kubernetes).
Check for internally impossible or stale statements (DMS migrating servers, resource policies on Redshift tables, retired tools) and prefer the option whose architecture is coherent.

blocks.body: (1) A 'migrate to serverless' answer may break a 15-minute or 6 MB limit. (2) Express workflows cannot wait for callbacks. (3) Streams keep data 24 hours. (4) FIFO has lower default throughput. (5) EventBridge has no ordering. (6) Some answers use retired tools or names; the intended architecture may still be right.

items: Decouple with durable buffers: SQS for buffering/queueing, SNS for fanout, EventBridge for rule-based routing and cross-account events, Step Functions for orchestration.
Lambda: 15-minute max, 10,240 MB memory, 6 MB sync payload, 1,000 default concurrency per Region (adjustable). Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes environments; reserved concurrency does not.

Containers: ECS simplest; EKS for Kubernetes manifests and portability; Fargate removes servers; EC2 capacity when you must control OS or hardware; EFS for shared file storage; EKS Auto Mode is now the recommended EKS approach over Fargate.

Databases: DynamoDB on-demand for unpredictable key-based load (2x previous peak instantly); provisioned for steady; Streams 24 hours; Aurora serverless min 0 ACU pauses, min 0.5+ does not, max 256 ACU; Data API via Secrets Manager; ElastiCache lazy loading plus TTL.
SQS: retention 4 days default up to 14; DLQ for failed messages; ReportBatchItemFailures to avoid reprocessing successful messages; FIFO 300/3,000 msg/s default.
Step Functions: Standard (1 year, exactly-once, state transition billing, .sync and callbacks) vs Express (5 min, at-least-once, high rate, no .sync).
Transfer Family: VPC internet-facing endpoint for Elastic IPs and source IP control; public endpoint cannot.

blocks.title: Key takeaways
blocks.body: Pick the most managed option that satisfies hard constraints; verify limits (15 minutes, 24 hours, 5 minutes, 14 days); match the database to the access pattern; recognize stale service names without discarding the underlying architecture.
